docs.text:
- **Abdominal (AAA):** often asymptomatic; risk factors smoking, age, male, family history. **Screening** (single ultrasound) offered to older men in many countries. Repair generally at **diameter ≥5.5 cm**, rapid growth, or if symptomatic. **Ruptured AAA** — sudden abdominal/back pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass — surgical emergency.
- **Thoracic aortic aneurysm** — associated with connective-tissue disease.

docs.title: Aortic & Peripheral Vascular Disease
docs.text:
- **Tear in the intima → blood tracks into the media**, creating a false lumen.
- **Stanford classification:** **Type A** involves the **ascending** aorta (surgical emergency); **Type B** is confined to the **descending** aorta (usually managed medically).
- **Presentation:** sudden, severe, **tearing/ripping** chest pain radiating to the **back**, **maximal at onset**; pulse/BP asymmetry between arms; may cause AR, tamponade, stroke, or limb/organ ischaemia. CXR: widened mediastinum. **Diagnosis: CT angiography** (aorta).
- **Management:** rapid control of **heart rate first, then BP** — IV **beta-blocker** (labetalol/esmolol) to a target HR ~60 and systolic ~100–120 mmHg (reduce shear stress/dP/dt), then vasodilator if needed. **Type A → emergency surgery; Type B → medical** (surgery/stenting if complicated).
- **Connective-tissue associations:** **Marfan** (fibrillin-1), Ehlers–Danlos (vascular type), Loeys–Dietz.

docs.title: Aortic & Peripheral Vascular Disease
docs.text:
- **Chronic limb ischaemia:** intermittent **claudication** → rest pain → tissue loss (critical limb ischaemia). Assess with **ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI)** (<0.9 abnormal; falsely high if calcified vessels in diabetes). Management: risk-factor control, antiplatelet + statin, supervised exercise, revascularisation for critical ischaemia.
- **Acute limb ischaemia — the 6 Ps:** **P**ain, **P**allor, **P**ulselessness, **P**erishing cold, **P**araesthesia, **P**aralysis. A surgical emergency (embolic or thrombotic) — urgent revascularisation.
- **Carotid disease:** stenosis is a stroke/TIA source; carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic significant stenosis.

docs.title: Aortic & Peripheral Vascular Disease
docs.text:
- **DVT & PE** share risk factors (**Virchow's triad**: stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial injury).
- **DVT:** unilateral leg swelling/pain; **Wells score** → D-dimer (if low probability) or Doppler ultrasound.
- **PE:** dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia; ECG usually sinus tachycardia (classic S1Q3T3 uncommon); **CT pulmonary angiogram** is the main diagnostic test (V/Q if contrast contraindicated). **Risk-stratify:** massive/**high-risk PE** (hypotension/shock) → **thrombolysis**; otherwise anticoagulate.
- **Treatment:** **DOAC** first-line for most VTE; consider thrombolysis for haemodynamically unstable PE; IVC filter if anticoagulation contraindicated.

docs.text:
| Definition | Narrowing and in final stages, occlusion of peripheral arteries due to atherosclerotic plaques |
| --- | --- |
| Risk Factors | Hyperlipidaemia, HTN, smoking (ROS-induced endothelial damage), DM (AGES), homocysteine, lifestyle (↑weight, ↓activity), haemodynamic factors |
| Aetiology | Insufficient tissue perfusion due to atherosclerosis in aorta/peripheral arteriesOften co-exists with CAD |
| Classification | Fontaine Classification of PAD |
| Stage I | Asymptomatic |
| Stage II | Pain of exertion (claudication): IIa > 200m, IIb <200m |
| Stage III | Ishcemic pain at rest |
| Stage IV | Necrosis/gangrene/ulcers: IVa- dry necrosis, IVb- infection of necrotic tissue |

**Presentation**

| Progression | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Silent | Asymptomatic |
| Intermittent claudication | Pain, cramps, paraesthesia distal to arterial occlusionExacerbated on exertion, relieved by rest/lowering affected limbsFemoropopliteal: calf claudicationAorticiliac (Leriche’s Syndrome)Level of aortic bifurcation/bilateral occlusion of iliac arteriesTriad: buttock/hip/thigh claudication, erectile dysfunction, ↓ femoral pulsesTibiofibular: foot claudication |
| Progression of Disease | 6P’s: pain, pallor, paralysis, paraesthesia, pulselessness, perishingly coldAs disease progresses 🡪 absent/diminished pulses, tropic changes (pallor, perishingly cold, ↓temp, ↓perspiration, atrophic skin, brittle nails)Paraesthesia and paralysis 🡪 irreversible ischemia |
| Ischemic rest pain | Typically, distal metatarsals Worse at night (↓CO) with rubor/elevation pallorRelieved by ↑ perfusion (hanging legs off bed- gravity, walking- exertion) |
| Critical limb ischemia | Resting pain, ulcers and/or tissue loss (gangrene which can become infected)Indicative of limb-threatening arterial occlusion |

**Investigations**

- Routine bloods: FBC, coags, fasting metabolic profile
- Ankle-Brachial Index ± exercise testing in normal resting ABI
- ABI= systolic ankle BP: systolic brachial BP
- >1.3 = calcified vessels
- 1.0–1.30 = normal value
- 0.91–0.99 = borderline
- 0.40– 0.90 = mild to moderate PAD → claudication
- < 0.40 = critical limb ischemia
- Duplex ultrasonography: volume/direction of blood flow
- Contrast CTA/MRA: good for large arteries (aorta, iliac, femoral) but difficult with tibial arteries
- Catheter-based angiography: invasive, superior resolution, can obtain in operating theatre before potential revascularisation

**Management**

- Conservative: smoking cessation, supervised graded exercise therapy, foot care, avoid cold temperatures
- Medical: aspirin, clopidogrel, statin, anti-hypertensive, hyperglycaemia control, PDE inhibitors (e.g. cilostazol) when smoking/exercise unsuccessful
- Revascularisation
- Indications: critical limb ischemia, failure of above Tx, clinically significant distress due to claudication, nil limitations due to other disease
- Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) ± stenting (minimally invasive, 1st line)
- Operative vasc

docs.title: Applied Skills
docs.text:
##### 12.1 Data Interpretation

###### ECG — the drill
Always present in the same order (Installment 1): **rate → rhythm → axis → P → PR → QRS → ST → T → QT**. Then pattern-recognise. High-yield patterns to spot in seconds:
- **ST elevation** in a territory → STEMI (name the leads and artery).
- **ST depression / T inversion** → ischaemia/NSTEMI.
- **Tall tented T waves** → hyperkalaemia.
- **Widespread saddle ST elevation + PR depression** → pericarditis.
- **Short PR + delta wave** → WPW.
- **Long QT** → torsades risk (drugs/electrolytes).
- **Dominant R in V1 + right axis** → RVH; **deep S in V1 + tall R in V5/6** → LVH.
- **AV dissociation** → complete heart block.

###### Other data
- **Troponin** — interpret as a *trend* with the clinical picture; a rise-and-fall + ischaemia = MI; a stable rise = injury (Installment 1).
- **BNP/NT-proBNP** — a normal value largely excludes HF.
- **CXR** — heart size, pulmonary oedema (ABCDE), effusions, mediastinal width, valve calcification, devices.
- **Echo report** — LVEF, wall motion, valves/gradients, chamber size, pericardium.
- **ABG in the crashing patient** — metabolic acidosis (lactate) in shock; type 1 respiratory failure in pulmonary oedema.

##### 12.2 OSCE Stations
- **Cardiovascular examination** — run the Installment 1 sequence smoothly; verbalise fluid status, JVP, apex, murmurs, and peripheral signs; offer to check obs, dip urine, ECG.
- **Focused murmur/JVP station** — time the murmur (systolic/diastolic), locate, use dynamic manoeuvres (RILE, Valsalva), and give the most likely lesion.
- **Device/anticoagulation counselling** — pacemaker/ICD basics; explaining DOAC vs warfarin, monitoring, and bleeding risk.
- **Counselling stations** — starting a statin (why, side effects, monitoring), AF anticoagulation (stroke vs bleeding trade-off), post-MI lifestyle and cardiac rehab, and breaking bad news in advanced heart failure (use a structured framework, e.g. SPIKES).
- **Prescribing stations** — the ACS bundle, acute pulmonary oedema, hyperkalaemia, and rate/rhythm control in AF.

##### 12.3 Emergency Scenarios — the protocols

###### Acute coronary syndrome (STEMI)
Recognise (ischaemic pain + ST elevation) → aspirin + P2Y12 + anticoagulation, analgesia, O₂ only if hypoxic → **reperfusion**: primary PCI if ≤120 min from diagnosis, else fibrinolysis <12 h (Installment 1).

###### Cardiac arrest / peri-arrest (Adult ALS)
- **Shockable (VF/pVT):** defibrillate → 2-min CPR cycles. **Adrenaline 1 mg** after the **3rd** shock (RCUK/ERC) — **note ANZCOR gives it after the 2nd shock** — then every 3–5 min; **amiodarone 300 mg** after the 3rd shock (150 mg after the 5th).
- **Non-shockable (PEA/asystole):** CPR + adrenaline 1 mg **as soon as possible**, then every 3–5 min.
- Treat **4 Hs & 4 Ts**.
- **Peri-arrest bradycardia** with adverse features: **atropine 500 µg IV** (repeat to 3 mg) → transcutaneous pacing / isoprenaline / adrenaline infusion → transvenous pacing.
- **Peri-arrest tachycardia**

docs.text:
##### A. Emergency Drug/Number Recall

| Scenario | Key action / dose |
|---|---|
| Shockable arrest | Adrenaline 1 mg after 3rd shock (ANZCOR: 2nd); amiodarone 300 mg after 3rd shock |
| Non-shockable arrest | Adrenaline 1 mg ASAP, then every 3–5 min |
| Adverse bradycardia | Atropine 500 µg IV (max 3 mg) → pacing |
| Adverse tachycardia | Synchronised DC cardioversion |
| SVT (stable) | Vagal → adenosine 6→12→18 mg |
| Hyperkalaemia (cardioprotect) | Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV |
| Hyperkalaemia (shift) | Insulin 10 U + 25 g glucose; salbutamol neb |
| Torsades | IV magnesium sulfate |
| STEMI reperfusion | PCI ≤120 min from diagnosis, else fibrinolysis <12 h |
| Dissection | IV β-blocker: HR ~60, SBP ~100–120 |

##### B. "See this → do this" (emergency ECG cues)

| ECG | Immediate thought |
|---|---|
| ST elevation in a territory | STEMI → reperfuse |
| Tall tented T waves | Hyperkalaemia → calcium + shift |
| Broad complex, regular, unwell | VT → cardiovert if unstable |
| Polymorphic VT, long QT | Torsades → magnesium |
| AV dissociation, bradycardia | Complete heart block → pace |
| Widespread saddle ST + PR depression | Pericarditis (not STEMI) |

##### C. The Whole-Series Master Index

**Foundations (Part 1)** — action potentials, EC coupling, cardiac cycle, PV loop, cardiac output, haemodynamics, BP regulation, coronary flow.
**Installment 1** — assessment, examination, ECG, investigations · coronary disease & ACS.
**Installment 2** — heart failure · arrhythmias & conduction.
**Installment 3** — valves · infective/inflammatory/pericardial · cardiomyopathies.
**Installment 4** — hypertension · aortic & peripheral vascular · congenital/inherited/special groups.
**Installment 5** — cardiovascular pharmacology.
**Installment 6** — applied skills, data interpretation, OSCE, emergencies *(this file)*.

**Highest-yield cross-cutting themes:** ACS reperfusion timing · HFrEF four pillars · AF anticoagulation (CHA₂DS₂-VA) · ECG pattern recognition · murmur identification · hyperkalaemia and cardiac-arrest protocols · aortic dissection · the ESC 2024 hypertension reclassification.

---

*End of Installment 6 — series complete. Suggested revision order: **Foundations → Installments 1–6**, revisiting Foundations and the ⚡ Quick Reference blocks by spaced repetition throughout.*

docs.title: Arrhythmias & Conduction Disorders
docs.text:
##### 4.1 Mechanisms
Three broad mechanisms: **re-entry** (a circuit — most tachyarrhythmias including AVNRT, AVRT, atrial flutter, VT), **enhanced automaticity** (an ectopic focus), and **triggered activity** (afterdepolarisations — e.g. torsades).

##### 4.2 Bradyarrhythmias and Conduction Disease
- **Sinus node dysfunction (sick sinus)**: inappropriate bradycardia, pauses, tachy-brady syndrome.
- **AV block**:
  - *First-degree*: PR >200 ms, every P conducts. Benign.
  - *Second-degree Mobitz I (Wenckebach)*: progressive PR lengthening until a dropped beat. Usually benign (AV nodal).
  - *Second-degree Mobitz II*: constant PR with intermittent dropped QRS. High risk of progression to complete block → **pace**.
  - *Third-degree (complete)*: AV dissociation — P waves and QRS independent; escape rhythm. **Cannon a waves**. Needs pacing.
- **Bundle branch / fascicular blocks** (see Installment 1 for WiLLiaM MaRRoW).

**Acute bradycardia with adverse features** (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, heart failure): **atropine 500 µg IV**, repeat to 3 mg; if inadequate → transcutaneous pacing / isoprenaline / adrenaline infusion; then transvenous pacing. **Pacing indications**: symptomatic bradycardia, complete heart block, Mobitz II, and symptomatic sinus node disease.

##### 4.3 Supraventricular Tachycardias
Narrow-complex, regular unless AF/flutter with variable block:
- **AVNRT** — commonest paroxysmal SVT; re-entry within the AV node.
- **AVRT** — accessory pathway (see WPW below).
- **Atrial flutter** — macro-re-entry; "sawtooth" flutter waves, atrial rate ~300, often 2:1 block giving ventricular rate ~150.
- **Focal atrial tachycardia**.

**Acute SVT management** (stable, regular narrow-complex): **vagal manoeuvres** (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage) → **adenosine 6 mg** rapid IV push, then 12 mg, then 18 mg (warn re transient chest tightness/flushing; contraindicated in asthma — use verapamil). Unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion.

**Wolff–Parkinson–White (WPW)**: accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) → **short PR + delta wave** on resting ECG. Risk: if AF occurs, rapid antegrade conduction down the pathway can degenerate to VF. **Avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs (adenosine, verapamil, digoxin, beta-blockers) in pre-excited AF** — they can accelerate pathway conduction. Definitive treatment: catheter ablation.

##### 4.4 Atrial Fibrillation — in depth
Commonest sustained arrhythmia; **irregularly irregular** pulse, absent P waves.
- **Classification**: paroxysmal (<7 days, self-terminating), persistent (>7 days), permanent.
- **Management framework (ESC 2024 "AF-CARE")**: **C** Comorbidity/risk-factor management · **A** Avoid stroke/thromboembolism · **R** Reduce symptoms (rate/rhythm) · **E** Evaluation and dynamic reassessment.
- **Rate control** (first-line for most): beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB (diltiazem/verapamil); digoxin if sedentary/HF.
- **Rhythm control**: cardioversion (electrical or pharmacological — flecainide if no struc

docs.title: Arrhythmias & Conduction Disorders
docs.text:
##### A. Mnemonics & Acronyms

| Acronym | Use |
|---|---|
| **NYHA I–IV** | HF symptom class (I none → IV at rest) |
| **The 4 Pillars** | ARNI/ACEi · Beta-blocker · MRA · SGLT2i (all Class I in HFrEF) |
| **LMNOP** | Acute pulmonary oedema: Lasix, Morphine, Nitrates, Oxygen/CPAP, Position (sit up) |
| **CXR "ABCDE"** | Alveolar oedema, Kerley B lines, Cardiomegaly, upper-lobe Diversion, Effusions |
| **CHA₂DS₂-VA** | AF stroke risk (ESC 2024, sex removed); ≥2 → anticoagulate |
| **CHA₂DS₂-VASc** | Older version, includes female Sex category |
| **HAS-BLED** | AF bleeding risk (manage modifiable factors, don't withhold OAC) |
| **4 Hs & 4 Ts** | Reversible causes of arrest |
| **WiLLiaM MaRRoW** | LBBB/RBBB on ECG (Installment 1) |

##### B. Spot Signs — *"See this → think this"*

| Sign | Think |
|---|---|
| Irregularly irregular pulse, no P waves | Atrial fibrillation |
| Sawtooth baseline, rate ~150 (2:1) | Atrial flutter |
| Short PR + delta wave | WPW (accessory pathway) |
| Cannon *a* waves, AV dissociation | Complete heart block |
| Progressive PR lengthening → dropped beat | Mobitz I (Wenckebach) |
| Constant PR, sudden dropped QRS | Mobitz II (→ pace) |
| Polymorphic VT twisting around baseline | Torsades de pointes (→ Mg²⁺) |
| Coved ST elevation V1–V2 | Brugada syndrome |
| S3 gallop + bibasal crackles + raised JVP | Congestive heart failure |

##### C. Disease Formulation Cards

> **HFrEF (systolic heart failure)**
> *One-liner:* impaired contractility, LVEF ≤40%. *Classic:* exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, raised JVP, displaced apex, S3. *Ix:* ↑NT-proBNP, echo (low EF). *Mx:* four pillars + loop diuretic; ICD/CRT if criteria met. *Buzz:* "start low, start all".

> **HFpEF (diastolic heart failure)**
> *One-liner:* HF symptoms with LVEF ≥50% + raised filling pressures. *Classic:* elderly, hypertensive, AF, obese, diabetic. *Mx:* SGLT2i + treat comorbidities/congestion; no strong prognostic drug list like HFrEF. *Buzz:* "stiff ventricle".

> **Acute pulmonary oedema**
> *One-liner:* acute decompensation → alveolar flooding. *Classic:* severe breathlessness, pink frothy sputum, bibasal crackles, distress, hypoxia. *Ix:* CXR bat-wing. *Mx:* sit up, O₂/CPAP, IV loop diuretic, IV nitrate. *Buzz:* LMNOP.

> **Atrial fibrillation**
> *One-liner:* disorganised atrial activity → irregular ventricular response. *Classic:* palpitations, irregularly irregular pulse, absent P waves. *Mx:* rate/rhythm control + anticoagulation by CHA₂DS₂-VA (DOAC preferred). *Buzz:* AF-CARE pathway.

> **Complete (3rd-degree) heart block**
> *One-liner:* total AV conduction failure → independent escape rhythm. *Classic:* syncope, bradycardia, cannon *a* waves, AV dissociation on ECG. *Mx:* atropine as temporiser → pacing. *Buzz:* P waves "march through" the QRS.

> **Wolff–Parkinson–White**
> *One-liner:* accessory pathway pre-excitation. *Classic:* short PR + delta wave; SVT episodes; danger in pre-excited AF. *Mx:* avoid AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF;

docs.title: Cardiac Electrophysiology
docs.text:
Atrial and ventricular myocytes have a resting potential near **−90 mV** and a characteristic long plateau. Five phases:
- **Phase 0 — rapid depolarisation:** fast voltage-gated **Na⁺** channels open → steep upstroke.
- **Phase 1 — early repolarisation:** Na⁺ channels inactivate; transient outward **K⁺** current (I_to).
- **Phase 2 — plateau:** inward **Ca²⁺** (L-type channels) balances outward **K⁺** → sustained depolarisation. This long plateau is unique to cardiac muscle and underlies the long refractory period.
- **Phase 3 — repolarisation:** Ca²⁺ channels close, delayed-rectifier **K⁺** efflux dominates → return toward baseline.
- **Phase 4 — resting potential:** stabilised by inward-rectifier K⁺ (I_K1); the **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase** restores gradients.

**🔗** Antiarrhythmic drug classes map onto these phases (Vaughan–Williams, Installment 5): Class I block phase-0 Na⁺; Class III block phase-3 K⁺ (prolong QT/refractoriness); Class IV block phase-2 Ca²⁺.

docs.title: Cardiac Electrophysiology
docs.text:
SA- and AV-nodal cells have **no stable resting potential** and no fast Na⁺ channels. Instead:
- **Phase 4 — spontaneous diastolic depolarisation:** the "funny" current **I_f** (Na⁺ influx) plus T-type Ca²⁺ drifts the membrane up to threshold → **automaticity**.
- **Phase 0 — upstroke:** driven by **L-type Ca²⁺** influx (slower than Na⁺-driven cells).
- **Phase 3 — repolarisation:** K⁺ efflux.

The **SA node** depolarises fastest, so it is the dominant pacemaker (overdrive suppression of slower sites).

**Intrinsic escape rates:** SA node **60–100/min** · AV node **40–60/min** · His–Purkinje/ventricle **20–40/min**.

**🔗** Ivabradine blocks I_f to slow the sinus rate without affecting contractility. Autonomic tone tunes the pacemaker: vagal (ACh) slows phase-4 drift; sympathetic (noradrenaline, β1) steepens it.

docs.title: Cardiac Electrophysiology
docs.h: 2.3 The conduction system and AV nodal delay
docs.text:
Impulse path: **SA node → atrial myocardium (internodal tracts) → AV node → bundle of His → left & right bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricular myocardium**, spreading apex-to-base.

The **AV node deliberately delays** conduction (~0.1 s; the PR interval). This lets atrial contraction complete ventricular filling (the "atrial kick") *before* the ventricles contract, and protects the ventricles from very fast atrial rates.

**🔗** In AF the irregular atrial impulses are filtered by the AV node — AV-nodal blockers (β-blockers, diltiazem, digoxin) are how we rate-control. In complete heart block, a slow ventricular escape rhythm takes over.

docs.title: Cardiac Electrophysiology
docs.text:
During the **absolute (effective) refractory period** (phases 0–2 and early 3) the cell cannot be re-excited — this prevents **tetany** (cardiac muscle must relax to refill) and limits re-entry. The **relative refractory period** (late phase 3) needs a stronger stimulus, and can propagate abnormally.

docs.title: Cardiomyopathies
docs.text:
##### 7.1 Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM)
Dilated, poorly contracting ventricles (systolic dysfunction). **Causes:** idiopathic/genetic, **alcohol**, peripartum, post-myocarditis, tachycardia-induced, drugs (**anthracyclines**, trastuzumab), haemochromatosis, thiamine deficiency. Presents as **HFrEF**, arrhythmia, or thromboembolism. Treat as heart failure (Installment 2).

##### 7.2 Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)
- **Genetics:** **autosomal dominant** sarcomere-gene mutations (commonly β-myosin heavy chain, myosin-binding protein C).
- **Pathophysiology:** asymmetric septal hypertrophy → **LV outflow tract obstruction** (in HOCM) and diastolic dysfunction; risk of **sudden cardiac death**.
- **Signs:** ejection-systolic murmur that gets **louder with Valsalva/standing** (reduced preload), jerky pulse, double apical impulse, S4.
- **SCD risk factors** (feed the ESC **HCM Risk-SCD** model): family history of SCD, **unexplained syncope**, **NSVT**, **massive LVH (≥30 mm)**, abnormal BP response to exercise; the model also weights age, LA diameter and LVOT gradient. (AHA/ACC additionally flag LVEF <50%, apical aneurysm, extensive LGE.)
- **Management:** **beta-blockers or verapamil** (avoid in significant obstruction with caution); **avoid dehydration, vasodilators (nitrates, ACEi) and digoxin** in obstructive disease; **ICD** if high SCD risk; septal reduction (myectomy or alcohol septal ablation) for refractory obstruction; **mavacamten** (cardiac myosin inhibitor) is a newer option. **Commonest cause of SCD in young athletes.**

##### 7.3 Restrictive Cardiomyopathy
Stiff, non-compliant ventricles → impaired filling with preserved (early) systolic function. **Causes:** **amyloidosis**, sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis, endomyocardial fibrosis. Overlaps clinically with constrictive pericarditis.

##### 7.4 Arrhythmogenic (Right Ventricular) Cardiomyopathy (ARVC)
Fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium → ventricular arrhythmias and SCD, often in young adults/athletes. ECG clues: **epsilon waves**, T-wave inversion V1–V3.

##### 7.5 Other
- **Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy** — apical ballooning post-stress, unobstructed arteries (Installment 1).
- **Peripartum cardiomyopathy** — HFrEF in late pregnancy to ~5 months postpartum.
- **Cardiac amyloidosis** — increasingly recognised: suspect with **HFpEF + LVH on echo but low-voltage ECG**, bilateral carpal tunnel, aortic stenosis in the elderly; diagnose with bone scintigraphy (DPD/PYP) ± biopsy. **Sarcoidosis** — heart block and VT in a young/middle-aged patient. **Haemochromatosis** — dilated/restrictive picture plus diabetes, bronze skin, arthropathy.

---

> **Aortic stenosis** — degenerative/bicuspid/rheumatic. Syncope/Angina/Dyspnoea; ESM → carotids, slow-rising pulse, soft S2. Severe: area <1 cm², gradient >40, velocity >4 m/s. Intervene if symptomatic or EF <50% (SAVR/TAVI). *Buzz:* "SAD".

> **Mitral stenosis** — rheumatic. Mid-diastolic rumble, loud S1, opening snap, malar flush, AF. Ix: echo. Mx: balloon valvuloplasty/surgery, anticoagulate if AF. *Buzz:* malar flush + tapping apex.

> **Cardiac tamponade** — effusion compressing the heart. Beck's triad, pulsus paradoxus, electrical alternans. Ix: echo (diastolic RV collapse). Mx: pericardiocentesis. *Buzz:* "water-bottle heart".

docs.title: Cardiovascular Pharmacology
docs.text:
##### 11.1 Antiplatelets and Anticoagulants
- **Aspirin** — irreversibly inhibits **COX-1** → less thromboxane A₂. Backbone of secondary prevention. Caution: GI bleeding/ulceration.
- **P2Y12 inhibitors** — block ADP-mediated platelet activation: **clopidogrel** (prodrug, variable metabolism), **ticagrelor** and **prasugrel** (more potent, preferred in ACS). *Prasugrel is contraindicated after prior stroke/TIA*; dose-reduce if <60 kg or ≥75 y. **Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT)** = aspirin + a P2Y12 inhibitor, default 12 months post-ACS.
- **Anticoagulants:**
  - **Warfarin** — vitamin K antagonist (factors II, VII, IX, X). Needs **INR** monitoring; many interactions; reversed with vitamin K/PCC. Still first-line for **mechanical valves** and **moderate–severe mitral stenosis**.
  - **DOACs** — direct factor **Xa inhibitors** (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) and the direct **thrombin inhibitor** dabigatran. Preferred over warfarin for AF and VTE; no routine monitoring; reduce dose for renal impairment/age/weight criteria; reversal agents (idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa for Xa inhibitors).
  - **Heparins** — unfractionated (IV, monitored by APTT, quickly reversible with protamine) and **LMWH** (subcutaneous, predictable). **Fondaparinux** in NSTE-ACS.

##### 11.2 Lipid-lowering Therapy
- **Statins** (e.g. atorvastatin) — inhibit **HMG-CoA reductase** → less hepatic cholesterol synthesis, upregulated LDL-receptors. First-line; high-intensity for secondary prevention. Side effects: myalgia/myopathy (rarely rhabdomyolysis), deranged LFTs; interactions (some via CYP3A4).
- **Add-on ladder** if LDL targets not met: **ezetimibe** (blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption) → **PCSK9 inhibitors** (monoclonal antibodies — evolocumab/alirocumab) or **inclisiran** (siRNA lowering PCSK9, twice-yearly) → **bempedoic acid**. **Icosapent ethyl** for residual high triglyceride risk.

##### 11.3 Antihypertensives
- **ACE inhibitors** (ramipril) — block angiotensin I→II conversion; also raise bradykinin (→ **dry cough**, rarely angioedema). Watch K⁺ and creatinine; **contraindicated in pregnancy** and bilateral renal artery stenosis.
- **ARBs** (losartan/candesartan) — block AT₁ receptor; alternative if ACEi cough.
- **Calcium-channel blockers:** *dihydropyridines* (amlodipine — vascular selective, cause ankle oedema/flushing) vs *non-dihydropyridines* (verapamil, diltiazem — rate-limiting, negatively inotropic; **don't combine verapamil with a beta-blocker** → bradycardia/asystole risk).
- **Thiazide-like diuretics** (indapamide) — see 11.4.
- **Beta-blockers, MRAs, alpha-blockers** — see relevant sections.

##### 11.4 Diuretics
- **Loop diuretics** (furosemide, bumetanide) — inhibit the **Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter** in the thick ascending limb; powerful; used in fluid overload/HF. Side effects: hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, ototoxicity, gout.
- **Thiazides/thiazide-like** (bendroflumethiazide, indapamide) — inhibit the **Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotr

docs.text:
##### A. Mnemonics & Acronyms

| Acronym | Use |
|---|---|
| **Vaughan–Williams I–IV** | Antiarrhythmics: I Na⁺ · II β-blocker · III K⁺ · IV CCB |
| **A/C/D** | HTN drug steps (Installment 4) |
| **4 Pillars** | HFrEF: ARNI/ACEi · β-blocker · MRA · SGLT2i |
| **DAPT** | Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12), 12 mo post-ACS |
| **Statin ladder** | Statin → ezetimibe → PCSK9i/inclisiran → bempedoic acid |

##### B. Drug ⇄ Effect / Side-effect Associations

| Cue | Drug |
|---|---|
| Dry cough / angioedema | ACE inhibitor (bradykinin) |
| Ankle oedema, flushing | Dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine) |
| Gynaecomastia + hyperkalaemia | Spironolactone |
| Yellow vision (xanthopsia), narrow therapeutic index | Digoxin |
| Thyroid + lung + corneal + skin toxicity | Amiodarone |
| Profound hypotension with sildenafil | Nitrates |
| Bradycardia/asystole if combined | Verapamil + beta-blocker |
| Reversal by idarucizumab | Dabigatran |
| Reversal by andexanet alfa | Factor Xa inhibitors |
| Warfarin still required | Mechanical valve / mod–severe mitral stenosis |

##### C. Drug-class Cards

> **Statins** — inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↓LDL, plaque stabilisation. First-line primary/secondary prevention. SE: myalgia/myopathy, ↑LFTs. *Buzz:* high-intensity after ACS.

> **ACE inhibitors** — block ATI→II, ↑bradykinin. Uses: HTN, HFrEF, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy. SE: dry cough, hyperkalaemia, ↑creatinine, angioedema; teratogenic. *Buzz:* check U&Es after starting.

> **Beta-blockers** — ↓rate/contractility/O₂ demand; disease-modifying in HFrEF & post-MI. SE: bradycardia, fatigue, bronchospasm; don't start in acute decompensated HF. *Buzz:* start when euvolaemic.

> **Loop diuretics** — block Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ (thick ascending limb); potent, for congestion. SE: ↓K⁺/Mg²⁺/Ca²⁺, ototoxicity, gout. *Buzz:* symptom relief, not mortality.

> **Digoxin** — Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibitor → +inotropy, vagal rate control. Narrow index; toxicity ↑ by ↓K⁺. Reverse with Digifab. *Buzz:* xanthopsia.

> **Amiodarone** — Class III (multi-channel). Broad-spectrum for VT/AF. SE across thyroid/lung/liver/skin/eyes; QT prolongation. *Buzz:* baseline TFT/LFT/CXR before starting.

docs.title: Congenital, Inherited & Special Groups
docs.h: Cardiology Notes — Congenital, Inherited & Special Groups
docs.text:
##### 10.1 Congenital Heart Disease
- **Atrial septal defect (ASD):** left-to-right shunt; **fixed splitting of S2**; may present in adulthood with AF/right heart strain.
- **Ventricular septal defect (VSD):** harsh **pansystolic** murmur at the left sternal edge (smaller defect = louder); commonest congenital lesion.
- **Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA):** **continuous "machinery" murmur**.
- **Coarctation of the aorta:** **radio-femoral delay**, upper-limb hypertension, **rib notching** on CXR; associated with bicuspid valve and Turner syndrome.
- **Tetralogy of Fallot** (commonest cyanotic lesion): **VSD, overriding aorta, RV outflow obstruction, RV hypertrophy** ("boot-shaped" heart); cyanotic "tet" spells.
- **Eisenmenger syndrome:** a long-standing left-to-right shunt raises pulmonary pressures until the shunt **reverses** (right-to-left) → cyanosis; once established, shunt closure is contraindicated.

##### 10.2 Inherited Cardiovascular Disease
- **Channelopathies** (long QT, Brugada, CPVT) and **inherited cardiomyopathies** (HCM, ARVC, DCM) — cross-reference Installments 2–3; **family screening and genetic counselling** matter.
- **Familial hypercholesterolaemia:** autosomal dominant (usually LDL-receptor); tendon xanthomata, very high LDL, premature coronary disease — treat aggressively and screen relatives (cascade testing).
- **Marfan syndrome:** fibrillin-1; tall, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, **aortic root dilatation/dissection** and MVP — needs aortic surveillance and often prophylactic root surgery.

##### 10.3 Cardiology in Special Groups
- **Pregnancy:** physiological rise in cardiac output/volume and fall in SVR unmasks or worsens disease (e.g. mitral stenosis); **peripartum cardiomyopathy**; several drugs are contraindicated (**ACEi/ARB, warfarin, spironolactone**) — labetalol, methyldopa and nifedipine are the usual antihypertensives.
- **Cardio-oncology:** anthracycline and trastuzumab cardiotoxicity, radiotherapy-related disease — baseline and serial cardiac monitoring.
- **Athlete's heart:** physiological adaptation (bradycardia, chamber enlargement, voltage criteria) that must be distinguished from HCM/ARVC.

---

docs.title: Congenital, Inherited & Special Groups
docs.text:
##### A. Mnemonics & Acronyms

| Acronym | Use |
|---|---|
| **A/C/D** | HTN drug steps: ACEi/ARB · CCB · thiazide-like Diuretic (→ spironolactone step 4) |
| **6 Ps** | Acute limb ischaemia: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Perishing cold, Paraesthesia, Paralysis |
| **Virchow's triad** | VTE: stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial injury |
| **Stanford A/B** | Dissection: A = ascending (surgery); B = descending (medical) |
| **ToF (VOPR)** | Tetralogy: VSD, Overriding aorta, Pulmonary/RVOT obstruction, RVH |
| **Conn's / ARR** | Primary aldosteronism → check aldosterone:renin ratio |

##### B. Spot Signs — *"See this → think this"*

| Sign | Think |
|---|---|
| Radio-femoral delay + upper-limb HTN + rib notching | Coarctation of the aorta |
| Fixed splitting of S2 | Atrial septal defect |
| Continuous "machinery" murmur | Patent ductus arteriosus |
| Tearing chest pain to the back, BP asymmetry, wide mediastinum | Aortic dissection |
| Pulsatile abdominal mass + hypotension + back pain | Ruptured AAA |
| Young woman, resistant HTN, renal bruit | Fibromuscular renal artery stenosis |
| Resistant HTN + hypokalaemia | Primary aldosteronism (Conn's) |
| Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, labile BP | Phaeochromocytoma |
| Tendon xanthomata + very high LDL + premature CAD | Familial hypercholesterolaemia |
| Tall, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, dilated aortic root | Marfan syndrome |

##### C. Disease Formulation Cards

> **Hypertension** — mostly essential; screen for secondary if young/resistant. Ix: confirm with ABPM/HBPM, assess end-organ damage. Mx: lifestyle + A/C/D algorithm; target ~120–129 systolic (ESC 2024, tolerated). *Buzz:* "elevated BP" is the new ESC in-between category.

> **Aortic dissection** — intimal tear, false lumen. Sudden tearing pain to back, BP/pulse asymmetry, wide mediastinum. Ix: CT angiogram. Mx: HR then BP control (IV β-blocker); Type A → surgery, Type B → medical. *Buzz:* "maximal at onset".

> **Ruptured AAA** — pulsatile mass + back/abdo pain + hypotension. Ix: urgent imaging/theatre. Mx: emergency repair. *Buzz:* don't delay for a scan if unstable.

> **Acute limb ischaemia** — sudden 6 Ps. Embolic (AF) or thrombotic. Mx: urgent revascularisation, heparin. *Buzz:* paralysis/paraesthesia = threatened limb.

> **Pulmonary embolism** — dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia. Ix: Wells → CTPA. Mx: DOAC; thrombolysis if haemodynamically unstable (massive PE). *Buzz:* S1Q3T3 (rare); sinus tachy is commonest.

> **Coarctation of the aorta** — upper-limb HTN, radio-femoral delay, rib notching; Turner/bicuspid links. Mx: repair/stent. *Buzz:* differential BP arms vs legs.

---

*End of Installment 4. Next: **Installment 5 — Section 11 (Cardiovascular Pharmacology & Prescribing)**.*

docs.title: Coronary Circulation
docs.text:
The **left main** coronary artery divides into the **LAD** and **circumflex**; the **right coronary** supplies the inferior wall and (in most people) the AV node. Two features are heavily examined:
- **Coronary flow is mainly diastolic.** During systole the contracting LV compresses its own intramural vessels, so the left ventricle is perfused chiefly in **diastole**. **🔗** **Tachycardia shortens diastole** and a low diastolic pressure both reduce coronary perfusion — why fast rates and hypotension worsen ischaemia.
- **Oxygen extraction is already near-maximal at rest** (~70–80%). The myocardium cannot extract much more, so increased demand must be met by **increased flow** (metabolic hyperaemia — adenosine, hypoxia → coronary vasodilatation), tightly **autoregulated** across a range of perfusion pressures.

**Myocardial O₂ supply–demand balance:** demand rises with **heart rate, contractility, and wall tension** (preload/afterload). **🔗** Anti-anginals work by tilting this balance — β-blockers cut rate/contractility (demand), nitrates cut preload (demand) and dilate coronaries (supply).

---

docs.title: Coronary Circulation
docs.text:
##### A. Key Equations & Normal Values

| Quantity | Formula / value |
|---|---|
| Cardiac output | CO = HR × SV (~5 L/min) |
| Stroke volume | SV = EDV − ESV (~70 mL) |
| Ejection fraction | EF = SV/EDV (~55–70%) |
| Blood pressure | BP = CO × SVR |
| Mean arterial pressure | MAP ≈ DBP + ⅓(SBP−DBP) = (2·DBP+SBP)/3 (~93 at 120/80) |
| Pulse pressure | PP = SBP − DBP (~40) |
| Fick (CO) | CO = VO₂ ÷ (CaO₂ − CvO₂) |
| Poiseuille | flow ∝ radius⁴ |
| Laplace | wall tension ∝ (pressure × radius) ÷ thickness |
| Normal volumes | EDV ~120 mL · ESV ~50 mL |
| Intrinsic rates | SA 60–100 · AV 40–60 · ventricle 20–40 /min |

##### B. Spot Associations — *"See this → recall this"*

| Cue | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Long AP plateau | Phase 2 Ca²⁺ influx (L-type) |
| Spontaneous phase-4 drift | I_f "funny" current → pacemaker automaticity |
| PR interval / AV delay | Allows atrial kick; protects ventricle from fast rates |
| S1 | Mitral + tricuspid closure (systole start) |
| S2 + dicrotic notch | Aortic + pulmonary closure (systole end) |
| S4 impossible in AF | Needs organised atrial contraction |
| Loop width | Stroke volume |
| Flow ∝ radius⁴ | Arterioles = main resistance vessels |
| Veins hold ~70% volume | Capacitance vessels |
| LV perfused in diastole | Tachycardia/hypotension → ischaemia |
| O₂ extraction ~75% at rest | Extra demand met by ↑flow, not ↑extraction |

##### C. Concept Cards

> **Fast-response action potential** — Phases 0 (Na⁺ in) → 1 (K⁺ out, transient) → 2 (Ca²⁺ plateau) → 3 (K⁺ out) → 4 (rest, −90 mV). Long plateau → long refractory period → no tetany. *Drug link:* Vaughan–Williams classes.

> **Pacemaker potential** — no stable rest; I_f drives phase-4 drift to threshold; Ca²⁺ upstroke. SA node fastest → dominant pacemaker. *Drug link:* ivabradine (I_f), autonomic tone.

> **Excitation–contraction coupling** — AP → L-type Ca²⁺ → CICR via RyR2 → Ca²⁺–troponin C → tropomyosin shift → cross-bridge cycling. Relaxation via SERCA + NCX. *Drug link:* digoxin (Na/K-ATPase → ↑Ca²⁺ → ↑inotropy).

> **Frank–Starling law** — ↑ preload (EDV/stretch) → ↑ contractile force → ↑ SV; matches output to venous return. *Clinical link:* curve is flattened in HFrEF → congestion instead of output.

> **Pressure–volume loop** — filling → isovolumetric contraction → ejection → isovolumetric relaxation. Width = SV; ESPVR slope = contractility. ↑preload widens; ↑afterload raises pressure & ↓SV; ↑contractility ↓ESV.

> **Baroreceptor reflex** — carotid sinus (CN IX) + aortic arch (CN X) → medulla → autonomic outflow. ↑BP → ↑vagal/↓sympathetic → ↓HR & vasodilate. Buffers acute BP swings (e.g. standing).

> **Coronary physiology** — LV perfused in diastole; near-maximal O₂ extraction at rest; demand set by HR, contractility, wall tension. *Clinical link:* the whole logic of angina and anti-anginal therapy.

---

*End of Part 1 (Foundations). This precedes **Installment 1 (Assessment & Coronary/ACS)** and underpins all six clinical installments. Recommended revisi

| Definition | Sx due to acute myocardial ischaemia ± infarction, attributable to obstruction of coronary arteries |
| --- | --- |
| Classification |  | ST Elevation | Cardiac Biomarkers |
| STEMI | + | + |
| NSTEMI | - | + |
| Unstable Angina | - | - |

- UNSTABLE ANGINA: ACS with no biomarker changes of myocardial damage; clinically defined:  ↑ frequency, duration (> 20m), ↓ threshold of exertion, ↓ response to treatment
- Angina at rest
- New onset of severe angina
- Angina that occurs after a recent episode of MI/post-procedure (e.g. PCI, CABG)

- MI is defined by evidence of myocardial necrosis and diagnosed with biomarker changesSymptoms of ischemia

- ECG changes (ST-T changes, new BBB, pathological Q waves)
- Imaging (↓myocardial viability, wall motion abnormality, intracoronary thrombus)
- If biomarkers unattainable, cardiac Sx + new ECG changes sufficient
- NSTEMI: myocardial infarction without ST elevation or BBB
- Partial/near-complete occlusion of a coronary artery
- STEMI: clinical features of ACS in addition to either: 1) ST elevation of at least 1mm in 2 contiguous limb leads, 2) ST elevation of at least 2mm in 2 contiguous chest leads or 3) new LBBBComplete occlusion of a coronary artery

**Epidemiology**

Globally, leading cause of death for men and women

**Normal Arterial Wall**

- INTIMASingle layer of endothelial cells
- Barrier b/w circulating blood and vessel wall
- Non-thrombogenic surface with vasodilator/anti-inflammatory properties

- MEDIASmooth muscle cells and ECM
- Contractile and elastic functions
- Synthesises inflammatory mediators (IL-6, TNF-α) 🡪 leukocyte proliferation + adhesion

- ADVENTITIA

- Nerves, lymphatics and blood vessels (vasa vasorum) 🡪 nourishes arterial wall cells

**Pathophysiology of an atherosclerotic wall **

- 1) endothelial dysfunction 2) accumulation of lipids within intima, 3) leukocytes and smooth muscle cells to vessel wall, 4) foam cells, 5) ECM deposition
- FORMATION OF A FATTY STREAK (LIPID-FILLED FOAM CELLS)Arterial endothelium injury (chemical/physical) 🡪 cytokines 🡪 cell surface adhesion molecules + impaired permeability 🡪 monocytes/T lymphocytes enter subendothelial space
- LDL bind to glycoproteins 🡪 accumulate within subendothelial space 🡪 oxidation by ROS
- Monocytes differentiate into macrophages which phagocytose LDL to form foam cells
- Impaired efflux of these cells leads to local accumulation in the plaque

- PLAQUE PROGRESSION:↑ platelet to damaged endothelium 🡪 release factors that cause smooth muscle cell migration into intima 🡪 proliferation 🡪 collagen + other ECM deposition 🡪 atherosclerotic plaque (raised focal lesion with thrombogenic lipid core covered by a firm, white, fibrous cap)
- Significant lumen narrowing 🡪 tissue ischaemia 🡪 angina pectoris

- PLAQUE DISRUPTION:Plaque causes ↓ in lumen size and ↓ ability to dilate/constrict artery when needed
- Vulnerable plaque: thin cap, ↑ lipid content/macrophages/haemodynamic stresses, ↓ SMC
- Stable plaque: thick

docs.title: Heart Failure
docs.text:
Heart failure is a clinical syndrome — symptoms (breathlessness, fatigue, ankle swelling) and signs (raised JVP, crackles, oedema) caused by a structural/functional cardiac abnormality producing raised intracardiac pressures or inadequate output.

**By ejection fraction** (drives treatment eligibility):
- **HFrEF** — LVEF ≤40% (reduced).
- **HFmrEF** — LVEF 41–49% (mildly reduced).
- **HFpEF** — LVEF ≥50% (preserved) — diagnosis needs *objective evidence* of raised filling pressures/structural change (e.g. raised NT-proBNP, LVH, LA enlargement, diastolic dysfunction).

**Other axes:** acute vs chronic; left vs right vs biventricular; and **high-output** failure (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, AV fistula, beriberi, pregnancy — the heart is normal but demand outstrips supply).

**NYHA functional class** (symptom burden, reassessed often): I (no limitation) · II (slight — symptoms on ordinary activity) · III (marked — symptoms on less-than-ordinary activity) · IV (symptoms at rest).

docs.title: Heart Failure
docs.text:
A drop in output triggers compensatory **neurohormonal activation** that is adaptive short-term but maladaptive long-term:
- **RAAS**: angiotensin II (vasoconstriction) and aldosterone (Na⁺/water retention) → afterload and congestion.
- **Sympathetic nervous system**: tachycardia, vasoconstriction, and direct myocyte toxicity.
- **Natriuretic peptides** (BNP/ANP): a counter-regulatory system (natriuresis, vasodilatation) — overwhelmed as disease progresses.
These pathways drive **adverse remodelling** (dilatation, hypertrophy, fibrosis). Every disease-modifying HF drug works by *blocking* one of these axes — which is why the "four pillars" together outperform any single agent.

docs.title: Heart Failure
docs.text:
Causes: ischaemic (commonest), hypertensive, valvular, cardiomyopathic, arrhythmic (tachycardia-induced), toxic (alcohol, anthracyclines, trastuzumab), infiltrative, congenital, high-output.
**Decompensation triggers** (learn these for the "why did they deteriorate" question): arrhythmia (esp. AF), ischaemia/MI, infection, non-adherence (drugs/salt/fluid), **NSAIDs**, negatively inotropic drugs, anaemia, thyroid disease, renal dysfunction, and IV fluids.

docs.title: Heart Failure
docs.text:
- **Clinical**: congestion (orthopnoea, PND, raised JVP, crackles, oedema, S3 gallop) vs low output (fatigue, cool peripheries, hypotension).
- **NT-proBNP** — high negative predictive value; a normal value largely excludes HF and gates echo. (Use **NT-proBNP** to monitor patients on sacubitril/valsartan, which raises BNP but not NT-proBNP.)
- **Echocardiography** — defines EF, cause, and reversible pathology.
- **CXR** — the ABCDE of failure: **A**lveolar oedema (bat-wing), **B** Kerley B lines, **C**ardiomegaly, **D** upper-lobe **D**iversion, **E**ffusions.

docs.title: Heart Failure
docs.h: 3.5 Chronic HFrEF Management — the Four Pillars
docs.text:
Foundational disease-modifying therapy, all four Class I, **"start low, start all"** (get all four classes on board at low dose early rather than sequential up-titration):
1. **ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) — or ACEi / ARB** if ARNI unsuitable.
2. **Beta-blocker** (bisoprolol, carvedilol, or metoprolol succinate — start when euvolaemic).
3. **MRA** (spironolactone or eplerenone — monitor K⁺ and renal function).
4. **SGLT2 inhibitor** (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin) — benefit **regardless of diabetes**; single fixed dose, easy to start.

**Symptom control:** **loop diuretics** (furosemide) relieve congestion but do *not* improve mortality.

**Device therapy** (in addition to optimal medical therapy):
- **ICD** for primary prevention: symptomatic HFrEF, **LVEF ≤35%** despite **≥3 months** of guideline therapy, expected survival >1 year. *Not* within 40 days of MI. (Ischaemic aetiology has the strongest evidence.)
- **CRT** (biventricular pacing) for **LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II–IV, QRS ≥150 ms with LBBB** (strongest indication); weaker for QRS 130–149 ms or non-LBBB.

**Other agents:** ivabradine (sinus rhythm, HR ≥70 on max beta-blocker), hydralazine/nitrate (esp. if ACEi/ARB not tolerated), vericiguat (worsening HF), IV iron for iron deficiency, digoxin (rate control/symptoms, no mortality benefit).

docs.title: Heart Failure
docs.h: 3.6 Acute Heart Failure / Acute Pulmonary Oedema
docs.text:
Emergency. Immediate management by the **LMNOP** memory aid:
- **L**asix (IV loop diuretic), **M**orphine (cautiously), **N**itrates (IV — if BP allows, reduce preload/afterload), **O**xygen (if hypoxic; **CPAP** for refractory), **P**osition (sit up).
Identify and treat the precipitant. Characterise haemodynamics as **wet/dry** (congestion) and **warm/cold** (perfusion): "wet & warm" is the commonest — diurese and vasodilate; "wet & cold" (cardiogenic shock) needs inotropes/support.

docs.title: Heart Failure
docs.text:
**Cardiogenic shock**: hypotension + hypoperfusion despite adequate filling. Manage the cause (revascularise if ischaemic), cautious inotropes/vasopressors (dobutamine, noradrenaline) as a bridge, and **mechanical circulatory support** (IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO, LVAD) in selected patients. **Transplantation** for end-stage disease; **palliative care** where appropriate.

docs.title: Hypertension
docs.text:
- **Measure properly:** seated, rested, correct cuff; confirm raised clinic readings with **ambulatory (ABPM)** or **home (HBPM)** monitoring to catch **white-coat** (high clinic, normal out-of-office) and **masked** (normal clinic, high out-of-office) hypertension.
- **⚠️ Guideline divergence — know which your exam uses:**
  - **ESC 2024:** *non-elevated* <120/70 · **"Elevated BP" 120–139/70–89** (new category) · **Hypertension ≥140/90**. Treatment target **120–129 mmHg systolic** if tolerated (relaxed in the frail/elderly).
  - **NICE:** stage 1 = clinic ≥140/90 (ABPM/HBPM ≥135/85); stage 2 = ≥160/100.
  - **ACC/AHA (2017):** hypertension defined lower, at ≥130/80.

docs.title: Hypertension
docs.text:
- **Primary (essential)** — ~90–95%; no single cause.
- **Secondary** — suspect if young, resistant, or with suggestive features. Causes:
  - **Renal:** parenchymal disease; **renovascular** (renal artery stenosis — atherosclerotic in older, fibromuscular dysplasia in young women).
  - **Endocrine:** **primary aldosteronism (Conn's)** — the commonest endocrine cause, look for hypokalaemia and a raised aldosterone:renin ratio; **phaeochromocytoma** (episodic headache, sweating, palpitations); **Cushing's**; thyroid/parathyroid disease.
  - **Coarctation of the aorta**, **obstructive sleep apnoea**, and drugs (NSAIDs, steroids, oral contraceptive, sympathomimetics, liquorice).

docs.title: Hypertension
docs.text: Hypertension-mediated organ damage: **LV hypertrophy**/heart failure, coronary disease, **stroke** and vascular dementia, **chronic kidney disease** and albuminuria, and **hypertensive retinopathy** (Keith–Wagener grades I–IV).

docs.title: Hypertension
docs.text:
- **Lifestyle first/always:** salt reduction, weight loss, exercise, alcohol moderation, DASH-style diet.
- **Pharmacological algorithm (A/C/D):**
  - **Step 1:** **ACEi/ARB** (**A**) — especially younger/diabetic/CKD; or a **calcium-channel blocker** (**C**) — especially older or Afro-Caribbean patients.
  - **Step 2:** combine A + C.
  - **Step 3:** add a **thiazide-like diuretic** (**D**) → A + C + D.
  - **Step 4 (resistant HTN):** add **spironolactone** (if K⁺ ≤4.5), or a beta-/alpha-blocker.
  - **Beta-blockers are no longer routine first-line** for uncomplicated hypertension (reserved for a compelling indication — angina, HF, post-MI, rate control, pregnancy).

docs.title: Hypertension
docs.text:
- **Hypertensive emergency** = severe hypertension **with acute end-organ damage** (encephalopathy, acute LV failure/pulmonary oedema, ACS, **aortic dissection**, acute kidney injury, eclampsia, papilloedema). **Urgency** = severely raised BP without acute organ threat.
- **Malignant/accelerated hypertension:** very high BP with grade III/IV retinopathy (haemorrhages, exudates, papilloedema) ± renal failure.
- **Principle:** in emergencies lower BP in a **controlled** way with IV agents (avoid precipitous drops → watershed infarction) — *except aortic dissection*, which needs rapid, aggressive control (see below). Uncomplicated urgency is managed with oral agents over hours–days.

---


---

docs.title: Hypertension
docs.text:
| Definition | Persistent systolic BP ≥ 140 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP ≥ 90 mm Hg |
| --- | --- |
| Classification | Category | Systolic | Diastolic |
| Optimal | <120 | <80 |
| Normal | 120-29 | 80-84 |
| High Normal | 130-39 | 85-89 |
| Grade 1 HTN | 140-59 | 90-99 |
| Grade 2 HTN | 160-79 | 100-109 |
| Grade 3 HTN | ≥180 | ≥110 |
| Isolated systolic HTN | ≥140 | <90 |
| Isolated systolic HTN with widened pulse pressure | ≥160 | <70 |

**Mechanism of BP control**

CENTRAL MECHANISM

- ↓BP 🡪 ↓ arterial pressure 🡪 ↓ stretch 🡪 ↓ afferent baroreceptor firing  🡪 ↑ efferent sympathetic and ↓ efferent parasympathetic 🡪  vasoconstriction, ↑ HR,   ↑ contractility,  ↑ BP
- Carotid massage ↑ carotid sinus pressure to ↓ HR

HORMONAL MECHANISMS

- Sympathetic activation 🡪 adrenal glands release adrenaline, noradrenaline and corticosteroids (volume control) 🡪 ↑ cardiac output, ↑ peripheral vasoconstriction
- Kidneys: ↑ renin (activate RAAS) and EPO (↑ RBC formation) 🡪 ↑ blood volume

ANP/BNP

- ANP: from atrial myocytes in response to ↑blood volume and atrial pressure via cGMP. Causes vasodilation, Na+ reabsorption at the RCT and dilates afferent + constricts efferent renal arterioles (causing diuresis and “aldosterone escape” mechanism)
- BNP:  from ventricular myocytes in response to  ↑ tension. Similar physiologic action to ANP, with longer half-life. Very good negative predictive value in diagnosing HF and Tx of HF (nesiritide)

**Aetiology**

- ESSENTIAL (PRIMARY) HTN (90%) related to CO and TPR
- SECONDARY HTN (10%):
- Renal (parenchymal disease, GN, pyelonephritis, polycystic kidney)
- Endocrine (1o hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing’s, ↑thyroid, ↑PTH, ↑Ca2+, gestational)
- Vascular (coarctation of aorta, renal artery stenosis)
- Drug-induced (oestrogens/OCP, MAOIs, cocaine, amphetamine, steroids, lithium, NSAIDs, decongestants, EtOH)
- HTN is associated with structural changes, remodelling and hypertrophy in resistance arterioles
- Isolated systolic HTN associated with progressive ↓ in vascular compliance

**Risk Factors**

↑ age, male, dyslipidaemia, obesity, DM, physical inactivity, ↑ salt/fatty diet, FHx; African American > Caucasian > Asian

**Features**

- HTN URGENCY: severe (≥ 180/≥ 120 mm Hg) hypertension without acute end-organ damage
- HTN EMERGENCY: severe HTN + acute end-organ damage; types are accelerated HTN (papilloedema) and malignant HTN (causing papilloedema and vascular damage e.g. retinal haemorrhage, bulging disc, mental status change, ↑ creatinine)
- ↓ K+ is an indicator of endocrine HTN (primary aldosteronism, endogenous/exogenous glucocorticoids)

**Differentials**

White coat syndrome (from anxiety)

**Investigations (use per indication)**

- Self-measurement of BP at home
- Bloods: EUCs, BSL, lipids, endocrine tests if suspected
- 12-lead ECG
- Urine: urinalysis, urinary protein excretion (DM, CKD)
- Renovascular HTN: renal U/S, MRA/CTA
- Echocardiography: LV dysfunction?

docs.h: Cardiology Notes — Infective, Inflammatory & Pericardial Disease

docs.title: Infective, Inflammatory & Pericardial Disease
docs.text:
- **Organisms:** *Staphylococcus aureus* (commonest overall; acute, IV drug use, prosthetic), *Streptococcus viridans* (subacute, poor dentition), *Enterococcus*, coagulase-negative staph (prosthetic), the HACEK group, *Streptococcus gallolyticus* (bovis — look for **colorectal cancer**), and culture-negative causes (Coxiella, Bartonella).
- **Peripheral signs — "FROM JANE":** **F**ever, **R**oth spots (retinal), **O**sler nodes (painful pulps — "Ouch"), **M**urmur (new/changed), **J**aneway lesions (painless palms/soles), **A**naemia, **N**ail splinter haemorrhages, **E**mboli.
- **Modified Duke criteria** (updated by **2023 Duke-ISCVID** — added CT/**PET-CT** imaging, new microbiology, and surgical/intraoperative findings as major criteria; the classic structure is still examined):
  - **Major:** persistently positive blood cultures with a typical organism; evidence of endocardial involvement (echo vegetation/abscess/new regurgitation; now also cardiac CT/PET-CT).
  - **Minor:** predisposing cardiac lesion or IV drug use; fever ≥38 °C; **vascular** phenomena (emboli, Janeway, mycotic aneurysm, septic pulmonary infarct); **immunologic** phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis); microbiological evidence not meeting a major criterion.
  - **Definite** = 2 major, *or* 1 major + 3 minor, *or* 5 minor.
- **Investigation:** **three sets of blood cultures** from different sites before antibiotics; **echo — TTE then TOE** (TOE more sensitive for vegetations, abscess, prosthetic valves).
- **Management:** prolonged **IV antibiotics** (empirical, then organism-directed, typically 4–6 weeks). **Surgery** for heart failure from valve destruction, uncontrolled/persistent infection or abscess, large/mobile vegetations with embolic risk, or prosthetic-valve involvement.
- **Prophylaxis:** now **restricted to the highest-risk patients** (prosthetic valve, previous IE, certain congenital disease) undergoing high-risk dental procedures — a big shift from historical blanket prophylaxis; know that guidance is conservative and varies by body.

docs.title: Infective, Inflammatory & Pericardial Disease
docs.text:
- **Acute pericarditis:** causes — viral/idiopathic (commonest), post-MI/**Dressler**, uraemia, autoimmune, TB, malignancy. Features: **sharp, pleuritic** chest pain, worse lying flat and **relieved by sitting forward**, pericardial **friction rub**. ECG: **widespread saddle-shaped (concave) ST elevation + PR depression**. Management: **NSAIDs + colchicine**.
- **Pericardial effusion → cardiac tamponade:** **Beck's triad** (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds), **pulsus paradoxus**, **electrical alternans**, globular "water-bottle" heart on CXR; echo is diagnostic (diastolic RV collapse). Treatment: **urgent pericardiocentesis**.
- **Constrictive pericarditis:** rigid/calcified pericardium restricts filling. **Kussmaul's sign**, pericardial **knock**, pericardial calcification. Distinguish from restrictive cardiomyopathy (imaging, haemodynamics).

docs.title: Infective, Inflammatory & Pericardial Disease
docs.text:
Inflammation of the myocardium — often **viral** (e.g. Coxsackie B). Spectrum from mild chest pain to fulminant heart failure or life-threatening arrhythmia. Raised troponin, ECG changes; **cardiac MRI** (oedema/late gadolinium) and sometimes biopsy. Largely **supportive** care; treat HF/arrhythmia; avoid strenuous exercise during recovery.

docs.text:
| Definition | Pericardial fluid, blood, pus or air accumulation within the pericardial space (↑pressure on heart) |
| --- | --- |
| Aetiology | HemopericardiumCardiac wall rupture (MI complication)Chest traumaAortic dissectionCardiac surgery (valve, CABG) | Serous pericardial effusionIdiopathicAcute pericarditis MalignancyPost-sternotomy syndromeUremicAutoimmune disordersHypothyroidism |
| Pathophysiology | ↓ elasticity of the pericardium → ∼ 150–200 mL of fluid → ↑ pressure in pericardial space → compression of heart (especially thin-walled RV)→ interventricular septum shifts towards the LV chamber → ↓ ventricular diastolic filling → ↓ SV (+ venous congestion) → ↓ cardiac output |
| Presentation | Initially asymptomaticClassic quartet: hypotension, ↑JVP, ↑HR, pulsus paradoxusDDx Pulsus Paradoxus: CP, severe obstructive pulmonary disease, tension pneumothorax, PE, cardiogenic shock, cardiac tamponadeBeck's triad: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins Retrosternal chest painLHF and RHF SxCardiogenic shock |
| Investigations | Echo: pericardial effusion, anechoic space bw peri- and epi-cardium, ↓EF, ↓ wall motionCXR: ↑ cardiac silhouette, clear lungs, globular "water bottle-shaped" heart contour (severe)ECG: ↓ voltage, electric alternans (pathognomonic variation in R amplitude)Pericardial fluid drainage: used to sample the effusion in cases of unclear aetiology |
| Management | Main: analgesia, NSAIDs, IVF (to ↑CO), echo-guided pericardiocentesisAvoid: diuretics and vasodilators (↓ venous return which ↓ LV preload and ↓CO)Other: treat purulent pericardiocentesis patients with Abx (confirm species and sensitivity) |

docs.title: Valvular Heart Disease
docs.text: For every lesion, examiners want the same five things: **cause → murmur → other signs → key investigation → when to intervene.**

docs.title: Valvular Heart Disease
docs.text:
- **Cause:** age-related **calcific/degenerative** (commonest >65), **bicuspid** valve (presents younger), rheumatic.
- **Symptoms — the ominous triad ("SAD"):** exertional **S**yncope, **A**ngina, **D**yspnoea. Onset of symptoms in severe AS signals poor prognosis and the need for intervention.
- **Signs:** ejection-systolic murmur (right 2nd space) radiating to the **carotids**, **slow-rising** pulse, **narrow** pulse pressure, soft/absent S2, S4, sustained heaving apex.
- **Severe AS:** valve area <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg, peak jet velocity >4 m/s (echo).
- **Intervention:** **symptomatic severe AS**, or **asymptomatic severe AS with LVEF <50%** → valve replacement. **SAVR** (surgical) vs **TAVI** (transcatheter) decided by age, surgical risk and anatomy — TAVI now standard for older/higher-risk patients and increasingly used across the risk spectrum.

docs.title: Valvular Heart Disease
docs.text:
- **Cause:** *acute* (infective endocarditis, aortic dissection) — a flash-pulmonary-oedema emergency; *chronic* (bicuspid, rheumatic, or **aortic root dilatation** — Marfan, connective-tissue disease, hypertension).
- **Signs:** early-**diastolic** decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge, best sitting forward in expiration; **collapsing (water-hammer) pulse**, **wide** pulse pressure. Eponymous peripheral signs: Corrigan's (visible carotid pulsation), de Musset's (head bob), Quincke's (nail-bed pulsation), Traube's (pistol-shot femorals), Duroziez's, and the **Austin Flint** murmur (mid-diastolic apical rumble).
- **Intervention:** symptomatic severe AR, or asymptomatic with **LVEF ≤50%** or a dilating LV/aortic root.

docs.title: Valvular Heart Disease
docs.text:
- **Cause:** almost always **rheumatic**.
- **Signs:** low-pitched mid-**diastolic** "rumble" at the apex (bell, left lateral position), **loud S1**, **opening snap**, **malar flush**, **tapping** non-displaced apex.
- **Complications:** **AF** (LA enlargement), pulmonary hypertension, systemic embolism.
- **Intervention:** percutaneous **balloon mitral valvuloplasty** (if suitable, non-calcified, no LA thrombus/significant MR) or surgery.

docs.title: Valvular Heart Disease
docs.text:
- **Cause:** *primary* (degenerative/**prolapse**, rheumatic, endocarditis) vs *secondary/functional* (LV dilatation, ischaemic — the valve is structurally normal).
- **Signs:** **pansystolic** murmur at the apex radiating to the **axilla**, soft S1, displaced thrusting apex, S3.
- **Acute MR** (papillary muscle rupture post-MI, endocarditis) → sudden severe pulmonary oedema — surgical emergency.
- **Intervention:** symptomatic/severe primary MR → repair (preferred) or replacement; transcatheter edge-to-edge repair for selected secondary MR.

docs.title: Valvular Heart Disease
docs.text: - **Tricuspid regurgitation:** usually *functional* (RV dilatation, pulmonary hypertension); also endocarditis (IV drug use). Pansystolic murmur louder on **inspiration**, **giant v waves**, pulsatile liver, ascites.

docs.title: Valvular Heart Disease
docs.text:
- **Mechanical** — durable but need **lifelong warfarin** (DOACs contraindicated); favoured in younger patients.
- **Bioprosthetic** — no long-term anticoagulation but **degenerate in ~10–15 years**; favoured in older patients.
- **Complications:** thrombosis, embolism, endocarditis, haemolysis, structural degeneration, anticoagulant-related bleeding.

docs.title: Valvular Heart Disease
docs.text:
- **Mechanism:** immune cross-reactivity (molecular mimicry) ~2–4 weeks after **group A streptococcal** pharyngitis.
- **Jones criteria** (evidence of preceding strep + 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor). **Major = "JONES"**: **J**oints (migratory polyarthritis), **O** ♡ carditis, subcutaneous **N**odules, **E**rythema marginatum, **S**ydenham chorea. **Minor:** fever, arthralgia, raised inflammatory markers, prolonged PR.
- **Chronic RHD:** predominantly **mitral stenosis**. High burden in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities — secondary penicillin prophylaxis is key.

---

docs.h: Cardiovascular (ANU) — RHEUMATIC FEVER — Valvular Heart Disease
docs.text:
| Definition | Inflammatory complication (2-4 weeks) of group A β-hemolytic streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis RHD: acute pancarditis as a GAS sequela or chronic cardiac valvular changes from ARF complications |
| --- | --- |
| Epidemiology | 5–15 years, ↑ incidence in developing countries |
| Aetiology | Antibodies cross-reactivity with nerve/myocardial proteins → type II hypersensitivity RHD: Aschoff bodies (rheumatic inflammation granuloma), Anitschkow cells (mononuclear cells in Aschoff bodies) |
| Jones Criteria | Diagnosed clinically: Jones Criteria (2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor) + preceding strep infection (Hx: Scarlet Fever, GAS pharyngitis culture, positive rapid Ag detection, ASOTs)Major CriteriaJoints (migratory polyarthritis, primarily large joints)♥ (pancarditis)Nodules (subcutaneous)Erythema marginatum (trunk/limbs; marginated rash)Sydenham chorea (cross-reactivity with basal ganglia)Minor criteria: 1. arthralgia, 2. fever, 3. ↑ acute phase reactants (ESR, CRP), 4. prolonged PR interval on electrocardiogram |
| Presentation | Valves (usually high-pressure e.g. mitral and aortic)Mitral valve (~70%): regurgitation/prolapse and late mitral stenosis (can be mixed in picture)Aortic valve (~30%): regurgitation, stenosisTricuspid valve (~10%)Motor and speech disordersNeuropsychiatric: inappropriate emotions, obsessive-compulsive |
| Investigations | Bloods: anaemia of chronic disease, leucocytosis, ↑ ASO antibodies against metabolites of GAS GAS confirmation: positive rapid strep antigen test, throad culture Echocardiogram: valvular pathology |
| Treatment | Arthritis/fever: bedrest, NSAIDS (/glucocorticoids), aspirin, ibuprofen/naproxenAntibiotics: oral penicillin V (1st line, acute course x 10d)Alternative Abx: amoxicillin, erythromycin, benzathine IM, cephalosporin, macrolidesCardiac valves: Surgery or interventional reconstructive measures ≥ 1 year after acute phase |
| Prognosis | Acute complications: myocarditis, conduction (sinus tachycardia, AF), valvulitis, pericarditisRheumatic heart disease: Acute pancarditis patient 🡪 ↑ risk of valvular heart defects ( mitral/aortic insufficiency/stenosis) and infective endocarditis (10-20 year latency) |
| Prevention | Primary: prompt Abx when GAS tonsillopharyngitis confirmed with throat culture/rapid strep testSecondary: Abx prophylaxis (IM penicillin G benzathine or oral macrolides in penicillin allergies)Duration depends on: nil carditis (5 years/until 21y/o), carditis (10 years/until 21), carditis and permanent valvular heart defects (10 years/until age 40) [for all: choose longer option] |

docs.title: Valvular Heart Disease
docs.h: Cardiovascular (ANU) — INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS — Valvular Heart Disease
docs.text:
| Definition | Infective inflammation of the cardiac endothelium, most commonly the valvesClassification: acute vs. subacute; native vs. prosthetic valve, R-sided vs. L-sidedValve leaflet vegeation: platelet-fibrin thrombi, WBCs, bacteria |
| --- | --- |
| Epidemiology | M>F, age > 60 y/o |
| Risk Factors | Pre-existing: previous IE, pre-damaged/prosthetic heart valves, congenital defects,  ↓ immunityBacteraemia: infected peripheral venous catheters, poor dentition, surgery, IVDU, various bacterial infections, haemodialysis |
| Aetiology | Pathogen | Characteristics |
| S.aureus (45-65%) | Most common acutely, affecting previously health valvesFatal within 6 weeks (if untreated) |
| Viridans streptococci (30%) | Most common subacutely, especially in pre- damaged mitral valves and prosthetic valves≥ 60 days after surgery |
| Enterococcus (<10%) | Multiple drug resistance, following nosocomial UTIs |
| Staphylococcus epidermis | Prosthetic heart valves |
| Gram-negative HACEK | Poor dental hygiene Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, Kingella kingae |
| Candida species | In immunosuppressed patients |

**Pathophysiology**

- Localized infection 🡪 bacteraemia 🡪 bacterial colonisation and thrombi formation on valve leaflets and chordae tendineaeValve destruction with ↓function
- Vessel occlusion/infarction from thrombo-emboli
- Immune complex against tissue antigens (GN, Osler Nodes)

- Mitral > aortic > tricuspid > pulmonary

**Presentation**

- ACUTE IE:
- Acute onset with rapid progression (days to weeks) and ↑ constitutional Sx
- Most common: S. aureus (can be caused by GAS, S. pneumoniae, N.gonorrhoeae)
- SUBACUTE IE:
- Insidious onset with slow progression (weeks to months) and ↓ constitutional Sx
- Most common: Streptococci
- PROSTHETIC VALVE IE:
- Early (<60d) vs. late (≥ 60d)
- S.epidermidis (early onset) or S.aureus (late onset)
- SYMPTOMS
- Constitutional: fever/chills, ↑HR, malaise, arthralgia, myalgia, cough, pleuritic chest pain
- Cardiac: murmur, CHF, arrthmias
- Mnemonic: Fever, Roth’s spots, Osler’s nodes, Murmur, Janeway lesions, Anemia, Nail-bed hemorrhages (i.e. splinter hemorrhages), Emboli
- Other: neurological (seizure, paresis), PE, splenomegaly, acute renal injury

**Duke Criteria**

- 1) 2 major, 2) 1 major + 3 minor OR 3) 5 minor
- Major diagnostic criteriaTwo separate blood cultures positive for typical pathogens
- Evidence of endocardial involvement in echocardiography (valve vegetations on TTE/TOE)
- A new valvular regurgitation (worsening of a pre-existing murmur is not sufficient)

- Minor diagnostic criteriaPredisposition (underlying heart disease or IV drug abuse)
- Fever ≥ 38°C
- Vascular (major arterial emboli, pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysms, Janeway lesions)
- Immunologic disorder (GN, rheumatoid factor, Osler nodes, Roth’s spots)
- Microbiology

- Only negative findings on TOE can reliably rule out endocarditis, as TTE is not

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
- Thyroxine (T4) and tri-iodothyronine (T3)
- Formed by iodine binding to tyrosine residues
- T3 is much more biologically active (3-8 x more potent) than T4­ (longer half-life)
- Hence, plasma concentration of free T4 much higher than T3
- Circulate while being bound by plasma proteins thyroid-binding globulin, albumin and transthyretin
- Unbound fraction is the active component  (‘free hormone’). Usually free T4 (0.03%) and free T3 (0.3%)
- 85% of T4 is converted into T3 or reverse T3 (RT3) in the peripheral tissue by tissue-specific deiodinases
- Type I: converts T4 into T3 for circulation in plasma; found in liver, kidney, thyroid and muscle
- Type II: produce high proportion of receptor-bound T3 themselves; found in pituitary, thyroid, cardiac and skeletal muscle, brown fat, and cerebral cortex
- Type III: converts T4 to rT3 and T3 to T2, hence inactivating hormones; found in placenta, developing brain and skin. RT3 is metabolically inactive but produced in times of stress to ↓ metabolic activity


---

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
![](notes/images/endocrinology-anu/img009.jpg)

- Stimulation: TRH (hypothalamus) stimulates TSH (pituitary), which stimulates follicular cells. May also be stimulated by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) in Graves disease
- Extrathyroid Regulation:
- Stimulation of thyroid by TSH, epinephrine, prostaglandins (cAMP stimulators)
- Negative feedback by free T3/T4 on the anterior pituitary to inhibit TSH and on hypothalamus to inhibit TRH
- Intrathyroid Autoregulation:
- There is varying thyroid sensitivity to TSH in response to iodide availability
- Wolff-Chaikoff: excess iodine temporarily inhibits thyroid peroxidase → ↑ iodine organification → ↑ T3/T4
- Jod-Basedow effect (opposite to Wolff-Chaikoff): thyrotoxicosis if a patient with iodine deficiency and partially autonomous thyroid tissue (e.g. autonomous nodule) is made iodine replete
- Increased activity of peripheral 5’deiodinase in hypothyroidism increases T3 production despite low T4 levels

docs.title: Adrenal Disorders
docs.text:
**Cushing's syndrome = chronic glucocorticoid excess** (of any cause). **Cushing's *disease* = the specific pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma.**

**Features:** central obesity, moon face, dorsocervical fat pad ("buffalo hump"), **purple striae >1 cm, easy bruising, thin skin, proximal myopathy**, hypertension, glucose intolerance/diabetes, osteoporosis, hirsutism, mood change; hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (esp. ectopic ACTH).

**Commonest cause overall is iatrogenic (exogenous steroids)** — always the first thing to exclude.

**Step 1 — confirm cortisol excess (screening tests, need ≥2 positive):**
- **Overnight/low-dose dexamethasone suppression test** (fails to suppress)
- **Late-night salivary cortisol** (loss of diurnal trough)
- **24 h urinary free cortisol** (elevated)

**Step 2 — find the source with ACTH:**

| | ACTH | Source | Next test |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ACTH-dependent** | **High/normal** | Pituitary (**Cushing's disease**, ~⅔) or **ectopic** ACTH (small-cell lung, carcinoid) | **High-dose DST** (pituitary suppresses, ectopic doesn't); **CRH test**; pituitary MRI; **inferior petrosal sinus sampling** if unclear |
| **ACTH-independent** | **Low/suppressed** | **Adrenal** adenoma/carcinoma (or bilateral hyperplasia) | Adrenal CT |

**Discriminator:** **very high ACTH + hypokalaemia + rapid onset + pigmentation** suggests **ectopic ACTH** (paraneoplastic). **Management:** treat the cause — transsphenoidal surgery (disease), adrenalectomy (adrenal), resect the ectopic source; medical control with **metyrapone/ketoconazole** meanwhile.

docs.title: Adrenal Disorders
docs.text:
**Primary (Addison's disease)** — the adrenal cortex itself fails, so **both cortisol AND aldosterone are lost**, and ACTH rises:
- **Causes:** **autoimmune adrenalitis** (commonest in developed world; may be part of autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes), **TB** (commonest worldwide), metastases, haemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen in meningococcaemia), adrenoleukodystrophy.
- **Features:** fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, **postural hypotension**, salt craving, GI upset, and — the discriminator — **hyperpigmentation** (palmar creases, buccal mucosa, scars) from **high ACTH/POMC (MSH activity)**.
- **Biochemistry:** **hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia** (aldosterone loss), hypoglycaemia, ± mild hypercalcaemia; **high ACTH**; **low cortisol failing to rise on short Synacthen**.

**Secondary** — pituitary ACTH deficiency (tumour, or **suppression by exogenous steroids** — the commonest cause):
- **Aldosterone is preserved** (RAAS-driven), so **no hyperkalaemia and no pigmentation** (ACTH is low). Cortisol low, ACTH low.

**Discriminator:** **pigmentation + hyperkalaemia = primary (Addison's); pale + normal potassium = secondary.**

**Addisonian (adrenal) crisis** *(emergency)* — hypotension/shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, hypoglycaemia, often precipitated by infection/surgery or steroid withdrawal: **IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately** + **aggressive IV 0.9% saline** (± glucose); don't wait for confirmatory tests (take a random cortisol/ACTH first if quick). **Steroid sick-day rules:** double oral glucocorticoid during intercurrent illness; switch to parenteral if vomiting; carry a steroid emergency card. Replacement: **hydrocortisone** (glucocorticoid) + **fludrocortisone** (mineralocorticoid) in primary disease.

docs.title: Adrenal Disorders
docs.text:
##### Primary aldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) ⚑
Autonomous aldosterone excess — **the commonest cause of secondary/endocrine hypertension**, and increasingly recognised (current guidance broadens screening toward **most people with hypertension**, not just the classic hypokalaemic case).
- **Presentation:** **hypertension** (often resistant), ± **hypokalaemia** (weakness, cramps, polyuria), metabolic alkalosis. Note many are **normokalaemic**.
- **Screening:** **aldosterone:renin ratio (ARR)** — **high aldosterone with suppressed renin**. (Stop interfering drugs where possible; spironolactone must be withheld.)
- **Confirm:** saline/fludrocortisone **suppression** (aldosterone fails to suppress).
- **Subtype/localise:** adrenal CT + **adrenal vein sampling** to separate a **unilateral adenoma** (→ **adrenalectomy**) from **bilateral hyperplasia** (→ **mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist: spironolactone or eplerenone**).

##### Phaeochromocytoma / paraganglioma
Catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal **medulla** (or extra-adrenal paraganglion). "**Rule of 10s**" (classic teaching, now looser): ~10% bilateral, ~10% extra-adrenal, ~10% malignant, ~a quarter **hereditary** (MEN 2, VHL, NF1, SDH mutations).
- **Presentation:** paroxysmal **headache, sweating, palpitations** with **labile/severe hypertension** (the classic triad); pallor, anxiety, weight loss; crises provoked by anaesthesia, contrast, β-blockade-first.
- **Diagnosis:** **plasma or 24 h urinary metanephrines/normetanephrines** (most sensitive) → then imaging (CT/MRI, MIBG). **Never biopsy.**
- **Management:** **α-blockade FIRST (phenoxybenzamine/doxazosin), then β-blockade** once α-blocked, with volume expansion, before surgical resection. **Giving a β-blocker first causes unopposed α-vasoconstriction → hypertensive crisis** — a classic exam trap.

##### Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)
Enzyme defect in cortisol synthesis (**21-hydroxylase deficiency, ~90%**) → low cortisol → high ACTH → adrenal hyperplasia and shunting into **androgens**.
- **Classic salt-wasting** (severe): neonatal **hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypotension** + **ambiguous genitalia** in girls / adrenal crisis in the first weeks. **17-hydroxyprogesterone is high.** Treat with glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid replacement.
- Non-classic (mild): later hirsutism/oligomenorrhoea (a PCOS mimic).

##### Adrenal incidentaloma
An adrenal mass found on imaging done for another reason. Two questions: **is it functioning?** (screen for phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's/autonomous cortisol, and — if hypertensive — Conn's) and **is it malignant?** (size >4 cm, irregular, high Hounsfield units, rapid growth → resect).

---

docs.title: Adrenal Disorders
docs.text:
**Adrenal cortex** (derived from mesoderm) and **medulla **(derived from neural crest)

![](notes/images/endocrinology-anu/img022.jpg)

![](notes/images/endocrinology-anu/img023.jpg)

Glucocorticoids: primarily cortisol

- Involved in the regulation of metabolism (counteracts insulin), supports blood pressure and vasomotor tone, and involved in regulation of behaviour and immunosuppression
- Stimulatory effects
- Hepatic gluconeogenesis
- Insulin resistance in peripheral tissues
- Protein catabolism and lipolysis
- Bone resorption
- Leukocytosis
- ↑ cardiac output, vascular tone, Na+ retention
- PTH release and urine calcium excretion
- Permissive effect on catecholamines
- Inhibitory effects: antiphlogistic (↓ inflammation)

Androgens: present as dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) in the adrenal cortex (intermediate male sex steroid )

- Minimal effect compared to the gonads
- Anabolic effects on muscles and bones
- Influences behaviour and CNS processes
- In men: sexual differentiation, spermatogenesis

Mineralocorticoids: primarily aldosterone → mainly regulated through renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)

- Act on nuclear mineralocorticoid receptors within the principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct
- Negative feedback to JGA by long loop (aldosterone → volume expansion) and short loop (angiotensin II → peripheral vasoconstriction)
- Aldosterone increases renal reabsorption of sodium (and water) and augments the excretion of potassium and protons → ↑ extracellular fluid, ↑ blood pressure, ↓ K+, ↑ pH

Adrenaline

- Catecholamines are synthesized from tyrosine in postganglionic sympathetic nerves (noaradrenaline) and chromaffin cells of adrenal medulla (adrenaline)
- Broken down into metanephrines and other metabolites (VMA, HVA) and excreted in urine
- Constricts blood vessels but dilates airways
- Increases RR, HR, BP and CO

Adrenal-sympathetic-thyroid link

- ACTH stimulates synthesis of DA and NA, and cortisol up-regulates the conversion of noradrenaline to adrenaline
- When stressed is sensed by the cortex, it activates the HPA axis and amplifies adrenaline production
- There is increased sympathetic drive to the adrenal medulla, leading to increased adrenaline release
- Simultaneously, high thyroid levels cause an increased expression of β-adrenoreceptors, and hence, an increased response to adrenaline
