docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — HIATUS HERNIA — Additional Notes
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: Protrusion of the upper stomach into the thorax, through a tear/weakness in the diaphragm
- RISK FACTORS: age (~60% of individuals >50), ↑ abdominal pressure (in obesity, pregnancy, coughing, heavy lifting), smoking, structural abnormalities
- PATHOGENESIS/CLASSIFICATION

![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img001.jpg)

- Type I – sliding hiatal hernia (95%): Protrusion of gastro-oesophageal junction followed by the body of the stomach through the oesophageal hiatus and above the diaphragm; ↓ lower oesophageal sphincter pressure ↑ GORD risk
- Type II – rolling (1%): Protrusion of the fundus and/or body of the stomach into the chest, with maintenance of the gastro-oesophageal junction below the diaphragm; ↑ risk of intermittent strangulation/ischemia/ischemic necrosis of stomach (🡪 mediastinitis, death)
- Type III – mixed (3%): Both GO junction + fundus above the diaphragmatic hiatus
- Type IV – mixed + complex (1%): other viscera (e.g. colon, spleen, pancreas, small intestine) within the hernia sac

- HISTORY: Sliding (Sx of GORD), Paraoesophageal (retrosternal fullness, N/V), GI bleeding/fever (O= ischemia/potential necrosis of stomach)
- EXAMINATION: bowel sounds in chest
- INVESTIGATIONSUpper GI series: first drink is very carbonated 🡪 gas build up 🡪 expands the stomach 🡪 second drink is a contrast agent 🡪 X-Ry 🡪 positive when stomach is partially/completely intrathoracic
- CT/MRI: better visualization if  upper GI is negative but diagnosis still suspected

- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: angina pectoris, GORD, pneumonia, gastric outlet obstruction
- TREATMENTSliding hiatus hernia: surgical repair not indicted in asymptomatic patients; treat as per GORD in symptomatic patients (medical/surgical)
- Paraesophageal hiatus hernia: surgical repair if failed medical management of GORD, dysphagia, early satiety, postprandial pain, vomiting

- COMPLICATIONS: GORD (most common), esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett’s oesophagus, oesophageal carcinoma and extra-oesophageal complications such laryngitis, pneumonia, asthma or coughing, strangulation (ischemia/necrosis)
- PROGNOSIS: good to excellent long-term outcomes in relatively small hiatus
- PREVENTION: avoid meals that are large/before bedtime, avoid nicotine/caffeine/fatty foods (↓LES tone)


---

docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — fobt — Additional Notes
docs.text:
- ADVANTAGES: non-invasive, quick, easy, cheap
- DISADVANTAGES: ↓ specific, false positive test results, requires follow-up investigations if positive
- Australians turning 50, 55, 60 or 65, who hold a Medicare/DVA card have a free FOBT kit sent which they can send to pathology. A positive result is followed by imaging of the whole colon, usually with colonoscopy
- The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program is currently inviting Australians turning 50, 55, 60, 64, 65, 70, 72 or 74 years of age to take part through FOBTs. However, NHMRC recommends FOBT screening every two years from 50
- Other screening strategies include 5-yearly flexible sigmoidoscopy with or without FOBT, double-contrast barium enema or 10-yearly colonoscopy

docs.text:
- DEFINITION: malignancy of extra- or intrahepatic bile ducts
- RISK FACTORS: 50-70 y/o, UC, PSC, liver fluke, intrahepatic stones
- Majority adenocarcinoma
- CLINICAL FEATURES: gradual Sx of biliary obstruction (jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools), anorexia, weight loss, RUQ pain, Courvoisier’s sign in CBD obstruction, hepatomegaly, metastases into portal vein/hepatic artery
- Klatskin tumour at the bifurcation of common hepatic duct
- INVESTIGATIONS
- LFTs: obstructive picture
- U/S or CT: dilated bile ducts
- ERCP/PTC: ?resectability, biopsy
- CXR/bone scan: metastatic work-up
- TREATMENT:
- Resectable: biliary drainage and wide excision margin (can do duct resection, Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy, liver resection, Whipple Procedure depending on location)
- Unresectable: stent or choledochojejunostomy (surgical bypass)
- Chemotherapy ± radiotherapy
- Transplantation in Klatskin tumours

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.h: Gastroenterology Master Notes — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
**Gallstones** — mostly **cholesterol** (or mixed); pigment stones with haemolysis. **Risk = the 5 Fs: Female, Fat, Forty, Fertile, Family history** (± rapid weight loss, ileal disease/bile-salt loss). Most are **asymptomatic** (leave alone).

**The spectrum — separate them by the presence of pain, fever, and jaundice (high yield):**

| Condition | Where the stone is | Pain | Fever/WCC | Jaundice | Key sign/test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Biliary colic** | Neck/cystic duct (transient) | RUQ, post-fatty meal, **<6 h, no fever** | No | No | US stones; settles |
| **Acute cholecystitis** | Impacted in cystic duct → inflamed GB | RUQ, **constant >6 h** | **Yes** | Usually no | **Murphy's sign +**; US: thick wall, pericholecystic fluid |
| **Choledocholithiasis** | **CBD** | RUQ | ± | **Yes (obstructive)** | ↑bilirubin/ALP; dilated CBD; **MRCP → ERCP** |
| **Ascending cholangitis** | CBD + **infection** | RUQ | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Charcot's triad** (RUQ pain + fever + jaundice); emergency |

*Discriminators: **biliary colic = pain only**; **cholecystitis = pain + fever + Murphy's** (but no jaundice); **cholangitis = pain + fever + jaundice (Charcot's triad)** — add **hypotension + confusion = Reynolds' pentad** (severe, needs urgent biliary drainage/ERCP).*

**Management:** cholecystitis → analgesia, IV antibiotics, and **laparoscopic cholecystectomy** (ideally within 1 week / same admission ⚑). CBD stones → **ERCP** clearance ± cholecystectomy. Ascending cholangitis → resuscitate, IV antibiotics, **urgent biliary decompression (ERCP)**.

**Other biliary:**
- **Murphy's sign:** arrest of inspiration on RUQ palpation (cholecystitis).
- **Mirizzi syndrome** — stone in the cystic duct compressing the CBD → obstructive jaundice.
- **Gallstone ileus** — a large stone erodes into the bowel (cholecysto-enteric fistula) → small-bowel obstruction; **Rigler's triad** (pneumobilia, obstruction, ectopic stone).
- **Courvoisier's law:** a **palpable, painless** gallbladder with jaundice is **unlikely to be gallstones** — think **malignant obstruction** (pancreatic/biliary cancer), because a chronically stone-diseased gallbladder is fibrotic and won't distend.
- **Cholangiocarcinoma** (PSC-associated, ↑CA19-9) and **gallbladder cancer** (porcelain gallbladder) — late, poor prognosis.

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
**Acute inflammation from premature enzyme activation** → autodigestion. **Causes — "I GET SMASHED"**: **I**diopathic, **G**allstones, **E**thanol, **T**rauma, **S**teroids, **M**umps, **A**utoimmune, **S**corpion, **H**yperlipidaemia/hypercalcaemia, **E**RCP, **D**rugs. **Gallstones and alcohol account for ~80%.**

**Diagnosis (2 of 3):** characteristic **epigastric pain radiating to the back**, **serum lipase (or amylase) >3× upper limit** (lipase more specific/sensitive), and/or characteristic **imaging** (CT/US). *Amylase can be normal if late-presenting or in alcoholic pancreatitis — lipase is better.*

Signs: epigastric tenderness, and (in severe/haemorrhagic disease) **Cullen's sign** (periumbilical bruising) and **Grey Turner's sign** (flank bruising).

**⚑ Severity assessment:**
- **Glasgow–Imrie score (PANCREAS)** at 48 h — **PaO₂ <8 kPa, Age >55, Neutrophils (WCC >15), Calcium <2, Renal (urea >16), Enzymes (LDH/AST high), Albumin <32, Sugar (glucose >10)**. **≥3 = severe** → HDU/ITU. (Ranson's and **APACHE II** and **CRP >150** are also used.)
- **Revised Atlanta classification** grades severity by **organ failure and complications**: **mild** (no organ failure/complications), **moderately severe** (transient organ failure <48 h and/or local complications), **severe** (**persistent organ failure >48 h**).

**Management:** **aggressive IV fluid resuscitation**, analgesia, oxygen, **early enteral nutrition** (NBM only if not tolerated; parenteral is last resort), treat the cause (**ERCP/cholecystectomy for gallstone pancreatitis**; alcohol withdrawal). **Antibiotics are not routine** — only for proven infected necrosis. Complications: **pancreatic necrosis** (± infection), **pseudocyst** (fluid collection weeks later — amylase-rich; drain if symptomatic), abscess, haemorrhage, **ARDS**, and later chronic pancreatitis/diabetes.

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
**Chronic pancreatitis** — irreversible fibrosis (commonest cause **alcohol**; also genetic, autoimmune/IgG4, obstruction). Presents with **chronic epigastric pain radiating to the back**, and the two failures: **exocrine** (steatorrhoea, weight loss, **low faecal elastase** → **pancreatic enzyme replacement, Creon**) and **endocrine** (diabetes). Imaging: **pancreatic calcification** on CT/AXR. Manage pain, alcohol cessation, enzyme/insulin replacement.

**Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma** — usually **head of pancreas**; classically **painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss** (**Courvoisier-positive** — palpable painless gallbladder), later epigastric/back pain, new-onset diabetes, thrombophlebitis migrans (Trousseau's sign). Risk: **smoking**, chronic pancreatitis, age, hereditary. Tumour marker **CA19-9**. Diagnose with **CT (pancreatic protocol) + EUS ± biopsy**. Most present **late/unresectable**; only ~20% are candidates for **Whipple's (pancreaticoduodenectomy)**; overall **poor prognosis**.

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Gallstone risk factors | **5 Fs: Female, Fat, Forty, Fertile, Family history** |
| RUQ pain <6 h, no fever, settles | **Biliary colic** |
| RUQ pain + fever + Murphy's, no jaundice | **Acute cholecystitis** |
| RUQ pain + fever + **jaundice** | **Ascending cholangitis (Charcot's triad)** |
| Charcot's triad + hypotension + confusion | **Reynolds' pentad** (severe cholangitis) |
| Definitive treatment of cholecystitis | **Laparoscopic cholecystectomy** |
| Emergency treatment of cholangitis | **Urgent biliary drainage (ERCP)** |
| Palpable **painless** gallbladder + jaundice | **Malignant obstruction** (Courvoisier's law) |
| Stone eroding into bowel → obstruction | **Gallstone ileus** (Rigler's triad) |
| Pancreatitis causes mnemonic | **I GET SMASHED** (gallstones + alcohol ~80%) |
| Best diagnostic enzyme in pancreatitis | **Lipase** (>3× ULN) |
| Periumbilical / flank bruising | **Cullen's / Grey Turner's sign** |
| Severity score at 48 h | **Glasgow–Imrie (PANCREAS), ≥3 = severe** |
| Atlanta "severe" pancreatitis | **Persistent organ failure >48 h** |
| Antibiotics in acute pancreatitis | **Only for infected necrosis** (not routine) |
| Fluid collection weeks after pancreatitis | **Pseudocyst** |
| Low faecal elastase + calcification + steatorrhoea | **Chronic pancreatitis** (give Creon) |
| Painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss + CA19-9 | **Pancreatic head cancer** |
| Curative pancreatic cancer operation | **Whipple's (pancreaticoduodenectomy)** |

##### Sources
Robbins & Cotran (biliary/pancreatic pathology); NICE NG118 (gallstone disease), NG104 (pancreatitis); IAP/APA and BSG pancreatitis guidance (revised Atlanta severity, no routine antibiotics, early enteral nutrition ⚑); Oxford Handbook of Clinical Surgery; Merck Manual Professional. docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — ACUTE PANCREATITIS — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: ↑ in incidence, age and sex dependent on aetiology (EtOh-related males, biliary tract-related females)
- AETIOLOGY: I – idiopathic, G – gallstones, E – ethanol, T – trauma, S – steroids, M – mumps/malignancies/microbiology, A – autoimmune (SLE, polyarteritis nodosa, Crohn’s Disease), S – scorpion stings/spider bites, H – hyperlipidaemia/hyperCa2+ (metabolic disorders), E – ERCP D – drugs (azathioprine, frusemide, oestrogen, antibiotics, acetaminophen, salicylates)
- PATHOGENESIS: Pancreatic acinar cells in the exocrine pancreas produce enzymes which are packaged into zymogens and released into the pancreatic duct via ductal cells. Proenzyme is activated at duodenal brush border, where trypsinogen is converted to trypsin, facilitating activation of other proenzymes. To prevent premature activation, zymogens are segregated into compartments, and contain ↓pH and ↓Ca2+. Once cellular injury pattern has initiated, cellular membrane trafficking becomes chaotic, leading to fusion of lysosomal and zymogen granules, enabling activation of trypsinogen to trypsin. Secretory vesicles are extruded across the basolateral membrane into the interstitium, where molecular fragments act as chemoattractants for inflammatory cells. Activated neutrophils exacerbate the problem by releasing superoxides/proteolytic enzymes 🡪 ↑vascular permeability 🡪 haemorrhage, oedema, pancreatic necrosis

In gallstone pancreatitis, mechanical obstruction of the pancreatic duct whereas in ethanol-related pancreatitis, pathogenesis is unknown. In rare genetic diseases, mutations prevent the physiological trypsin breakdown required normally to stop proteolysis

- CLASSIFICATIONS
- Oedematous – pancreatic parenchyma and surrounding retroperitoneal structures are
- Haemorrhagic – bleeding into the parenchyma engorged with interstitial fluid and inflammatory cell infiltration
- PATHOLOGY
- Mild (interstitial)- peri-pancreatic fat necrosis, interstitial oedema
- Severe (necrotic)- peri/intra-pancreatic fat necrosis/haemorrhage/infection; systemic toxic factors and peritoneal space (multi-organ failure)
- HISTORY
- Sharp epigastric pain that radiates to the back, eased by forward flexion (Inglefinger’s sign)
- Post-prandial, fever, N/V, steatorrhoea, anorexia, ↓BP, jaundice (bile duct obstruction), hypovolemic shock (🡪 renal failure), ARDS (SIRS, sepsis, severe sepsis, septic shock, multi-organ dysfunction), coma, tetany (transient hypoCa2+)
- EXAMINATION: rigidity, guarding, abd distension (from paralytic ileus), Cullen’s sign (periumbilical ecchymosis), Grey-Turner’s signs (flank ecchymosis), ↓BP, ↑HR
- ![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img019.jpg)
INVESTIGATIONS
- ↑ Lipase (?EtOH- related; x3 reference range; starts rising 4-8 hrs after onset peaks at 24 hrs and lasts for 8-14 days)
- ↑ Amylase (more pancreas-?gallstone-related; x3 reference range; starts rising 2-12 hrs peaks at 48 hrs and lasts for 3-5 days)
- FBC, CRP (severity), IgG (acute), ALT&

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — CHRONIC PANCREATITIS — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: persistent/irreversible pancreatic inflammation with cell loss (from necrosis), inflammation, fibrosis
- AETIOLOGY: idiopathic, EtOH (>90%), cystic fibrosis
- PATHOGENESIS: unrelenting injury to the pancreas 🡪 fibrosis and chronic pancreatitis and ↓ amylase and lipase
- RISK FACTORS: EtOH, smoking, coeliac disease
- HISTORY: dull epigastric pain that radiates to the back, and relieved by sitting forward; weight loss and steatorrhea (different from acute), N/V, jaundice, ascites, GI bleed, malabsorption (chronic diarrhoea, steatorrhea, weight loss, fatigue), endocrine insufficiency (frank initially vs pancreatogenic after surgery types of diabetes)
- EXAMINATION: abd distension, skin lesions (circulating pancreatic lipase 🡪 fat necrosis)
- INVESTIGATIONS
- Bloods- normal amylase/lipase (fibrin has destroyed much of the enzyme- forming capacity; may be elevated in acute exacerbations), ↑ glucose/ALP/bilirubin (biliary obstruction)
- Abd U/S- structural changes, cavities, duct irregularity, calcification
- CT Scan- focal/diffuse enlargement of the pancreas
- Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP): most accurate test, shows beading off main pancreatic duct (from alternating dilatation and stenosis)
- Other- 72 hour faecal fat test for exocrine function; secretin test (gold standard)- measures exocrine function but difficult to perform, unpleasant, expensive; pancreatic polypeptide response to a test meal (blunted PP response to feeding in severe disease)
- Diabetes mellitus- in 75% with calcific pancreatitis and 30% of non-calcific (due to ↑ glucose tolerance and ↓ insulin level)
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: acute pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, biliary colic, peptic ulcer, AAA
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT
- Lifestyle (psychiatric, ↓fatty foods, ↓smoking, ↓EtOH)
- Pain management- oral analgesia (narcotics titrated to lowest effective dose) with analgesia-enhancing agents e.g. gabapentin
- Tread IDMM with insulin if needed
- Oral enzyme replacement (especially lipase) by resting pancreas negative feedback
- Somatostatin to ↓ exocrine secretion and CKK release
- Interventional- block visceral afferent nerve conduction to treat obstructions of the main pancreatic duct
- Spinchterotomy- if duct dilated, remove stones from pancreatic duct
- Surgery- Indications: failure of medical tx, debilitating pain, pseudocyst complications (persistence, haemorrhage, infection, rupture), CBD obstruction, fistula, pancreatic cancer
- Minimal - pancreatic duct decompression, extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy, celiac plexus block
- Options:  pancreticojejunostomy (drain pancreatic duct if dilated), resect pancreas if duct contracted (most severe disease usually in the head of the gland) with Whipple Procedure (pancreticoduodenectomy) ± Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy, or total pancretectomy (where aforementioned has failed to give pain relief)

- COMPLICATIONS: exocrine insufficiency, DM, calcification, duct obstruction, cancer
- PROGNOSI

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — Pancreatic cancer — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: 4th most common in relation to mortality
- RISK FACTORS: age, smoking, ↑ fat, ↓ fibre, EtOH, DM, chronic pancreatitis, gastrectomy, cholecystectomy, African
- PATHOLOGY
- Ductal adenocarcinoma most common 75-80%; can have others e.g. endocrine, acinar cell, mucinous cystic and intra-ductal papillary mucinous
- CLINICAL FEATUREs
- Vague abd pain with weight loss ± jaundice in a patient over 50 yr old is pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise
- Head (70%)- weight loss, obstructive jaundice, steatorrhea, vague constant and mid-epigastric pain (worse at night, radiate to back), Courvoisier’s sign (painless jaundice, with palpable epigastric mass = pancreatic cancer, Trousseau's Sign (spontaneous peripheral venous thrombosis, often associated with pancreatic/other)
- Body/tail (30%)- tends to present later + usually inoperable, weight loss, vague epigastric pain, <10% jaundiced, sudden onset DM
- FHx
- INVESTIGATIONS: ↑ALP, ↑bilirubin, Ca19-9 (most useful serum marker), U/S or CT (evaluates metastases + resectability), ± ERCP/MRI/EUS/Bone Scan for staging/metastases
- TREATMENT
- Resectable (10-20%)
- No involvement of liver, peritoneum, vasculature or distant sites
- Whipple procedure (pancreoduodenectomy) for cure <5% mortality
- Distal pancreatectomy ± splenectomy, lymphadenectomy if carcinoma of midbody/tail
- Non-resectable Palliation: Endoscopic stenting or double bypass procedure (choledochoenterostomy + gastroenterostomy)‚
- Chemotherapy (gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel, FOLFIRNOX) ± radiotherapy

- PROGNOSIS : 5 year survival is 1%

docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — Jaundice — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
- CLINICAL PRESENTATION: dark urine/pale stools, pruritis (cholestasis), abdominal pain (stone/pancreatic tumour causing obstructive jaundice), painless (?pancreatic cancer), kernicterus
- KEY QUESTIONS: Alcohol, Billirubin, Cirrhosis (VARICES), Drug overdose (e.g. panadol, nEoplasms, Familial (autoimmune, hemochromatosis, a1-antitrypsin deficiency, Gilbert’s syndrome, Wilson’s), Gall bladder/pancreas, Hepatitis (IVDU, unprotected sex, overcrowding, poor sanitation)
- INVESTIGATIONS: FBC, EUC, INR, BSL, LFTs (↑AST/ALT=liver damage; GGT=EtOH), serology for Ab in Viral Hepatitis, amylase/lipase, US/CT, endoscopic US, MRCP/ERCP, percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography, liver biopsy

|  | Pre-hepatic | Hepatic | Post-hepatic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Total bilirubin | N/↑ | ↑ | ↑ |
| Conjugated bilirubin | N | ↑ | ↑ |
| Unconjugated bilirubin | ↑ | ↑ | N |
| Urine bilirubin | Not present | Present | Present |
| Urine urobilinogen | N/↑ | ↓ | ↓ |
| Urine colour | N | Dark | Dark |
| Stool colour | N | N/pale | Pale |
| LFTs | N | ↑ | ↑ |

- PRE-HEPATIC JAUNDICE when there is ↑ haemolysis 🡪 liver cannot process ↑ bilirubin 🡪 ↑ unconjugated bilirubin (not water soluble) in blood-stream. Caused by ↑ haemolysis (thalassemia, sickle-cell, spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, malaria, uaemia) or ↓ uptake/conjugation (Gilbert’s syndrome, porto-systemic shunt)
- HEPATIC JAUNDICE when there is acute/chronic liver injury 🡪 ↓ ability to metabolize and excrete bilirubin thus an ↑ unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin. Caused by cirrhosis (alcoholic, Wilson’s, haemochromatosis), infection (viral hepatitis), and drug-induced (paracetamol toxicity)
- POST-HEPATIC JAUNDICE caused by an interruption to the drainage of bile containing conjugated bilirubin that prevents delivery of bile from liver/gallbladder to duodenum. Caused by obstruction in lumen (choledocholithiasis), obstruction in wall (cholangiocarcinoma, choledocal cyst), and obstruction by compression (head of pancreas cancer, Mirrizi syndrome)

docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — primary sclerosing cholangitis vs primary biliary cholangitis — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
|  | Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis | Primary Biliary Cholangitis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | Biliary tree narrowing from scarring/fibrosis of bile ducts (intra and/or extrahepatic bile ducts) | Chronic granulomatous inflammation and fibrous obliteration of intra-hepatic bile ducts |
| Epidemiology | Male 20-40s | Females 50-60s > 90% |
| Aetiology | Primary- Commonly UCSecondary- long-term choledocholithiasis, cholangiocarcinoma, trauma, post-ERCP, HIV/AIDS, IgG4-related disease) | Autoimmune- Sjogren’s Disease (most commonly), RA, scleroderma, thyroiditis |
| Microscopic Features | Concentric “onion-skin” fibrosis around bile ducts | Florid duct lesion (granulomas) |
| Symptoms | Insidious onsetFatigue & pruritusEpisodic bacterial cholangitis secondary to biliary obstruction | Usually asymptomaticPruritus & fatigue 🡪 jaundice, melanosis, cholestasis 🡪 hepatocellular failure, portal HTN, ascites↑ incidence of osteoporosis |
| Investigations | AMA -ve↑ ALP (hallmark), ↑ bilirubin, ↑AST, pANCA (30-80%), ↑ IgMERCP/MRCP (narrowing and dilatations of ducts 🡪 “beaded” appearance of bile ducts)Liver biopsy shows fibrous, obliterative cholangitis | Anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA+)IgM↑ALP, GGT, bilirubin in later stages↑ lipidsLiver biopsy shows florid duct lesion (granulomas)Normal bile ducts on MRCP/ERCP |
| Treatment | Endoscopic sphincterotomy/ERCP + biliary stentAbx ± drainage of pusLiver transplant in advanced diseasePotential MRCP to monitor for cholangiocarcinoma (controversial) | UrsodiolCholestyramine (pruritis, ↑cholesterol)Ca2+/Vit D (low bone density)/bisphosphonateMonitor for thyroid diseaseLiver transplant in advanced disease |
| Prognosis | Unfavourable regardless of treatmentLong-term complications of cirrhosis and cholangiocarcinoma | Long-term complication of cirrhosis |
| Shared hepatic features | Autoimmune hepatitis, Cholestatic liver cirrhosis, pruritus, fatigue |

docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — cholelithiasis (gallstones) — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
- ![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img021.jpg)
DEFINITION: presence of gallstones in the gallbladder
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: 10-15% of population, M>F, ↑ in elderly
- PATHOGENESIS
- Bile is produced in pancreas and stored in gallbladder. Composition of bile is 92% water, 6% bile salts, 0.3% bilirubin and 1.7% fats (cholesterol, fatty acid, lecithin) and it aids in the digestion of lipids.
- CHOLESTEROL GALLSTONES: Formation dependent on cholesterol supersaturation of bile,  crystalisation-promoting factors within bile, and stasis of gall bladder (supersaturation of bile 🡪 cholesterol crystallisation 🡪 sludge🡪 stone)
- Risk Factors: 5Fs (fair, fat, forties, female- oestrogen , OCP, fertile- multiparity)
- BLACK PIGMENT GALLSTONES: Calcium bilirubinate + network of mucin glycoproteins interfaced with salts such as CaCO3/Ca3(PO4)2. Seen in  haemolytic conditions in which there is chronic ↑ bilirubin s e.g. cirrhosis, chronic haemolysis
- BROWN PIGMENT GALLSTONES: calcium bilirubinate + calcium salts of fatty acids; almost always found in bile stasis (strictures, dilation) and/or biliary infection
- CLINICAL PRESENTATION: asymptomatic (80%), biliary colic (10-25%), cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis (8-15%), cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis, gallstone ileus, empyema of gallbladder, liver abscess, gall bladder perforation with bile peritonitis
- HISTORY: Biliary colicky pain when gallstone transiently impacted in cystic duct (chronic RUQ dull pain exacerbated after fatty meal, radiates to R shoulder tip/scapula), N/V, potentialchest pain, nil peritoneal/systemic findings
- INVESTIGATIONS
- Bloods (to rule out complications)- FBC, EUC, LFT (↑GGT, ALP), pancreatic enzymes (?pancreatitis), INR/PT
- Urinalysis
- Abdominal U/S (inflammation, obstruction, localisation of stone):Gallbladder wall thickening >4mm, oedema (double-wall sign), sludge, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy’s sign
- Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP): non-invasive to visualise ampullary region, biliary and pancreatic anatomy
- Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP): can obtain biopsy sample (risk of pancreatitis 10%)
- HIDA Scan (less common but technetium-99 injected into vein and excreted into bile 🡪 visualisation of biliary tree occlusion)
- Percutanteous Transhepatic Cholangiography  (via hepatic parenchyma for proximal bile duct obstruction or when ERCP fails/unavailable; requires prophylactic ABx, contraindicated in coagulopathy/ascites/sepsis/lung disease)
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: PUD, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, acute pancreatitis, acute cholangitis
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT: only if symptomatic; analgesia, NBM, IVF, Abx (Cef/met), endoscopic sphincterotomy (free passage of common bile duct stones), Ursodeoxycholic acid (for cholesterol stones to ↓ cholesterol absorption, dissolve cholesterol stones for uncomplicated and infrequent biliary colic or those with ↑ surgical morbidity/mortality risk; sl

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — acute cholecystitis — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: Inflammation of the gallbladder
- AETIOLOGY: Gallstones (95%), infections, starvation, TPN
- RISK FACTORS: ↓ fibre, ↓ physical activity, DM, trauma
- PATHOGENESIS: Stasis of gallbladder 🡪 bile becomes trapped 🡪 irritation and increased pressure 🡪 inflammatory process and oedema 🡪 bacterial invasion 🡪 gallbladder wall becomes thickened with subserosal haemorrhage, pericholecystic fluid present 🡪 mucosa may show hyperaemia and patchy necrosis (loss of venous initially and then arterial) 🡪 5-10% develop ischemia and necrosis 🡪 perforation (less likely to perforate due to greater compliance and volume)
- HISTORY: RUQ pain (intense, prolonged > 6 hrs 🡪 radiates to R shoulder tip; post-prandial), fever, anorexia, N/V
- EXAMINATION
- Boas Sign- hyperaesthesia (↑ or altered sensitivity) below the R scapula can be a symptom in acute cholecystitis
- Murphy’s sign – inspire deeply while the examiner palpates the area of the gallbladder fossa just beneath the liver edges
- Other- palpable gallbladder, peritonism, ↑HR, febrile
- INVESTIGATIONS: FBC (↑WBC with left shift), ↑CRP, EUC, LFT, albumin, INR, amylase/lipase, U/S (thickened walls > 3 mm, pericolic fluid, CBD dilation > 6mm, shadow of stone, sonographic Murphy’s sign); HIDA scan (if U/S is inconclusive to show cystic duct obstruction); CT scan (less sensitive then U/S)
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: biliary colic, acute cholangitis, peptic ulcer, acute pancreatitis, appendicitis
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT:
- Conservative- analgesia (NSAIDs), IVF, electrolyte correction, NBM, antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole)
- Lap cholecystectomy- four small cuts 0.5-2.5 cms made in the abdomen; a telescope passed into one to see the abdomen and ports into the other cuts; CO2 is blown into abdomen to lift the abdominal wall from the liver, gallbladder, small bowel, stomach and other organs; forceps and scissors used to help remove gall bladder; metal clips to block ducts and arteries leading to gall bladder (which stay in body); gallbladder removed and CO2 allowed to escape following by closure with staples/stitches. Sometimes, contrast medium is injected and x-rays are taken of the bile duct
- RISKS: infection, shoulder pain, excess bleeding, perforation, air embolus, hernia, adhesions, lung collapse, heart attack/stroke, DVT, anaphylaxis to contrast/anaesthetic
- COMPLICATIONS: gangrenous cholecystitis, perforation of gallbladder

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — ascending cholangitis — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: ascending bacterial infection in association with partial or complete obstruction of the bile ducts
- AETIOLOGY: cholelithiasis, benign stasis, iatrogenic (during cholecystectomy)
- PATHOGENESIS: biliary obstruction and stasis🡪 increases intrabiliary pressure 🡪 increases permeability of ductules 🡪 permits translocation of bacteria into biliary tract; >90% of cases involve mixed growth of gram-negative (e.g. E.coli and Klebsiella) and gram-positive (e.g. Enterococcus)
- Mnemonic common bacteria in biliary tract KEEPS (Klebsiella, Enterococcus, E.Coli/Enterobacter, Proteus/Pseudomonas, Serratia)
- HISTORY
- Charcot’s triad – RUQ pain + fever + jaundice (usually the one missing)
- Reynold’s pentad – Charcot’s triad + confusion + hypotension
- N/V, abdominal distension, ileus, acholic stools, tea-coloured urine (↑direct bilirubin)
- INVESTIGATIONS: FBC (↑ WBC), LFTs (↑bilirubin, ↑ALP/GGT, potentially ↑AST/ALT), ↑CRP, U/S (dilated bile duct, common bile duct stones), blood culture, CT contrast (level + reason for obstruction, bile culture, removal of stones if needed, drainage of bile with catheter), ERCP
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: acute cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, acute diverticulitis, appendicitis, hepatic abscess, peptic ulcer disease
- TREATMENT: analgesia, NBM, IVF, IV ABx (empiric coverage for colonic bacteria), ± NGT, biliary decompression (ERCP + sphincterotomy with stone extraction and/or stent insertion), cholecystectomy (in all patients unless contraindicated)

docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — gallstone ileus — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
- PATHOGENESIS: ↑ inflammation causing a cholecystoenteric fistula (usually duodenal) 🡪 gallstone enters gut 🡪 impacts ileocecal valve 🡪 true bowel obstruction
- RIGLER’S TRIAD: pneumobilia, SBO, gallstone
- BOUVERET’S SYNDROME: gastric outlet/duodenal obstruction caused by a gallstone passing through cholecytogastric/ cholecystoduodenal fistula
- INVESTIGATIONS: AXR (pneumobilia, gallstone, air fluid levels, dilated small intestine), CT (biliary tract air, obstruction, gallstone)
- TREATMENT: fluid resus, NGT decompression, surgery (enterolithotomy + removal of stone), close fistula/manage expectantly, cholecystectomy not usually performed

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — carcinoma of the gall bladder — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
- RISK FACTORS: ↑ stones, age, female, polyps, chronic infection, abnormal pancreaticobilliary duct junction
- Majority adenocarcinoma
- SYMPTOMS: asymptomatic until late 🡪 RUQ pain, palpable RUQ mass, Courvoisier’s gallbladder, jaundice (50%), local extension to liver/stomach/duodenum, metastasis to liver/lung/bone
- INVESTIGATIONS
- U/S: mural thickening, calcifications, fixed mass
- EUS: staging, sampling bile for cytology
- Abd CT: polypoid mass, mural thickening, liver invasion, nodal involvement, distant metastases
- MRI/MRCP: malignant vs benign
- TREATMENT: open cholecystectomy to avoid tumour seeding of peritoneal cavity ± en bloc wedge resection of 2-5cm underlying liver ± dissection of hepatoduodenal lymph nodes
- PROGNOSIS: Poor 5 -year survival (10%) due to late detection

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.h: Gastroenterology Master Notes — Clinical Assessment & Investigation

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
**Cardinal symptoms and what they localise:**

| Symptom | Key discriminators |
|---|---|
| **Dysphagia** | Solids-then-liquids progressive = **mechanical** (stricture/cancer); solids **and** liquids from the start = **motility** (achalasia). Painful swallowing (odynophagia) = oesophagitis/candida. |
| **Dyspepsia** | Epigastric pain/burning; relation to meals (duodenal ulcer often *relieved* by food; gastric ulcer *worsened*). Screen for **ALARM** features. |
| **Abdominal pain** | Site (map to foregut/midgut/hindgut), character (colicky = obstruction/biliary; constant = inflammation/peritonism), radiation (epigastric → back = pancreatitis/AAA). |
| **Altered bowel habit** | New change >6 weeks in >50s = red flag; alternating = IBS/obstruction; nocturnal/weight loss = organic. |
| **Rectal bleeding** | Bright red on paper/coating stool = anorectal; mixed in/darker = higher; **melaena** (black tarry) = upper GI. |
| **Jaundice** | Pale stool + dark urine + itch = obstructive; painless = malignancy until proven otherwise (Courvoisier). |

**⚑ ALARM / red-flag symptoms** mandating **urgent upper GI endoscopy / 2-week-wait referral**: **A**naemia (iron-deficiency), **L**oss of weight, **A**norexia, **R**ecent onset/progressive symptoms, **M**elaena/haematemesis, **S**wallowing difficulty (dysphagia). Add **new dyspepsia in anyone ≥55** with weight loss, and any upper-abdominal mass. (NICE NG12.)

**Signs of chronic liver disease** (worth a systematic hand-to-abdomen sweep): palmar erythema, **Dupuytren's**, leuconychia, clubbing, **spider naevi** (>5, SVC distribution), gynaecomastia, **caput medusae**, splenomegaly, ascites, testicular atrophy. **Signs of decompensation:** jaundice, **asterixis** (flap) + encephalopathy, ascites, variceal bleeding, easy bruising (coagulopathy).

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.h: 3.2 Liver Function Tests and Their Interpretation
docs.text:
**First split every abnormal LFT into a *pattern*, not a list of numbers:**

| | **Hepatocellular** | **Cholestatic (obstructive)** |
|---|---|---|
| Dominant rise | **ALT/AST** (transaminases) | **ALP + γGT + bilirubin** |
| Meaning | Hepatocyte injury | Bile-flow obstruction (intra- or extra-hepatic) |
| Examples | Viral/alcoholic/autoimmune hepatitis, ischaemia, drugs, MASH | Gallstone, pancreatic/biliary cancer, PBC, PSC, drugs |

**Reading the enzymes:**
- **ALT** is more liver-specific than AST. **AST:ALT ratio >2** suggests **alcoholic** liver disease (and advanced fibrosis); **ALT > AST** is typical of viral hepatitis and MASLD.
- **Transaminases in the thousands** = a narrow differential: **ischaemia ("shock liver"), paracetamol/toxins, acute viral hepatitis** (± autoimmune).
- **Raised ALP** — is it liver or bone? Check **γGT**: **↑ALP + ↑γGT = hepatobiliary**; ↑ALP with **normal** γGT = **bone** (Paget's, mets, growth) or placenta (pregnancy).
- **Bilirubin** — see the pre-/intra-/post-hepatic split (Section 1.4).

**⚑ True tests of hepatic *function* (not just damage)** — these tell you how sick the liver actually is:
- **Albumin** (low = chronic synthetic failure, but also sepsis/nutrition) — long half-life.
- **Prothrombin time / INR** — the **most useful acute marker of synthetic function** (clotting factors have a short half-life, so PT/INR rises early in acute liver failure). *ALT/ALP tell you there is injury; INR and bilirubin tell you the liver is failing.*

**Non-invasive fibrosis assessment (⚑ replaces routine biopsy for staging in many settings):** simple scores (**FIB-4**, NAFLD fibrosis score), the **Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF)** blood test, and **transient elastography (FibroScan)**. A "**non-invasive liver screen**" for unexplained abnormal LFTs = viral serology (Hep B/C), autoantibodies + immunoglobulins (AIH, PBC), ferritin/transferrin saturation (haemochromatosis), caeruloplasmin (Wilson's, if <40y), α₁-antitrypsin, coeliac serology, lipids/glucose (MASLD), and an **ultrasound**.

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
**Endoscopy:**
- **OGD (gastroscopy)** — dyspepsia with ALARM features, dysphagia, haematemesis/melaena, surveillance (Barrett's, varices), biopsy (coeliac, *H. pylori*).
- **Colonoscopy** — the gold standard for colorectal assessment; investigation of altered bowel habit/rectal bleeding/iron-deficiency anaemia, IBD assessment, polyp/cancer diagnosis and removal, surveillance.
- **Flexible sigmoidoscopy** — left colon/rectum (e.g. acute UC where full colonoscopy risks perforation).
- **Capsule endoscopy** — obscure small-bowel bleeding/Crohn's (contraindicated if stricturing — risk of capsule retention).

**Imaging:**

| Modality | Best for |
|---|---|
| **Ultrasound** | First-line for gallstones, biliary dilatation, liver texture/ascites, portal flow |
| **CT** | Acute abdomen (obstruction, perforation, ischaemia, collections), cancer staging |
| **MRCP** | **Non-invasive** imaging of the biliary/pancreatic ducts (stones, strictures, PSC beading) |
| **ERCP** | **Therapeutic** biliary intervention (stone extraction, stenting, sphincterotomy) — not first-line diagnostic (risk of pancreatitis) |
| **EUS** | Staging oesophageal/pancreatic tumours; sampling; assessing CBD stones |
| **Erect CXR / AXR** | Free air under the diaphragm (perforation); dilated loops/obstruction |

*Discriminator: **MRCP looks, ERCP acts.** Use MRCP to diagnose, ERCP to treat.*

**Stool and serology (know the "one test" for each disease):**

| Test | Points to |
|---|---|
| **Faecal calprotectin** | **Organic bowel inflammation** — distinguishes **IBD from IBS** (raised in IBD, normal in IBS) |
| **Faecal immunochemical test (FIT)** | Occult blood — bowel-cancer **screening** and symptomatic triage |
| **Faecal elastase** (low) | **Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency** (chronic pancreatitis) |
| ***C. difficile* toxin/GDH** | Antibiotic-associated / pseudomembranous colitis |
| **Anti-tTG (IgA) + total IgA** | **Coeliac disease** (must be **on a gluten-containing diet**) |
| **Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA)** | **Primary biliary cholangitis** |
| **ASMA / anti-LKM1, ↑IgG** | **Autoimmune hepatitis** |
| **pANCA + MRCP beading (+ IBD)** | **Primary sclerosing cholangitis** |
| **Ferritin ↑, transferrin sat ↑** | **Haemochromatosis** |
| **Caeruloplasmin ↓** (<40y) | **Wilson's disease** |

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Solids-then-liquids progressive dysphagia | **Mechanical** (stricture/cancer) |
| Solids **and** liquids dysphagia from the outset | **Motility disorder** (achalasia) |
| ALARM features (upper GI) | Anaemia, Loss of weight, Anorexia, Recent/progressive, Melaena/haematemesis, Swallowing difficulty |
| Duodenal ulcer pain vs meals | **Relieved** by food (gastric ulcer worsened) |
| Hepatocellular LFT pattern | **↑↑ALT/AST** |
| Cholestatic LFT pattern | **↑ALP + ↑γGT + ↑bilirubin** |
| AST:ALT ratio **>2** | **Alcoholic** liver disease |
| Transaminases in the thousands | Ischaemia, paracetamol/toxin, acute viral hepatitis |
| ↑ALP, **normal** γGT | **Bone** (or placental) source |
| Best acute marker of synthetic function | **PT/INR** |
| Distinguishes IBD from IBS | **Faecal calprotectin** (↑ in IBD) |
| Low faecal elastase | **Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency** |
| "Looks vs acts" on the biliary tree | **MRCP diagnoses, ERCP treats** |
| Free air under diaphragm | **Perforation** (erect CXR) |
| Coeliac serology caveat | Must be tested **on gluten** (+ check total IgA) |

##### Sources
NICE NG12 (suspected cancer referral / ALARM features) and CG184 (dyspepsia); Kumar & Clark and Oxford Handbook (LFT interpretation, examination); BSG guidance (non-invasive liver screen, fibrosis assessment); Merck Manual Professional. Fibrosis-assessment and referral thresholds ⚑ cross-checked against current NICE/BSG guidance.

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — alcoholic liver disease — Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: liver damaged as a result of chronic, heavy alcohol ingestion
- PATHWAYS OF ALCOHOL METABOLISM
- EtOH 🡪 alcohol dehydrogenase 🡪 acetalydehyde 🡪 acetaldehyde dehydrogenase 🡪 acetate; Reduction of NAD to NADH (however when there is ↑NADH in relation to NAD this inhibits gluconeogenesis and increases fatty acid oxidation to promote fatty infiltration in the liver)
- Cytochrome P450 E21 pathway that enerates free radicals through oxidation of NADPH to NADP. Chronic alcohol use upregulates cytochrome P450 E21, thus producing more free radicals
- Via hepatic macrophages (Kupffer cells): Chronic EtOH exposure activates this third site of metabolism 🡪 TNF-α production 🡪 ROS in the mitochondria

![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img022.jpg)

- STAGES
- Fatty liver: abnormal lipid retention within hepatocytes due to shift from metabolism to catabolism that ↑ lipid globule size and displace hepatocytes; nil jaundice, mildly tender, hepatomegaly, mildly ↑ transaminases
- Alcoholic hepatitis (reversible): Inflammation of liver due to excessive EtOH 🡪 hepatocytes swell up with ↑ fat, water, protein and malllory filaments 🡪 block bile ducts + cholestasis 🡪 Kupffer cells become overloaded 🡪 neutrophils/macrophages migrate and trigger an inflammatory response 🡪 necrotic damage
- Alcoholic cirrhosis (irreversible): hepatic cell death, inflammation, nodular regeneration, scarring/fibrosis; deranged vascular perfusion,  ↓ function of new hepatocytes, green tint from bile stasis
- HISTORY: RUQ abdominal discomfort, weight loss (malnutrition), weight gain (ascites)
- ABDOMINAL EXAM reveals stigmata of chronic liver disease: finger clubbing, palmar erythaema, Dupuytren’s contracture, asterixis, signs of jaundice, venous collaterals, spider naevi, gynaecomastia, ascites and pitting oedema, hepatomegaly for fatty liver and hepatitis, but liver size is decreased with cirrhosis
- INVESTIGATIONS: CAGE, LFT (AST:ALT > 2:1, ↑GGT, ↑bilirubin, ↓albumin), FBC (↓Hb, ↑MCV, ↑WBC), U/S  for cirrhosis, CT for hepatosplenomegaly/varices/nodular texture/ascites, liver biopsy (swollen hepatocytes, Mallory bodies, neutrophils, fibrosis in speace of Disse), Hepatitis serology (Hep B surface antigen, anti-Hep B IgG, Hep X antibodies), fluid/stool chart, serial weights (ascites), copper studies (wilson’s), iron studies (haemochromatosis), INR to assess function
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, haemochromatosis, biliary obstruction, cholecystitis
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT

- Alcohol cessation –naltrexone for addiction, Valium for withdrawal, rehab, AA, Drug & EtOH referral, counselling
- Nutritional support –dietician referral, thiamine, B12, folate, correct electrolyte and glucose abnormalities
- Weight reduction; smoking cessation
- Cease drugs metabolised by liver and
- Prednisolone (in those with ↑INR and ↑bilirubin) and monitor INR (may need Vit K)
- Monitor GCS for Wernicke’s and assess renal function
- Repla

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatic Physiology
docs.h: Gastroenterology Master Notes — Gastrointestinal & Hepatic Physiology
docs.text: *The exam tests physiology as the substrate for the drugs and the diseases: acid secretion → PPIs and ulcers; bile/enterohepatic circulation → gallstones and B₁₂; bilirubin handling → the jaundice split; portal anatomy → varices. Learn the loop, and the clinical section reads off it.*

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatic Physiology
docs.text:
##### Gastric acid
The **parietal cell** (body/fundus) secretes H⁺ via the **H⁺/K⁺-ATPase ("proton pump")** — the final common step and the target of PPIs. Three stimulants converge on it, each with its own receptor:

| Stimulant | Source | Receptor on parietal cell | Blocked by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Histamine** | ECL cells | H₂ | H₂-antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) |
| **Gastrin** | G cells (antrum) | CCK₂/gastrin | — (indirectly, via ↓ECL histamine) |
| **Acetylcholine** | Vagus | M₃ (muscarinic) | (antimuscarinics) |

Histamine is the **dominant/amplifying** pathway — which is why H₂-blockers work and why gastrin and ACh act partly *through* ECL histamine release. **Somatostatin** (D cells) is the master brake: it inhibits gastrin, histamine and acid. **Prostaglandins** (mucosal) inhibit acid and stimulate the protective mucus/bicarbonate layer — hence **NSAIDs (↓prostaglandins) cause ulcers**.

**Three phases of secretion:** **cephalic** (sight/smell/taste → vagal, ~30%), **gastric** (distension + peptides → gastrin, ~60%), **intestinal** (small, then inhibitory as chyme enters duodenum). **Intrinsic factor**, also from the parietal cell, is essential for **B₁₂ absorption in the terminal ileum** — lose the parietal cells (autoimmune/pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy) and you lose both acid and B₁₂.

##### Pancreatic exocrine secretion
Two components, two hormones:
- **Acinar cells → digestive enzymes** (amylase, lipase, proteases as inactive zymogens — trypsinogen activated by enterokinase to trypsin, which activates the rest). Driven by **CCK** (from I cells, in response to fat and protein).
- **Ductal cells → bicarbonate-rich alkaline fluid** that neutralises gastric acid. Driven by **secretin** (from S cells, in response to duodenal acid).

*Memory hook: **S**ecretin from **S**-cells for **S**odium bicarbonate (the "wash"); **C**CK for **C**ontents/enzymes and gall-bladder **C**ontraction.*

##### Bile and the enterohepatic circulation
Hepatocytes secrete **bile** (bile salts, cholesterol, phospholipids, bilirubin) into canaliculi → the biliary tree → stored/concentrated in the gall bladder → released on **CCK** (gall-bladder contraction + sphincter of Oddi relaxation) after a fatty meal. **Bile salts emulsify fat** into micelles for absorption. ~95% of bile salts are **reabsorbed in the terminal ileum** and recycled (the **enterohepatic circulation**) — so **terminal ileal disease/resection (Crohn's) causes bile-salt malabsorption** (→ watery diarrhoea, gallstones, and fat/fat-soluble-vitamin malabsorption).

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatic Physiology
docs.text:
- **Swallowing:** oral (voluntary) → pharyngeal → oesophageal (peristalsis). The **lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS)** relaxes to let the bolus through; failure of LOS relaxation = **achalasia**; incompetent LOS = **GORD**.
- **Stomach:** receptive relaxation/**accommodation** (vagally mediated — lost after vagotomy), mixing (antral contractions), and controlled **emptying**. Liquids empty fast, solids slower.
- **Migrating motor complex (MMC):** the "housekeeper" — cyclical fasting-state sweeps that clear residue; driven by **motilin** (the target of erythromycin as a prokinetic).
- **Small/large bowel:** segmentation (mixing) and peristalsis (propulsion); the **gastrocolic reflex** (eating → colonic mass movement → urge to defecate). **Defecation** relies on the recto-anal inhibitory reflex and voluntary external anal sphincter (pudendal, S2–4).
- **The enteric nervous system** ("the gut's own brain": myenteric/Auerbach = motility; submucosal/Meissner = secretion) runs the gut semi-autonomously, modulated by the vagus and sympathetics. Loss of enteric ganglia = **Hirschsprung's** (aganglionic segment → functional obstruction).

**The gut hormones worth knowing:**

| Hormone | Source | Main action | Exam hook |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Gastrin** | G cells (antrum) | ↑Acid | ↑↑↑ in **Zollinger–Ellison** |
| **CCK** | I cells (duodenum) | Gall-bladder contraction, pancreatic enzymes, satiety | Fat/protein trigger |
| **Secretin** | S cells (duodenum) | Pancreatic/biliary **bicarbonate**, ↓acid | Acid trigger |
| **GIP** | K cells | ↑Insulin (incretin) | — |
| **GLP-1** | L cells (ileum) | ↑Insulin, ↓glucagon, ↓emptying, satiety | Basis of **GLP-1 agonists** |
| **Somatostatin** | D cells | Inhibits nearly everything | Octreotide (varices, VIPoma) |
| **Motilin** | M cells | MMC / gastric emptying | Erythromycin agonist |
| **Ghrelin** | Stomach (fundus) | **Hunger** ("ghrowling") | ↑ before meals |

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatic Physiology
docs.text:
- **Carbohydrate:** salivary/pancreatic amylase → oligosaccharides → brush-border disaccharidases (lactase, sucrase) → monosaccharides absorbed (SGLT1, GLUT). **Lactase deficiency → lactose intolerance** (osmotic diarrhoea, bloating).
- **Protein:** pepsin (stomach) + pancreatic proteases → amino acids/peptides absorbed.
- **Fat:** bile-salt emulsification + pancreatic lipase → micelles → absorbed → chylomicrons. Fat malabsorption → **steatorrhoea** (pale, greasy, floating, offensive stool) + deficiency of **fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K** (K → coagulopathy).

**Site of absorption (high yield):**

| Nutrient | Main site |
|---|---|
| Iron, folate, calcium | **Duodenum / proximal jejunum** |
| Most nutrients (carbs, protein, fat) | Jejunum |
| **Vitamin B₁₂ (with intrinsic factor), bile salts** | **Terminal ileum** |
| Water, electrolytes, short-chain fatty acids | Colon |

*Discriminator: **terminal ileal disease (Crohn's, resection) = B₁₂ deficiency + bile-salt diarrhoea + gallstones**; proximal small-bowel disease (coeliac) = iron/folate deficiency.*

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatic Physiology
docs.text:
The liver has a **dual blood supply** — ~75% from the **portal vein** (nutrient-rich, deoxygenated, draining the gut) and ~25% from the **hepatic artery** — mixing in the sinusoids. The functional acinus is zoned: **zone 1 (periportal)** is best oxygenated; **zone 3 (pericentral/centrilobular)** is most susceptible to **ischaemia** and to **paracetamol/toxic** injury (highest cytochrome P450 activity).

**Functions (a memory frame):** **Synthetic** (albumin, clotting factors — all except VIII, so a rising **INR/PT** is an early marker of failing synthesis), **Metabolic/detoxifying** (drugs; **ammonia → urea** — lost in liver failure → encephalopathy), **Storage** (glycogen, vitamins A/D/B₁₂, iron, copper), **Immune** (Kupffer cells), and **Excretory** (bilirubin, bile).

**Bilirubin metabolism — the basis of the jaundice split:**
1. Haem breakdown → **unconjugated (indirect)** bilirubin — fat-soluble, albumin-bound, **not water-soluble → not in urine**.
2. Hepatocyte **conjugation** by UGT1A1 → **conjugated (direct)** bilirubin — water-soluble.
3. Excreted in bile → gut bacteria → **urobilinogen** (some reabsorbed) and **stercobilin** (brown stool).

| Type | Bilirubin raised | Urine | Stool | Classic causes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Pre-hepatic** | Unconjugated | Normal (no bilirubin; ↑urobilinogen) | Normal | Haemolysis, **Gilbert's** |
| **Hepatic** | Both | Dark (bilirubin +) | Normal/pale | Hepatitis, cirrhosis |
| **Post-hepatic (obstructive)** | Conjugated | **Dark** (bilirubin +) | **Pale** | Gallstone, pancreatic Ca, stricture |

*Discriminator: **pale stool + dark urine + itch = obstructive (conjugated)**; unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with otherwise normal LFTs and no bilirubinuria = **Gilbert's or haemolysis**.*

---

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatic Physiology
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Final step of gastric acid secretion (drug target) | **H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump)** |
| Dominant/amplifying acid stimulant | **Histamine** (via H₂ on ECL/parietal) |
| Master inhibitor of acid | **Somatostatin** |
| Why NSAIDs cause ulcers | ↓Prostaglandins → ↓mucus/bicarbonate barrier |
| Hormone driving pancreatic **bicarbonate** | **Secretin** (acid trigger) |
| Hormone driving gall-bladder contraction + enzymes | **CCK** (fat/protein trigger) |
| Where B₁₂ + bile salts are absorbed | **Terminal ileum** |
| Where iron + folate are absorbed | Duodenum / proximal jejunum |
| Hunger hormone | **Ghrelin** |
| Incretin behind GLP-1 agonists | **GLP-1** (L cells) |
| Liver zone hit by paracetamol/ischaemia | **Zone 3 (pericentral)** |
| Earliest marker of failing hepatic **synthesis** | **↑INR/PT** (short-half-life factors) |
| Clotting factor NOT made by the liver | **Factor VIII** |
| Unconjugated bilirubin in urine? | **No** (fat-soluble) — so bilirubinuria = conjugated |
| Pale stool + dark urine + itch | **Obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice** |

##### Sources
Guyton & Hall *Textbook of Medical Physiology* and Ganong (secretion, motility, gut hormones, absorption, bilirubin); Kumar & Clark *Clinical Medicine* (clinical correlation); Robbins & Cotran (hepatic zonation, injury patterns). Stable physiology — not web-searched.

docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — GASTROINTESTINAL STROMAL TUMOUR — Gastrointestinal & Hepatic Physiology
docs.text:
- Most common mesenchymal neoplasm of GI tract
- Derived from interstitial cells of Cajal (Auerbach’s plexus 🡪 autonomous pacemaker function 🡪 peristalsis)
- RISK FACTORS/AETIOLOGY: tyrosine kinase mutations (75-80%), Type IA neurofibromatosis, Carney’s triad
- Most common in stomach (50%), proximal SI (25%) but can occur anywhere along GI tract
- SIGNS/SYMPTOMS: vague abdominal mass, feeling of abdominal fullness with secondary bleeding or anaemia
- Often incidental finding on CT, laparotomy, endoscopy
- TREATMENT: Surgical resection (resection > 2cm, endoscopy <2cm), localised GIST (surgical resection, lymphadenectomy, adjuvant chemo with Imatinib), advanced disease (palliative intent chemo Imatinib, metastectomy)
- PROGNOSIS: Metastatic potential depends on tumour size (>10cm), mitotic activity (>5 figures), nuclear pleomorphism, location (extra-gastric location); metastases to liver, omentum, peritoneum, nodal

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.h: Gastroenterology Master Notes — Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.text: *Written as prose + tables (paired with the anatomy SVG sheet). Anatomy earns marks in three predictable places: referred/localising pain by embryological origin, the arterial watershed zones behind ischaemic bowel, and the **portosystemic anastomoses** behind varices.*

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.h: 2.1 The gut tube and its embryological blood supply
docs.text:
The gut develops as three regions, each with its **own artery** and **own referred-pain level** — this is why abdominal pain localises the way it does:

| Region | Extent | Artery | Referred (visceral) pain |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Foregut** | Mouth → mid-2nd part of duodenum (+ liver, gall bladder, pancreas, spleen) | **Coeliac trunk** (T12) | **Epigastric** |
| **Midgut** | Mid-duodenum → proximal 2/3 transverse colon | **SMA** (L1) | **Periumbilical** |
| **Hindgut** | Distal 1/3 transverse colon → upper rectum | **IMA** (L3) | **Suprapubic/hypogastric** |

*Classic application: **appendicitis** — early **periumbilical** pain (midgut visceral) that later **localises to the right iliac fossa (McBurney's point)** once the parietal peritoneum is irritated (somatic).* Foregut acid/ulcer pain is **epigastric**.

**Watershed zones** (between two arterial territories, vulnerable to ischaemia): the **splenic flexure** (SMA/IMA — "Griffiths' point") and the **rectosigmoid junction** (IMA/internal iliac — "Sudeck's point"). Ischaemic colitis classically hits the **splenic flexure**.

**Peritoneum:** the **peritoneal cavity** (potential space) with intraperitoneal organs (stomach, most small bowel, transverse & sigmoid colon, spleen) vs **retroperitoneal** ones. *Memory hook for retroperitoneal — **"SAD PUCKER"**: Suprarenal glands, Aorta/IVC, Duodenum (2nd–4th parts), Pancreas (except tail), Ureters, Colon (ascending/descending), Kidneys, (o)Esophagus, Rectum.* The **lesser sac** communicates with the greater sac through the **epiploic (omental) foramen of Winslow**.

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.text:
- **Oesophagus** (~25 cm): three **constrictions** where things lodge/strictures form — cricopharyngeus, aortic arch/left main bronchus, diaphragmatic hiatus. Upper third **striated** muscle, lower third **smooth**. The **Z-line (squamocolumnar junction)** is where oesophageal squamous meets gastric columnar epithelium — the site of **Barrett's** metaplasia. The lower oesophagus drains partly into the **portal system** (left gastric vein) → **oesophageal varices**.
- **Stomach:** cardia, fundus, body, antrum, pylorus. **Gastric gland cell types:** parietal (acid + IF), chief (pepsinogen), G cells (gastrin, antrum), ECL (histamine), D cells (somatostatin), mucous/foveolar (mucus).
- **Duodenum** (C-shaped, mostly retroperitoneal): four parts wrapping the pancreatic head. The **ampulla of Vater** (2nd part) is where the **common bile duct + main pancreatic duct** enter, guarded by the **sphincter of Oddi**. The **duodenojejunal flexure** is fixed at the **ligament of Treitz** — the anatomical **upper/lower GI-bleed boundary** (bleeding proximal to it = "upper").

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.h: 2.3 Small bowel, large bowel and anorectum
docs.text:
| Feature | Jejunum | Ileum |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Upper/left | Lower/right (→ terminal ileum at caecum) |
| Wall/lumen | Thicker wall, wider lumen | Thinner, narrower |
| Plicae circulares | Tall, frequent | Sparse |
| Vasa recta / arcades | Long vasa recta, few arcades | Short vasa recta, many arcades |
| Lymphoid tissue | Less | **Peyer's patches** (→ typhoid, terminal-ileal Crohn's) |

The **large bowel** is recognised by **taeniae coli**, **haustra**, and **appendices epiploicae**. The **appendix** arises from the caecum; the taeniae converge on its base (surgical landmark). **McBurney's point** = 1/3 along a line from the ASIS to the umbilicus.

**Anal canal — the dentate (pectinate) line is a watershed**, and everything about it splits above/below:

| | Above dentate line | Below dentate line |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Endoderm (hindgut) | Ectoderm |
| Epithelium | Columnar | Squamous |
| Sensation | **Insensate** (autonomic) | **Somatic (very painful)** — pudendal |
| Venous drainage | Portal (superior rectal) | Systemic (inferior rectal) |
| Cancer type | Adenocarcinoma | Squamous cell carcinoma |

*Application: internal haemorrhoids (above) are **painless** and bleed; an anal fissure/external thrombosed pile (below) is **exquisitely painful**. The rectum is another **portosystemic anastomosis** → rectal varices (not the same as haemorrhoids).*

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.text:
- **Liver:** functionally divided by the portal/hepatic-vein anatomy into **8 Couinaud segments** (each with its own inflow/outflow — the basis of segmental resection). The **porta hepatis** transmits the **portal triad**: portal vein (posterior), hepatic artery (left), common bile duct (right — "**ducts to the right**").
- **Biliary tree:** canaliculi → interlobular ducts → right & left hepatic ducts → **common hepatic duct** → joined by the **cystic duct** → **common bile duct (CBD)** → through the pancreatic head → ampulla of Vater. **Calot's (cystohepatic) triangle** — bordered by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior liver edge — contains the **cystic artery**; it is the key dissection landmark in cholecystectomy.
- **Pancreas** (retroperitoneal, except the tail): head (+ uncinate) cradled in the duodenal C, neck, body, tail (→ splenic hilum). Main duct (Wirsung) joins the CBD at the ampulla. Its intimate posterior relations — CBD, portal/SMA vessels, duodenum — explain why **pancreatic head cancer causes painless obstructive jaundice** and why the disease presents late.

**Portosystemic anastomoses — the four sites and their varices (very high yield):**

| Site | Portal vein tributary | Systemic vein | Clinical result of portal hypertension |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lower oesophagus** | Left gastric | Azygos | **Oesophageal varices** (the dangerous ones) |
| **Umbilicus** | Paraumbilical | Epigastric | **Caput medusae** |
| **Rectum** | Superior rectal | Middle/inferior rectal | **Rectal varices** |
| **Retroperitoneal/bare area** | Colic, splenic | Retroperitoneal | (silent) |

---

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Foregut artery + pain location | **Coeliac trunk**; epigastric |
| Midgut artery + pain location | **SMA**; periumbilical |
| Hindgut artery + pain location | **IMA**; suprapubic |
| Why appendicitis pain "moves" | Periumbilical (visceral midgut) → RIF (somatic peritoneal) |
| Colonic ischaemia watershed | **Splenic flexure** (SMA/IMA, Griffiths' point) |
| Retroperitoneal organs mnemonic | **SAD PUCKER** |
| Upper vs lower GI-bleed anatomical boundary | **Ligament of Treitz** (DJ flexure) |
| Site of Barrett's metaplasia | **Z-line** (squamocolumnar junction) |
| Painful vs painless anal lesions | Below dentate = painful (somatic); above = painless |
| Cancer type below dentate line | **Squamous cell** (above = adenocarcinoma) |
| Portal triad "duct" position | CBD to the **right** |
| Contents/landmark of Calot's triangle | **Cystic artery** (cholecystectomy landmark) |
| Why pancreatic head cancer → painless jaundice | Head compresses the CBD; presents late |
| Most dangerous portosystemic varices | **Oesophageal** (left gastric ↔ azygos) |

##### Sources
Gray's Anatomy / Last's Anatomy and Moore's *Clinically Oriented Anatomy* (gut rotation, arterial supply, peritoneum, anal canal, biliary/pancreatic relations); Kumar & Clark (portosystemic anastomoses, clinical correlation). Stable anatomy — not web-searched.

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — Gastroesophageal Varices — Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: dilated portosystemic collaterals, usually in the lower 1/3 of the oesophagus. Usually 30% of cirrhotic patients have varices and it accounts for 10-30% of all cases of upper GI bleeding.
- PATHOPHYSIOLOGY : Intrahepatic vascular resistance (due to deranged hepatic vascular architecture) and splanchnic blood flow become increased in cirrhosis 🡪 portal hypertension 🡪 portosystemic collaterals 🡪 exacerbated by decreased albumin due to functional loss of liver in cirrhosis causing imbalance in osmotic pressures 🡪 tensions become too great and these varices rupture 🡪 oesophageal bleed
- CLINICAL PRESENTATION: massive hematemesis, EtOH abuse, portal HTN, ascites, vomiting
- INVESTIGATIONS: FBC, EUC, coagulation studies, Fe studies, group and hold, LFTs
- MANAGEMENT
- Acute Treatment: haemodynamic stability (IVF, blood transfusion), somatostatin-ocreotide (↓vasodilatory hormones 🡪 splanchnic vasoconstriction and ↓ portal inflow), Abx (third gen e.g. cephalosporin), endoscopic variceal ligation (adrenaline injection, banding, diathermy), PPI, stop NSAIDS/anticoags
- Chronic Treatment: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) may be beneficial to ↓ portal HTN

![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img003.jpg)

stomach and small intestine

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — anal fissure — Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: split/tear in the anal mucosa or anal canal
- CLASSIFICATION: acute (spontaneously heal after 1/2 weeks), chronic (persisting for longer than 6 weeks, often associated with indurated edges, skin tag, visible anal spincter fibres at base)
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: often young adults aged 15 – 40, M=F
- AETIOLOGY: passage of hard stool, nitric oxide synthase deficiency, chronic constipation, excessive wiping, inflammation, Crohn’s disease, anal injury, pregnancy, rectal cancer, opiate analgesia
- PATHOGENESIS: 90% posterior midline of anal canal (poor circulation); other 10% in anterior midline; circulation further reduced by the spasm of the internal anal sphincter which results in insufficient blood supply (🡪 ischemia) to heal the split in the skin. Patient then avoids defaecation in fear experiencing the pain 🡪  formation of harder stools which tears the anoderm at the next time of defaecation 🡪 self-perpetuating cycle
- HISTORY: pain/tearing sensation on defecation, fresh blood on stool/paper, anal spasm
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: constipation, sarcoidosis (abnormal nodules), Crohn’s disease, anal carcinoma
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT: ↑ fibre, ↓ fluid intake, analgesia, stool softeners, GTN (prevents sphincter spasm, increases blood flow and promotes healing), surgical sphincterectomy/botulinum toxin


---

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — haemorrhoids — Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.text:
- ![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img015.jpg)
DEFINITION: vascular structures in the anal canal which become problematic when swollen/inflamed
- Internal – superior haemorrhoidal veins, above dentate line, portal circulation
- External – inferior haemorrhoidal veins, below dentate line, systemic circulation
- AETIOLOGY: ↑ intra-abdominal pressure (chronic constripation, pregnancy, obesity, portal HTN, heavy lifting)
- PATHOGENESIS: normal anatomical and functional components of the anal canal and pathological only when they cause symptoms. Increase in pressure 🡪 decreases venous return 🡪 engorgement of vascular cushions 🡪 rectal bleeding when epithelial lining torn
- HISTORY
- Internal haemorrhoids- painless rectal bleeding, rectal fullness/discomfort, mucous discharge, engorged vascular cushions usually at 3,7, 11 o’clock positions in lithotomy position1st degree: bleed but do not prolapse through the anus
- 2nd degree: bleed, prolapse with straining, spontaneous reduction
- 3rd degree: bleed, prolapse, requires manual reduction
- 4th degree: bleed, permanently prolapsed, cannot be manually reduced
- External haemorrhoids- severe perianal pain in thrombosed haemorrhoids, perianal massDilated venules (mildly symptomatic) vs. thrombosed haemorrhoids (v painful)

- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: anal fissure, rectal prolapse
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT: avoid straining, ↑ fibre, topical corticosteroids, stool softeners, topical steroids, surgical (rubber band ligation/sclerotherapy, haemorrhoidectomy in severe disease)
- COMPLICATIONS: anaemia, thrombosis (acute perianal pain and appearance of a tender nodule adjacent to the anal canal; resolves itself within a few weeks but may leave perianal skin tag)

docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — anal neoplasm — Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.text:
SCC OF ANAL CANAL (ABOVE DENTATE LINE)

- Most common (75%)
- HPV infection 🡪 ↑ risk for anal squamous intraepithelial lesion (high grade and low grade)
- Clinical features: anal bleeding, pain, mass, ulceration, pruritis, 25% asymptomatic
- Treatment: chemo, radio, surgery
- Prognosis: 80% 5-yr survival

MALIGNANT MELANOMA OF ANAL CANAL

- 3rd most common site for primary malignant melanoma after skin, eyes
- Aggressive, distant metastases
- Treatment: wide excision or APR ± chemoradiation
- Prognosis:<5%5yrsurvival

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — ANAL FISTULA — Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.text:
- ![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img017.jpg)
DEFINITION: abnormal communication between the epithelialized surface of the anal canal and the perianal skin
- AETIOLOGY: post-operative, trauma, anal fissure, malignancy, radiation proctitis
- PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Originate from anal glands (b/ww internal and external anal sphincter and drain into anal canal)🡪 glands become blocked 🡪 build-up of contents in tunnel 🡪 abscess
- SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS: pain, bloody/purulent discharged, pruritis ani, systemic Sx in infection
- DIAGNOSIS: generally clinical (opening of fistula, painful, redness, induration, discharge), but can use anoscopy, probing (to find both openings), fistulogram, proctoscopy, sigmoidoscopy
- TREATMENTIdentificationInternal opening (Goodsall’s Rule)- fistulas originating anterior to a transverse line through the anus will have a straight course and exit anteriorly, whereas those originating posterior to the transverse line will begin in the midline and have a curved tract
- Fistula tract- proving/fistulography under anaesthesia

- SurgeryFistulotomy: unroof tract from external to internal opening, drainage, heal by secondary intention
- Low-lying fistula (no external sphincter involvement( 🡪 primary fistulotomy
- High-lying fistula (involves external sphincter)🡪 stages fistulotomy with Seton suture placed through tract to promote drainage, fibrosis, ↓ incontinence, delineates anatomy and to spare muscle cutting.

- Post-operative: sitz baths, irrigation, packing to ensure healing proceeds from inside to outside

- COMPLICATIONS: recurrence, fecal incontinence (rare)

docs.title: Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — portal hypertension — Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Anatomy
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: HTN in the hepatic portal system, made up of the portal vein and its branches that drain from most of the intestine to the liver; defined as a hepatic venous pressure gradient > 5 mmHg
- PATHOPHYSIOLOGY (PRESSURE= FLOW X RESISTANCE): pre-sinusoidal (portal vein thrombosis), sinusoidal (cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis), post-sinusoidal (RHF, hepatic vein thrombosis, constrictive pericarditis)
- COMPLICATIONS: GI bleeding (varices), ascites, encephalopathy, thrombocytopenia, renal dysfunction, sepsis
- TREATMENT: B- blockers (↓ bleeding from varicies), nitrates (vasodilator), TIPS (↓ portal venous pressure and complications such as variceal bleeding)

docs.title: GI & Hepatic Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.h: Gastroenterology Master Notes — GI & Hepatic Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
*The consolidated drug section. Organised by target; the discriminators are the mechanism, the classic adverse effect, and the exam "trap."*

##### 9.1 Acid suppression and gut motility drugs

**⚑ Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs — omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole):** irreversibly block the **H⁺/K⁺-ATPase**; first-line for GORD, peptic ulcers, *H. pylori* regimens, and NSAID gastroprotection. **Long-term harms to know:** hypomagnesaemia, **B₁₂/iron malabsorption**, increased **fracture** risk, **C. difficile** and enteric infection, **microscopic colitis**, hyponatraemia, and masking of gastric cancer symptoms. **Deprescribe/review long-term PPIs** where no ongoing indication (⚑ — over-prescription is a real exam/QI theme).

**H₂-receptor antagonists (famotidine):** block histamine H₂ on the parietal cell — weaker acid suppression. *(Ranitidine was withdrawn over NDMA contamination — don't quote it as first-line. ⚑)*

**Antacids/alginates** (Gaviscon) — symptomatic reflux relief.

**Prokinetics:** **metoclopramide** (D₂ antagonist — **extrapyramidal side effects**, avoid in young/Parkinson's), **domperidone** (D₂, doesn't cross BBB but **QT prolongation**), **erythromycin** (motilin agonist).

**Antiemetics — by receptor target (high yield):**

| Drug | Target | Best for | Watch |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ondansetron** | 5-HT₃ antagonist | Chemo, post-op | Constipation, **QT** |
| **Metoclopramide/domperidone** | D₂ antagonist | Gastric stasis, GI causes | EPSEs / QT |
| **Cyclizine** | H₁ antihistamine | Motion, vestibular, mechanical | Antimuscarinic |
| **Hyoscine** | Antimuscarinic | Motion sickness, secretions | Dry mouth |
| **Aprepitant** | NK₁ antagonist | Chemo (delayed) | — |

**Laxatives:** bulk (ispaghula), osmotic (**lactulose, macrogol**), stimulant (senna, bisacodyl), softeners. **Antidiarrhoeals:** **loperamide** (avoid in acute infective/inflammatory colitis — precipitates megacolon). **Antispasmodics:** mebeverine, hyoscine (IBS).

##### 9.2 IBD, biologic and immunomodulator therapy

- **5-ASAs (mesalazine, sulfasalazine):** topical anti-inflammatory for **UC** (induction + maintenance); sulfasalazine can cause reversible **oligospermia**, rash.
- **Corticosteroids:** flares only (not maintenance); **budesonide** (high first-pass metabolism → fewer systemic effects) for ileocaecal Crohn's/microscopic colitis.
- **Thiopurines (azathioprine, mercaptopurine):** steroid-sparing maintenance — **check TPMT activity first** (low TPMT → myelosuppression); monitor FBC/LFTs; risk of pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, lymphoma/skin cancer.
- **Methotrexate:** Crohn's maintenance; folate, teratogenic, hepatotoxic, pneumonitis.
- **⚑ Biologics & small molecules (the modern step-up):** **anti-TNF** (infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab), **anti-integrin** (vedolizumab — gut-selective), **anti-IL-12/23** (ustekinumab) and **anti-IL-23** (risankizumab, mirikizumab), **JAK inhibitors** (tofacitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib), **S1P modulators** (ozanimod

docs.text:
*Synthesis only — no new facts; every discriminator here traces back to the section notes. This is the **source of truth** for the Section 10 "Key Differentials Quick-Reference" (that section is a view of this document). Organised three ways: **A** by presenting syndrome, **B** signature lookup tables, **C** confusable pairs. British/Australian spelling.*

---

##### Part A — By Presenting Syndrome

###### A1. Dysphagia
| If you also see… | Think | Clincher |
|---|---|---|
| Progressive **solids → liquids** + weight loss | **Oesophageal cancer / stricture** | OGD + biopsy |
| **Solids and liquids together** from the start | **Achalasia / motility** | Barium "bird's-beak", manometry |
| Atopic young adult, food bolus stuck | **Eosinophilic oesophagitis** | ≥15 eosinophils/hpf |
| Iron-deficiency anaemia + web | **Plummer–Vinson** | — |
| Regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, neck lump | **Pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's)** | Barium (don't blind-scope) |

###### A2. Dyspepsia / epigastric pain
- **Pain relieved by food** → **duodenal ulcer**; **worse with food + weight loss** → **gastric ulcer** (biopsy — could be cancer).
- **ALARM features** (anaemia, weight loss, dysphagia, melaena, ≥55 new) → **urgent OGD**.
- Radiating to the **back** → pancreatitis (lipase) or AAA. Epigastric + cardiac risk → exclude **MI**.

###### A3. Right-upper-quadrant pain
| Clue | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| Post-fatty-meal pain <6 h, no fever | **Biliary colic** |
| Constant pain + fever + **Murphy's sign** | **Acute cholecystitis** |
| Pain + fever + **jaundice** (Charcot's triad) | **Ascending cholangitis** |
| + hypotension + confusion (Reynolds' pentad) | **Severe cholangitis** → urgent ERCP |
| RUQ pain + deranged transaminases | **Hepatitis** |
| RUQ + right-shoulder tip, sexually active woman | **Fitz-Hugh–Curtis** (perihepatitis) |

###### A4. Jaundice
- **Pale stool + dark urine + itch** = **obstructive (post-hepatic)** → US then MRCP/ERCP.
- **Painless** obstructive jaundice + palpable gallbladder (**Courvoisier**) = **pancreatic/biliary malignancy**.
- Jaundice + **AST:ALT >2** = alcohol; + thousands of transaminases = ischaemia/paracetamol/acute viral.
- Isolated **unconjugated** with normal LFTs, on fasting = **Gilbert's**; with anaemia/↑LDH/↓haptoglobin = **haemolysis**.

###### A5. GI bleeding
| Clue | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| **Melaena + raised urea** | **Upper GI bleed** (ulcer/varices) |
| Retching/vomiting **then** haematemesis | **Mallory–Weiss** |
| Chronic liver disease + massive haematemesis | **Variceal bleed** (terlipressin + antibiotics) |
| Painless large-volume fresh PR blood, elderly | **Diverticular** / angiodysplasia |
| Altered habit + weight loss + PR blood | **Colorectal cancer** |
| Bloody diarrhoea + pain | **Colitis** (IBD/infective/ischaemic) |
| Bright red on paper only | **Haemorrhoids / fissure** |

###### A6. Chronic diarrhoea
- **Bloody + urgency + systemic** → **IBD** (calprotectin ↑).
- **Steatorrhoea + weight loss** → malabso
