docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — crohn’s disease — GI & Hepatic Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: Chronic transmural GIT inflammation that may involve the entire GIT from mouth to perianal area
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: Bimodal distribution (15-40 years, 60-80 years), M=F, ↑ incidence in Caucasians and Ashkenazi Jews
- PATHOGENESIS: Current theory involves inappropriate mucosal immune response to commensal bacteria in the gut lumen in a genetically susceptible host that might have been exposed to environmental triggers. Initially inflammatory infiltrate around intestinal crypts 🡪 ulceration of superficial mucosa 🡪 progresses to involve deeper layers 🡪 thickens the bowel wall 🡪 scarring, luminal narrowing, stricture formation 🡪 obstruction + ↓absorption.
- Most common location is ileum and ascending colon.
- VIENNA CLASSIFICATION OF CD

![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img012.jpg)

- RISK FACTORS: Caucasian, age, FHx, smoking, OCP, ↑refined sugar
- HISTORYCharacteristic triad – abdominal pain (cramping/constant usually in RLQ/peri-umbilical regions; exacerbated by eating), diarrhoea (possible constipation/obstipation in obstruction), weight loss
- Fevers, fatigue, haematochezia (microscopic/gross), oral (ulcers, mouth/gum pain), oesophageal (dysphagia, odynophagia), gastroduodenal (upper abd pain, gastric outlet obstruction), perianal (pain, skin tags, anal fissures, abscesses)

- INVESTIGATIONS
- FBC (anaemia, leucocytosis), iron studies (to demonstrate consistency with iron deficiency), serum B12, serum folate, CMP (in severe/chronic disease 🡪 ↓albumin, ↓cholesterol, ↓ Ca2+), CRP and ESR, stool testing, AXR (bowel wall thickening, bowel/colonic dilatation, calcification, sacroiliitis, abscess), CT abdomen (localisation of disease, fistula, abscess, extra-mural complications), MRI abdomen/pelvis (when IV contrast contraindicated)
- Colonoscopy/gastroscopy: exploration, tissue biopsy, skip lesions (focal ulceration adjacent to normal mucosa), polypoid mucosal changes (cobblestone appearance)
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: UC, IBS, CRC, infectious colitis (diarrhoea, acute Sx, infections with Shigella/ Salmonella/  Campylobacter/ E.Coli/ C.Diff/ CMV)
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT
- Lifestyle: smoking cessation, fluids in acute exacerbations, enteral diet for symptomatic management, supplementation (Vit D, Ca2+, Mg2+, Zn, Fe, B12)
- PharmacologyFor mild disease: 5-ASA compounds (aminosalicylates) e.g. sulfazaline/mesalamine (↑ effective in mild UC)
- For moderate disease: immunomodulators e.g. 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP, azathioprine, and methotrexate (less often) often used to maintain remission and as steroid-sparing agents; may require >3 mo for beneficial effect
- For severe disease: biologics (anti-TNF agents) e.g. Infliximab IV or adalimumab SC and proven for effective treatment of fistulae and medically refractory CD
- For flares: steroids e.g. prednisolone, methylprednisolone or IV hydrocortisone + antibiotics (metronidazole/ ciprofloxacin)

- Surgery: generally reserved for medically refractory disease and complicati

docs.h: Gastroenterology Master Notes — GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen

docs.title: GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.text:
**Upper GI bleed = bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz** → **haematemesis** (fresh red or "coffee-ground") and/or **melaena** (black, tarry, offensive — digested blood; ~50 mL is enough). Brisk upper bleeding can present as fresh PR blood (haematochezia) with haemodynamic compromise.

**Causes (know the top few):**

| Cause | Clue |
|---|---|
| **Peptic ulcer** (commonest) | NSAID/*H. pylori*; posterior duodenal → gastroduodenal artery |
| **Oesophageal/gastric varices** | Chronic liver disease/portal hypertension; often massive |
| **Mallory–Weiss tear** | **Vomiting/retching → then haematemesis** (e.g. after alcohol) |
| **Oesophagitis/gastritis** | Reflux, alcohol, drugs |
| **Malignancy** | Weight loss, dyspepsia |
| **Dieulafoy lesion / angiodysplasia** | Recurrent obscure bleeding |

**Immediate management (ABCDE + resuscitate first, scope second):**
1. **A–B–C**, two large-bore cannulae, bloods incl. **crossmatch**, **group & save**, U&E (**urea disproportionately raised** — digested blood protein), LFTs, clotting, VBG/lactate.
2. **Fluid resuscitation**; **⚑ restrictive red-cell transfusion — transfuse at Hb <70 g/L, target 70–90 g/L** (a restrictive strategy improves survival — Villanueva; over-transfusion worsens variceal bleeding). Correct coagulopathy/platelets; reverse anticoagulation as indicated.
3. **Risk-score:**
   - **Glasgow–Blatchford score (GBS)** — used **pre-endoscopy** to decide admission; **a score of 0–1 may allow safe outpatient management**. Based on urea, Hb, systolic BP, pulse, melaena, syncope, hepatic/cardiac disease.
   - **Rockall score** — **post-endoscopy**, predicts rebleeding/mortality (age, shock, comorbidity, diagnosis, stigmata of recent haemorrhage).
4. **Endoscopy within 24 h** (immediately after resuscitation if unstable/variceal).

**Non-variceal (e.g. peptic ulcer):** **endoscopic haemostasis** — two modalities (adrenaline injection **plus** a second: clips/thermal/haemospray). **⚑ Give PPI *after* endoscopic therapy** for high-risk stigmata (not routinely before). Test and treat *H. pylori*; stop NSAIDs.

**Variceal bleed (a distinct pathway — high yield):**
- **Terlipressin** (splanchnic vasoconstrictor) **+ prophylactic antibiotics** (e.g. ceftriaxone — reduces mortality) started **immediately**, even before endoscopy.
- **Endoscopic band ligation** (oesophageal); **injection/glue** or **balloon tamponade (Sengstaken–Blakemore)** as a bridge for uncontrolled bleeding; **TIPS** (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) for refractory bleeding.
- **Secondary prevention:** **non-selective β-blocker (propranolol/carvedilol)** + repeat banding.

docs.title: GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.text:
**Bleeding distal to the ligament of Treitz** → usually **fresh/dark red PR blood** (haematochezia). **Causes by likelihood/age:**

| Age / pattern | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Older, painless, large-volume | **Diverticular disease** (commonest), **angiodysplasia** |
| Older, altered habit/weight loss | **Colorectal cancer** |
| Any age, bloody diarrhoea + pain | **Colitis** (IBD, infective, ischaemic) |
| Bright red on paper/around stool | **Haemorrhoids / anal fissure** |
| Young | Meckel's diverticulum, IBD, polyps |

**Approach:** resuscitate as above; **exclude a brisk upper GI source** (a bleeding duodenal ulcer can mimic lower bleeding — consider OGD/NG aspirate, and note the **raised urea** of an upper bleed). Investigate with **colonoscopy** (once stable/prepped); **CT angiography** for active brisk bleeding (can go to embolisation). Most lower GI bleeds settle spontaneously.

*Discriminator: **melaena + raised urea = upper**; fresh red PR blood with normal urea = lower. **Massive haematochezia with shock can still be a fast upper bleed** — don't be caught out.*

docs.title: GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.h: 6.3 The acute abdomen — obstruction, perforation, ischaemia
docs.text:
**Bowel obstruction:**

| | **Small-bowel obstruction** | **Large-bowel obstruction** |
|---|---|---|
| Commonest causes | **Adhesions** (previous surgery), **hernias** | **Colorectal cancer**, **volvulus**, diverticular stricture |
| Vomiting | **Early**, bilious | Late |
| Distension | Less | **More** |
| Pain | Colicky, central | Colicky, lower |
| AXR | Central loops, **valvulae conniventes** (cross the full width) | Peripheral loops, **haustra** (partial) |

Features: **colicky pain, vomiting, distension, absolute constipation** (no flatus), tinkling then absent bowel sounds. Management: **"drip and suck"** (NBM, IV fluids, **NG tube** decompression), correct electrolytes, imaging (**CT** to find cause/level and spot ischaemia); surgery for a cause needing it or for **strangulation/ischaemia** (fever, tachycardia, peritonism, ↑lactate — the sign a simple obstruction has become an emergency).
- **Sigmoid volvulus** — elderly/constipated/institutionalised; **"coffee-bean" sign** on AXR; decompress with a **flatus tube/sigmoidoscopy**.
- **Caecal volvulus** — younger; usually needs surgery.
- Mnemonic for the causes of distension — **the 6 Fs:** Fat, Fluid, Flatus, Faeces, Fetus, "Fatal growth" (tumour).

**Perforation and peritonitis:** sudden severe pain, rigid "board-like" abdomen, involuntary guarding, rebound tenderness, absent bowel sounds, shock. **Free air under the diaphragm on erect CXR** (or free gas on CT). Causes: perforated peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, appendicitis, obstruction, cancer, ischaemia. Management: resuscitate, IV antibiotics, analgesia, and usually **urgent laparotomy**.

**Mesenteric ischaemia (acute):** the classic **"pain out of proportion to examination"** — severe central pain with an initially soft abdomen. Causes: **SMA embolus (AF!)**, SMA thrombosis, mesenteric venous thrombosis, non-occlusive (low-flow). **Metabolic acidosis + raised lactate** is the red flag. Diagnose **CT angiography**; this is a surgical emergency (revascularisation/resection) — high mortality if delayed.
- **Ischaemic colitis** (a milder, more common cousin) — the **splenic-flexure watershed**, transient bloody diarrhoea + LIF pain, "thumbprinting" on imaging; usually managed conservatively.

**Appendicitis:** central (periumbilical, visceral) pain **migrating to the right iliac fossa** (McBurney's, somatic), anorexia, low-grade fever, RIF tenderness/guarding, Rovsing's/psoas signs. Largely a **clinical diagnosis** (imaging/US/CT if uncertain, especially to avoid missing other pathology in women); treat with **appendicectomy** (± antibiotics).

**The acute abdomen by quadrant (a rapid triage):**

| Location | Think first |
|---|---|
| **RUQ** | Cholecystitis/biliary, hepatitis, right lower-lobe pneumonia |
| **Epigastric** | Peptic ulcer/perforation, pancreatitis, MI, AAA |
| **RIF** | Appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian, Crohn's, mesenteric adenitis |
| **LIF** | Diverticulitis, colitis, ovarian, constipation |
| **Loin → groin** |

docs.title: GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Black tarry offensive stool | **Melaena** (upper GI bleed) |
| Urea disproportionately raised with GI bleed | **Upper** GI bleed (digested blood protein) |
| Vomiting/retching **then** haematemesis | **Mallory–Weiss tear** |
| Transfusion threshold in GI bleed | **Hb <70 g/L**, target 70–90 ⚑ |
| Pre-endoscopy risk score (can allow outpatient) | **Glasgow–Blatchford (0–1)** |
| Post-endoscopy risk score | **Rockall** |
| When to give PPI in bleeding ulcer | **After** endoscopic therapy ⚑ |
| Immediate drugs in variceal bleed | **Terlipressin + prophylactic antibiotics** |
| First-line endoscopic therapy for oesophageal varices | **Band ligation** |
| Bridge for uncontrolled variceal bleed | **Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken–Blakemore)** → TIPS |
| Secondary prevention of variceal bleed | **Non-selective β-blocker + banding** |
| Commonest cause of lower GI bleed | **Diverticular disease** |
| Small-bowel vs large-bowel AXR sign | **Valvulae conniventes** (full width) vs **haustra** |
| Obstruction management | **"Drip and suck"** (NBM, IV fluids, NG) |
| "Coffee-bean" sign on AXR | **Sigmoid volvulus** |
| Board-like rigid abdomen + free air | **Perforation/peritonitis** |
| Pain **out of proportion** + AF + ↑lactate | **Acute mesenteric ischaemia (SMA embolus)** |
| Central pain migrating to RIF | **Appendicitis** |
| Must-exclude test in any woman with acute abdomen | **β-hCG** (ectopic) |

##### Sources
NICE CG141/NG12 (acute upper GI bleeding, transfusion, risk scoring); **Villanueva NEJM** (restrictive transfusion ⚑); BSG/BASL variceal-haemorrhage guidance (terlipressin, antibiotics, banding, TIPS); Oxford Handbook of Clinical Surgery and Kumar & Clark (acute abdomen, obstruction, ischaemia); Merck Manual Professional. Transfusion threshold and timing of PPI flagged ⚑ and cross-checked against NICE and the restrictive-transfusion trial evidence.

docs.title: GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — MALLORY-WEISS TEAR — GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: non-transmural/ oesophageal laceration (partial thickness tear) at or near the gastro-oesophageal junction
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: M>F, 3-15% of upper GI bleeding, incident ↑ with age
- PATHOGENESIS: secondary to sudden ↑ in intra-abdominal pressure from retching/vomiting against a closed glottis 🡪 distension 🡪 acute gastro-oesophageal laceration 🡪 bleeding from submucosal arteries
- RISK FACTORS: condition causing retching/vomiting/straining, hiatus hernia, heavy EtOH
- HISTORY:  hematemesis ± melaena (classically following an episode of retching); sudden large hematemesis (can be fatal); may be accompanies by epigastric/back pain
- INVESTIGATIONS:Bloods- FBC (Hb, Hct, platelets usually unremarkable in acute settings), INR, EUC, LFT, Group and Hold
- Flexible oesophagogastrodueodenoscopy: focal lesions with normal appearing adjacent mucosa (as opposed to other ulcerative, diffuse diseases); most tears heal within 24-48 hours (won’t be seen if endoscopy delayed)
- Chest XRay- contrast swallow

- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: Oesophagitis, Boerhaave’s syndrome, peptic ulcer, oesophageal varices, oesophageal cancer
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT: Most tears heal spontaneously however if bleeding doesn’t cease, endoscopic intervention with adrenaline injection ± haemoclip placement/thermal therapy/band ligation.  Evaluate fluid loss and replace with IVF/electrolytes and blood transfusion if necessary. Cease NSAIDS/anticoagulants and start antigastric acid therapy (PPI/H2 antagonists), anti-emetics (ondansetron/promethazine). Surgery should be reserved for situations where endoscopic haemostasis of bleeding has failed or transmural oesophageal perforation is a problem
- PROGNOSIS: Portal hypertension and coagulopathy are risk factors for re-bleeding (occurs in ~8-15% of cases). High risk factors for re-bleeding include >65 y/o, hematemesis at presentation, hemodynamic instability, alcoholism, aspirin/NSAID use and comorbidities.

docs.title: GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — small bowel obstruction — GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: normal flow of intraluminal contents interrupted in small bowel
- AETIOLOGY (MNEUMONIC SHAVING):
- Strictures
- Hernias (3rd; incisional, internal or external hernia)
- Adhesions (1st)
- Volvulus
- Intussusception
- Neoplasm (2nd; primary vs metastases from colon/ovarian/pancreatic/gastric)
- Gallstone (biliary-enteric fistula)
- TOP 3 causes (mneumonic ABC)- Adhesions, Bulge (hernias), Cancer
- TYPES: Partial: portion of intestinal lumen is occluded, allows passage of some gas & fluid, ↓ risk of strangulation
- Complete: the lumen of the intestine is occluded, no passage of gas or stool, ↑risk of strangulation
- Closed-loop: segment of intestine is obstructed both proximally and distally e.g. in volvulus ↑ intraluminal pressure from gas and fluid that cannot escape, ↑ riskof strangulation due to bowel wall ischemia

- PATHOGENESIS:
- Proximal to blockage 🡪 progressive dilatation
- Distal to blockage 🡪 decompression as luminal contents pass.
- Bowel wall become oedematous and loses normal absorptive function 🡪 fluid sequestered into bowel lumen.
- Ongoing emesis 🡪 metabolic alkalosis losing Na, K, H and CL.
- If bowel dilatation excessive 🡪 intramural vessels become compromised 🡪 perfusion to wall of intestine reduced 🡪 ischemia 🡪 necrosis + perforation
- RISK FACTORS: prior abd/pelvic surgery, abd wall/groin hernia, intestinal inflammation, prior irradiationHistory: N/V, distension, relative constipation in partial obstruction, obstipation (no stool/gas) in complete obstruction, feculent vomiting (late disease), Sx of adhesions/bulge/cancer
- Proximal SI- profuse vomiting, rarely feculent, more epigastric discomfort as opposed to pain
- Mid-late SI- cramping crescendo-decrescendo peri-umbilical pain (poorly localised), vomiting following pain

- EXAMINATION: dehydration, abd exam (surgical scars, hernias, distension, abnormal masses, “tinkling”/muffled bowel sounds, hyper resonance to percussion)
- INVESTIGATIONS:Vitals- SIRS criteria (?ischemia)
- Bloods- FBC, EUC, ABG (lactate acidosis in ischemia), Group & Hold, LFTs, BUN
- Urinalysis
- Erect and supine AXR (dilated looks of bowel >3mm in SB, >6mm in LB, >9mm in caecum; air fluid levels, proximal bowel dilatation + distal bowel collapse, ?pneumoperitoneum, paucity of air in colon)
- CT scan can show obstruction and sites of ischemia (dilated loops of bowel, air fluid level, sites of ischemia, aetiology, transition point for point of obstruction, donut sign/kinks for adhesion)Ischemic bowel/strangulation pneumatosis intestinalis, thickened bowel wall, air in portal vein, free intraperitoneal fluid, differential wall enhancements (↓ IV contrast uptake in affected bowel)

- Angiography for acute mesenteric arterial occlusion
- Water-soluble contrast medium (WSCM) is recommended for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes in patients undergoing nonoperative management

- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: ileus, LBO
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENTSimple (conservative) vs. Complete

docs.title: GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — large bowel obstruction — GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: Normal flow of intraluminal contents interrupted in large bowel
- AETIOLOGY: top 3 causes- 1. CRC, 2. Volvulus (sigmoid > caecal) 3. Diverticulitis; can also be caused by chronic constipation, IBD stricture, radiation stricture, volvulus or adhesions
- PATHOGENESIS: proximally, progressive dilatation; distally, decompression as luminal contents pass
- HISTORY:Open loop (10-20%; safer)- incompetent ileocecal valve allows relief of colonic pressure as contents reflux into ileum (similar presentation to SBO)
- Closed loop (80-90%; dangerous)-competent ileocaecal valve resulting in proximal/distal occlusions
- Insidious onset compared to SBO, deep cramping hypogastric pain

- ABD EXAMINATION: distension, abnormal masses, hyper-resonance
- INVESTIGATIONS: bloods (FBC, EUC, CEA), erect/supine AXR, CT abd (site, aetiology, complications)

![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img014.jpg)

- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: ileus, toxic megacolon (commonly associated with C. Diff, Hx of ABx use), SBO (earlier pain that is more superior, Hx of abdo surgery/hernia repair)
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT
- Conservative: 75% of LBO ultimately requires surgery, supportive (IV fluids, electrolyte replacement, analgesia)
- Surgery: usually requires resection + temporary diverting colostomy; volvulus requires sigmoidoscopy to decompress and followed by operative reduction; stomas used if not safe/unable to anastomose/defunctioning to let it join before being used
- COMPLICATIONS: ischemia, necrosis, perforation, anastomotic leak from surgery

docs.title: GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — acute appendicitis — GI Bleeding & the Acute Abdomen
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: acute inflammation of the appendix
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: Early teens-late 40s
- AETIOLOGY: faecal matter, lymphoid hyperplasia (↑ lymphocytes in the lymph nodes)
- PATHOGENESIS: Faecolith/enlarged lymphoid follicles/ inspissated barium/parasites/tumours 🡪 appendiceal luminal obstruction 🡪 lumen distal to obstruction fills with mucus 🡪 closed-loop obstruction 🡪 ↑ intraluminal pressure 🡪 distension 🡪 bacteria (e.g. E Coli) rapidly colonisation 🡪 intraluminal pressure > venous pressure 🡪 ↓ drainage 🡪 engorgement/congestion of appendix 🡪 inflammatory response 🡪 spreads to serosa/parietal peritoneum 🡪 RLQ pain 🡪 small arterioles thrombosed 🡪 ischemia 🡪 necrosis 🡪 perforation 🡪 bacteria and pus leak out from dying appendix wall 🡪 fistula/absess
- PAIN: Initially, inflammation irritates visceral peritoneum 🡪 referred pain to umbilical area (embryonic midgut; visceral afferent fibers from appendix follow same nerve  distribution of small intestine; T10 origins). Disease progression 🡪 irritates parietal peritoneum 🡪 localised RLQ pain (McBurney’s Point; pain carried by somatosensory T12 nerves with specific dermatomal distribution)
- RISK FACTORS: ↓dietary fibre
- HISTORY: onset over 12-24 hours, constant umbilical pain that shifts to the RLQ, anorexia (↓ appetite), N/V, fever
- EXAMINATION: Vitals abnormal, McBurney’s Sign (tenderness 2/3 between ASIS and umbilicus), Rosving’s Sign (R-sided pain upon deep left palpation), Psoas Sign (RLQ pain on passive extension of right hip), Obturator Sign (pain with passive flexion and internal rotation of right hip); peritonism upon rupture
- ![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img018.jpg)
INVESTIGATIONS:
- Bloods- FBC (mild leucocytosis with left shift; leucocytosis > 20,000=probable perforation; Hb/MCV for blood loss anaemia), EUC, LFT, CRP, pancreatic enzymes, bHCG
- Urinalysis
- CXR- pneumoperitoneum
- U/S- thick-walled appendix, excludes gynae causes e.g. ovarian cyst/ectopic pregnancy/tubo-ovarian abscess
- Abdominal and pelvic CT scan- enlarged appendix (>6mm), peri-appendiceal stranding, faecolith presence, inflammatory changes
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: mesenteric adenitis, viral gastroenteritis, meckel’s diverticulitis, intussusception, right-sided ureteric stone, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT: ABCD, NBM, IVF, analgesia, MAG ABx, anti-emetics, appendicectomy
- COMPLICATIONS: perforation, peritonitis, sepsis/septic shock, abscess, carcinoma,
- PROGNOSIS: Rapid treatment yields good prognosis

docs.title: Hepatology
docs.h: 7.1 Jaundice and the approach to abnormal LFTs
docs.text:
**Jaundice** (visible when bilirubin >~50 µmol/L) splits three ways — this algorithm underlies most hepatology data questions (see also Section 1.4):

| Type | Bilirubin | Other LFTs | Urine/stool | Causes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Pre-hepatic** | Unconjugated ↑ | Otherwise normal | Normal urine, normal stool | **Haemolysis, Gilbert's** |
| **Hepatic** | Both ↑ | ↑↑ALT/AST | Dark urine | Hepatitis, cirrhosis, drugs |
| **Post-hepatic** | Conjugated ↑ | ↑ALP/γGT | **Dark urine, pale stool, itch** | **Gallstone, pancreatic/biliary Ca, stricture, PBC/PSC** |

**Inherited hyperbilirubinaemias:** **Gilbert's syndrome** (common, benign; reduced UGT1A1 → **isolated unconjugated** hyperbilirubinaemia, jaundice on **fasting/stress/illness**, otherwise normal LFTs — no treatment, reassure); Crigler–Najjar (severe unconjugated); **Dubin–Johnson / Rotor** (conjugated, benign).

docs.title: Hepatology
docs.text:
**Acute liver failure = acute liver injury + coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) + hepatic encephalopathy in someone without pre-existing cirrhosis** (classified by the jaundice-to-encephalopathy interval: hyperacute/acute/subacute).

**Causes:** **paracetamol overdose** (commonest in the UK/West), viral hepatitis (commonest worldwide — A/B/E), drug reactions (idiosyncratic DILI), ischaemia, Wilson's, Budd–Chiari, acute fatty liver of pregnancy, amanita mushroom poisoning. Complications drive the danger: **encephalopathy + cerebral oedema, coagulopathy/bleeding, hypoglycaemia, AKI, sepsis, multi-organ failure**.

**⚑ Paracetamol overdose (very high yield):**
- Toxic metabolite **NAPQI** depletes glutathione → hepatocyte necrosis (zone 3).
- **Plot the paracetamol level against time on the treatment nomogram** — a **single line at 100 mg/L at 4 h → 15 mg/L at 15 h** is now used for everyone (the "high-risk" line was abolished in the UK, treating more people). Bloods: paracetamol level (≥4 h post-ingestion), LFTs, **INR**, U&E, VBG/lactate, glucose.
- **Antidote: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)** — replenishes glutathione. Give **immediately if**: level above the nomogram line; **staggered/uncertain-time** overdose; or presenting late with abnormal INR/ALT. Don't wait for a level if presentation is late or staggered.
- **King's College criteria for transplant referral (paracetamol ALF):** **arterial pH <7.30** after resuscitation, **OR all three of** — **INR >6.5 (PT >100 s)**, **creatinine >300 µmol/L**, and **grade III/IV encephalopathy**. (An arterial **lactate >3.5 mmol/L** early, or >3.0 after fluid resuscitation, is an additional adverse marker.)

docs.title: Hepatology
docs.text:
**Cirrhosis** = diffuse **fibrosis + regenerative nodules** (irreversible architectural distortion) → two problems: **portal hypertension** and **hepatic synthetic/detoxifying failure**. Commonest causes: **alcohol, MASLD/MASH, chronic viral hepatitis (B/C)**; then autoimmune, PBC/PSC, haemochromatosis, Wilson's, α₁-antitrypsin.

**Compensated vs decompensated** — **decompensation** is defined by the appearance of **jaundice, ascites, variceal bleeding, or encephalopathy**. **Severity scores:**
- **Child–Pugh (A/B/C)** — **"ABCDE": Albumin, Bilirubin, Clotting (INR/PT), Distension (ascites), Encephalopathy**. Grades severity/surgical risk.
- **⚑ MELD / MELD-Na** — bilirubin, INR, creatinine (+ **sodium**) — used for **transplant prioritisation** and prognosis; MELD-Na now standard (adds hyponatraemia as an adverse factor).

**The complications set (learn these six as a block):**

**1. Variceal bleeding** — see Section 6.1 (terlipressin + antibiotics + banding; NSBB + banding for prevention).

**2. Ascites** — portal hypertension + **hypoalbuminaemia** + splanchnic vasodilatation/RAAS activation → Na⁺/water retention. Diagnose and **always tap (diagnostic ascitic tap)**:
- **Serum–ascites albumin gradient (SAAG)**: **≥11 g/L = portal hypertension** (transudate: cirrhosis, heart failure, Budd–Chiari); **<11 g/L** = other (malignancy, TB, pancreatitis, nephrotic).
- **Management:** **salt restriction + spironolactone** (± furosemide), **fluid restriction if Na⁺ <125**, therapeutic paracentesis (with **albumin cover** for large volumes), and **TIPS** for refractory ascites.

**3. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)** — infection of ascites **without a surgical source**. Suspect in any decompensation/fever/abdominal pain/encephalopathy in an ascitic patient. **Diagnosis: ascitic neutrophils (PMN) ≥250 cells/mm³.** Commonest organism **E. coli**. **Treat with IV cefotaxime/piperacillin-tazobactam + IV albumin** (reduces hepatorenal syndrome/mortality). **Secondary prophylaxis: oral ciprofloxacin/norfloxacin.**

**4. Hepatic encephalopathy** — **ammonia** and other toxins cross to the brain → confusion, **asterixis (flap)**, altered consciousness (graded I–IV). **Precipitants (treat these!): GI bleed, infection/SBP, constipation, dehydration/diuretics, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives, high protein load.** **Treatment: lactulose** (traps ammonia in the gut, ≥2–3 soft stools/day) + **rifaximin** (non-absorbed antibiotic, reduces ammonia-producing flora) + correct the precipitant.

**5. Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS)** — functional renal failure from splanchnic vasodilatation → renal vasoconstriction, in advanced liver disease, **with structurally normal kidneys** (diagnosis of exclusion — no other cause, no response to volume). Treat: **terlipressin + albumin**; definitive = **liver transplant**.

**6. Hepatocellular carcinoma** — see 7.3 surveillance below.

**⚑ HCC surveillance:** **6-monthly liver ultrasound (± AFP)** in patients with **cirrhosis**

docs.title: Hepatology
docs.text:
**The core split — route and chronicity:**

| Virus | Genome/route | Acute/chronic | Key points |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hep A** | RNA, **faeco-oral** | Acute only | Travel/shellfish; **vaccine**; self-limiting |
| **Hep B** | **DNA**, blood/sexual/vertical | Acute → **chronic** (esp. neonatal) | Vaccine (surface antigen); serology below; ↑HCC |
| **Hep C** | RNA, **blood-borne** (IVDU) | Mostly **chronic** | **Curable with DAAs** ⚑; no vaccine |
| **Hep D** | RNA, needs **HBsAg** | Co/super-infection with B | Worsens B |
| **Hep E** | RNA, **faeco-oral** (pork, water) | Acute; **chronic in immunosuppressed** | Dangerous in **pregnancy** |

**⚑ Hepatitis B serology (a guaranteed exam grid):**

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **HBsAg** | **Surface antigen — current infection** (acute or chronic if >6 months) |
| **Anti-HBs** | **Immunity** — vaccination or cleared infection |
| **Anti-HBc IgM** | **Acute/recent** infection |
| **Anti-HBc IgG** | **Past exposure** (present in chronic and resolved; absent after vaccination) |
| **HBeAg** | **High infectivity / active replication** |
| **Anti-HBe** | Lower infectivity (seroconversion) |
| **HBV DNA** | Viral load (monitors treatment) |

*Discriminators: **Anti-HBs alone (no anti-HBc) = vaccinated.** HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM = acute. HBsAg >6 months + anti-HBc IgG = chronic. HBeAg positive = highly infectious.* Chronic B treated with **tenofovir/entecavir** (or pegylated interferon) — suppressive, not curative.

**⚑ Hepatitis C** — screen with **anti-HCV antibody**, confirm active infection with **HCV RNA (PCR)**. **Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)** — **pangenotypic regimens** such as **sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (12 weeks)** or **glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (8 weeks)** — achieve **>95% cure (SVR12)**, well tolerated. This has transformed HCV from a chronic disease into a curable one (older interferon/ribavirin regimens are obsolete).

docs.title: Hepatology
docs.text:
**Alcohol-related liver disease** — a spectrum: **fatty liver (steatosis, reversible) → alcoholic hepatitis → cirrhosis.** Clues: **AST:ALT >2**, ↑γGT, ↑MCV, ↑IgA. **Alcoholic hepatitis** (jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, systemically unwell) — severity by **Maddrey's discriminant function** (≥32 = severe) or **Glasgow Alcoholic Hepatitis Score**; severe disease may be treated with **corticosteroids** (assess response with the Lille score). Manage alcohol withdrawal (**chlordiazepoxide**, **thiamine/Pabrinex** to prevent **Wernicke's**), nutrition, and abstinence (the single most important intervention).

**⚑ MASLD / MASH (the 2023 renaming):** what used to be **NAFLD → is now MASLD** (metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease), and **NASH → MASH** (steatohepatitis). The change is more than cosmetic: diagnosis now requires **hepatic steatosis PLUS ≥1 cardiometabolic risk factor** (overweight/obesity, type 2 diabetes/dysglycaemia, hypertension, dyslipidaemia) — a **positive** definition rather than "fatty liver by exclusion of alcohol." A new category, **MetALD**, covers MASLD with a moderate/increased alcohol intake. It is now a leading cause of chronic liver disease. Management: **weight loss (≥7–10%)**, treat the metabolic risk factors, exercise; assess fibrosis (**FIB-4/elastography**). *(Any older material calling this "NAFLD/NASH" is out of date — flag ⚑.)*

docs.title: Hepatology
docs.h: 7.6 Autoimmune, cholestatic and inherited liver disease
docs.text:
**Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH)** — young/middle-aged **women**, may present acutely or as chronic hepatitis/cirrhosis; **↑IgG, ASMA / anti-LKM1**, interface hepatitis on biopsy. **Steroid-responsive** (prednisolone + azathioprine).

**The two cholestatic autoimmune diseases (don't mix them up):**

| | **Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)** | **Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)** |
|---|---|---|
| Who | **Middle-aged women** | **Men**, associated with **UC** |
| Target | Small intrahepatic bile ducts | Intra- **and** extra-hepatic ducts |
| Antibody | **Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA)** | **pANCA** (no specific antibody) |
| Imaging | — | **MRCP: "beaded" strictures** |
| Hallmark symptom | **Itch + fatigue**, xanthelasma | Cholestasis, cholangitis episodes |
| Cancer risk | — | **Cholangiocarcinoma**, colorectal (with UC) |
| Treatment | **Ursodeoxycholic acid** (+ obeticholic acid) | ERCP for dominant strictures; transplant; no drug alters course |

**The three inherited metabolic liver diseases (each has a signature):**

| Disease | Defect | Signature findings | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Haemochromatosis** | **HFE (C282Y)** → iron overload (AR) | **↑Ferritin, ↑transferrin saturation**; "bronze diabetes," arthralgia, cardiomyopathy, hypogonadism | **Venesection** |
| **Wilson's disease** | ATP7B → copper overload (AR); think **<40 y** | ↓Caeruloplasmin, ↑urinary copper, **Kayser–Fleischer rings**, neuropsychiatric signs | **Penicillamine / trientine, zinc** |
| **α₁-antitrypsin deficiency** | SERPINA1 (PiZZ) | Liver disease **+ early emphysema**; low serum A1AT; PAS-positive globules | Supportive; ± transplant |

*Discriminators: young patient + liver + **neuropsychiatric/eye signs = Wilson's**; middle-aged + **bronze skin/diabetes/arthralgia = haemochromatosis**; liver + **basal emphysema = α₁-antitrypsin**.*

---

docs.title: Hepatology
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Isolated unconjugated bilirubin, jaundice on fasting, normal LFTs | **Gilbert's syndrome** |
| Commonest cause of acute liver failure in UK/West | **Paracetamol overdose** |
| Paracetamol antidote + mechanism | **N-acetylcysteine** (replenishes glutathione) |
| King's College criteria (paracetamol) | pH <7.30, **or** all of: INR >6.5, creatinine >300, grade III/IV encephalopathy |
| Child–Pugh components | **Albumin, Bilirubin, Clotting, Distension (ascites), Encephalopathy** |
| Transplant-allocation score | **MELD-Na** ⚑ |
| SAAG ≥11 g/L | **Portal hypertension** (cirrhosis, HF, Budd–Chiari) |
| Ascitic neutrophils ≥250/mm³ | **Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis** |
| SBP treatment | **IV cefotaxime + IV albumin** |
| Encephalopathy treatment | **Lactulose + rifaximin** (+ treat precipitant) |
| Functional renal failure in cirrhosis, normal kidneys | **Hepatorenal syndrome** (terlipressin + albumin) |
| HCC surveillance | **6-monthly ultrasound ± AFP** in cirrhosis ⚑ |
| Anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative | **Vaccinated** |
| HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM | **Acute hepatitis B** |
| HBeAg positive | **High infectivity** |
| Hepatitis C treatment | **Direct-acting antivirals — curative (>95% SVR)** ⚑ |
| Hepatitis dangerous in pregnancy | **Hepatitis E** |
| AST:ALT >2, ↑γGT, ↑MCV | **Alcoholic liver disease** |
| New name for NAFLD/NASH | **MASLD / MASH** ⚑ |
| AMA-positive, itchy middle-aged woman | **Primary biliary cholangitis** |
| pANCA, UC, beaded ducts on MRCP | **Primary sclerosing cholangitis** |
| ↑Ferritin + ↑transferrin saturation, bronze diabetes | **Haemochromatosis** (venesect) |
| Young + liver + Kayser–Fleischer rings | **Wilson's disease** |
| Liver disease + early basal emphysema | **α₁-antitrypsin deficiency** |

##### Sources
Robbins & Cotran (hepatic pathology); EASL/AASLD guidance (acute liver failure, cirrhosis complications, HCC surveillance, HCV DAAs); NICE NG50 (cirrhosis), CG165 (hepatitis B); UK paracetamol-overdose guidance (single-nomogram line, NAC ⚑); **AASLD/EASL/ALEH 2023 MASLD nomenclature** (⚑); BSG/BASL. Paracetamol nomogram/King's criteria, MELD-Na, HCC surveillance, HCV cure, and the MASLD renaming all flagged ⚑ and cross-checked against ≥2 current sources.

docs.title: Hepatology
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — viral hepatitis — Hepatology
docs.text:
- CLINICAL FEATURES
- Mostly subclinical
- Flu-like prodrome 🡪 jaundice by 1-2 weeks (N/V, anorexia, headaches, fatigue, myalgia, low-grade fever, arthralgia, urticaria especially HBV)
- Icteric (clinical jaundice) phase 🡪 pale stools, dark urine, hepatosplenomegaly, RUQ pain, cervical lymphadenopathy
- Hx of IVDU, tattoo, blood transfusion, unprotected sex, travel, non-immunized, endemic regions (poor sanitation)
- HEP ARNA virus with faecal-oral transmission
- Hx: travel, fatigue, nausea, arthralgia, fever, jaundice
- Diagnosed by ↑transaminases, + anti-HAV IgM [note: + anti-HAV IgG (=immunity from prior infection/recent disease]

- HEP BTransmitted via sexual activity/blood/IVDU
- Acute (+ve HBsAg, HBeaG, IgM)
- Chronic (+ve HBsAg, HBeaG, IgG, AST, ALT)
- Resolved infection (anti HBs +, IgG, Anti-HBe)
- Immunization (anti-HBs)

- HEP CRNA requires blood borne/IVDU transmission (not sex)
- Ab (+) and HCV-RNA (+) = INFECTED (chronic carrier)
- Ab (-) and HCV-RNA (+) = ACUTE (just got the virus and haven’t had enough time to mount a response i.e. Ab is low)
- Ab (+) and HCV-RNA (-) = someone who has been TREATED

- HEP DRequires Hep A; causes more aggressive disease

- INVESTIGATIONS: ↑ AST, ALT (AST: ALT < 1), hepatitis serology (IgM antibody directed to the virus), cirrhosis on biopsy
- TREATMENT: hepatocellular carcinoma screening with U/S, anti-virals Tenofovir/adefovir, inteferon alpha + ribavirin, cease ETOH (increases risk of disease progression), educate about blood and sexual practices, diet (↓Na, ↑protein, fluid restriction), liver transplant

docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — wilson’s disease — Hepatology
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: autosomal recessive defect in copper metabolism (gene ATP7B)
- CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: Asterixis, Basal ganglia degeneration (parkinsonism), Ceruloplasmin decreases (copper carrying decreases), Cirrhosis, Corneal deposits (Kayser-Fleischer ring), Cerebellum (dysarthria, dysphagia, incoordination, ataxia), Dementia/psychosis
- Suspected if ↑ liver enzymes with clinical manifestations at young age

docs.title: Hepatology
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: liver damage with diffuse architectural distortion, replacement with scar tissue, regenerative nodules
- STAGES
- Stage 1- compensated, asymptomatic, 10-20 yr survival with normal lie expectancy
- Stage 2- decompensation, development of complications
- AETIOLOGY: alcoholic/non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, chronic viral hepatitis, drugs (methotrexate, paracetamol), haemochromatosis, AI hepatitis, PBC, Gilbert’s, Wilson’s alpha anti-trypsin deficiency, occupational exposure to hepatotoxins (e.g. vinyl chloride)

![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img023.jpg)

- CLINICAL PRESENTATION: RUQ pain, N/V, fatigue, easy bruising, anorexia, pruritus, gynaecomastia, splenomegaly
- COMPLICATIONS: Varices, Ascites/Anemia, Renal failure (pre-renal from over-diuresis 🡪 ATN 🡪 HRS), Infections, Coagulopathy, Encephalopathy, Sepsis/
- Portal HTN 🡪 ventilation-perfusion mismatch 🡪 intrapulmonary shunting/limitation of oxygen diffusion 🡪 hepatopulmonary syndrome 🡪 dyspnoea, platypnoea, orthodeoxia
- INVESTIGATIONS
- Bloods-↓platelet (earliest finding) 🡪 ↑INR 🡪 ↓albumin 🡪 ↑bilirubin 🡪 ↓glucose (pre-terminal)
- Fibrotest- combination of clinical and biochemical markers to predict degree of fibrosis
- Imaging- U/S, CT (varices, nodular liver texture, splenomegaly, ascites), gastroscopy
- TREATMENT: treat underlying disorder, ↓ insults (EtOH, heptotoxic drugs, immunize for Hep A/B), manage complications, liver transplantation (if no EtOH for > 6 months, use MELD score)
- ![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img024.jpg)
PROGNOSIS
- Child-Pugh Score for Severity
- MELD- Na score for transplant to predict 3 month survival and used to stratify patients on transplant list; based on creatinine, INR, bilirubin and serum Na+
- Usual causes of death in cirrhosis: renal failure (hepatorenal syndrome), sepsis, GI bleed, or HCC

docs.text:
- DEFINITION: potentially reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome secondary to liver disease
- PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: porto systemic shun taround hepatocytes and ↓ hepatocellular function ↑ systemic toxins (believed to be ammonia from gut, fatty acids, amino acids etc) which go to the brain
- PRECIPITATING FACTORS: Haemorrhage in Gi tract/ HypoK+, Excess protein, Paracentesis, Alkalosis/Anaemia, Trauma, Infection, Colon surgery, Sedatives

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
**First split mechanical vs motility** (see Section 3): progressive **solids → liquids** = mechanical; **solids and liquids together** = motility.

- **Achalasia** — failure of LOS relaxation + loss of peristalsis (degenerate myenteric plexus). Dysphagia to solids **and** liquids, regurgitation, weight loss. **Barium swallow: "bird's-beak"** tapering; **manometry** is diagnostic (↑LOS pressure, incomplete relaxation, aperistalsis). Small long-term **oesophageal cancer** risk. Treat: pneumatic dilatation, **Heller myotomy/POEM**, or botulinum toxin. *(Beware **pseudoachalasia** — a fundal/GOJ tumour mimicking it in older patients.)*
- **Diffuse oesophageal spasm** — intermittent chest pain + dysphagia; "corkscrew" oesophagus.
- **Systemic sclerosis** — smooth-muscle atrophy → absent lower peristalsis + **incompetent** LOS → severe reflux/stricture (the opposite pattern to achalasia).
- **Eosinophilic oesophagitis** — atopic young adults, food bolus impaction, rings/furrows; ≥15 eosinophils/hpf on biopsy; treat with PPI, topical steroids (swallowed fluticasone/budesonide), diet.
- **Structural:** **strictures** (peptic, from reflux), **Schatzki ring**, and **oesophageal webs** — the web of **Plummer–Vinson syndrome** (web + **iron-deficiency anaemia** + glossitis; premalignant).
- **Pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum)** — elderly, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, gurgling neck lump; barium swallow diagnostic (avoid blind endoscopy/NG).

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: 4.2 GORD, Barrett's oesophagus and oesophageal cancer
docs.text:
**GORD** — LOS incompetence → retrograde acid. Heartburn, acid regurgitation, worse lying/bending; atypical: chronic cough, hoarseness, dental erosion. Diagnosis is usually **clinical**; endoscope only if **ALARM** features or refractory. Management ladder: lifestyle (weight, avoid triggers, smaller/earlier meals) → **PPI** → consider **fundoplication** for refractory/volume reflux. Complications: oesophagitis, peptic stricture, **Barrett's**.

**⚑ Barrett's oesophagus** — chronic reflux drives **metaplasia** of lower-oesophageal squamous → **columnar (intestinal) epithelium** — a premalignant change (adenocarcinoma). Confirmed on biopsy. **Surveillance** is length- and dysplasia-stratified: non-dysplastic short segment (<3 cm) roughly every **3–5 years**, longer segments every **2–3 years**; **any dysplasia → endoscopic therapy** (radiofrequency ablation ± endoscopic mucosal resection) rather than watchful waiting. *(Older texts undertreat dysplasia — RFA/EMR now standard for low- and high-grade dysplasia. ⚑)*

**Oesophageal cancer — the treatment-defining split:**

| | **Adenocarcinoma** | **Squamous cell carcinoma** |
|---|---|---|
| Site | **Lower third** / GOJ | **Upper two-thirds** |
| Risk factors | **GORD, Barrett's, obesity** | **Smoking, alcohol**, hot drinks, achalasia, Plummer–Vinson |
| Trend (West) | Now the **commonest** in the West ⚑ | Commonest worldwide |

Presents with **progressive dysphagia + weight loss**; diagnose by **OGD + biopsy**, stage with CT/PET + **EUS**. Most present late (poor prognosis).

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: 4.3 Peptic ulcer disease, *H. pylori* and gastritis
docs.text:
**Two big causes: *H. pylori* and NSAIDs** (± aspirin, steroids, physiological stress). *H. pylori* (Gram-negative, urease-positive) drives most **duodenal** ulcers; NSAIDs feature more in **gastric** ulcers.

| | Duodenal ulcer | Gastric ulcer |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency | Commoner (~4:1) | Less common |
| Pain vs food | **Relieved** by eating (worse at night/when hungry) | **Worsened** by eating (→ weight loss, food fear) |
| *H. pylori* | ~90% | ~70% |
| Malignant potential | Essentially none | **Can be malignant — always biopsy + repeat scope to confirm healing** |

**⚑ *H. pylori* testing:** non-invasive **urea breath test** or **stool antigen** (stop PPI ~2 weeks, antibiotics ~4 weeks before, to avoid false negatives); or biopsy-based (**CLO/rapid urease test**, histology) at endoscopy. Confirm eradication with a urea breath test.

**⚑ *H. pylori* eradication (guidance has shifted — ACG 2024):** because **clarithromycin resistance is now high**, empirical clarithromycin triple therapy is discouraged. **First-line is optimised bismuth quadruple therapy** — a **PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole for 14 days** — which does not depend on clarithromycin susceptibility. Clarithromycin-based triple therapy (PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin) is reserved for regions/patients with proven low resistance and **no prior macrolide exposure**. (In UK practice, a 7-day PPI-based triple regimen is still commonly first-line per local guidance, but bismuth quadruple therapy is the salvage/high-resistance choice — flag both.)

**Complications of PUD:** bleeding (posterior duodenal ulcer → **gastroduodenal artery**), **perforation** (anterior duodenal ulcer → peritonitis, free air), **gastric outlet obstruction** (succussion splash, vomiting).

**Zollinger–Ellison syndrome** — a **gastrinoma** (± MEN1) → massive acid → **multiple/refractory/distal** ulcers + diarrhoea; **very high fasting gastrin**.

**Gastritis:** *H. pylori* (antral), autoimmune (**pernicious anaemia** — anti-parietal/intrinsic-factor antibodies, achlorhydria, B₁₂ deficiency, ↑gastric-cancer risk), NSAID/chemical, stress.

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: 4.4 Gastric cancer and upper-GI malignancy clues
docs.text:
Mostly **adenocarcinoma**. Risk: *H. pylori*, pernicious anaemia, smoking, salt/smoked diet, previous partial gastrectomy. Presentation: dyspepsia + weight loss, anaemia, early satiety, epigastric mass; **linitis plastica** (diffuse "signet-ring" infiltration → rigid "leather-bottle" stomach). **Metastatic clues (eponyms):** **Virchow's node** (left supraclavicular, Troisier's sign), **Sister Mary Joseph nodule** (periumbilical), **Krukenberg tumour** (ovarian mets), acanthosis nigricans. Diagnose OGD + biopsy; stage CT + EUS ± laparoscopy.

Briefly: **GISTs** (c-KIT/CD117, treat with **imatinib**) and **gastric MALT lymphoma** (*H. pylori*-driven — **eradication can be curative**).

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| "Bird's-beak" on barium swallow | **Achalasia** |
| Dysphagia to solids **and** liquids from the start | **Achalasia / motility disorder** |
| Food bolus impaction in an atopic young adult | **Eosinophilic oesophagitis** |
| Oesophageal web + iron-deficiency anaemia | **Plummer–Vinson** |
| Regurgitation of undigested food + halitosis + neck gurgle | **Pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's)** |
| Metaplasia at the Z-line | **Barrett's oesophagus** |
| Any dysplasia in Barrett's | **Endoscopic therapy (RFA/EMR)** ⚑ |
| Lower-third oesophageal cancer + reflux/obesity | **Adenocarcinoma** |
| Upper-two-thirds oesophageal cancer + smoking/alcohol | **Squamous cell carcinoma** |
| Ulcer pain **relieved** by eating | **Duodenal ulcer** |
| Ulcer pain **worsened** by eating + weight loss | **Gastric ulcer** (biopsy — could be cancer) |
| First-line *H. pylori* eradication (high resistance) | **Bismuth quadruple therapy × 14 days** ⚑ |
| Multiple refractory distal ulcers + diarrhoea + ↑gastrin | **Zollinger–Ellison (gastrinoma)** |
| Bleeding posterior duodenal ulcer vessel | **Gastroduodenal artery** |
| Left supraclavicular node in gastric cancer | **Virchow's (Troisier's sign)** |
| Periumbilical metastatic nodule | **Sister Mary Joseph nodule** |
| *H. pylori*-driven gastric lymphoma curable by eradication | **MALT lymphoma** |

Robbins & Cotran (oesophageal/gastric pathology, Barrett's, gastric cancer); NICE CG184/NG12 (dyspepsia, referral); **ACG 2024 Clinical Guideline on Treatment of *H. pylori*** (bismuth quadruple first-line ⚑); BSG Barrett's surveillance guidance (⚑); Merck Manual Professional. Eradication regimen and Barrett's dysplasia management flagged ⚑ and cross-checked against ACG 2024 and BSG.

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — GORD — Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus, resulting in symptoms/complications
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: 10-20% of people in Western countries
- RISK FACTORS: transient relaxation or low basal tone of the LES, hiatus hernia, acid hyper secretion, Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (gastrin secreting tumour), ↑ BMI, smoking/EtOH/caffeine
- AETIOLOGY: ↓resting LES pressure, pathologically ↑ intra-gastric pressure
- DIAGNOSISHistory: Heartburn (retrosternal area, postprandial, exacerbated by bending/recumbence)
- Associated: regurgitation, dysphagia, metallic taste in mouth, hiatus hernia, cough (atypical), chest pain (mimic angina pectoris; uncommon), globus sensation (lump in throat; uncommon), hematemesis (O)

- INVESTIGATIONSpH monitoring:  Catheter in oesophagus for 24 hours, electrodes every 5 – 10cm apart, [atient notes time of the event/symptoms which can be correlated with pH readings and if correlating pH <4 then GORD can be expected
- Endoscopy with biopsy – patients with troublesome dysphagia, odynophagia, GI bleeding, anaemia, weight loss or anorexia
- Oesophageal manometry (assessing movement/peristalsis and pressure) – dysphagia

- MANAGEMENT:Lifestyle: ↓EtOH/coffee/spices /citrus juices; elevate head off bed, weight loss
- Medical: antacids (Mg(OH)2), H2 receptor antagonists (e.g. ranitidine), PPI (e.g. omeprazole/esomeprazole; maintenance therapy)
- Surgical: Nissen Fundoplication (Upper portion of stomach is wrapped around the oesophagus, effectively creating a new sphincter; many modifications are utilised)
- Indications for surgery include: Failed optimal medical management (most frequent indication), high volume reflux, severe oesophagitis by endoscopy, benign stricture,  Barrett’s oesophagus, upper respiratory Sx (laryngitis, nocturnal asthma, cough, aspiration)

- COMPLICATIONS: BARRETT’S OESOPHAGUS (metaplasia of stratified squamous esophageal cells into columnar epithelium with ↑ malignant potential for oesophageal cancer; diagnosed via biopsy; consider oesophagectomy in high-grade dysplasia), Erosive Oesophagitis, stricture, PUD, chronic laryngitis (△ voice quality, persistent cough, globus sensation)
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: Peptic ulcer disease, eosinophilic oesophagitis, CAD, achalasia
- PROGNOSIS: usually a good response to PPI, low adenocarcinoma risk (0.1% at 7 years follow-up)

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — oesophageal cancer — Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: M:F=3:1, 50-60 y/o onset, upper (20-33%)/middle (33%)/lower (33-50%)
- Regardless of type, is aggressive and spreads rapidly due to the extensive lymphatic network in the submucosa
- OESOPHAGEAL SCC (arise from the skin cells lining oesophagus, affecting upper 2/3 of oesophagus)
- ↑ risk in males; rarely seen < 30 y/o’; most common worldwide (incidence has fallen that adenocarcinoma has become most common)
- Causative factors: Smoking, EtOH, hot liquids, underlying oesophageal disease e.g. strictures/diverticula/achalasia
- Lesions are subtle and can be missed on endoscopy
- OESOPHAGEAL ADENOCARCINOMA (arise from the glandular cells present in lower 1/3 of oesophagus)
- ↑ risk in males; rarely seen < 40 y/o
- Causative factors: Gastric metaplasia from gastric reflux (GORD), Barrett’s oesophagus, smoking, EtOH
- HISTORY: progressively worsening dysphagia (first solids than liquids) with or without odynophagia, frequently asymptomatic (late presentation), constitutional symptoms, regurgitation and aspiration, anaemia, dyspepsia, hematemesis
- DIRECT HEMATOGENOUS, OR LYMPHATIC SPREAD- trachea (coughing), recurrent laryngeal nerves (hoarseness, vocal paralysis), aortic, liver, lung, bone, celiac and mediastinal nodes
- EXAMINATION: palpable supraclavicular lymph nodes
- INVESTIGATIONS
- Barium swallow (show narrowing); endoscopic biopsy and assess resectability (early lesions appear as plaques, nodules or ulcerations and advanced lesions appear as strictures); endoscopy ultrasound EUS (visualize local disease and nodal involvement); CT chest, abdomen and pelvis or PET Scan (metastatic workup to evaluate spread to adjacent 
![](notes/images/general-surgery-and-gastroenterology-anu/img002.jpg)
tissues/distanct organs); bronchoscopy ± thoracoscopy (rule out airway invasion)
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: achalasia, oesophageal strictures
- TUMOUR STAGING
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENTConservative: pain management, nutrition/electrolyte/fluid replacement
- Surgical: Oesophagectomy (open vs. minimally invasive) depending on depth of tumour invasion into oesophageal wall, size of lesion, lymphovascular invasion, extent of Barrett’s mucosa, comorbid conditions and patient’s age; Endoscopic reception
- Other therapies: chemoradiotherapy, speech pathology to help with dysphagia
- Adenocarcinoma requires oesophagectomy and SCC treated non-surgically with tumour staging
- If early stage, consider an oesophagectomy (transthoracic or trans-hiatal). Stomach/colon used for reconstruction
- If locally advanced, multimodal therapy with concurrent external beam radiation and chemotherapy (cisplatin and 5-FU). May need curative esopagectomy if disease responds well.
- If there is distant metastatic disease, treat with systemic therapy and palliate symptoms (oesophageal stent)
- Adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation are recommended for post-operative node positive disease

- COMPLICATIONS: metastases – commonly in the liver, lungs, pleura and bone
- PROGNOISI

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — OESOPHAGITIS — Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
- PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: When acid reflux from the stomach is frequent and persistent, the result is damage to the lining of the oesophagus. This is known as reflux oesophagitis or peptic oesophagitis.
- CLINICAL PRESENTATION:  heart burn, dysphagia (intermittent with first few swallows), odynophagia, chronic cough, solid foods only but can progressively worsen, PMHx of atopy, GORD or toxin ingestion
- INVESTIGATIONS: Barium swallow and X-ray or endoscopy
- COMPLICATIONS: oesophageal stricture, Barrett’s oesophagus oesophageal Cancer

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — Achalasia — Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: failure of smooth muscle relaxation at LES, ↑ LES pressure and progressive ↓ of peristaltic function.
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: ↑ in young women and middle-aged men
- TYPESPrimary Achalasia: unknown aetiology 🡪 inflammatory degeneration of Auerbach’s/myenteric plexus  + selective loss of post-ganglionic inhibitory neurons🡪 increased LES pressure (stimulatory neurons sole effectors of smooth muscle) 🡪 incomplete relaxation of LES with swallowing
- Secondary Achalasia: can be due to malignancy, Chagas disease, Parkinsons, myasthenia gravis or scleroderma

- NORMAL SWALLOWING: Oral phase (Tongue 🡪 food bolus 🡪 oropharynx), Pharyngeal phage (sensory signals through glossopharyngeal, vagus and trigeminal nerve to the swallowing centre in the medulla and pons causing closure of the opening to the pharynx), Oesophageal phase (vagal stretch receptors detect distension via the bolus and induce a vagovagal reflex, during which motor nerves induce a wave of contractions and causes relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter)
- CLINICAL PRESENTATION: dysphagia (starting from solids 🡪 liquids), weight loss, vomiting/regurgitation, postprandial chest pain
- EXAMINATION: oesophageal enlargement
- RISK FACTORS: Allgrove syndrome (achalasia, alacrima and adrenal insufficiency), AI diseases, FHx, Chagas disease
- INVESTIGATIONS: CXR (shows no air in stomach and a dilated oesophagus), barium studies (birds beak narrowing of oesophagus at LES, dilated oesophagus and loss of peristalsis), endoscopy to rule out malignancy, clinical features of scleroderma, oesophageal manometry
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: oesophageal carcinoma (Pseudo-achalasia when cancer invades myenteric plexus), CTD, reflux/eosinophilic oesophagitis
- COMPLCIATIONS: aspiration pneumonia, GORD, oesophagus SCC (caused by mucosal injury)
- MANAGEMENT: Ca2+ channel blockers (nifedipine), botulinum toxin A injection, LES dilation (bougie/endoscopic balloon dilatation; mechanical dilatation of the lower oesophageal sphincter using a balloon with a sufficiently forceful mechanical stretch to rupture the muscle fibres)


---

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — barrett’s oesophagus — Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: metaplastic columnar epithelium replaces the stratified squamous epithelium that normally lines the distal esophagus (intestinal metaplasia)
- AETIOLOGY: Long-standing GORD (gastric acid secretion + reflux)
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: > 50 y/o, M>F, Caucasians, smokers, overweight, hiatus hernia, reflux Sx
- PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: endoscopy shows erythematous epithelium in distal oesophagus, need biopsy for diagnosis
- Pre-malignant changes categorized as low/high-grade dysplasia 🡪 can progress to adenocarcinoma
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT: 1. Acid suppression (high-dose PPI/surgical fundoplication), 2. endoscopy every 3 year if no dysplasia, 3. Regular surveillance + biopsy, endoscopic ablation/resection or oesophagectomy

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — gastric cancer — Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: 50-59 y/o, M>F
- AETIOLOGY: compensatory epithelial cell proliferation via gastric atrophy (H.Pylori gastritis, pernicious anaemia, previous partial gastrectomy), host-related (blood type A, HNPCC, hereditary diffuse gastric carcinoma HDGC, gastric adenomatous polyps), environmental (smoking, EtOH, smoked/salted food)
- PATHOGENESIS: Gastric dysplasia 🡪 gastric adenocarcinoma 🡪 early cancer limited to the mucosa + submucosa, regardless of lymph node status 🡪 malignant epithelial tumour, originating from glandular epithelium of the gastric mucosa
- CLASSIFICATIONS
- Intestinal type: irregular tubular structures (frequently ulcerative) 🡪 intestinal metaplasia commonly in lesser curvature of antrum
- Diffuse type: poorly/un-differentiated + lacking gland formation 🡪 infiltrate gastric wall 🡪 secretes mucous into interstitium 🡪 large pools of mucous/colloid in tumour cell 🡪 pushes to nucleus to periphery 🡪 Signet Ring Cell
- HISTORY: Clinical suspicion (ulcer fails to heal, lesion on greater curvature of stomach/cardia)
- Insidious onset + late presentation (post-prandial abdominal fullness, vague epigastric pain, anorexia, constitutional symptoms, burping, N/V, dyspepsia, dysphagia, hepatomegaly/epigastric mass, hematemesis, fecal occult blood, melena, iron-deficiency anaemia)
- Metastasis (distal lymph nodes, peritoneum, Krukenburg ovarian, liver, lung, brain)

- EXAMINATION:
- Palpable abdominal mass, ascitesSigns of metastases- Virchow’s node (left supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph’s node (periumbilical), Irish node (left axillary), Blumer’s shelf (mass in pouch of Douglas), Krukenberg tumour (metastases to ovary)
- Less commonly, Acanthosis nigricans (thickening and darkening of skin, particularly in axilla) or Leser-Trelat sign (seborrhoeic keratoses all over skin)

- INVESTIGATIONS: Upper GI endoscopy + biopsy; EUS; immunohistochemistry (HER2);  CT chest, abdomen and pelvis or PET scan- looks for metastases
- CLINICAL STAGES OF GASTRIC CANCER- TNM system used to classify cancer into rudimentary stagesStage 0 – limited to inner lining of stomach
- Stage I – second or third layers of stomach (1A) or to second layer and nearby lymph nodes (1B)
- Stage II – second layer and more distant lymph nodes, to the third layer with nearby lymph nodes, or all four layers with no lymph nodes
- Stage III – third layer and more distant lymph nodes, or to fourth layer and nearby tissues and lymph nodes
- Stage IV – spread to nearby tissues and more distant lymph nodes, or metastasised to other organs

- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: PUD, benign polyp
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENTProximal lesions: Total gastrectomy and Roux en Y esophagojejunostomy
- Distal lesions: Distal gastrectomy or subtotal gastrectomy (5-6 cm margins)
- Palliation: gastric resection to decrease bleeding/relive obstruction + radiation therapy
- Adjuvant and palliative chemotherapy
- Low grade – endoscopically; High grade – surgical

- COMPLICATIONS: metastases, malnutrition, g

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — complications of gastric surgery — Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
- The anatomical changes that result after gastrectomy affect the emptying time of the stomach. Symptoms include ↓ tolerance for large meals, rapid emptying food into small intestine (“dumping”), abdominal cramping pain, diarrhoea, light-headedness after eating, ↑HR, and sharp ↓ in blood sugars.
- ALKALINE REFLUX GASTRITIS: duodenal bilious reflux into stomach 🡪 gastritis/oesophagitis; Tx: bile acid sequestrant (e.g. H2 Blocker) + surgical (Bilroth 1/II 🡪 Roux-en-Y conversion)
- AFFERENT LOOP SYNDROME: bile + pancreatic secretions 🡪 intermittent mechanical obstruction and distention of afferent limb 🡪 post-prandial distension, RUQ pain, N/biious vomiting anaemia; Tx: conversion to Roux-en-Y
- DUMPING SYNDROME: hyperosmotic chime released into small bower 🡪 post-prandial Sx, epigastric fullness/pain, emesis, nausea, diarrhoea, palpitations, dizziness, ↑HR, diaphoresis; Tx: small multiple meals, surgery
- BLIND-LOOP SYNDROME: bacterial overgrowth of colonic gram-neg bacteria in afferent limb🡪 diarrhoea, malnutrition, abd pain, hypoCa2+, anaemia/weakness; Tx: broad-spectrum ABx, conversion to Billroth I
- POSTVAGOTOMY DIARRHOEA: bile salts in colon inhibit water resorption; Tx: medical, surgery

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — peptic ulcer disease — Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: Break in the mucosal lining of the stomach/duodenum > 5mm in diameter, with a depth to the submucosa
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: ↑incidence with age, M=F
- AETIOLOGY: H. pylori infection (90% of duodenal, 60% of gastric), NSAID use, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, malignancy. Only 5% of population of H.Pylori are symptomatic.
- PATHOGENESIS: Imbalance between gastric acid that damages the gastroduodenal mucosal defenses (mucus HCO3-, tight junctions b/w epithelial cells, process of restitution) that normally limits the injury.
- NSAID 🡪 inhibits COX-1 🡪 inhibits synthesis of certain prostaglandins responsible for protective mucous laye.
- H Pylori 🡪 inflammation 🡪 ↑gastric secretion + disruption of tight junctions in stomach and impairs somatostatin in antrum of duodenum 🡪 ↑gastrin 🡪 gastric acid hypersecretion.
- Gastric ulcers usually due to NSAID use and duodenal ulcer due to H. pylori infection

- RISK FACTORS: smoking, ICU patients, H.Pylori infection, NSAID, ↑ age, FHx/PMHx
- PREVENTION: careful NSAID use, prophylactic PPI (especially in ICU), avoidance of smoking/EtOH
- HISTORY: Gastric- epigastric pain exacerbated by eating (1-2 hours postprandial), heartburn, chest discomfort, early satiety, hematemesis
- Duodenal- epigastric pain 2-5 hrs after eating, melena more common (than hematemesis), heartburn uncommon

- EXAMINATION: epigastric tenderness, pallor, ‘pointing sign’ (patient pointing at site of pain with one finger)
- INVESTIGATIONS
- Urea breath test: Urea-labelled isotope swallowed 🡪 wait for 15 minutes 🡪 H.Pylori converts urea to ammonia to CO2 🡪 patient breath tested for CO2 🡪 If positive, H.Pylori positive
- Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy: Allows visualization of ulcers and also for biopsy (+ rapid urease test ); H.Pylori (single ulcer), NSAID (multiple, shallow ulcers), malignancy (heaped-up margins, necrotic centre ulcers)
- Stool haem test: often performed, but usually negative
- FBC: anaemic, evidence of GI Bleeding
- Serology for H.Pylori- can remain positive after treatment
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: stomach cancer, GORD, acute pancreatitis, coeliac disease
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT
- Goals: 1. Treat underlying cause 2. Inhibit hypersecretion of acid (pH >6  ↓  pepsin which ↓ fibrin clot degradation)
- Cessation of NSAID, smoking, EtOH if possible
- Triple Therapy (PPI + 2ABx)
- Acid Suppression- PPI e.g. emomeprazole: inhibits parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase pump which secretes acid (heals most ulcers even if NSAIDs continued). H2 antagonists e.g. ranitidine can be used; except less effective.
- If there is H. pylori– 2 antibiotics are usually clarithromycin AND amoxicillin (or metronidazole if penicillin allergic)
- In actively bleeding ulcer 🡪 blood transfusion, PPI
- In perforated ulcer 🡪 endoscopy to stop bleeding or surgery (adrenaline injection, coagulation, endoscopic clips)
- Indications for Surgery: haemorrhage, rebleed in hospital, perforation, gastric outlet obstruction, refractory to medical/endoscopic manag

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — APPENDICULAR CARCINOMA — Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: 50% present as acute appendicitis, spreads rapidly to lymph nodes, ovaries, and peritoneal surfaces
- CLINICAL PRESENTATION: ascites, bloating, appendicitis pain, changes in bowel function
- TREATMENT: appendectomy (only treatment when tumour <1.5cm), right hemicolectomy (with nearby blood vessels + lymph nodes; no stoma required), debulking/cytoreduction surgery (doctor removes as much tumour as possible, usually followed by chemotherapy), chemotherapy

docs.title: Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — hepatocellular carcinoma — Oesophageal & Gastric Disorders
docs.text:
- RISK FACTORS: Hep B/C, haemochromatosis, cirrhosis, EtOH, smoking, DM, [note: statins are protective]
- HISTORY: chronic liver disease Sx, upper abd pain, weight loss, early satiety
- EXAMINATION: palpable liver mass, jaundice
- INVESTIGATIONS
- Bloods- FBC, LFTs, EUC
- Screening with AFP + ultrasound
- CT chest/abdo with contrast
- Percutaneous biopsy + histology: only when uncertain, risk of spreading tumour along needle track
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: cavernous haemangioma, focal nodular hyperplasia, adenoma (all benign neoplasms), metastatic liver disease (from CRC, but also lung, breast, gall bladder, pancreas, ovary, uterus, kidney, prostate)
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT
- Resection for patients with: solitary HCC confined to the liver, no radiographic evidence of invasion of hepatic vasculature, no evidence of portal hypertension, well-preserved hepatic function
- Other treatment options include liver transplant, radiofrequency ablation, transarterial chemoembolisation
- COMPLICATIONS: paraneoplastic (hypoglycaemia, hyperCa2+, erythrocytosis, watery diarrhoea), metastases to lung/intra-abd lymph nodes/bone/adrenal gland/brain (in order), intraperitoneal bleeding due to tumour rupture
- PROGNOSIS: freq diagnosed late due to absence of Sx2 thus following diagnosis median survival ~ 6-20 months

docs.title: Small & Large Bowel Disorders
docs.h: Gastroenterology Master Notes — Small & Large Bowel Disorders

docs.title: Small & Large Bowel Disorders
docs.text:
**Malabsorption** presents with steatorrhoea, weight loss, and deficiency states (iron/folate → anaemia; B₁₂; fat-soluble vitamins; osteomalacia). Causes span mucosal (coeliac, Crohn's), luminal (pancreatic insufficiency, bile-salt deficiency), and structural (short bowel, bacterial overgrowth).

**⚑ Coeliac disease** — T-cell-mediated sensitivity to **gliadin (gluten)** → **villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intraepithelial lymphocytes** in the **proximal small bowel** (hence **iron/folate** deficiency). Associations: **dermatitis herpetiformis** (itchy extensor vesicles — IgA, treat with dapsone), type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid, **IgA deficiency**, Down syndrome. Long-term risk: osteoporosis, hyposplenism, and **enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL)** / small-bowel adenocarcinoma.
- **Serology:** **anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA (anti-tTG) + total IgA** (to catch IgA deficiency → then use IgG-based tests). Endomysial antibody (EMA) is confirmatory. **Must be tested while eating gluten.**
- **⚑ Diagnosis:** historically duodenal **biopsy** (villous atrophy) was mandatory in adults. Current guidance now supports a **"no-biopsy" diagnosis in adults** with **anti-tTG ≥10× the upper limit of normal** *plus* a positive EMA on a second sample (mirroring the established paediatric ESPGHAN pathway) — otherwise biopsy still confirms. **HLA-DQ2/DQ8** has high negative predictive value (absence largely excludes coeliac).
- Treatment: **lifelong gluten-free diet**; pneumococcal vaccination (hyposplenism).

Other malabsorption: **bile-salt malabsorption** (terminal ileal disease → watery diarrhoea, SeHCAT test, treat with colestyramine); **small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO)** (hydrogen breath test, rotating antibiotics); **tropical sprue**; **Whipple's disease** (*Tropheryma whipplei* — arthralgia, weight loss, diarrhoea, PAS-positive macrophages).

docs.title: Small & Large Bowel Disorders
docs.text:
**Crohn's disease vs ulcerative colitis — the core discriminators:**

| Feature | **Crohn's disease** | **Ulcerative colitis** |
|---|---|---|
| Distribution | **Mouth → anus**, any part; **skip lesions**; terminal ileum classic | **Colon only**, from **rectum** proximally, **continuous** |
| Depth | **Transmural** | **Mucosa/submucosa** |
| Histology | **Non-caseating granulomas**, cobblestoning | Crypt abscesses, goblet-cell depletion |
| Smoking | **Worse** with smoking | **Protective** (paradox) |
| Complications | **Strictures, fistulae, abscesses, perianal disease**, B₁₂ malabsorption, gallstones | **Toxic megacolon**, higher **colorectal cancer** risk |
| Antibodies | ASCA+ | pANCA+ |
| Surgery | Not curative (recurs at anastomoses) | Colectomy is **curative** of the colitis |

**Shared extraintestinal manifestations** — some track disease activity, some don't:

| Manifestation | Note |
|---|---|
| Enteropathic **arthritis** (peripheral) | Tracks gut activity |
| **Erythema nodosum** | Tracks activity |
| **Pyoderma gangrenosum** | Independent of activity |
| Anterior **uveitis / episcleritis** | Eye |
| **Primary sclerosing cholangitis** | Strongly linked to **UC**; independent of activity |
| Sacroiliitis / ankylosing spondylitis | HLA-B27-linked |

**Assessing acute severe UC — Truelove & Witts** (severe = **>6 bloody stools/day** plus any systemic feature: temp >37.8°C, HR >90, Hb <105 g/L, ESR >30). This is a **medical emergency**: admit, IV fluids, **IV hydrocortisone**, VTE prophylaxis, stool chart, daily AXR (watch for **toxic megacolon**: transverse colon >6 cm — high perforation risk). Rescue therapy (**infliximab** or ciclosporin) if no response by **day 3**; **colectomy** if failing. Investigate: **faecal calprotectin** raised, endoscopy + biopsy, exclude infection/*C. difficile*.

**Medical management (⚑ the therapeutic landscape has expanded):**
- **UC:** topical/oral **5-ASA (mesalazine)** for mild–moderate (induction + maintenance); corticosteroids for flares; step up to **biologics** (anti-TNF infliximab/adalimumab/golimumab, anti-integrin **vedolizumab**, anti-IL-12/23 **ustekinumab**, anti-IL-23 **mirikizumab**), **JAK inhibitors** (**tofacitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib**) and **S1P modulators** (**ozanimod, etrasimod**).
- **Crohn's:** 5-ASAs are less effective; use **budesonide/steroids** to induce, **thiopurines/methotrexate** and **biologics** (anti-TNF, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab) to maintain; **smoking cessation** is essential.

docs.title: Small & Large Bowel Disorders
docs.h: 5.3 Irritable bowel syndrome and functional disorders
docs.text: A **positive diagnosis** (not just exclusion): **Rome IV** — recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week over 3 months, related to defecation and/or a change in stool frequency/form; subtypes IBS-C/-D/-M. **Exclude red flags** (age >50 new symptoms, weight loss, PR bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, family history of bowel cancer/IBD, anaemia) — check **FBC, CRP, coeliac serology, and faecal calprotectin** (normal in IBS). Management: education/reassurance, diet (**low-FODMAP** with dietitian), fibre adjustment, antispasmodics, and symptom-directed drugs (loperamide, laxatives, low-dose tricyclics, linaclotide).

docs.title: Small & Large Bowel Disorders
docs.h: 5.4 Diverticular disease and other colonic conditions
docs.text:
**Diverticulosis** (herniation of mucosa through the muscle wall at vessel points, commonest **sigmoid**; from low-fibre diet/raised intraluminal pressure) → **diverticular disease** (symptomatic) → **acute diverticulitis** (inflammation/infection: LIF pain, fever, raised inflammatory markers — "**left-sided appendicitis**"). Diagnose acutely with **CT**; classify complicated disease by **Hinchey** (I abscess→ IV faeculent peritonitis).
- **⚑ Management shift:** for **uncomplicated** acute diverticulitis in a systemically well patient, **antibiotics are no longer routinely required** (NICE NG147) — analgesia, fluids and review. Antibiotics/admission for complicated disease (abscess → drainage; perforation/peritonitis → surgery, e.g. Hartmann's).
- Complications: abscess, perforation, fistula (**colovesical → pneumaturia/faecaluria**), stricture, and **lower GI bleeding**.

**Other colonic conditions:** **angiodysplasia** (arteriovenous malformations, painless bleeding/iron deficiency, right colon, associated with aortic stenosis — Heyde's); **ischaemic colitis** (splenic-flexure watershed, "thumbprinting" on AXR, usually settles); **microscopic colitis** (chronic watery diarrhoea, normal endoscopy, abnormal biopsy — collagenous/lymphocytic; drug-associated, e.g. PPIs/NSAIDs); **radiation enteritis**.

docs.title: Small & Large Bowel Disorders
docs.text:
Nearly all arise via the **adenoma–carcinoma sequence** (APC → KRAS → p53). **Hereditary syndromes** (worth spotting):

| Syndrome | Genetics | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| **FAP** | APC (AD) | **Hundreds–thousands of polyps**, ~100% cancer → prophylactic colectomy; **Gardner** variant (osteomas, desmoids) |
| **Lynch (HNPCC)** | Mismatch-repair genes (AD) | Fewer polyps, **right-sided**, younger; also endometrial/others; **Amsterdam criteria** |
| Peutz–Jeghers | STK11 | Hamartomas + **mucocutaneous pigmentation** |
| MUTYH-associated polyposis | MUTYH (AR) | Polyposis |

**⚑ Screening (England):** **FIT (faecal immunochemical test)** home kit every **2 years**, now offered from **age 50 to 74** (the programme has been extended down from 60 to 50 — fully rolling out across the over-50s from 2025). A positive FIT → **colonoscopy**. In symptomatic patients, **FIT is also used to triage** urgent referral.

**Presentation by side:** **left-sided/rectal** → change in bowel habit, PR bleeding, obstruction, tenesmus; **right-sided** → **iron-deficiency anaemia**, weight loss, occult bleeding, later obstruction (wider lumen). **Any iron-deficiency anaemia in a man or post-menopausal woman is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise.**

**Referral/diagnosis:** 2-week-wait for red-flag features (FIT-supported); **colonoscopy + biopsy**; stage with **CT chest/abdomen/pelvis + MRI rectum** (rectal cancer) + CEA baseline. **Staging: TNM** (has largely replaced Dukes' — ⚑; Dukes A confined to bowel wall → D distant metastases). Management: **surgical resection** (the only cure) ± neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (rectal) + adjuvant chemotherapy (node-positive); palliative chemo/biologics for metastatic disease.

---

docs.title: Small & Large Bowel Disorders
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Villous atrophy + iron/folate deficiency + dermatitis herpetiformis | **Coeliac disease** |
| Coeliac first-line serology | **Anti-tTG IgA + total IgA** (on gluten) |
| Adult no-biopsy coeliac criteria | **tTG ≥10× ULN + positive EMA** ⚑ |
| PAS-positive macrophages, arthralgia, weight loss | **Whipple's disease** |
| Skip lesions, transmural, granulomas, perianal disease | **Crohn's** |
| Continuous colitis from the rectum, crypt abscesses | **Ulcerative colitis** |
| Smoking **protective** | **Ulcerative colitis** |
| IBD strongly linked to PSC | **Ulcerative colitis** |
| Truelove & Witts severe UC threshold | **>6 bloody stools/day + a systemic feature** |
| Transverse colon >6 cm in acute UC | **Toxic megacolon** |
| UC rescue therapy if no response by day 3 | **Infliximab or ciclosporin** |
| Positive diagnostic criteria for IBS | **Rome IV** |
| Normal calprotectin, red-flags excluded, pain + habit change | **IBS** |
| "Left-sided appendicitis" | **Acute diverticulitis** |
| Uncomplicated diverticulitis + systemically well | **No routine antibiotics** ⚑ |
| Pneumaturia/faecaluria | **Colovesical fistula** (diverticular) |
| Painless colonic bleeding + aortic stenosis | **Angiodysplasia (Heyde's)** |
| Thousands of polyps, APC gene | **FAP** |
| Right-sided cancer, young, MMR genes, endometrial risk | **Lynch (HNPCC)** |
| Bowel-cancer screening test + age (England) | **FIT, 2-yearly, age 50–74** ⚑ |
| Iron-deficiency anaemia in an older man | **Colorectal cancer until proven otherwise** |

##### Sources
Robbins & Cotran (IBD, coeliac, colorectal neoplasia); NICE NG151 (coeliac — no-biopsy adult pathway ⚑), NG147 (diverticular disease — antibiotics ⚑), NG12/DG56 (colorectal cancer, FIT), ECCO/BSG IBD guidance (biologics/JAK/S1P ⚑); UK NSC / NHS bowel-cancer screening (age-50 extension ⚑); Merck Manual Professional. Coeliac no-biopsy criteria, diverticulitis antibiotics, IBD advanced therapies, and screening age all flagged ⚑ and cross-checked against current NICE/BSG/NSC guidance.

docs.title: Small & Large Bowel Disorders
docs.h: General Surgery & Gastroenterology (ANU) — boerhaave’s syndrome — Small & Large Bowel Disorders
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: spontaneous transmural oesophageal perforation
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: Very rare, 50-70 y/o, more common in males
- AETIOLOGY: Iatrogenic (endoscopy/paraoesophageal surgery), repeated/forceful retching/vomiting, forceful swallowing
- PATHOGENESIS:
- Excessive intraluminal pressure leads to tear
- Most frequent site in the left posterolateral aspect, 3-5cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction
- Overlying pleura can also tear 🡪 mediastinum/pleural cavity are contaminated with oesophageal contents
- Left chest is affected more than right chest
- DIAGNOSIS
- History: severe chest/neck/upper abd. pain, Hx of severe retching/vomiting, other causes of ↑ intrathoracic pressure, hematemesis not typically seen; dysphagia/odynophagia over time (+ patient deterioration)
- Examination: Obs (↓ grade fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, dyspnoea, ↓BP), Hamman sign (air escapes into the mediastinum 🡪 heart beating against air-filled tissues🡪 mediastinal crunch)
- INVESTIGATIONS
- Oesophogram: If perforation in abdomen, use gastograffin (barium causes peritonitis); if perforation above diaphragm, use barium (gastrograffin causes pneumonitis)
- CT chest: With thoracic perforations, mediastinal widening and pleural effusion with or without pneumothorax
- DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES: MI, pancreatitis, lung abscess, pericarditis, spontaneous pneumothorax
- TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT: NBM, broad-spectrum IV ABx, IV PPI, drainage of fluid collections/debridement of infected & necrotic tissue, surgical consultation
- INDICATIONS FOR SURGERY: diffuse extravasation, extension of perforation, clinical deterioration (persistent fevers/sepsis), progression of pneumomediastinum/pneumothorax, empyema
- COMPLICATIONS: septicaemia, mediastinitis, massive pleural effusion, empyema, pneumothorax, sepsis, abscess
- PROGNOSIS: Dependent on early recognition and appropriate intervention (Within 24 hours= ~75% survival rate)
