docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.h: Haematology & Oncology Notes — Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
*Sources: Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; BSH guidelines (ITP, TTP, VTE, DIC, massive haemorrhage, transfusion); NICE NG158 (VTE), NG89; AABB 2023/2025 red-cell transfusion guidelines; SHOT (Serious Hazards of Transfusion) reports; StatPearls. Scope: the bleeding and clotting disorders, anticoagulation, and the transfusion medicine a finalist must manage acutely. TTP and the ABO transfusion reaction are emergencies — flagged throughout.*

---

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
Distinguish two bleeding phenotypes at the bedside — it points straight at the mechanism:

| Feature | **Platelet-type** (primary haemostasis) | **Coagulation-type** (secondary haemostasis) |
|---|---|---|
| Bleeding site | **Mucocutaneous** — petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, menorrhagia, gums | **Deep** — haemarthroses, muscle haematoma, retroperitoneal |
| Timing | Immediate after injury | **Delayed** (plug forms then fails) |
| Causes | Thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, VWD | Haemophilia, DIC, warfarin, liver disease |

Then read the **coagulation screen** (PT/APTT/fibrinogen/platelets — see Section 3.4) to localise the defect.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
Low platelets arise from **reduced production** (marrow failure/infiltration, drugs, alcohol, B12/folate), **increased destruction** (immune/consumption), or **sequestration** (hypersplenism).

**Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)** — isolated thrombocytopenia, autoantibody-mediated. Children: post-viral, acute, self-limiting. Adults: chronic; secondary to SLE, CLL, HIV, *H. pylori*. Diagnosis of exclusion (normal film otherwise, no other cause). **Treat only if bleeding or platelets very low** — first-line **corticosteroids ± IVIG**; second-line TPO-receptor agonists (eltrombopag/romiplostim), rituximab, splenectomy.

**Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)** ⚑ — **a haematological emergency.** Deficiency of **ADAMTS13** (the VWF-cleaving protease; autoantibody in acquired form) → ultra-large VWF multimers → platelet-rich microthrombi → **microangiopathic haemolysis**. The **pentad** (rarely all present): **MAHA (schistocytes) + thrombocytopenia + neurological signs + renal impairment + fever.** **Coagulation screen is normal** (unlike DIC). **Do NOT give platelet transfusions** (fuels thrombosis) unless life-threatening haemorrhage. Treatment is **urgent plasma exchange** + steroids (± caplacizumab, rituximab).

**Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)** — MAHA + thrombocytopenia + **acute kidney injury**, predominantly in **children after Shiga-toxin *E. coli* O157 (bloody diarrhoea)**; renal-dominant, neurology usually milder. Mainly supportive; **avoid antibiotics** in typical STEC-HUS (may increase toxin release). Atypical HUS (complement dysregulation) → eculizumab.

**Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)** — IgG antibodies to **platelet factor 4–heparin** complexes, 5–10 days after starting heparin (sooner if re-exposed); a **fall in platelets >50% + paradoxical thrombosis** (not bleeding). Use the **4Ts score**. Management: **stop all heparin, start a non-heparin anticoagulant** (argatroban, danaparoid, fondaparinux); **do not give platelets**; warfarin only once platelets recover.

**Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)** — systemic activation of coagulation (sepsis, malignancy — esp. **APL**, obstetric, trauma) consuming clotting factors and platelets → simultaneous **bleeding and thrombosis**. Labs: **↓platelets, ↑PT + ↑APTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑↑D-dimer, schistocytes.** Treat the **cause**; supportive component replacement (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate) only if bleeding.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
**Haemophilia** — **X-linked recessive**, so affects males; deep bleeding (haemarthroses, muscle bleeds). **A** = factor **VIII** deficiency (commoner); **B** ("Christmas disease") = factor **IX**. **Isolated prolonged APTT, normal PT/platelets/VWF.** Severity tracks factor level (<1% severe). Treat with **factor concentrate/recombinant factor** (or emicizumab prophylaxis for haemophilia A); desmopressin for mild A. Avoid IM injections/NSAIDs.

**Von Willebrand disease (VWD)** — **the commonest inherited bleeding disorder**; autosomal (usually dominant). VWF does two jobs — platelet adhesion **and** carrying factor VIII — so it causes **mucocutaneous (platelet-type) bleeding** and can prolong the APTT (low factor VIII). Type 1 (partial quantitative, commonest), 2 (qualitative), 3 (complete). Treat with **desmopressin (DDAVP)** ± VWF-containing concentrate; tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeds.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
**Virchow's triad** underlies venous thromboembolism (**DVT/PE**). Risk factors: surgery/immobility, malignancy, pregnancy/oestrogen, previous VTE, and **inherited/acquired thrombophilias**:

| Inherited | Acquired |
|---|---|
| **Factor V Leiden** (commonest; APC resistance) | **Antiphospholipid syndrome** |
| Prothrombin G20210A | Malignancy |
| Protein C / protein S / antithrombin deficiency | Pregnancy, oestrogens, nephrotic syndrome |

**Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)** — arterial **and** venous thrombosis, **recurrent miscarriage**, thrombocytopenia; antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein-I). Paradox: **prolonged APTT in vitro but thrombotic in vivo.** Long-term **warfarin** (DOACs are inferior in triple-positive/arterial APS ⚑); aspirin + LMWH in pregnancy.

**Diagnosis of VTE:** risk-stratify (Wells score) → **D-dimer** to exclude if low probability → **Doppler USS** (DVT) or **CTPA** (PE; V/Q if contrast contraindicated). **Provoked** (transient risk factor) vs **unprovoked** VTE guides duration. **Cancer-associated thrombosis** — historically LMWH; **⚑ DOACs (edoxaban, apixaban, rivaroxaban) are now first-line for most, with caution in GI/GU tumours** (bleeding).

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
| Drug | Target | Monitoring | Reversal ⚑ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Unfractionated heparin** | Antithrombin → IIa & Xa | **APTT** (or anti-Xa) | **Protamine sulfate** |
| **LMWH** (enoxaparin) | Antithrombin → mainly Xa | Usually none (anti-Xa if renal/pregnancy/extremes of weight) | Protamine (partial) |
| **Warfarin** | Vitamin-K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X | **INR** | **Vitamin K**; **PCC** (Prothrombin Complex Concentrate) for major bleeding; FFP if PCC unavailable |
| **Dabigatran** | Direct thrombin (IIa) | None routine | **Idarucizumab** |
| **Apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban** | Direct factor **Xa** | None routine | **Andexanet alfa** (or PCC) |

Key safety points: **warfarin is teratogenic** (use LMWH in pregnancy); it has an **initial procoagulant effect** (protein C falls first) → bridge with heparin/LMWH when starting for acute thrombosis; countless interactions (CYP450). **DOACs** are renally cleared (avoid/reduce in severe renal impairment) and are **contraindicated in antiphospholipid syndrome (triple-positive) and mechanical heart valves** ⚑ (warfarin only there).

---

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
**ABO** is the critical system — antibodies are **naturally occurring IgM** and cause immediate intravascular haemolysis if mismatched. **Group O = universal red-cell donor; group AB = universal recipient. Group AB plasma is the universal plasma (FFP) donor** (opposite of red cells). **RhD**: RhD-negative patients can form anti-D after exposure → matters in transfusion and in **pregnancy (haemolytic disease of the newborn; give anti-D prophylaxis).**

**Pre-transfusion testing:** **Group & save** (ABO/RhD + antibody screen, no unit assigned) for possible need; **crossmatch** (units physically/electronically matched) when transfusion is likely. Emergency: **O-negative** (or group-specific) blood before crossmatch completes.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
| Component | Contains | Main indication |
|---|---|---|
| **Red cells** | RBCs | Symptomatic anaemia / significant blood loss |
| **Platelets** | Platelets | Thrombocytopenic bleeding or prophylaxis (e.g. <10 ×10⁹/L, or pre-procedure) |
| **Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)** | All clotting factors | Bleeding + coagulopathy (↑PT/APTT), DIC, warfarin reversal only if PCC unavailable |
| **Cryoprecipitate** | Fibrinogen, VWF, VIII, XIII | **Low fibrinogen** (<1.5 g/L, or <2 in obstetric haemorrhage), DIC |

**Restrictive transfusion is the default.** For **most haemodynamically stable inpatients, transfuse at Hb <70 g/L**, aiming for **70–90 g/L**; use **<80 g/L** for patients with **chronic cardiovascular disease** or post-cardiac surgery. **⚑ Exception — acute coronary syndrome/acute MI:** the **2025 AABB guideline now suggests a more liberal strategy (transfuse to keep Hb around 80–100 g/L)**, a shift from the older uniform restrictive threshold, based on the MINT trial and meta-analyses; this remains an area where sources differ, so state both the general restrictive rule and the acute-MI exception. Transfuse **one unit at a time and reassess** in non-bleeding patients.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
**Acute (within 24 h):**

| Reaction | Mechanism | Recognition | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Acute haemolytic (ABO incompatibility)** ⚑ | IgM against wrong ABO group — usually a **clerical error** | Fever, loin/back pain, hypotension, dark urine, DIC — **during** transfusion | **STOP immediately**, resuscitate (fluids), check identity, inform lab; can be fatal |
| **Febrile non-haemolytic** | Anti-leucocyte antibodies/cytokines | Isolated fever/rigors | Slow/stop, antipyretic; usually continue cautiously |
| **Allergic / urticarial** | Antibodies to donor plasma proteins | Itch, urticaria | Antihistamine, slow rate |
| **Anaphylaxis** | Often **IgA deficiency** with anti-IgA | Hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema | STOP, adrenaline, resuscitate |
| **TACO** (circulatory overload) | Volume overload | **Hypertension**, dyspnoea, raised JVP, pulmonary oedema | Slow/stop, **diuretics, O₂**, sit up |
| **TRALI** | Donor anti-leucocyte antibodies → pulmonary capillary leak | **Hypotension**, dyspnoea, bilateral infiltrates within 6 h | STOP, respiratory support; report |
| **Bacterial contamination** | Contaminated unit (esp. platelets, stored at room temp) | High fever, rigors, shock | STOP, cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics |

**TACO vs TRALI** — both cause acute dyspnoea/pulmonary oedema during/after transfusion; **TACO is hypertensive and fluid-overloaded (responds to diuretics); TRALI is hypotensive with normal filling pressures (do not diurese, support ventilation).**

**Delayed:** delayed haemolytic reaction (days later, falling Hb, positive DAT), transfusion-associated GvHD (irradiate products for at-risk patients), iron overload (chronic transfusion), post-transfusion purpura.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
**Major haemorrhage protocol** — activate for loss of one blood volume in ~24 h or rapid ongoing loss. Give **red cells, FFP and platelets in a balanced ratio** (empirically ~1:1:1 until guided by results), replace **fibrinogen (cryoprecipitate) if <1.5 g/L**, give **tranexamic acid** (early, especially in trauma — CRASH-2), keep the patient warm, and correct calcium (citrate chelation), acidosis and coagulopathy (the "lethal triad": hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy). Reverse anticoagulants (PCC for warfarin, specific agents for DOACs). Obstetric and trauma haemorrhage have dedicated pathways.

---

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Mucocutaneous bleeding + immediate | Platelet-type (thrombocytopenia/VWD) |
| Deep/delayed bleeding (haemarthrosis) | Coagulation-type (haemophilia) |
| MAHA + thrombocytopenia + neuro + renal + fever, **normal clotting** | TTP (ADAMTS13) — plasma exchange, **no platelets** ⚑ |
| MAHA + AKI in a child after bloody diarrhoea | HUS (STEC O157) |
| Platelets ↓>50% + thrombosis 5–10 days into heparin | HIT — stop heparin, non-heparin anticoagulant |
| ↓platelets + ↑PT/APTT + ↓fibrinogen + ↑↑D-dimer | DIC |
| Commonest inherited bleeding disorder | Von Willebrand disease |
| Isolated ↑APTT, X-linked, haemarthrosis | Haemophilia (A = VIII, B = IX) |
| Thrombosis + miscarriage + ↑APTT that won't correct | Antiphospholipid syndrome — warfarin (not DOAC) ⚑ |
| Universal red cell donor / universal plasma donor | O red cells / AB plasma |
| Default restrictive transfusion threshold | Hb <70 (80 if cardiac disease) |
| Acute-MI transfusion target ⚑ | More liberal (~80–100 g/L) per 2025 AABB |
| Fever + loin pain + shock during transfusion | Acute haemolytic (ABO) — STOP, resuscitate |
| Hypertensive pulmonary oedema post-transfusion | TACO — diurese |
| Hypotensive bilateral infiltrates <6 h | TRALI — support, don't diurese |
| Anaphylaxis to transfusion | Consider IgA deficiency |
| Warfarin major-bleed reversal | Vitamin K + PCC |
| Dabigatran / factor Xa DOAC reversal | Idarucizumab / andexanet alfa |
| Antidote to heparin | Protamine sulfate |

##### Sources
Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; BSH guidelines (ITP, TTP/ADAMTS13, HIT, DIC, VTE, transfusion, massive haemorrhage); NICE NG158 (VTE) and NG89; **AABB 2023 red-cell transfusion thresholds and 2025 AABB acute-MI guideline** (the liberal-threshold shift, MINT trial); SHOT reports (reaction epidemiology); StatPearls. ⚑ The acute-MI transfusion target and DOAC-first cancer-associated thrombosis reflect changes from older textbooks; sources still differ on the MI target (restrictive vs liberal), so both are stated.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
The commonest cancers (UK/Australia): **breast, prostate, lung, bowel** dominate incidence; **lung** remains a leading cause of cancer death. **Screening** targets common cancers with a detectable pre-clinical phase and effective early treatment:

| Programme (UK) ⚑ | Population | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **Breast** | Women ~50–71, every 3 years | Mammography |
| **Bowel** | ~50/60–74 (varies by nation) | **FIT (faecal immunochemical test)** home kit ± colonoscopy |
| **Cervical** | Women 25–64 | **Primary HPV testing** (cytology if HPV+) ⚑ |

(Australia mirrors these: **BreastScreen** 50–74, **National Bowel Cancer Screening** with iFOBT 50–74, **Cervical Screening** 25–74 with 5-yearly primary HPV.) **Prostate has no national screening programme** (PSA's poor specificity). **Lung-cancer low-dose CT screening** for high-risk ever-smokers is being rolled out ⚑.

**Prevention:** smoking cessation (lung, bladder, head & neck, oesophagus), HPV vaccination (cervical, anal, oropharyngeal), hepatitis B vaccination (HCC), alcohol/obesity reduction, sun protection (melanoma). **Hereditary predisposition** worth recognising: **BRCA1/2** (breast, ovarian, prostate, pancreatic), **Lynch/HNPCC** (colorectal, endometrial — MMR genes), **FAP** (APC — colorectal), **Li–Fraumeni** (TP53 — sarcoma, breast, brain), **MEN** syndromes, **retinoblastoma (RB1)**.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Diagnosis needs **tissue** (Section 3.5). **Staging** describes extent — **TNM** (Tumour, Node, Metastasis) → stage groups I–IV — while **grade** describes differentiation (how abnormal the cells look). Both feed prognosis alongside **performance status** and molecular markers. **Urgent (2-week-wait) referral** pathways (NICE NG12) route red-flag presentations quickly.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- **Surgery** — the main curative modality for localised solid tumours; also diagnostic, palliative (bypass, fixation), and reconstructive.
- **Radiotherapy** — ionising radiation damaging tumour DNA. **Radical** (curative), **adjuvant** (post-op), **neoadjuvant** (shrink pre-op), **palliative** (bone pain, cord compression, SVCO, bleeding). Toxicity is **acute** (mucositis, skin erythema, diarrhoea — inflammation of the irradiated field) vs **late** (fibrosis, stricture, second malignancy). Brachytherapy = internal source.
- **Systemic anticancer therapy** — reaches disseminated disease (see 8.4).

**Treatment intent:** **neoadjuvant** (before primary treatment), **adjuvant** (after, to kill micrometastases), **radical/curative**, or **palliative** (symptom control, prolong life). Naming the intent is expected in every oncology answer.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
| Class | Examples | Mechanism | Signature toxicity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cytotoxic chemotherapy** | (see Section 11) | Damage DNA/mitosis of dividing cells | Myelosuppression, alopecia, mucositis, N&V, infertility |
| **Targeted small molecules** | Imatinib, erlotinib/osimertinib (EGFR), TKIs | Block specific driver kinases | Rash, diarrhoea (mechanism-specific) |
| **Monoclonal antibodies** | Rituximab (CD20), trastuzumab (HER2), bevacizumab (VEGF), cetuximab (EGFR) | Block surface targets/ligands | Infusion reactions; trastuzumab cardiotoxicity; bevacizumab bleeding/HTN |
| **Immunotherapy — checkpoint inhibitors** ⚑ | Pembrolizumab/nivolumab (PD-1), atezolizumab (PD-L1), ipilimumab (CTLA-4) | Release the brakes on T cells | **Immune-related adverse events (irAEs)** — colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies |
| **CAR-T cell therapy** ⚑ | For refractory B-cell malignancies | Engineered autologous T cells | **Cytokine release syndrome (CRS)**, neurotoxicity |
| **Hormonal therapy** | Tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors, GnRH agonists, anti-androgens | Block hormone-driven growth | Menopausal symptoms, bone loss, thromboembolism (tamoxifen) |

**Immunotherapy is the major recent shift** — checkpoint inhibitors have transformed melanoma, lung, renal and many other cancers, but their toxicity is **autoimmune** and can affect any organ; management is steroids/immunosuppression and holding the drug, not the usual chemo supportive care. ⚑

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
**Cancer pain — WHO analgesic ladder:** non-opioid (paracetamol/NSAID) → weak opioid (codeine) → strong opioid (morphine), with adjuvants (dexamethasone, gabapentinoids for neuropathic pain, bisphosphonates for bone pain). Anticipate and prescribe for **constipation** (co-prescribe laxatives with opioids), **nausea**, and breakthrough pain (~1/6 of the 24-h dose). Learn basic **opioid conversion** (e.g. oral→subcut morphine divide by 2; morphine→oxycodone roughly divide by 1.5–2). **Anticipatory/end-of-life prescribing:** subcut morphine (pain/dyspnoea), midazolam (agitation), haloperidol/levomepromazine (nausea/agitation), hyoscine/glycopyrronium (secretions). Involve palliative care early; recognise the dying patient and address holistic (psychological, spiritual, family) needs.

docs.text:
Commonest cancer in women. Presentation: painless lump, nipple change/discharge, skin tethering/peau d'orange, axillary node. **Triple assessment** = **clinical exam + imaging (mammography/USS) + core biopsy** — the exam mantra. Types: **ductal (commonest) vs lobular**; in-situ (DCIS) vs invasive. **Receptor subtypes drive treatment ⚑:**

| Subtype | Marker | Treatment lever |
|---|---|---|
| **ER/PR positive** | Hormone receptor + | **Endocrine therapy** (tamoxifen pre-menopause; aromatase inhibitor post-menopause) |
| **HER2 positive** | HER2 amplified | **Anti-HER2** (trastuzumab, pertuzumab) |
| **Triple-negative** | ER−/PR−/HER2− | Chemotherapy (± immunotherapy/PARP inhibitor if BRCA); worst prognosis |

Management combines **surgery** (wide local excision + radiotherapy, or mastectomy) with **sentinel lymph node biopsy**, ± adjuvant chemo/radio/endocrine/anti-HER2. **BRCA1/2** carriers: earlier onset, higher risk, consider risk-reducing surgery and **PARP inhibitors**. Spread: bone, lung, liver, brain.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
Leading cancer killer; strongly smoking-related. Presentation: cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, recurrent pneumonia, or a paraneoplastic/metastatic syndrome. **Two big groups:**

**Non-small cell (NSCLC, ~85%)** — adenocarcinoma (commonest, including non-smokers), squamous (central, cavitating, **PTHrP → hypercalcaemia**), large cell. **⚑ Molecular panel guides targeted therapy in adenocarcinoma:** **EGFR** (osimertinib), **ALK** and **ROS1** rearrangements (targeted TKIs), **KRAS G12C** (sotorasib/adagrasib), **BRAF, MET, RET, NTRK**; **PD-L1** expression guides immunotherapy. Test every advanced non-squamous NSCLC.

**Small cell (SCLC, ~15%)** — central, aggressive, early metastasis, strongly smoking-related; **neuroendocrine** origin → **paraneoplastic syndromes** (SIADH, ectopic ACTH → Cushing's, **Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome**). Rarely surgical; chemo ± immunotherapy ± radiotherapy.

**Paraneoplastic map (high-yield):** **squamous → PTHrP (hypercalcaemia)**; **small cell → SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert–Eaton**; any → clubbing/HPOA, hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy. **Pancoast tumour** (apex) → Horner's syndrome + arm/brachial-plexus symptoms. **Mesothelioma** — pleural malignancy from **asbestos** (long latency); pleural plaques, effusion.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Third commonest cancer. Adenocarcinoma via the **adenoma–carcinoma sequence** (APC → KRAS → TP53). Risk: age, IBD, diet, **FAP** (hundreds of polyps, APC — near-100% cancer risk, prophylactic colectomy) and **Lynch/HNPCC** (MMR genes; also endometrial). Presentation by side: **left/rectal** → change in bowel habit, PR bleeding, tenesmus, obstruction; **right** → occult bleeding/**iron-deficiency anaemia**, mass. **Screening: FIT** (see 8.1). Diagnosis: colonoscopy + biopsy; staging CT + MRI rectum + **CEA** baseline. Treatment: surgical resection ± adjuvant chemo (FOLFOX); rectal cancer often neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy. **⚑ Molecular:** **RAS/BRAF** status (anti-EGFR **cetuximab** only works in **RAS wild-type**); **MMR/microsatellite-instability (MSI-high)** predicts immunotherapy response and flags Lynch. Spread: **liver** (portal drainage) → lung.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
**Prostate** — commonest male cancer; adenocarcinoma of the peripheral zone. Often asymptomatic (screen-detected) or LUTS/bone pain (**osteoblastic** mets → bone scan). **PSA** raised but non-specific (BPH, prostatitis, catheter, DRE). **Gleason score / ISUP grade groups** grade aggressiveness; risk stratification guides active surveillance vs radical prostatectomy/radiotherapy vs **androgen deprivation therapy (ADT)** for advanced disease.

**Renal cell carcinoma** — "internist's tumour": haematuria, flank pain, mass (triad is late); **paraneoplastic** (polycythaemia via EPO, hypercalcaemia, hypertension, Stauffer's syndrome); left varicocele (renal vein). Surgery; TKIs/immunotherapy for advanced.

**Bladder** — **painless visible haematuria** is bladder cancer until proven otherwise (cystoscopy). Mostly **transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma** (smoking, aromatic amines/dye/rubber; squamous with schistosomiasis). TURBT ± intravesical BCG/chemo, or cystectomy.

**Testicular** — commonest solid cancer in **young men (20–40)**; painless testicular lump. **Seminoma** vs **non-seminomatous germ cell tumours**. **Markers:** **AFP + β-hCG** (raised in NSGCT; **AFP is NOT raised in pure seminoma**), LDH. Spreads to **para-aortic nodes**. Highly curable (orchidectomy + platinum-based chemo).

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- **Oesophageal** — **adenocarcinoma** (lower third; GORD/Barrett's/obesity — rising ⚑) vs **squamous** (upper two-thirds; smoking, alcohol). Progressive dysphagia + weight loss. Poor prognosis.
- **Gastric** — adenocarcinoma; *H. pylori*, smoking, diet, pernicious anaemia; **Virchow's node**, Sister Mary Joseph nodule, Krukenberg (transcoelomic to ovary). Signet-ring/linitis plastica.
- **Pancreatic** — ductal adenocarcinoma (head): **painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss** (Courvoisier: palpable non-tender gallbladder + jaundice → not gallstones), new diabetes, thrombophlebitis migrans (Trousseau). **CA 19-9**. Usually advanced at diagnosis; Whipple if resectable.
- **Hepatocellular carcinoma** — on a background of **cirrhosis (hepatitis B/C, alcohol, NAFLD)**; **AFP**; surveillance USS in cirrhosis. Treatment by liver function/stage (resection, transplant, ablation, TACE, systemic).

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- **Ovarian** — presents **late** with vague bloating/abdominal distension/early satiety; **CA-125**; **epithelial** (commonest), linked to **BRCA**; risk with age, nulliparity, ovulation. Surgery + platinum chemo ± PARP inhibitors (BRCA).
- **Endometrial** — **post-menopausal bleeding** is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise (TV-USS endometrial thickness → hysteroscopy + biopsy); oestrogen-driven (obesity, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen, PCOS, Lynch). Usually early-stage, good prognosis.
- **Cervical** — **HPV (16/18)**-driven squamous (and adeno); post-coital/intermenstrual bleeding; prevented by **HPV vaccination + screening** ⚑.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.h: 9.7 Skin, CNS, head & neck, unknown primary
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- **Melanoma** — UV/sun exposure; the **ABCDE** rule (Asymmetry, Border, Colour, Diameter >6 mm, Evolving). Prognosis by **Breslow thickness** (depth). **⚑ BRAF V600 mutation** → BRAF/MEK inhibitors; checkpoint immunotherapy has transformed advanced disease. Spreads widely (including brain).
- **Non-melanoma skin cancer** — **basal cell carcinoma** (commonest, "rodent ulcer", rolled pearly edge, rarely metastasises) vs **squamous cell carcinoma** (can metastasise; arises in sun-damaged skin/actinic keratosis).
- **CNS** — primary **gliomas** (glioblastoma — poor prognosis) and meningiomas, but **metastases are the commonest brain tumours** (lung, breast, melanoma, renal, colorectal); present with headache (worse in morning/on lying), seizures, focal deficit, raised ICP.
- **Head & neck** — squamous cell; smoking/alcohol, and rising **HPV-positive oropharyngeal** cancer (better prognosis).
- **Carcinoma of unknown primary** — metastatic cancer with no identifiable primary despite workup; treat by immunohistochemistry-guided likely origin.

---

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: **The most important oncology emergency.** Definition (NICE CG151): a patient on anticancer treatment with **neutrophils ≤0.5 ×10⁹/L** (some use ≤1.0 with expected fall) **and either temperature >38°C or other signs/symptoms of clinically significant sepsis.** **Management is time-critical: broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam) within 1 hour — the "door-to-needle" rule — BEFORE waiting for the neutrophil count or imaging.** Full sepsis-six/cultures, assess with the **MASCC score** to identify low-risk patients. Never delay antibiotics. ⚑

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Massive tumour-cell breakdown (spontaneous or on starting treatment) in **high-turnover cancers — Burkitt lymphoma, ALL, high-grade lymphomas, bulky disease**. The metabolic quartet: **↑potassium, ↑phosphate, ↑urate → ↓calcium** (and AKI from urate/phosphate crystals). **Cairo–Bishop** criteria classify laboratory vs clinical TLS. **Prevent** in at-risk patients: **IV hydration** + **allopurinol** (lower risk) or **rasburicase** (higher risk/established TLS — recombinant urate oxidase; **contraindicated in G6PD deficiency**). Treat hyperkalaemia; avoid calcium unless symptomatic; renal support if needed.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Vertebral metastasis/collapse compressing the cord — **breast, lung, prostate, myeloma, renal**. Red flags: **new/progressive back pain (worse lying/coughing), a sensory level, limb weakness, bladder/bowel dysfunction.** **⚑ Management (NICE NG234): give dexamethasone 16 mg immediately, arrange whole-spine MRI as soon as possible and within 24 hours, and deliver definitive treatment (surgical decompression or radiotherapy) as soon as possible and within 24 hours.** Nurse flat with neutral spine alignment until stability assessed. Outcome depends on treating **before** paraplegia is established — act on suspicion.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Obstruction of SVC flow — commonly **lung cancer, lymphoma**. Facial/neck/arm swelling, distended veins, plethora, dyspnoea, headache; **Pemberton's sign** (facial congestion on raising the arms). Usually subacute but can be an emergency (airway/cerebral oedema). Investigate with CT; treat with corticosteroids, **endovascular stenting** (fast relief), and treat the underlying tumour (radiotherapy/chemo depending on histology — get tissue if feasible first).

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Commonest life-threatening metabolic complication of cancer. Mechanisms: **PTHrP** (squamous lung/head-neck, renal, breast — humoral), **osteolytic** bone metastases/myeloma, and **calcitriol** production (lymphoma). "**Bones, stones, groans, psychic moans**" + polyuria/dehydration. Management: **aggressive IV 0.9% saline rehydration** first, then an **IV bisphosphonate** (zoledronic acid) — or **denosumab** if refractory/renal impairment; treat the cancer. (Calcium-axis physiology cross-referenced from the endocrine build.)

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- **Raised ICP / brain metastases** — headache, vomiting, papilloedema, focal signs, seizures; **dexamethasone** for vasogenic oedema, urgent imaging, neurosurgery/radiotherapy.
- **Catastrophic haemorrhage** (e.g. carotid blowout, tumour erosion) — often a palliative event; crisis medication.
- **Chemotherapy extravasation** — a vesicant leaking into tissue; stop infusion, aspirate, agent-specific antidote/cold or warm compress.
- **Immunotherapy toxicity (irAEs)** ⚑ — checkpoint-inhibitor colitis/pneumonitis/hepatitis/hypophysitis; recognise and treat with **corticosteroids** (not standard anti-infective/supportive care), hold the drug.

---

docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Bowel-cancer screening test ⚑ | FIT (faecal immunochemical test) |
| Cervical screening primary test ⚑ | HPV testing |
| BRCA cancers | Breast, ovarian, prostate, pancreatic |
| Lynch cancers | Colorectal + endometrial (MMR) |
| Breast triple assessment | Exam + imaging + core biopsy |
| Breast subtype dictating anti-HER2 therapy | HER2-positive |
| Triple-negative breast + BRCA drug | PARP inhibitor |
| NSCLC adenocarcinoma targets ⚑ | EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS-G12C, PD-L1 |
| Squamous lung paraneoplastic | PTHrP → hypercalcaemia |
| Small cell lung paraneoplastic trio | SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert–Eaton |
| Pancoast tumour signs | Horner's + arm/brachial plexus |
| Asbestos pleural malignancy | Mesothelioma |
| Anti-EGFR (cetuximab) works only if… | RAS wild-type colorectal |
| Painless obstructive jaundice + palpable gallbladder | Pancreatic head cancer (Courvoisier) |
| Painless visible haematuria | Bladder cancer until proven otherwise |
| Young man, painless testicular lump, AFP+βhCG | Testicular (AFP not raised in seminoma) |
| Post-menopausal bleeding | Endometrial cancer until proven otherwise |
| Late bloating + CA-125 | Ovarian cancer |
| Melanoma prognosis measure / target ⚑ | Breslow thickness / BRAF V600 |
| Commonest brain tumour overall | Metastasis |
| Neutropenic sepsis rule ⚑ | Antibiotics within 1 h, before counts/imaging |
| TLS electrolytes | ↑K, ↑PO₄, ↑urate, ↓Ca |
| Rasburicase contraindication | G6PD deficiency |
| MSCC management ⚑ | Dex 16 mg + whole-spine MRI ≤24 h + treatment ≤24 h |
| Facial swelling + Pemberton's sign | SVCO |
| Hypercalcaemia of malignancy first step | IV saline then bisphosphonate |
| Checkpoint-inhibitor colitis/pneumonitis treatment ⚑ | Corticosteroids, hold drug |

##### Sources
NICE NG12 (suspected cancer/2-week-wait), **NG234 (spinal metastases/MSCC — 16 mg dexamethasone, MRI & treatment within 24 h)**, **CG151 (neutropenic sepsis — ≤0.5 neutrophils + fever/sepsis, antibiotics within 1 h)**, tumour-specific NICE guidelines; Cancer Research UK & NHS/Australian screening programmes; AJCC/TNM 8th edition; ESMO/NCCN (NSCLC molecular panel, colorectal RAS/MMR, melanoma BRAF); BSH TLS guideline (Cairo–Bishop, rasburicase); Robbins; StatPearls. ⚑ Molecular panels, immunotherapy/irAEs, FIT and primary-HPV screening, and low-dose-CT lung screening reflect current practice beyond older textbooks; screening ages/intervals vary between UK nations and Australia (both sets given).

| DEFINITION | Neoplasm in the stomach |
| --- | --- |
| EPIDEMIOLOGY | 50-59 y/o, M>F |
| AETIOLOGY | Compensatory epithelial cell proliferation via gastric atrophy (H.Pylori gastritis, pernicious anaemia, previous partial gastrectomy)Host-related (blood type A, HNPCC, hereditary diffuse gastric carcinoma HDGC, gastric adenomatous polyps)Environmental (smoking, EtOH, smoked/salted food) |
| PATHOGENESIS | Gastric dysplasia 🡪 gastric adenocarcinoma 🡪 early cancer limited to the mucosa + submucosa, regardless of lymph node status 🡪 malignant epithelial tumour, originating from glandular epithelium of the gastric mucosa |
| CLASSIFICATION | Intestinal type: irregular tubular structures (frequently ulcerative) 🡪 intestinal metaplasia commonly in lesser curvature of antrumDiffuse type: poorly/un-differentiated + lacking gland formation 🡪 infiltrate gastric wall 🡪 secretes mucous into interstitium 🡪 large pools of mucous/colloid in tumour cell 🡪 pushes to nucleus to periphery 🡪 Signet Ring Cell |
| PRESENTATION | Clinical suspicion Ulcer fails to healLesion on greater curvature of stomach/cardiaInsidious onset + late presentationPost-prandial abdominal fullnessVague epigastric painAnorexiaConstitutional symptomsBurpingN/VDyspepsiaDysphagiaHepatomegaly/epigastric massHematemesisFecal occult bloodMelena, iron-deficiency anaemiaMetastasis: distal lymph nodes, peritoneum, Krukenburg ovarian, liver, lung, brain |
| EXAMINATION | Palpable abdominal mass, ascitesSigns of metastases- Virchow’s node (left supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph’s node (periumbilical), Irish node (left axillary), Blumer’s shelf (mass in pouch of Douglas), Krukenberg tumour (metastases to ovary)Less commonly, Acanthosis nigricans (thickening and darkening of skin, particularly in axilla) or Leser-Trelat sign (seborrhoeic keratoses all over skin) |
| INVESTIGATIONS | Upper GI endoscopy + biopsyEUSImmunohistochemistry (HER2)CT chest, abdomen and pelvis or PET scan- looks for metastases |
| STAGING | TNM system used to classify cancer into rudimentary stagesStage 0 – limited to inner lining of stomachStage I – second or third layers of stomach (1A) or to second layer and nearby lymph nodes (1B)Stage II – second layer and more distant lymph nodes, to the third layer with nearby lymph nodes, or all four layers with no lymph nodesStage III – third layer and more distant lymph nodes, or to fourth layer and nearby tissues and lymph nodesStage IV – spread to nearby tissues and more distant lymph nodes, or metastasised to other organs |
| DIFFERENTIALS | PUD, benign polyp |

| DEFINITION | Neoplasia of the colon or rectum |
| --- | --- |
| EPIDEMIOLOGY | 3rd most common cancer, ~70 y/o median age |
| AETIOLOGY | Genetic factors Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP): autosomal dominant affecting APC gene with ↑polyps usually in rectumHereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch) – type I predominant colorectal cancer; type II involves other cancers especially uterine, ovarian and breastPredisposing conditions: adenomas, IBD, DM, acromegaly, FHxEnvironmental factors: increased weight, ↑ energy intake, ↑inactivity, smoking, ETOH) |
| COLORECTAL POLYP | Polyp: protuberance into the lumen of normally flat colonic mucosaTubular polyps (69-80%)- small <2 cm, pedunculated, lower malignant potential, even distribution, easier to removeVillous polyps (10%)- large > 2cm, sessile, higher malignant potential, left-sided predominance |
| PATHOGENESIS | Dysplastic adenomatous polyps + inactivation of tumour-suppressor and DNA repair genes + activation of oncogenes → cells gains advantage in growth without apoptosis → adenocarcinoma (95% of case) ![](notes/images/oncology-anu/img017.jpg) |
| PRESENTATION |  | Right Colon (25%) | Left Colon (35%) | Rectum (30%) |
| Information | Asymptomatic Weakness, weight loss, occult blood loss, mucusUlcerating lesions 🡪 chronic, insidious blood loss without a change stool appearance | Constipation ± overflow diarrhea, hematochezia, abd cramps, mucusStool more formed, thus tumours tend to impede its passage 🡪 cramps, obstruction, perforation | Constipation ± overflow diarrhea, tenesmus, hematochezia, mucus, pseudo-diarrhea |
| Signs | Fe deficiency anemia, RLQ mass (uncommon) | Bright blood on PR, LBO | Palpable mass, bright blood on PR |

EXAMINATION

GI exam (signs of anaemia, palpable abd mass, increased liver span in metastases, Virchow’s node, DRE mass/bloody stool on glove)

INVESTIGATIONS

- FBC, Carcinogenic embryonic antigen (CEA) to monitor response of Tx
- FOBT (sensitive, not specific, cheap)
- CT chest/abd/pelvis, colonoscopy (allows for biopsy for histological analysis
- Air contrast barium enema (“apple core” lesion) + sigmoidoscopy
- Pelvic MRI/endorectal US for rectal cancer
- Coags/stool OCP & MCS in active bleeding
- LFTs for metastases

TUMOUR STAGING

Duke’s staging is no longer used 🡪 **TNM staging used**

TREATMENT

- LOCAL EXCISION OR SURGICAL RESECTION: min 12 regional lymph nodes for staging, aim for adequate margins of excision, entails division of blood vessels, ileocolic + middle colic vessels, branches of the superior mesenteric R ant hemicolectomy – caecum, ascending colon and proximal 1/3 of transverse colon, with anastomosis

- Ant resection – resection of rectosigmoid colon, with anastomosis
- Hartmann’s procedure – resection of rectosigmoid colon with closure of rectal stump and end colostomy
- Abdomino-peritoneal resection – carcinomas in the distal

docs.text:
| EPIDEMIOLOGY | Most common endocrinological malignancyW>FMedian age of diagnosis is 40 – 45 years |
| --- | --- |
| TYPES | Papillary Thyroid cancerTissue of origin: thyrocytesEpidemiology: most common type of thyroid cancer (~80% of cases), 30-50 y/o peak incidenceDifferentiation: well-differentiatedAetiology: associated with RET/PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations; ionising radiationFeatures: lymphatic metastasis (often detected first), may be multi-focalCytology: psammoma bodies, “orphan annie” eyes nuclei, nuclear groovesPrognosis: most identified in early stages and have excellent prognosis (>90% at 5-years) |
| Follicular thyroid cancerTissue of origin: thyrocytesEpidemiology: ~10% of cases, 40-60 y/o peak incidenceDifferentiation: well-differentiatedGenetics: associated with PAX8-PPAR-γ rearrangement and RAS mutationCytology: uniform follicles, vascular/capsular invasionFeatures: haematogenous metastasis to lung/bone, rarely multifocal, vascular/capsular invasionDifficult to diagnose by FNA because distinction between benign and malignant follicular neoplasms rests largely on evidence of invasion into vessels, nerves, or adjacent structuresPrognosis: less favourable (in comparison) as most patients present with stage IV disease |
| Anaplastic thyroid cancerTissue of origin: thyrocytesEpidemiology: ~1-2% cases; >60 year old peak incidenceDifferentiation: poorly differentiated, aggressive cancerFeatures: rapid local growth, lymphatic and haematogenous metastasisPrognosis: poor and most patients die within 6 months of diagnosis |
| Thyroid lymphomaOften arises in the background of Hashimoto’s thyroiditisRapidly expanding thyroid mass |
| Medullary thyroid cancerTissue of origin: parafollicular C cellsEpidemiology: <10% of cases; 50-60 y/o peak incidenceCytology: ovoid cells of C cell origin, amyloid in the stromaFeatures: sometimes a genetic predisposition to multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) in 25% or it can be sporadic (in 75%)Prognosis: 50% survival rate at 5 years |
| RISK FACTORS | History of head and neck irradiationIodine deficiency |
| PRESENTATION | Early symptoms: rare noticeable; firm/painless thyroid nodules	Late symptomsIncreased nodule size (>4cm)Vocal cord paralysis → hoarse voiceHorner’s syndromePossible SVC obstructionDyspnoeaDysphagiaPalpable thyroid nodule – hard in consistencyCervical lymphadenopathy |
| INVESTIGATIONS | Serum TSH: usually normalSerum calcitonin: high in medullary cancerFine-needle biopsy and cytology studyI-123 thyroid scan and uptake: ↓ tracer uptake suggests a malignant non-functioning (cold) noduleUltrasound: hypoechoic thyroid lesions with irregular margins > 1 cm; microcalcificationsStaging: CXR, abdominal U/S, neck CT/MRT, bone scan/PET scan, familial screening |
| MANAGEMENT | Total/radical thyroidectomyPapillary or follicular: radioactive iodine ablation 4-6 weeks post-surgery, hemithyroidectomy in papillary is sufficient, TSH suppression with high-dose levothyroxine

docs.h: Oncology (ANU) — ovarian cancer — Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
| Aetiology | Genetic predisposition: BRCA 1/2 mutation, HNPCC syndrome, Peutz-Jegher’s Syndrome, Lynch II (colon, breast, endometrium, ovary)Hormonal imbalance and menstrual cycle: ↑ number of lifetime ovulations, infertility, early menarche, late menopause, PCOSProtective factors: OCP, pregnancy/breast-feeding, salpingectomy, BSO |
| --- | --- |
| Epidemiology | Second most common gynaecological cancerMedian age of diagnosis is in the 60sMost patients are diagnosed at stage III or IV65% epithelial (hereditary predisposition) and 35% non-epithelial |
| Pathology | Epithelial | ~70% of malignant ovarian tumoursThese may be benign, malignant or borderlineCytadenoma/cystadenocarcinoma: serous is most aggressive type, frequently bilateral, psammoma bodies are typicalMucinous: 75% benignEndometroid: associated with  endometriosis or endometrial cancerClear cell |
| Germ Cell | Teratoma: Dermoid cyst (90%) and can contain any type of tissue (e.g. hair, teeth)Strume ovarri (endometrial differentiation into thyroid tissue, very rare, may produce thyroxine)ImmatureDysgerminoma: histologically equivalent to male seminomaYolk sac tumour: childhood/adolescenceNon-gestational choriocarcinoma: rare, extremely malignant, normally accompanied by b-HCF production |
| Sex-cord-stromal | Oestrogen-producing: granulosa/theca cell tumourAndrogen-producing: Sertoli-Leydic cell tumour (very rarely)Ovarian fibroma: benign, can cause Meig’s syndrome |
| Metastases | 10-15%GI tract, breast or endometrial cancer are primary tumours often found in ovariesKrukenberg tumour: bilateral ovarian metastases from an undifferentiated gastric carcinoma |

**Presentation**

- Early features: are vague and ill-defined
- Pelvic mass/pain
- Ascites
- Early satiety

- Nausea/vomiting
- Change in bowel habits
- Pleural effusion
- Sister-Mary-Joseph nodule:  palpable lymph node

**Investigations**

- CA-125 levels: elevated in 80% of cases; useful in tracking progression of the disease and the response to treatment
- Tumour markers: Ca-125 in endothelial, AFP in yolk sac, B-HCG in non-gestational choriocarcinoma, inhibin B in granulosa cell tumour
- CT : “omental caking”; abnormal thickening of greater omentum
- Transvaginal ultrasound (gold standard): malignant tumours have irregularly thickened septa with indistinct borders and possible free fluid (ascites)
- FNA is contraindicated!

**FIGO Staging**

- I: growth limited to ovaries
- II: growth involving one or both ovaries with pelvic extension or primary peritoneal cancer
- III: tumour involving one or both ovaries with peritoneal implants outside the pelvic and/or positive retroperitoneal nodules
- IV: distant metastasis beyond peritoneal cavity

**Management**

- Early: hysterectomy, BSO, excision of peritoneum/lymph nodes/omentum
- Advanced disease
- Surgical debulking
- Chemotherapy: indicated in all pts as adjuvant therapy; carboplatin ± paclitaxel are first line
- Radiotherapy: rarely used

- Definition: single temperature of

- 38.3 or 38+ lasting an hour
- Presence of neutrophil count <0.5/109/l and or

- Investigations: FBC, EUCs, LFTs, blood cultures, CXR, UA, cultures

docs.h: Oncology (ANU) — Hypercalcaemia — Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- Definition: >2.6mmol/L, in 10-20% advanced cancers (breast, kidney, lung, prostate, head/neck, multiple myeloma)
- Epidemiology: most common oncological emergency
- Osteolytic hypercalcaemia: direct bone invasion → osteoclast activating factor → bone resorption
- Paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia: tumour cells secrete PTHrP which induces bone resorption
- Clinical presentation: nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, disorientation (stones, bones, groans, psychiatric overtones)
- Investigations: biochemistry (PTH), ECG, bone scan, PET-CT
- Management:

- Hydration + diuresis: 1-2L isotonic saline over 2 hours with 30-40mg of frusemide (expand intravascular volume + enhance calcium excretion)
- Bisphosphonates: inhibit osteoclasts e.g. Zolendronic acid (4mg infusion in 100mls NS over 15 mins), ibandronate (6mg/2 hour infusion or 50mg PO daily), pamidronate (90mg IV over 1-2 hours). These drugs may cause osteonecrosis of jaw following dental procedures so ensure dental work first
- RANKL inhibitor e.g. denosumab 120mg subcutaneous monthly

docs.h: Oncology (ANU) — Superior vena cava syndrome — Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- Definition: obstruction of flow through SVC due to extrinsic compression (lung cancer, lymphomas, other) or intrinsic compression (thrombosis associated with central venous devices)
- Obstructed flow: venous collaterals from azygos, internal mammary, lateral thoracic, paraspinous, oesophageal venous systems – central venous pressures stay elevated
- Clinical presentation: dyspnoea, headache, oedema/change in colour in areas drained, venous distension of neck/upper chest/arms, cough, Pemberton’s sign
- Diagnosis: CXR (mediastinal widening), CT CAP with contrast, tissue Dx
- Treatment:
- Supportive: head elevation, glucocorticoids (dex 4mg q6h), loop diuretics
- Definitive: radiotherapy to malignant mass, chemo if sensitive, SVC stent, removal of central venous device

docs.h: Haematology & Oncology Notes — Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
*Sources: Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; Guyton & Hall Physiology; Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease; StatPearls. Scope: the foundational biology that the clinical sections lean on — haematopoiesis, red/white cells, haemostasis, the hallmarks of cancer, and the marrow/lymphoreticular anatomy. Anatomy is written as prose + tables and paired with the anatomy SVG sheet.*

---

docs.title: Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
All blood cells derive from a single **pluripotent haematopoietic stem cell (HSC)** in the bone marrow, defined by two properties: **self-renewal** and **multipotency**. The HSC divides into a **common myeloid progenitor** (→ red cells, granulocytes, monocytes, platelets) and a **common lymphoid progenitor** (→ B, T and NK cells). **This myeloid/lymphoid fork is the single most useful anatomy in haematology** — it is the backbone of leukaemia and lymphoma classification.

**Sites of haematopoiesis across life** — a migration you should be able to recite:

| Stage | Primary site |
|---|---|
| 0–2 months (embryo) | Yolk sac |
| 2–7 months (foetus) | **Liver & spleen** |
| 5 months → birth → adult | **Bone marrow** |
| Adult | Axial skeleton + proximal femora/humeri (red marrow); peripheral long bones convert to yellow (fatty) marrow |

**Extramedullary haematopoiesis** (reversion to hepatic/splenic production, causing hepatosplenomegaly) is a red flag for chronic marrow stress — thalassaemia, myelofibrosis, severe chronic haemolysis. On the film it shows as a **leukoerythroblastic picture**: nucleated red cells + immature myeloid cells + tear-drop cells spilling into the blood. *Clue → cause:* leukoerythroblastic film → **marrow infiltration** (malignancy, myelofibrosis) until proven otherwise.

**Key growth factors** (each maps to a drug):

| Factor | Made by | Drives | Therapeutic analogue |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Erythropoietin (EPO)** | Renal peritubular cells (in response to hypoxia via HIF) | Red cell production | Epoetin/darbepoetin (renal anaemia) |
| **Thrombopoietin (TPO)** | Liver | Platelet production | Romiplostim, eltrombopag (ITP) |
| **G-CSF** | Endothelium, macrophages | Neutrophil production | Filgrastim (post-chemo neutropenia, stem-cell mobilisation) |

docs.title: Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
Erythropoiesis takes ~7 days: pronormoblast → normoblast (extrudes its nucleus) → **reticulocyte** (still contains RNA — the marker of active production) → mature biconcave erythrocyte (lifespan ~120 days, no nucleus/mitochondria, relies on glycolysis and the pentose phosphate shunt for reducing power).

**Three raw materials** the marrow needs, each with its own deficiency anaemia: **iron** (haem synthesis; deficiency → microcytic), **B12 and folate** (DNA synthesis; deficiency → megaloblastic macrocytic).

**Haemoglobin** is a tetramer of two α and two β-like globin chains, each cradling a haem (iron + protoporphyrin) that binds one O₂:

| Type | Chains | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **HbA** | α₂β₂ | ~97% of adult Hb |
| **HbA₂** | α₂δ₂ | ~2–3%; **raised in β-thalassaemia trait** |
| **HbF** | α₂γ₂ | Dominant foetal Hb; higher O₂ affinity; persists/rises in β-thalassaemia, sickle cell |

The **oxygen dissociation curve** is sigmoid (cooperative binding). *Right shift* (offloads O₂ to tissues) = ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺/↓pH (Bohr), ↑temperature, ↑**2,3-BPG**. *Left shift* (holds O₂) = the opposites, plus **HbF** and carboxyhaemoglobin. Memory hook: "**exercising muscle is hot, acidic, and CO₂-rich → curve shifts right → O₂ released**."

**Red cell breakdown:** senescent cells are removed by splenic macrophages. Haem → **biliverdin → unconjugated bilirubin** (bound to albumin, water-insoluble); globin recycled; iron recycled. Free plasma Hb is mopped up by **haptoglobin**. This is why **intravascular haemolysis** produces the pattern *↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, ↑unconjugated bilirubin, haemoglobinuria*.

docs.title: Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
| Cell | Lineage | Job | "Goes up with…" |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Neutrophil** | Myeloid | Bacterial/fungal phagocytosis | Bacterial infection, steroids, stress, tissue necrosis |
| **Lymphocyte** | Lymphoid | Adaptive immunity (B→antibody, T→cell-mediated) | Viral infection, CLL, pertussis |
| **Monocyte** | Myeloid | Becomes tissue macrophage; antigen presentation | Chronic infection (TB), CMML |
| **Eosinophil** | Myeloid | Parasites, allergy | **Allergy, parasites, drugs, Hodgkin, EGPA** (mnemonic: NAACP) |
| **Basophil** | Myeloid | Histamine, allergy | **CML** (basophilia is a clue), allergy |

The **differential white cell count** is a diagnostic instrument, not a footnote: a **neutrophilia with left shift** points to bacterial infection; a **lymphocytosis of mature smear cells** points to CLL; **eosinophilia** narrows to allergy/parasites/drugs/Hodgkin/vasculitis; **basophilia** flags a myeloproliferative process.

docs.title: Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
Haemostasis is the balance between clotting and bleeding. Two arms:

**Primary haemostasis (the platelet plug)** — endothelial injury exposes collagen; **von Willebrand factor (VWF)** bridges collagen to platelet **GpIb**; platelets activate, release ADP/thromboxane A₂, and aggregate via **GpIIb/IIIa** cross-linked by fibrinogen. *Disorders here → **mucocutaneous** bleeding: petechiae, epistaxis, menorrhagia, gum bleeding.*

**Secondary haemostasis (the coagulation cascade)** — a protease relay ending in a fibrin mesh. Two entry routes converge on a common path:

| Pathway | Factors | Measured by |
|---|---|---|
| **Extrinsic** ("tissue factor") | VII | **PT / INR** |
| **Intrinsic** ("contact") | XII, XI, IX, VIII | **APTT** |
| **Common** | X, V, II (prothrombin→thrombin), I (fibrinogen→fibrin), XIII (cross-links) | Both |

Memory hooks that pay off constantly: **"PT tests the Extrinsic; use warfarin's INR"** (VII has the shortest half-life, so PT/INR is the first to rise on warfarin). **"APTT tests the Intrinsic — think haemophilia and heparin."** **Vitamin-K-dependent factors = 2, 7, 9, 10 (+ protein C & S)** — the warfarin targets. Factor **VIII is the only clotting factor not made in the liver** (made by endothelium), so it stays normal or high in liver disease.

**Fibrinolysis:** plasminogen → **plasmin** (by tPA) dissolves fibrin, releasing **D-dimer** (a fibrin degradation product — sensitive but not specific for thrombosis).

**Natural anticoagulants** (lose these → thrombophilia): **antithrombin** (inhibits thrombin & Xa — the heparin target), **protein C & protein S** (inactivate factors Va and VIIIa; vitamin-K-dependent). **Factor V Leiden** makes factor V resistant to protein C → commonest inherited thrombophilia.

**Virchow's triad** (why thrombi form): **stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability.** Every VTE risk factor slots into one of the three.

docs.title: Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
Cancer is a genetic disease of somatic cells: a clone acquires mutations that let it proliferate without restraint and spread. The **hallmarks of cancer** (Hanahan & Weinberg) are the exam-friendly organising frame:

- **Self-sufficiency in growth signals** (oncogene activation)
- **Insensitivity to anti-growth signals** (tumour-suppressor loss)
- **Evading apoptosis** (e.g. p53 loss, BCL-2 overexpression)
- **Limitless replicative potential** (telomerase)
- **Sustained angiogenesis** (VEGF — the bevacizumab target)
- **Tissue invasion & metastasis**
- (enabling) **Genome instability** and **tumour-promoting inflammation**
- (emerging) **Deregulated metabolism** (Warburg effect) and **evading immune destruction** (the checkpoint-inhibitor rationale)

**Three gene classes:**

| Class | Normal role | In cancer | Inheritance of mutation | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Oncogene** | Promote proliferation | **Gain of function** — one hit enough (dominant) | Usually somatic | RAS, MYC, HER2, BCR-ABL1 |
| **Tumour-suppressor gene** | Brake proliferation | **Loss of function** — **two hits** (Knudson) | Can be germline (familial cancer) | **TP53** (p53), RB1, APC, BRCA1/2 |
| **DNA-repair gene** | Fix DNA errors | Loss → mutator phenotype | Germline in Lynch, xeroderma | MLH1/MSH2 (Lynch), BRCA |

**Knudson's two-hit hypothesis:** tumour-suppressors need both alleles knocked out. In hereditary cancer syndromes (retinoblastoma, Li–Fraumeni, Lynch, FAP) the person inherits one defective allele, so a single somatic "second hit" causes cancer — explaining younger age and bilateral/multifocal tumours.

**Carcinogenesis is multistep:** *initiation* (irreversible mutation from a carcinogen) → *promotion* (clonal expansion) → *progression* (further mutations, malignant phenotype). Illustrated best by the **adenoma–carcinoma sequence** in colorectal cancer (APC → KRAS → TP53).

**Invasion & metastasis:** loss of E-cadherin, basement-membrane degradation (matrix metalloproteinases), intravasation, survival in the circulation, extravasation at a distant site, angiogenesis. Routes: **lymphatic** (carcinomas typically) vs **haematogenous** (sarcomas, and carcinomas to lung/liver/bone/brain) vs **transcoelomic** (ovarian, gastric → peritoneum, e.g. Krukenberg tumour).

**Paraneoplastic syndromes** — remote effects not due to mass/metastasis, often via ectopic hormone secretion or autoimmunity (SIADH & ectopic ACTH in small cell lung cancer, PTHrP in squamous cancers, Lambert–Eaton). High-yield because they can be the presenting clue.

**Nomenclature** — worth being crisp: **-oma** usually benign (adenoma, lipoma); **carcinoma** = malignant epithelial; **sarcoma** = malignant mesenchymal (bone, muscle, fat); **-blastoma** = embryonal (neuroblastoma); **leukaemia/lymphoma/myeloma** = haematological. Exceptions that are malignant despite "-oma": **melanoma, lymphoma, myeloma, seminoma, glioblastoma.**

---

docs.title: Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
The marrow is the factory. **Red (haematopoietically active) marrow** in adults is confined to the **axial skeleton** — vertebrae, sternum, ribs, pelvis, skull — plus the **proximal femur and humerus**. Peripheral long-bone marrow is **yellow (fatty)** and can reconvert to red under haematopoietic stress. The marrow niche pairs developing cells with stromal cells and sinusoids; only mature cells cross the sinusoidal wall into blood.

**Clinical anatomy:** the standard **bone marrow biopsy site is the posterior superior iliac spine (posterior iliac crest)** — an **aspirate** samples cells for morphology/cytogenetics/flow, while a **trephine** takes a core of intact architecture for cellularity and infiltration. The sternum can be aspirated (not trephined) but is rarely used. A **"dry tap"** (no aspirate obtained) itself suggests **fibrosis (myelofibrosis) or a packed marrow**.

docs.title: Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
Lymph nodes are bean-shaped filters on the lymphatic highways. **Architecture, outside-in:** **cortex** (B-cell follicles with germinal centres) → **paracortex** (T cells) → **medulla** (plasma cells, macrophages). Afferent lymphatics enter the convex surface; a single efferent leaves the hilum. **Reactive lymphadenopathy** expands the germinal centres; **lymphoma** effaces the architecture; **metastatic carcinoma** seeds the subcapsular sinus first.

Lymph ultimately drains to the venous system via the **thoracic duct** (drains everything except the right upper body → left subclavian/IJV junction) and the **right lymphatic duct** (right head, neck, arm, thorax).

**Clinically important node groups:**

| Node | Drains / signals |
|---|---|
| **Cervical** | Head, neck; also lymphoma, nasopharyngeal/thyroid cancer |
| **Supraclavicular — Virchow's node (left)** | **"Troisier's sign"** — GI (gastric), thoracic malignancy via thoracic duct |
| **Axillary** | Breast, upper limb — central to breast-cancer staging (sentinel node) |
| **Inguinal** | Lower limb, perineum, anal canal, vulva |
| **Para-aortic** | Testicular cancer spreads here (testis descends from the abdomen, so drainage is para-aortic, **not** inguinal — a classic exam point) |

*Assessing lymphadenopathy:* rubbery/painless (lymphoma), hard/fixed/matted (carcinoma), tender/mobile (reactive/infective). Generalised lymphadenopathy → think lymphoma/leukaemia, HIV, EBV, TB, sarcoid, connective-tissue disease.

docs.title: Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ, in the **left hypochondrium along the 9th–11th ribs** (so a normal spleen is not palpable). Two functional tissues: **red pulp** (mechanical filter — culls old/abnormal red cells and removes intra-erythrocytic inclusions, "pitting") and **white pulp** (immune surveillance — the body's largest collection of lymphoid tissue, key for opsonising encapsulated organisms).

**Functions:** filtration, immunity (antibody production, filtering encapsulated bacteria), reservoir (platelets — a third of the platelet mass is pooled here), and reactivation of haematopoiesis in disease.

**Hyposplenism / post-splenectomy** — loss of filtration and antibody function → **overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI)** from **encapsulated organisms** (*Strep pneumoniae, H. influenzae b, N. meningitidis*). Hence vaccinate + lifelong prophylactic penicillin. Film clues to hyposplenism: **Howell–Jolly bodies, target cells, Pappenheimer bodies, thrombocytosis.**

**Splenomegaly — the pattern matters.** *Massive* splenomegaly (crosses the midline / reaches the pelvis): **CML, myelofibrosis** (and, worldwide, chronic malaria & visceral leishmaniasis). *Moderate:* portal hypertension, lymphoma, haemolysis. **Hypersplenism** = an enlarged spleen pooling and destroying cells → cytopenias.

docs.title: Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
**Primary lymphoid organs** (where lymphocytes are made and educated): **bone marrow** (B cells mature here; T-cell precursors born here) and the **thymus** (T cells mature — positive/negative selection teaches self-tolerance). **Secondary lymphoid organs** (where they meet antigen): lymph nodes, spleen, MALT (tonsils, Peyer's patches).

The thymus (anterior mediastinum) involutes after puberty. **Thymic pathology is exam-relevant through its associations:** **thymoma** links to **myasthenia gravis**, red cell aplasia, and hypogammaglobulinaemia; the anterior-mediastinal mass differential is the **"4 Ts": Thymoma, Teratoma (germ cell), Thyroid (retrosternal), Terrible lymphoma.**

---

docs.title: Physiology, Cancer Biology & Anatomy
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Leukoerythroblastic film (nucleated RBCs + immature myeloid + tear-drops) | Marrow infiltration/myelofibrosis until proven otherwise |
| Only clotting factor not made in the liver | Factor VIII (endothelium) → normal in liver disease |
| Vitamin-K-dependent factors | II, VII, IX, X (+ protein C & S) |
| Which test rises first on warfarin & why | PT/INR — factor VII has the shortest half-life |
| Commonest inherited thrombophilia | Factor V Leiden (activated protein C resistance) |
| Heparin's natural target | Antithrombin |
| Right-shift of O₂ curve | ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺, ↑temp, ↑2,3-BPG (exercising muscle) |
| Raised HbA₂ | β-thalassaemia trait |
| Two-hit gene class | Tumour-suppressor (Knudson) |
| One-hit, dominant gene class | Oncogene |
| "-oma" words that are actually malignant | Melanoma, lymphoma, myeloma, seminoma, glioblastoma |
| Testicular cancer nodal spread | Para-aortic (not inguinal) |
| Left supraclavicular node + GI cancer | Virchow's node / Troisier's sign |
| Post-splenectomy film | Howell–Jolly bodies, target cells, thrombocytosis |
| Massive splenomegaly (2 haem causes) | CML, myelofibrosis |
| Bone marrow biopsy site | Posterior superior iliac spine |
| "Dry tap" on aspirate | Myelofibrosis / packed marrow |
| Anterior mediastinal mass "4 Ts" | Thymoma, Teratoma, Thyroid, Terrible lymphoma |

##### Sources
Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology (haematopoiesis, haemostasis, red-cell physiology); Guyton & Hall (O₂ dissociation curve, coagulation); Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (hallmarks of cancer, oncogenes/tumour-suppressors, metastasis, Knudson two-hit); StatPearls (splenic function, hyposplenism, marrow anatomy). No threshold disagreements at this foundational level.

| Epidemiology | M>F, peak incidence 50-60 years (middle age to elderly) |
| Aetiology | Idiopathic (most cases), ionising radiation, hydrocarbons (benzene)Philadelphia chromosome found in > 90% |
| Pathophysiology | Reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and 22 → formation of the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) → fusion of ABL and BCR genes on chromosome 22 → BCR-ABL gene → active tyrosine kinase with increased enzyme activity →uncontrolled granulocyte proliferation |

Increasing Basophilia is a sign of acceleration!Blood film: extreme leukocytosis with mid-stage progenitor cellsCytochemistry: ↓leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) → distinguished featureCytogenetics: confirmation of BCR-ABL (Philadelphia chromosome) fusion geneBone marrow: myeloid hyperplasia with left shift, ↑ megakaryocytes, mild fibrosis |

- Benign: adenoma, angiomyolipoma, oncocytoma, hyperdense cysts

docs.h: Rheumatology & Immunology (ANU) — Rheumatoid arthritis — Additional Notes
docs.text:
| Definition | Chronic inflammatory autoimmune disorder characterised by symmetric and erosive synovitis of peripheral joints and extra-articular features |
| --- | --- |
| Epidemiology | F>M, peak incidence ~ 20-40 years |
| Aetiology | Autoimmune disorder of unknown aetiology where there is immune tolerance breakdown → autoreactivity. Hypotheses suggest the following factors:Genetic predisposition: HLA-DR4/DR1 in ~93% of patientsEnvironmental: infections, tobaccoHormonal: improves during pregnancy, worsens after birth |
| Pathophysiology | Initially, non-specific inflammation affects the synovial tissue, which is later amplified by activation of T cells (autoimmune response)With time, inflammatory joint effusion, synovial hypertrophy, and progressive destruction and deterioration of cartilage and bone (with ↑TNF and upregulation of RANK-L) |
| Presentation | COURSES OF DISEASEVariable course of exacerbations and remissions Monocyclic=single episode; polycyclic=relapsing/remitting; progressive patternsARTICULAR MANIFESTATIONSPolyarthritis: symmetric joint involvement (tender, swollen), small joints affected, most commonly in hands and feet (MCP, PIP, MTP but not DIP)Morning stiffness > 1 hour but impreoves with use, worsens with wrest“Rheumatoid hand”: swan neck, boutonniere, Z-line deformity, ulnar deviationHammer/mallet/claw toe: as a result of chornic synovitisAtlanto-axial subluxation: C-spine instability, neurological impingementEXTRA-ARTICULAR MANIFESTATIONSConstitutional: low-grade fever, myalgia, malaise, night sweatsRheumatoid nodules: non-tender, firm, subcutaneous lumps on the skinLungs: pulmonary fibrosis, pleural effusion, pleuritis, pulmonary nodulesEye: keratoconjunctivitis sicca, scleritis, episcleritisEndocrine/exocrine glands: secondary Sjogren syndrome, Xerostomia, Hashimoto’s thyroiditisHaematological: anaemia of chronic diseaseMusculoskeletal: tenosynovitis, bursitis, carpal tunnel syndromeHeart: pericarditis, myocarditis, myocardial infarction, stroke, CHFRenal: amyloidosisVascular: peripheral vasculitis, Raynaud’s, purpura, necrosing fingertips, rheumatoid neuropathy |
| 2010 ACR/EULAR Classification | ![](notes/images/rheumatology-and-immunology-anu/img006.jpg) |

docs.h: Anaphylaxis ⚑ (emergency — highest yield in this section)

docs.title: Anaphylaxis ⚑ (emergency — highest yield in this section)
docs.h: Immunology & Allergy Master Notes — Anaphylaxis ⚑ (emergency — highest yield in this section)
docs.parent: Anaphylaxis ⚑ (emergency — highest yield in this section)
docs.text:
**Definition:** a severe, life-threatening, generalised **Type I** hypersensitivity reaction — sudden onset with rapidly progressing **Airway, Breathing and/or Circulation** problems, usually with skin/mucosal changes.

**Recognition:**

- Sudden onset and rapid progression after exposure (food, drug, insect sting, latex, contrast).
- **A** — swelling, hoarseness, stridor. **B** — wheeze, tachypnoea, fatigue, hypoxia. **C** — hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, collapse.
- ⚑ **Skin/mucosal changes are absent in 10–20% of cases** — their absence does not exclude anaphylaxis.
- ⚑ **Isolated GI symptoms without A/B/C problems do not usually indicate anaphylaxis** (though abdominal pain and vomiting can feature in sting/venom anaphylaxis).

**Immediate management (Resuscitation Council UK 2021):**

1. Remove the trigger if possible (stop the infusion; remove the stinger).
2. **Position** — ⚑ **lie the patient flat** (legs raised if hypotensive), or sit up if breathing is the dominant problem. **Do not stand or walk the patient** — postural change from supine to standing is associated with cardiovascular collapse and death.
3. **IM adrenaline immediately** into the **anterolateral thigh (middle third)** — the single most important intervention, given even if IV access is available.
4. High-flow oxygen, IV fluid bolus for hypotension.
5. **Repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes** if A/B/C problems persist.
6. If refractory after two doses → senior/critical care help, IV adrenaline infusion by an experienced clinician only.

**IM adrenaline doses (1:1000):**

| Age | Resuscitation Council UK dose |
|---|---|
| Adult and child >12 years | **500 micrograms (0.5 mL)** |
| Child 6–12 years | 300 micrograms |
| Child 6 months–6 years | 150 micrograms |
| Child <6 months | 100–150 micrograms |

*(⚑ ANZCOR/ASCIA use a weight-based structure: 0.5 mg if >50 kg and ≥12 years, 0.3 mg for >20 kg/≥5 years, 0.15 mg for 7.5–20 kg — the adult dose agrees; know the local framing. Auto-injectors commonly deliver 300 micrograms, with 500-microgram devices available.)*

**⚑ What has changed from older textbooks:**

- **Corticosteroids are no longer routinely recommended** in the initial management of anaphylaxis — no good evidence they prevent biphasic reactions, and early steroid use may be associated with worse outcomes.
- **Antihistamines are not a treatment for anaphylaxis** — may be used afterwards for cutaneous symptoms only, and must never delay adrenaline.
- **Fixed observation periods have been replaced by risk-stratified observation.**

**Risk-stratified observation after resolution (RCUK 2021 / NICE NG258):**

| Observe for | When |
|---|---|
| **2 hours** | Good response to a single dose of adrenaline, prompt treatment, complete resolution, access to help, adequate supervision |
| **6 hours** | Two doses of IM adrenaline needed, or previous biphasic reaction |
| **12 hours** | >2 doses needed, severe asthma or severe respiratory compromise, possible continuing alle

docs.text:
| Definition | Life-threatening type I hypersensitivity reaction which can lead to distributive shock (circulatory failure) |
| --- | --- |
| Aetiology | Exaggerated immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction that leads to systemic vasoactive mediator release (histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins and smooth muscle reactive chemicals) → increased vascular permeability, and vasodilationAllergic (foods e.g. nuts/shellfish, stings, drugs e.g. penicillin/NSAIDs/ACE-I)Non-allergic (exercise-induced) |
| Presentation | Skin or mucous membranes: flushing, urticaria, pruritus, erythema, swelling of the eyelids, or angioedemaRespiratory: nasal congestion, cough, sneezing, hoarseness, chest tightness, stridordyspnoea (bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema)Cardiovascular: hypotension, tachycardia, chest pain (myocardial ischemia due to hypoxia and hypotension)GI: abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting (especially in food allergies) |
| Criteria for Diagnosis | Acute onset (within 1 hour of exposure) with involvement of the skin, mucosal tissue and at least one of the following: 1) respiratory compromise or 2) hypotension/end-organ dysfunctionLikely exposure to an allergenReduced blood pressure after exposure to a KNOWN allergen |
| Differentials | Septic shock, asthma, angioedema |
| Management | Withdrawal of offending agent if applicable (e.g., in drug reactions)Airway: examination of airway and intubation if obstruction seems imminent (+ “B” and “C”)IM adrenaline (1:1000) 0.3 – 0.5 mg in lateral thighPaediatric dose of adrenaline: 0.01 mg/kg IM up to 0.5mg q5-15minPositioning: The patient should be placed in a recumbent/supine position with elevation of the lower extremitiesO2 by facemaskIf patient is hypotensive: volume replacement with crystalloid (normal saline 1–2 L IV rapid bolus)Bronchospasm and no benefit of adrenaline: nebulized salbutamolAntihistamines (competitive inhibition of histamine at receptor, reducing histamine-mediated effects and symptoms e.g., increased vascular permeability, vasodilation, swelling, pruritus)H1 antihistamine (e.g., diphenhydramine) IV for urticariaH2 antihistamine (e.g., ranitidine) IVHydrocortisone 100mg IV/methylprednisolone 1mg/kg IV x 24 hoursContinuous monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, heart function, and pulse oximetry; urine output should also be monitored in hypotensive patients receiving resuscitation.Monitor for 4-6 hours in ED minimum and arrange follow up within 24-48 hours (educate about potential second biphasic reaction and avoidance of allergens) |

docs.title: Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)
docs.h: Immunology & Allergy Master Notes — Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)
docs.text:
Chronic, intensely pruritic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease, usually beginning in early childhood (onset typically **3–6 months**; affects ~10–15% of children, many improve with age).

**Pathogenesis:** skin barrier dysfunction (⚑ **filaggrin** loss-of-function mutations are a major genetic contributor) plus a **Th2-skewed** immune response with raised IgE.

**Distribution changes with age — the classic exam discriminator:**

| Age | Distribution |
|---|---|
| **Infantile (<2 years)** | Cheeks, face, scalp, **extensor** surfaces (nappy area typically spared) |
| **Childhood (2–12 years)** | **Flexures** — antecubital and popliteal fossae, wrists, ankles, neck |
| **Adult** | Flexures, hands, face/eyelids; lichenification from chronic scratching |

**Associated signs:** Dennie–Morgan infraorbital fold, xerosis, lichenification, post-inflammatory pigment change.

**Complications:** bacterial superinfection (*S. aureus* — weeping, golden crust) and ⚑ **eczema herpeticum** (HSV superinfection — rapidly worsening painful clustered vesicles/punched-out erosions, systemic upset; a dermatological emergency needing **systemic aciclovir**).

**Management ladder:** identify and avoid triggers → **liberal emollients** (the mainstay, used even when clear) → topical corticosteroid of potency matched to site and severity → topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/pimecrolimus) for face/flexures → phototherapy → systemic immunosuppression or biologics (**dupilumab — anti-IL-4Rα**) ⚑ in severe refractory disease.

**Discriminator:** atopic dermatitis = **flexural and itchy**; psoriasis = **extensor, well-demarcated, silvery scale**, onset later; seborrhoeic dermatitis = greasy scale in sebaceous areas (scalp, nasolabial folds).

docs.h: Rheumatology & Immunology (ANU) — PLASMA PROTEINS ASSOCIATED WITH INFLAMMATORY REACTIONS (play a role in innate immunity) — Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)
docs.text:
- ACUTE PHASE PROTEINS: liver releases 30 acute-phase reactants, including CRP, ferritin, fibrinogen, α1-antitrypsin, haptoglobin, procalcitonin, IL-6
- NOTABLE NEGATIVE ACUTE PHASE REACTANTS: albumin, transferrin, anti-thrombin
- COMPLEMENT SYSTEM: after stimulation from Ab-complexes by pathogens → compliment activation →enhance functions of antibodies and phagocytesClassical pathway: IgM or IgG binds to pathogen (via C1)
- Alternative pathway: direct activation by pathogen rather than Ab-Ag complexes (via C3)
- Causes: opsonisation (C3), bacteria lysis (C5-9) and activation of mast cells/granulocytes (C3/C4/C5)

- PRO-INFLAMMATORY CYTOKINESIFN-α: ↑MHC I expression
- IFN-β: stimulates NK cells and cytotoxic
- IFN-γ: activated macrophages
- TNF-α: pyrogenic, cytotoxic, mediates septic shock
- Interleukins: IL-1, 2, 4, 6
- Arachidonic acid derivatives: PGE2/PGI2 increases pain sensation, vasodilation, and inhibits platelet aggregation and  leukotrienes which cause chemotaxis, exudation and bronchoconstriction

docs.h: Rheumatology & Immunology (ANU) — Atopic Dermatitis — Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)
docs.text:
| Definition | Chronic inflammatory and pruritic skin disease that typically manifests in early child hoodOften associated with other atopic diseases e.g. asthma, allergic rhinitis |
| --- | --- |
| Epidemiology | 10-15% of all children are affected with an age of onset between 3-6 months of ageDisease often improves with age |
| Aetiology | Incompletely understoodGENETIC: polygenic inheritance of predisposition for increased IgE formation and sensitisation in which abnormal Th2 response in the skin → cytokine overproduction → excessive IgE production → allergic dermatitisTRIGGERS: dust, heat, dry/humid climates, emotional stress, infections, skin irritation |
| Presentation | Intense pruritis and dry skinINFANTILE AD (<2 YEARS): eczema (cheeks, face, head, extensors), Dennie-Morgan fold (below eye)CHILDHOOD AD (2-12 YEARS): eczema (flexural creases, skin folds, lichenified lesions (thickened skin)ADULT/ADOLESCENT AD (> 12 YEARS): LICHENIFIED lesions and pruritis of flexor surfaces of extremities), nummular eczema (coin-shaped)ASSOCIATED: asthma, allergic rhinitis, xerosis |
| Diagnostic Criteria | Essential: pruritis, eczema (maculopapular, erythematous lesions that can also have scale, crusting, oozing, or blistering)Important features: early age of onset, atopy, xerosis |
| Differentials | Seborrheic dermatitis (usually more greasy lesions), psoriasis (onset in adolescent years) |
| Management | Avoid triggers e.g. pets, dust, mites, pollens, foods, chemical/clothing irritants, heats, stressKeep skin moist with moisturisers and emollients (reduce skin evaporation to ↑ hydration)In severe AD can add topical steroids, calcineurin inhibitors (immunosuppressant), phototherapy (narrow band UVB) or systemic therapy (cyclosporine, azathioprine, methotrexate) |

Autoimmunity

DEFINITION: Immune reaction against the body’s own cells, due to a loss of immunological tolerance

PRESUMED PATHOGENESIS

- Autoreactive B lymphocytes are eliminated in the bone marrow, spleen, or lymph nodes (can be detected)
- T lymphocytes that attack the body's own cells are amended in the thymus or destroyed in peripheral lymphoid tissues (e.g., lymph nodes, adenoids, Peyer's patches) due to a lack of stimulation (usually cannot detect specific antibodies)
- If the selection mechanisms fail, this results in the immune cells attacking the body's own cells

CAUSES

- Previous infection e.g. GBS, RF through molecular mimicry
- Genetic predisposition
