docs.title: Hypersensitivity Reactions (Types I–IV)
docs.h: Immunology & Allergy Master Notes — Hypersensitivity Reactions (Types I–IV)
docs.text:
**Mnemonic — "ACID":** **A**llergic/Anaphylactic (I), **C**ytotoxic (II), **I**mmune complex (III), **D**elayed (IV).

| Type | Mechanism | Timing | Classic examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I — Immediate** | IgE-mediated mast cell/basophil degranulation → histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes | **Minutes** | Anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, atopic asthma, food/drug allergy, urticaria |
| **II — Antibody-mediated (cytotoxic)** | IgG/IgM bind antigen **on a cell surface** → complement activation, lysis or phagocytosis | Hours–days | Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction (ABO), Goodpasture's/anti-GBM, ITP, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, Graves' disease and myasthenia gravis (receptor-stimulating/blocking variants), pernicious anaemia, rheumatic fever |
| **III — Immune complex** | Antibody binds **soluble circulating antigen** → complexes deposit in tissue → complement-driven inflammation | Days–weeks | SLE, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, serum sickness, Arthus reaction, polyarteritis nodosa (HBV) |
| **IV — Delayed, T-cell-mediated** | Pre-sensitised T cells → macrophage activation; **no antibody involved** | **48–72 hours** | Contact dermatitis (nickel), Mantoux/tuberculin test, graft-versus-host disease, type 1 diabetes, granulomatous disease |

**The discriminators that separate them:**

- **Type I vs Type IV** — both can present as a "rash after exposure". Type I is **minutes** and IgE-mediated; Type IV is **48–72 hours** and T-cell-mediated. Contact dermatitis appearing two days after a new watch strap is Type IV.
- **Type II vs Type III** — the question is **where the antigen is**. Type II: antigen is **fixed on a cell/tissue surface**. Type III: antigen is **soluble in the circulation** and the complex deposits later.
- ⚑ Some classifications place Graves' disease in a "**Type V**" (receptor-stimulating) category; most UK/Australian teaching keeps it within Type II — know both framings exist.

**Testing:** skin prick testing and specific IgE for Type I; patch testing for Type IV contact dermatitis. **Discriminator: prick = immediate/IgE; patch = delayed/T-cell.**

docs.title: Innate versus Adaptive Immunity
docs.h: Immunology & Allergy Master Notes — Innate versus Adaptive Immunity
docs.text:
| | Innate | Adaptive |
|---|---|---|
| **Speed** | Immediate (minutes–hours) | Days (needs priming) |
| **Specificity** | Pattern recognition (PAMPs via toll-like receptors) | Antigen-specific receptors |
| **Memory** | None | **Yes — the basis of vaccination** |
| **Components** | Neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells, complement, physical barriers, acute-phase proteins | T cells (cellular), B cells/antibody (humoral) |

**Acute-phase response.** The liver releases **positive** acute-phase reactants — CRP, ferritin, fibrinogen, haptoglobin, α1-antitrypsin, procalcitonin — driven mainly by **IL-6**. **Negative** acute-phase reactants fall: albumin, transferrin, antithrombin. **Discriminator:** a raised ferritin in an inflamed patient is an **acute-phase artefact, not evidence of iron overload** — check transferrin saturation.

**Complement — the three pathways converging on C3:**

- **Classical** — IgM or IgG immune complexes activate via C1.
- **Alternative** — direct activation by pathogen surfaces via C3 (no antibody needed).
- **Lectin** — mannose-binding lectin binds carbohydrate on pathogens.

**Complement functions:** opsonisation (**C3b**), membrane attack complex/cell lysis (**C5–C9**), and anaphylatoxins (**C3a, C4a, C5a**) which activate mast cells and recruit granulocytes.

*(Complement consumption as an SLE activity marker — low C3/C4 in flare — is in the MSK build Section 1.4.)*

**Cytokines worth knowing by name:** IFN-α (↑MHC I expression), **IFN-γ** (activates macrophages — the granuloma cytokine), **TNF-α** (pyrogenic, mediates septic shock), **IL-1** (fever), **IL-6** (acute-phase response). **Arachidonic acid derivatives:** prostaglandins (pain sensitisation, vasodilation) and leukotrienes (chemotaxis, exudation, bronchoconstriction — hence leukotriene antagonists in asthma).

docs.title: Lymphoid Organs and Lymphatic Drainage
docs.h: Immunology & Allergy Master Notes — Lymphoid Organs and Lymphatic Drainage
docs.text:
**Primary** (where lymphocytes mature): bone marrow (B-cell maturation) and thymus (T-cell maturation). **Secondary** (where immune responses are mounted): spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches.

**The lymph node — three zones** (a classic single-mark question):

| Zone | Contains | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Follicle (cortex)** | **B cells** | B-cell localisation and proliferation; germinal centres in active response |
| **Paracortex** | **T cells** | T-cell zone; enlarges in viral infection, underdeveloped in DiGeorge |
| **Medulla** | Reticular cells, macrophages, plasma cells | Communicates with efferent lymphatics |

**Lymphatic drainage — the two-duct rule:** the **right lymphatic duct** drains the right side of the body **above the diaphragm**; the **thoracic duct** drains everything else, emptying at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins. (This is why a left supraclavicular node — **Virchow's node** — signals abdominal malignancy.)

**Spleen.** Splenic macrophages remove encapsulated bacteria opsonised by IgM and complement.

- **Splenic dysfunction** (post-splenectomy, sickle cell autosplenectomy, coeliac disease): ↓IgM → ↓complement activation → ↓C3b opsonisation → susceptibility to encapsulated organisms.
- **Post-splenectomy blood film: Howell–Jolly bodies** (nuclear remnants — the classic finding), target cells, thrombocytosis and lymphocytosis (loss of sequestration).
- **Management:** vaccinate against pneumococcus, Hib, meningococcus (ideally **≥2 weeks pre-splenectomy**), annual influenza, and **lifelong prophylactic penicillin**.

**Thymus.** Anterosuperior mediastinum; immature T cells in the cortex, mature in the medulla. Hypoplastic in **DiGeorge** syndrome and **SCID**. **Thymoma** — associated with **myasthenia gravis** and SVC obstruction.

docs.title: Primary Immunodeficiency — Pattern Recognition
docs.h: Immunology & Allergy Master Notes — Primary Immunodeficiency — Pattern Recognition
docs.text:
The exam skill is **inferring the defective arm of the immune system from the infection pattern**, not memorising rare syndromes.

| Defect | Infection pattern — the giveaway | Typical age at presentation | Named examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **B-cell / antibody (humoral)** | Recurrent **sinopulmonary** infection with **encapsulated** bacteria (*S. pneumoniae*, *H. influenzae*), giardia; enteroviral infections | **After ~6 months** (once maternal IgG wanes) — the timing is the clue | X-linked (Bruton's) agammaglobulinaemia (male, absent B cells, no tonsils/nodes), **CVID** (later onset, autoimmunity and lymphoma risk), **selective IgA deficiency** (commonest primary immunodeficiency; often asymptomatic; ⚑ **anaphylaxis to blood products containing IgA**) |
| **T-cell / cellular** | **Opportunistic and intracellular** infection — PCP, CMV, persistent candidiasis, disseminated BCG/mycobacteria, chronic viral illness; failure to thrive | Early infancy | **DiGeorge** (22q11 deletion) — thymic hypoplasia, hypocalcaemia/tetany, cardiac outflow defects, dysmorphism ("CATCH-22"); **SCID** (both arms — a paediatric emergency) |
| **Phagocyte** | Recurrent **skin and deep abscesses**, poor wound healing, **catalase-positive** organisms (*S. aureus*, *Serratia*, *Aspergillus*, *Burkholderia*) | Early childhood | **Chronic granulomatous disease** (NADPH oxidase defect — ⚑ diagnosed with the **dihydrorhodamine (DHR)** flow cytometry test, historically NBT); **leucocyte adhesion deficiency** (delayed umbilical cord separation, no pus formation) |
| **Complement** | Recurrent ***Neisseria*** infection (meningococcal/gonococcal) with terminal pathway defects; early classical-pathway (C1–C4) deficiency → **SLE-like disease** | Any age | Terminal complement (C5–C9) deficiency; **C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency → hereditary angioedema** |

**Hereditary angioedema — the anaphylaxis mimic worth separating out:** C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency → **bradykinin-mediated** angioedema. **Non-pruritic, non-urticarial** swelling (often facial, laryngeal or abdominal), frequently with a family history, triggered by trauma/dental work or **ACE inhibitors**, and — critically — **does not respond to adrenaline, steroids or antihistamines**. Treatment is **C1-inhibitor concentrate or icatibant** (bradykinin B2 antagonist). **Discriminator:** urticaria and itch point to histamine/anaphylaxis; their absence with recurrent episodic swelling points to bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

**Secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency is far commoner than primary:** HIV, malignancy (especially haematological), iatrogenic (chemotherapy, steroids, biologics, rituximab-induced hypogammaglobulinaemia), malnutrition, splenectomy, chronic renal/liver disease, ageing. **In an adult with recurrent infection, think acquired first.**

**When to investigate for primary immunodeficiency — "SPUR":** **S**evere, **P**ersistent, **U**nusual (opportunistic organism/site), or **R**ecurrent infections; plus f

- TYPES: congenital or acquired (infection, malnutrition, aging, malignancy, iatrogenic e.g. chemo)
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: individual deficiencies are rare

Arthocentesis

- DIAGNOSTIC: determine cause of pain or swelling in the joint
- THERAPEUTIC: removal of excess fluid may help lessen pain and improve antibiotic
- SYNOVIAL FLUID CHARACTERISTIC:
- Crystals: gout (urate), pseudogout (pyrophosphate)
- WCC: bacterial septic; may be slightly elevated in RA, psoaritic and reactive arthritis
- Blood: hemarthrosis from trauma or fracture
- Fat: fracture
- Non-inflammatory: OA

Hypersensivity

- HYPERSENSITIVITY: the immune system, which normally serves a protective role, has a harmful effect. The hypersensitivity reactions can be memorized with the mnemonic ACID: A – Allergic/Anaphylactic/Atopic (Type I); C – Cytotoxic (Type II); I – Immune complex deposition (Type III); D – Delayed (Type IV)
- ALLERGY: abnormal immunological response to an otherwise harmless environmental stimulus
- AUTOIMMUNITY: abnormal immunological response directed against an antigen that is actually part of the body itself

| Management | Supportive: fluid (maintain BP, ↓cerebral perfusion), bed rest, ↑ head of bed, monitor vitalsTreat: IV antibiotics if bacterial, IV acyclovir (10 mg/kg/8h IV over 1h) until HSV encephalitis is ruled outVaccinations after recovery |
| Complications | HSV encephalitis 🏳 has a high mortality rateComplications: stroke, seizures, memory loss, hypothalamic/autonomic dysfunction |

docs.title: Antimicrobial Pharmacology
docs.h: Infectious Disease Master Notes — Antimicrobial Pharmacology

docs.title: Antimicrobial Pharmacology
docs.text:
**Mechanism:** inhibit penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking in the bacterial cell wall → bactericidal.

**Bactericidal vs bacteriostatic** — bactericidal agents kill (cell-wall inhibitors: beta-lactams, glycopeptides; plus aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole); bacteriostatic agents inhibit replication and rely on host immunity. Mnemonic **"ECSTaTIC"**: Erythromycin, Clindamycin, Sulfamethoxazole, Trimethoprim, Tetracyclines, Chloramphenicol. (The distinction matters most in immunosuppression, endocarditis and meningitis, where bactericidal therapy is preferred.)

**CNS penetration:** beta-lactams generally cross into the CNS only when the meninges are inflamed — the exceptions with reliably good CNS penetration are **ceftriaxone and aztreonam** (part of why ceftriaxone is the empirical meningitis agent). Elimination is primarily renal (ceftriaxone is both renal and biliary — hence use without renal dose adjustment).

| Class | Spectrum progression | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Penicillins | Narrow (Gram+) → broader | Benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin, flucloxacillin (anti-staphylococcal, beta-lactamase-stable), piperacillin-tazobactam (broad, antipseudomonal + beta-lactamase inhibitor) | Amoxicillin-clavulanate adds beta-lactamase cover |
| Cephalosporins | Generations broaden Gram-negative cover, generally lose some Gram-positive | 1st gen (cefalexin — Gram+ skin), 3rd gen (ceftriaxone — meningitis, gonorrhoea, broad), ceftazidime (antipseudomonal) | **Enterococcus and Listeria are intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins** |
| Carbapenems | Broadest — Gram+, Gram−, anaerobes | Meropenem, imipenem | Reserve/Watch-tier — for ESBL and severe polymicrobial infection; **not active against MRSA or *E. faecium*** |
| Monobactams | Gram-negative only | Aztreonam | **Safe in severe penicillin allergy** (no cross-reactivity) |

**Beta-lactam allergy — the exam-favourite discriminator:** true cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is **low (~1–2%)**, much lower than historically taught (⚑ the old "10%" figure is outdated) — a documented mild penicillin rash does not contraindicate cephalosporins; **anaphylaxis** to penicillin is the scenario that mandates avoiding all beta-lactams (aztreonam is safe here). Carbapenems have minimal cross-reactivity with penicillins.

docs.title: Antimicrobial Pharmacology
docs.text:
| Class | Target | Examples | Key toxicity/notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aminoglycosides | 30S ribosome | Gentamicin, amikacin | **Nephrotoxic, ototoxic** — narrow therapeutic index, requires level monitoring; synergy with beta-lactams for endocarditis |
| Macrolides | 50S ribosome | Azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin | Atypical cover, QT prolongation, GI upset; CYP3A4 interactions (clarithromycin > azithromycin) |
| Tetracyclines | 30S ribosome | Doxycycline | Atypicals, Lyme, acne; **avoid in pregnancy and children <8** (teeth/bone deposition); photosensitivity |
| Clindamycin | 50S ribosome | — | Anaerobes, **toxin suppression** in necrotising fasciitis/toxic shock; **highest C. difficile risk of any class** |
| Linezolid | 50S ribosome | — | MRSA/VRE cover; **serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs** (weak MAOI), thrombocytopenia with prolonged use |

docs.title: Antimicrobial Pharmacology
docs.text:
| Drug | Mechanism | Key use | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vancomycin (glycopeptide) | Inhibits cell wall synthesis (different site to beta-lactams) | MRSA, C. diff (oral, severe disease) | Nephrotoxic, needs level monitoring; **red man syndrome** if infused too fast (histamine, **not** allergy) |
| Fluoroquinolones | DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV inhibition | Ciprofloxacin (Gram-negative/atypical), levofloxacin (adds pneumococcal cover) | ⚑ **Tendon rupture, aortic aneurysm/dissection risk, QT prolongation** — increasingly restricted; avoid in pregnancy, caution in elderly/steroid use |
| Metronidazole | DNA damage (anaerobic activation) | Anaerobes, C. difficile, protozoa (giardia, amoebiasis, trichomonas) | **Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol** |
| Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) | Folate synthesis inhibition (sequential blockade) | UTI, PCP prophylaxis/treatment, some MRSA | **Hyperkalaemia**, interacts with warfarin/methotrexate |
| Rifampicin | RNA polymerase inhibition | TB, meningococcal/Hib prophylaxis | Potent **CYP450 inducer**, red/orange body fluids |
| Daptomycin | Cell membrane disruption | MRSA/VRE bacteraemia | **Inactivated by pulmonary surfactant — never use for pneumonia** |

docs.title: Antimicrobial Pharmacology
docs.text:
**Antifungals:** azoles (fluconazole — *Candida*; itraconazole/voriconazole — *Aspergillus*; CYP450 interactions), echinocandins (caspofungin — invasive candidiasis, fungal cell wall synthesis), amphotericin B (broad but nephrotoxic, reserved for severe/resistant invasive fungal disease).

**Antivirals:** aciclovir/valaciclovir (HSV/VZV — thymidine kinase-dependent activation), oseltamivir (influenza, neuraminidase inhibitor, most effective within 48h of onset), antiretrovirals (Section 4).

docs.title: Antimicrobial Pharmacology
docs.text:
Now the global standard for antimicrobial stewardship and increasingly examined directly:

- **Access** — narrow-spectrum, first/second-line for common infections, low resistance potential (amoxicillin, flucloxacillin, gentamicin, doxycycline, nitrofurantoin). WHO/UN target: **≥60–70% of antibiotic use should be Access-tier by 2030**.
- **Watch** — higher resistance potential or reserved for specific syndromes (ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, macrolides, vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam). Use judiciously.
- **Reserve** — last-resort for confirmed/suspected multidrug-resistant infection (colistin, linezolid, newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor combinations for carbapenem-resistant organisms). Requires ID/microbiology input in most settings.

docs.title: Antimicrobial Pharmacology
docs.text:
Four core mechanisms — every resistant organism uses at least one:

1. **Enzymatic inactivation** — beta-lactamases (**ESBL** — hydrolyses most penicillins/cephalosporins, often still susceptible to carbapenems; **AmpC** — inducible, hydrolyses cephalosporins including some 3rd-gen; **carbapenemases** — CRE).
2. **Target modification** — altered PBP (**MRSA** — *mecA* gene, altered **PBP2a**), altered ribosomal target (macrolide resistance), altered DNA gyrase (fluoroquinolone resistance), altered vancomycin target (**VRE**).
3. **Efflux pumps** — actively pump the drug out (tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones).
4. **Reduced permeability** — porin loss (Gram-negatives, especially *Pseudomonas*, *Acinetobacter*).

**Worked examples:** MRSA — altered PBP2a; treat with vancomycin, linezolid, or daptomycin (not pneumonia). ESBL-producing Enterobacterales — resistant to penicillins and most cephalosporins; **carbapenems remain first-line** for serious infection. CRE ⚑ — top global priority pathogen; Reserve-tier agents and ID input. VRE — altered vancomycin binding target; linezolid or daptomycin.

##### Rapid-Recall Discriminators — Section 2

| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Beta-lactam mechanism | Inhibits PBPs → blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking |
| Bacteriostatic mnemonic | "ECSTaTIC" — erythromycin, clindamycin, sulfamethoxazole, trimethoprim, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol |
| Beta-lactams with reliable CNS penetration | Ceftriaxone and aztreonam (others need inflamed meninges) |
| Intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins | *Enterococcus* and *Listeria* |
| Safe beta-lactam in severe penicillin anaphylaxis | Aztreonam (monobactam) |
| True penicillin–cephalosporin cross-reactivity ⚑ | Low (~1–2%), not the old "10%" figure |
| Nephrotoxic + ototoxic, needs level monitoring | Aminoglycosides |
| Switches off exotoxin production (nec fasc/TSS) | Clindamycin |
| Highest C. difficile risk antibiotic class | Clindamycin |
| MRSA/VRE cover + serotonin syndrome risk | Linezolid |
| Never use for pneumonia (surfactant inactivates it) | Daptomycin |
| Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol | Metronidazole |
| Tendon rupture / aortic dissection risk ⚑ | Fluoroquinolones |
| Potent CYP450 inducer, red body fluids | Rifampicin |
| WHO stewardship framework ⚑ | AWaRe (Access/Watch/Reserve) |
| ESBL — still usually susceptible to | Carbapenems |
| MRSA mechanism | Altered PBP2a (*mecA* gene) |
| VRE mechanism | Altered vancomycin-binding cell wall target |

**Sources:** WHO AWaRe antibiotic book (2024–25 edition); IDSA 2026 AMR guidance (ESBL/AmpC/CRE/DTR-Pseudomonas/CRAB); BNF; Kumar & Clark; StatPearls. Beta-lactam cross-reactivity rate cross-checked against current allergy/immunology society position statements.

docs.h: Infectious Disease (ANU) — MECHANISM OF ACTION — Antimicrobial Pharmacology
docs.text:
Bactericidal

- Kill bacteria by inhibiting cell wall synthesis
- “Very finely proficient at ccell murder”: vancomycin, fluoroquinolones, penicillin, aminoglycosides, cephalosporins, carbapenems, metronidazole

Bacteriostatic

- Arrest bacterial growth, by interfering with bacterial protein production, DNA replication, bacterial cellular metabolism
- “ECSTaTIC”: erythromycin, clindamycin, sulfamethoxazole, trimethoprim, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol

docs.h: Infectious Disease (ANU) — beta-lactam antibiotics — Antimicrobial Pharmacology
docs.text:
- Includes penicillin, carbapenem’s, aztreonam and cephalosporins
- Mechanism of action:
- Inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins which inhibits peptidoglycan cross-linking
- Beta-lactam antibiotics are bactericidal
- CNS penetration: only when meninges are inflamed
- Exceptions: ceftriaxone and aztreonam always have good CNS penetration
- Route of elimination: primarily renal (ceftriaxone is both renal and biliary)
- General adverse effects
- Penicillin allergy (hypersensitivity reactions)
- Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
- Beta-lactamase inhibitors
- Beta-lactamases, which are usually produced by gram-negative and anaerobic organisms, can split the beta-lactam ring and render certain beta-lactam antibiotics ineffective
- Beta-lactamase inhibitors increase the spectrum of antibiotic activity (mnemonic CAST): Clavulanic Acid, Sulbactam, Tazobactam

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.h: Infectious Disease Master Notes — Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.text: *The highest-yield section. Exact empiric agents vary by local antibiogram — the finals skill being tested is the **logic** (likely organism → severity → allergy/resistance risk → source control), not a single "correct" drug name.*

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.text:
Every empiric decision runs through the same four questions, in order:

1. **What organism(s) are most likely**, given the site of infection and how it was acquired (community vs hospital vs healthcare-associated)?
2. **How severe** is the presentation — does the patient need broad empirical cover now (sepsis, immunosuppression) or can narrower/oral therapy wait for cultures?
3. **What increases resistance risk** — recent antibiotics (last 3 months), recent hospitalisation, known colonisation (MRSA/ESBL), travel, care-home residence?
4. **Is there a source that needs physical control** — antibiotics alone will not cure an abscess, empyema, infected line, or obstructed/infected kidney.

Then **de-escalate**: narrow the regimen once culture and sensitivity results return — broad empirical cover is a bridge, not a destination.

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.h: 3.2 Respiratory *(full clinical detail — Respiratory build Section 7)*
docs.text:
**CAP:** severity-stratify with **CURB-65** (Confusion, Urea >7, RR ≥30, BP <90/60, age ≥65) — 0–1 = outpatient (amoxicillin ± macrolide if atypical suspected), 2 = consider admission (amoxicillin + macrolide), ≥3 = severe, IV broad-spectrum (co-amoxiclav/ceftriaxone + macrolide) ± ICU. Atypical cover added when Mycoplasma/Legionella/Chlamydophila suspected.

**HAP/VAP:** broader empirical cover reflecting nosocomial flora (Pseudomonas, MRSA, resistant Enterobacterales) — typically an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam or 3rd/4th-gen cephalosporin), adding vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA risk factors.

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.h: 3.3 Urinary *(full clinical detail — Renal build Section 8)*
docs.text:
| Syndrome | Typical organism | Empiric logic |
|---|---|---|
| Uncomplicated cystitis | *E. coli* (commonest by far) | Short-course oral agent (nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim) — AWaRe Access-tier first-line |
| Pyelonephritis | *E. coli*, other Enterobacterales | Broader oral/IV cover (co-amoxiclav, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone if severe) — needs tissue penetration, not just urinary concentration |
| Catheter-associated UTI | Broader flora, higher resistance | **Only treat if symptomatic** (asymptomatic bacteriuria in a catheterised patient is not treated except in pregnancy or pre-urological-procedure) |

⚑ ESBL-producing *E. coli* in UTI is rising (~15–20% in some populations) — if first-line therapy has failed or ESBL risk factors are present, escalate empirically rather than repeating the same class.

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.text:
| Syndrome | Organism | Empiric logic |
|---|---|---|
| Cellulitis (non-purulent) | Group A strep, *S. aureus* | Flucloxacillin (or cephalosporin/clindamycin if penicillin-allergic) |
| Purulent cellulitis/abscess | *S. aureus* (consider MRSA) | **Drainage is the treatment** — antibiotics adjunctive; add MRSA cover if risk factors |
| Necrotising fasciitis ⚑ | Often polymicrobial (Type I) or Group A strep (Type II) | **Surgical emergency** — urgent debridement, broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam + **clindamycin** for toxin suppression) |

**Discriminator:** pain out of proportion to clinical signs, rapid spread, crepitus/skin necrosis, systemic toxicity → necrotising fasciitis; don't wait for imaging to call surgery.

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.h: 3.5 Intra-abdominal and Biliary *(full clinical detail — GI build)*
docs.text: Typically polymicrobial (Gram-negatives + anaerobes) — empiric cover needs both (co-amoxiclav, or a cephalosporin/quinolone **plus metronidazole**). **Source control** (drainage/surgery) is as important as antibiotic choice — cholangitis and perforation are surgical/interventional emergencies first.

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.h: 3.6 Bone and Joint *(full clinical detail — MSK build Section 5.5)*
docs.text: ⚑ **Aspirate/culture before starting antibiotics** wherever possible (unless critically unwell). *S. aureus* commonest; empirical flucloxacillin (or vancomycin if MRSA risk); add ceftriaxone for *N. gonorrhoeae* in young sexually active adults.

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.h: 3.7 CNS *(full clinical detail — Neurology build Section 8.5)*
docs.text: Bacterial meningitis — empirical therapy **must not be delayed** for imaging or LP in a septic/deteriorating patient: **ceftriaxone** (covers meningococcus and pneumococcus) ± **amoxicillin** (age <3 months, >50 years, or immunocompromised — to cover *Listeria*, which is cephalosporin-resistant) ± **dexamethasone** (reduces neurological sequelae, especially pneumococcal — give with or just before first antibiotic dose).

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.h: 3.8 Bloodstream/Endovascular *(full clinical detail — Cardiology build Section 6.1)*
docs.text:
**Sepsis of unknown source ("blind stab"):** broad empirical cover (piperacillin-tazobactam, or 3rd-gen cephalosporin + metronidazole) pending cultures and source identification, following the Sepsis Six bundle.

**Infective endocarditis (empirical):** typically vancomycin + gentamicin (or ampicillin/vancomycin + gentamicin per local protocol) to cover staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci; **three sets of blood cultures before starting antibiotics** wherever the patient is stable enough.

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.h: 3.9 Neutropenic Sepsis *(full clinical detail — Haem/Onc build Section 10.1)*
docs.text: ⚑ **Antibiotics within 1 hour**, before blood counts or imaging results are back — the exam's favourite "don't wait" scenario. Broad-spectrum antipseudomonal monotherapy (piperacillin-tazobactam) standard first-line; escalate per local protocol/MASCC risk score.

docs.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.text:
**Single dose** (or short course), given **within 60 minutes before incision** (timing is the exam point — too early or too late both reduce efficacy), chosen to cover expected flora (cefazolin for clean surgery, added anaerobic cover for bowel surgery). **Prolonging prophylaxis beyond the peri-operative window does not reduce infection risk** and increases resistance/C. diff risk.

##### Rapid-Recall Discriminators — Section 3

| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| CAP severity score | CURB-65 |
| CAP with hyponatraemia + deranged LFTs + water exposure | *Legionella* — add atypical cover |
| Commonest UTI organism | *E. coli* |
| Asymptomatic bacteriuria in a catheterised patient | Don't treat (except pregnancy/pre-urological-procedure) |
| Purulent skin abscess — the actual "treatment" | Drainage (antibiotics adjunctive) |
| Pain out of proportion + rapid spread + crepitus | Necrotising fasciitis — urgent surgery |
| Antibiotic added for toxin suppression in nec fasc/TSS | Clindamycin |
| Intra-abdominal empiric cover needs to include | Anaerobic cover (e.g. metronidazole) |
| Before antibiotics in suspected septic arthritis | Aspirate/culture first (unless critically unwell) |
| Empirical meningitis antibiotic covering meningo + pneumococcus | Ceftriaxone |
| Added in meningitis if age <3mo/>50/immunosuppressed | Amoxicillin (Listeria cover) |
| Before starting antibiotics in suspected endocarditis | Three sets of blood cultures (if stable enough) |
| Neutropenic sepsis antibiotic timing ⚑ | Within 1 hour, before counts/imaging |
| Surgical prophylaxis timing | Within 60 minutes pre-incision, single dose/short course |
| ESBL UTI rising — what changes | Escalate empirically if risk factors/prior failure, don't repeat same class |

**Sources:** WHO AWaRe antibiotic book; NICE (CAP, UTI, meningitis, neutropenic sepsis, SSTI guidance); BNF; IDSA. Empiric agent choices illustrate the reasoning framework — defer to local antibiogram in practice.

docs.h: Infectious Disease (ANU) — empiric antibiotic theraPY — Empiric Antibiotic Therapy by Syndrome
docs.text:
- Choose antibiotics to cover for most likely and lethal organisms for the type of infection prior to obtaining laboratory results (usually reserved for serious infections)
- Adjust antibiotic(s) based on C&S
- If causative organism identified, use antibiotic to which organism is sensitive
- If causative organism not identified, re-evaluate need for ongoing antimicrobial therapy (and continue with empiric antibiotics if indicated)

docs.title: Microbiology Foundations
docs.h: Infectious Disease Master Notes — Microbiology Foundations

docs.title: Microbiology Foundations
docs.text:
Cocci — the clustering/chaining split is the first branch point:

| Organism | Arrangement | Key test | Notable disease |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Staphylococcus aureus* | Clusters | **Coagulase-positive** | Skin/soft tissue, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, toxic shock, food poisoning (preformed toxin) |
| Coagulase-negative staphylococci (*S. epidermidis*) | Clusters | Coagulase-negative | Line/prosthetic infections (biofilm) |
| *Streptococcus pyogenes* (Group A) | Chains | Beta-haemolytic, **bacitracin-sensitive** | Pharyngitis, cellulitis/erysipelas, necrotising fasciitis, rheumatic fever, PSGN |
| *Streptococcus agalactiae* (Group B) | Chains | Beta-haemolytic, bacitracin-resistant | Neonatal sepsis/meningitis (maternal screening) |
| *Streptococcus pneumoniae* | Pairs (diplococci) | Alpha-haemolytic, **optochin-sensitive** | CAP, meningitis, otitis media |
| Viridans streptococci | Chains | Alpha-haemolytic, **optochin-resistant** | Subacute infective endocarditis (dental procedures) |
| *Enterococcus* (faecalis/faecium) | Pairs/chains | Grows in bile/salt | UTI, endocarditis, intra-abdominal — **intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins**; VRE a major resistance concern |

**Gram-positive rods:** *Listeria monocytogenes* (neonatal/elderly/immunosuppressed meningitis, unpasteurised dairy, motile at room temp), *Clostridium* species (spore-forming anaerobes — *C. difficile* colitis, *C. perfringens* gas gangrene, *C. tetani* tetanus, *C. botulinum* botulism), *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* (pseudomembranous pharyngitis, exotoxin).

docs.title: Microbiology Foundations
docs.text:
**Enterobacterales (the "coliforms"):** *E. coli* (commonest UTI/intra-abdominal pathogen), *Klebsiella pneumoniae* (UTI, pneumonia — mucoid, hypervirulent strains), *Proteus mirabilis* (**urease-producing → struvite stones**), *Salmonella*/*Shigella* (enteric), *Enterobacter*, *Citrobacter*, *Serratia* (nosocomial, AmpC-associated).

**Non-fermenters:** *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* (nosocomial, burns, CF, ventilator-associated pneumonia; intrinsically resistant to many agents — needs antipseudomonal cover), *Acinetobacter baumannii* (ICU, multidrug-resistant — CRAB a major concern ⚑).

**Fastidious Gram-negatives:** *Neisseria meningitidis* (meningococcal meningitis/sepsis, non-blanching rash), *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* (gonorrhoea), *Haemophilus influenzae* (epiglottitis, otitis media, COPD exacerbation — much rarer invasive disease since Hib vaccination).

docs.title: Microbiology Foundations
docs.text:
**Atypical respiratory pathogens** (no cell wall or intracellular — **don't respond to beta-lactams**): *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* (young adults, walking pneumonia, cold agglutinins), *Chlamydophila pneumoniae/psittaci*, *Legionella pneumophila* (water sources, **hyponatraemia, deranged LFTs** — legionella urinary antigen).

**Spirochaetes:** *Treponema pallidum* (syphilis), *Borrelia burgdorferi* (Lyme disease), *Leptospira* (leptospirosis — water/rodent exposure).

**Mycobacteria:** *M. tuberculosis* (see respiratory build for full TB detail), atypical mycobacteria (immunocompromised).

**Fungi:** *Candida* (mucosal/invasive, line infections), *Aspergillus* (invasive in neutropenia, ABPA in asthma/CF), *Cryptococcus neoformans* (HIV-associated meningitis), *Pneumocystis jirovecii* (HIV-associated pneumonia — Section 4).

docs.title: Microbiology Foundations
docs.text:
Innate vs adaptive — full immunology detail is in the immunology/allergy build; here the relevant point is the **inflammatory cascade in sepsis**: pathogen recognition (PAMPs via toll-like receptors) → cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) → vasodilation, capillary leak, coagulation activation → organ hypoperfusion.

**Sepsis definitions ⚑ (Sepsis-3):**

- **Sepsis** = life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection — operationalised as a rise in **SOFA score ≥2** from baseline.
- **Septic shock** = sepsis + vasopressor requirement to maintain **MAP ≥65 mmHg** despite adequate fluid resuscitation, with **lactate >2 mmol/L**.
- ⚑ **SIRS criteria are no longer part of the formal sepsis definition** (too non-specific) but are still widely taught/used as a bedside screening trigger.
- **qSOFA** (bedside, no labs): RR ≥22, altered mentation, SBP ≤100 — ≥2 flags risk, prompts full assessment (not a diagnostic tool itself).

**Sepsis Six** (management bundle, first hour): give O₂, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids; measure lactate, monitor urine output.

##### Rapid-Recall Discriminators — Section 1

| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Clusters, coagulase-positive | *S. aureus* |
| Chains, beta-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive | Group A strep (*S. pyogenes*) |
| Diplococci, alpha-haemolytic, optochin-sensitive | *S. pneumoniae* |
| Alpha-haemolytic, optochin-resistant, subacute IE post-dental | Viridans streptococci |
| Intrinsically cephalosporin-resistant Gram-positive | *Enterococcus* |
| Motile, unpasteurised dairy, neonatal/elderly meningitis | *Listeria* |
| Urease-producing → struvite (staghorn) stones | *Proteus mirabilis* |
| Intrinsically multi-resistant, needs antipseudomonal cover | *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* |
| No cell wall — beta-lactams won't work | Atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella) |
| Hyponatraemia + deranged LFTs + pneumonia | *Legionella* |
| Sepsis formal definition (Sepsis-3) | Organ dysfunction (SOFA ≥2 rise) from dysregulated host response to infection |
| Septic shock definition | Vasopressors needed for MAP ≥65 despite fluids + lactate >2 |

**Sources:** Sepsis-3 (JAMA 2016, still the operative definition); WHO AWaRe antibiotic book; Kumar & Clark; Robbins & Cotran; StatPearls. Sepsis-3 definitions cross-checked against Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidance.

docs.h: Infectious Disease (ANU) — INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS — Microbiology Foundations
docs.text:
| Definition | Infective inflammation of the cardiac endothelium, most commonly the valvesClassification: acute vs. subacute; native vs. prosthetic valve, R-sided vs. L-sidedValve leaflet vegetaions platelet-fibrin thrombi, WBCs, bacteria |
| --- | --- |
| Epidemiology | M>F, age > 60 y/o |
| Risk Factors | Pre-existing: previous IE, pre-damaged/prosthetic heart valves, congenital defects,  ↓ immunityBacteraemia: infected peripheral venous catheters, poor dentition, surgery, IVDU, various bacterial infections, haemodialysis |
| Aetiology | Pathogen | Characteristics |
| S.aureus (45-65%) | Most common acutely, affecting previously health valvesFatal within 6 weeks (if untreated) |
| Viridans streptococci (30%) | Most common subacutely, especially in pre- damaged mitral valves and prosthetic valves≥ 60 days after surgery |
| Enterococcus (<10%) | Multiple drug resistance, following nosocomial UTIs |
| Staphylococcus epidermis | Prosthetic heart valves |
| Gram-negative HACEK | Poor dental hygiene Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, Kingella kingae |
| Candida species | In immunosuppressed patients |

**Pathophysiology**

- Localized infection 🡪 bacteraemia 🡪 bacterial colonisation and thrombi formation on valve leaflets and chordae tendineaeValve destruction with ↓function
- Vessel occlusion/infarction from thrombo-emboli
- Immune complex against tissue antigens (GN, Osler Nodes)

- Mitral > aortic > tricuspid > pulmonary

**Presentation**

- ACUTE IE:
- Acute onset with rapid progression (days to weeks) and ↑ constitutional Sx
- Most common: S. aureus (can be caused by GAS, S. pneumoniae, N.gonorrhoeae)
- SUBACUTE IE:
- Insidious onset with slow progression (weeks to months) and ↓ constitutional Sx
- Most common: Streptococci
- PROSTHETIC VALVE IE:
- Early (<60d) vs. late (≥ 60d)
- S.epidermidis (early onset) or S.aureus (late onset)
- SYMPTOMS
- Constitutional: fever/chills, ↑HR, malaise, arthralgia, myalgia, cough, pleuritic chest pain
- Cardiac: murmur, CHF, arrthmias
- Mnemonic: Fever, Roth’s spots, Osler’s nodes, Murmur, Janeway lesions, Anemia, Nail-bed hemorrhages (i.e. splinter hemorrhages), Emboli
- Other: neurological (seizure, paresis), PE, splenomegaly, acute renal injury

**Duke Criteria**

- 1) 2 major, 2) 1 major + 3 minor OR 3) 5 minor
- Major diagnostic criteriaTwo separate blood cultures positive for typical pathogens
- Evidence of endocardial involvement in echocardiography (valve vegetations on TTE/TOE)
- A new valvular regurgitation (worsening of a pre-existing murmur is not sufficient)

- Minor diagnostic criteriaPredisposition (underlying heart disease or IV drug abuse)
- Fever ≥ 38°C
- Vascular (major arterial emboli, pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysms, Janeway lesions)
- Immunologic disorder (GN, rheumatoid factor, Osler nodes, Roth’s spots)
- Microbiology

- Only negative findings on TOE can reliably rule out endocarditis, as TTE is not

| Infection | Organism | Features | Treatment |

docs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV
docs.text: **HSV** — genital ulcers, recurrent; aciclovir/valaciclovir for episodes and suppression. **HPV** — genital warts (low-risk types **6/11**) vs oncogenic types (**16/18** → cervical cancer); vaccination is primary prevention. **Hepatitis B/C** — sexually transmissible; full detail in the GI/hepatology build.

docs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV
docs.text: **Trichomoniasis** (*Trichomonas vaginalis*, protozoan) — frothy discharge, **"strawberry cervix"**; metronidazole. **PID** — ascending infection (chlamydia/gonorrhoea commonest), a clinical syndrome not a single organism — cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, fever; **empirical broad cover started on clinical suspicion, don't wait for swab results** (fertility risk from delay).

docs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV
docs.text:
**Virology:** retrovirus, infects CD4+ T cells via **gp120** binding **CCR5/CXCR4** co-receptors; reverse transcriptase converts RNA to DNA for integration.

**Natural history:** seroconversion (2–4 weeks post-infection) — flu-like illness, often missed; high viral load, highly infectious → clinical latency (years, progressive CD4 decline) → AIDS-defining illness.

**Staging by CD4 count — the exam-favourite table:**

| CD4 count (cells/μL) | Risk |
|---|---|
| >500 | Usually asymptomatic |
| 200–500 | Bacterial infections, TB, shingles, oral candidiasis |
| **<200** | **PCP**, oesophageal candidiasis — AIDS-defining |
| **<100** | Toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis |
| **<50** | CMV retinitis, disseminated MAC |

**Diagnosis:** **4th-generation antigen/antibody combo test** (detects p24 antigen + antibodies — narrows the window period); confirmatory testing per local algorithm.

**ART classes:** NRTIs (tenofovir, lamivudine, abacavir — **HLA-B\*5701 screening before abacavir**), NNRTIs (efavirenz, rilpivirine), **integrase inhibitors** (dolutegravir, bictegravir — ⚑ now first-line backbone; high barrier to resistance, well tolerated), protease inhibitors (darunavir/ritonavir-boosted — less first-line now). **Standard modern regimen: 2 NRTIs + an integrase inhibitor.**

**PEP:** started **within 72 hours** of significant exposure, continued **28 days**. **PrEP:** tenofovir/emtricitabine for ongoing high-risk exposure.

##### Rapid-Recall Discriminators — Section 4

| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Often asymptomatic bacterial STI | Chlamydia |
| Single painless genital ulcer | Primary syphilis (chancre) |
| Rash on palms and soles + lymphadenopathy | Secondary syphilis |
| Fever/myalgia hours after first syphilis treatment | Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (not allergy) |
| Frothy discharge + strawberry cervix | Trichomoniasis |
| PID — when to start treatment | Empirically, on clinical suspicion — don't wait for swabs |
| HIV window-period test | 4th-gen antigen/antibody combo (p24 + antibody) |
| CD4 <200 AIDS-defining infection | PCP pneumonia |
| CD4 <100 | Toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis |
| CD4 <50 | CMV retinitis, disseminated MAC |
| Screen before starting abacavir | HLA-B\*5701 |
| Modern first-line ART backbone ⚑ | 2 NRTIs + integrase inhibitor |
| PEP window | Within 72 hours, 28-day course |

**Sources:** BASHH UK guidelines; CDC STI treatment guidelines; WHO HIV clinical staging; DHHS/BHIVA ART guidelines; Kumar & Clark; StatPearls.

docs.h: Infectious Disease Master Notes — Systemic, Opportunistic and Travel-Related Infection
docs.text:
##### 5.1 Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO)

**Classic definition:** fever **>38.3°C** on several occasions, lasting **>3 weeks**, with no diagnosis after **1 week** of inpatient investigation (or equivalent outpatient work-up).

**The four-category differential:**

1. **Infective** (commonest overall) — TB (often extrapulmonary/disseminated), abscess (intra-abdominal, dental), infective endocarditis, atypical/zoonotic infection.
2. **Malignant** — lymphoma (esp. Hodgkin — **Pel-Ebstein fever**), renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, leukaemia.
3. **Autoimmune/inflammatory** — adult-onset Still's disease, giant cell arteritis/PMR, vasculitis, SLE.
4. **Other** — drug fever (diagnosis of exclusion — resolves on stopping the culprit), factitious fever, familial Mediterranean fever, thyrotoxicosis.

**Work-up logic:** repeat, thorough history (travel, occupation, animal/sexual contact, drugs) and examination are more valuable than a shotgun panel; then a staged approach — basic bloods/cultures/urinalysis/CXR, then imaging (CT chest/abdo/pelvis), then targeted biopsy or PET-CT. **Avoid empirical antibiotics or steroids before a diagnosis** — they mask the underlying process.

##### 5.2 Opportunistic Infections — the Immunosuppressed-Host Framework

Match the defect to the pathogen (a recurring exam logic):

| Immune defect | Setting | Typical pathogens |
|---|---|---|
| **Neutropenia** | Chemotherapy, marrow failure | Gram-negative bacteraemia, invasive fungal (*Aspergillus*, *Candida*) |
| **T-cell/cellular** | HIV, transplant on calcineurin inhibitors, high-dose steroids | PCP, CMV, TB, *Cryptococcus*, *Toxoplasma*, *Listeria* |
| **B-cell/humoral (antibody)** | Myeloma, CLL, splenectomy | **Encapsulated organisms** — *S. pneumoniae*, *H. influenzae*, *N. meningitidis* |
| **Complement deficiency** | Terminal complement (C5–9) deficiency | **Recurrent *Neisseria* infections** |
| **Biologic therapy** (anti-TNF, JAK inhibitors) | RA, IBD on biologics | **TB reactivation** (screen before starting), serious bacterial infection |

**Asplenia/splenectomy** — lifelong risk from encapsulated organisms; requires vaccination (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib) and prophylactic penicillin, especially in the first years post-splenectomy and in children.

##### 5.3 Travel and Vector-Borne Infection

**Malaria** — *Plasmodium* species (**falciparum** most severe — cerebral malaria, blackwater fever, high parasitaemia); cyclical fever classically taught but often irregular. **Always test (thick and thin films) in a febrile returned traveller regardless of prophylaxis history.** Severe falciparum: **IV artesunate**.

**Dengue** — mosquito-borne (*Aedes*), fever + retro-orbital headache + myalgia (**"breakbone fever"**) + rash; warning signs for severe dengue (plasma leakage, bleeding, shock) — abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy.

**Enteric (typhoid) fever** — *Salmonella typhi*; stepwise fever, **relative bradycardia**, **rose

docs.text:
##### Part A — By Presenting Syndrome

**A1. Fever with no obvious source.** Sepsis Six bundle first (O₂, cultures, IV antibiotics, fluids, lactate, urine output) → broad empirical cover pending source. If >3 weeks, undiagnosed → PUO framework.

**A2. Fever in the immunosuppressed patient.** Match defect to pathogen: neutropenic → Gram-negative/fungal (antibiotics within 1 hour); T-cell defect (HIV/transplant) → PCP/CMV/TB/Cryptococcus/Toxoplasma; asplenic/B-cell → encapsulated organisms.

**A3. Fever in the returned traveller.** Always test for malaria (thick/thin films) regardless of prophylaxis. Consider dengue, typhoid by exposure/region and symptom pattern.

**A4. New diarrhoea in hospital / post-antibiotic.** Think C. difficile — check the antibiotic history ("4 Cs"), send toxin testing, stop the culprit, start oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin.

**A5. Genital ulcer / discharge.** Painless single ulcer → syphilis. Painful, recurrent → HSV. Purulent discharge → gonorrhoea/chlamydia. Frothy + strawberry cervix → trichomoniasis.

**A6. New HIV diagnosis / risk assessment.** Stage by CD4; screen for opportunistic infection at diagnosis if CD4 low; start ART (2 NRTIs + integrase inhibitor); PEP within 72h; PrEP for ongoing risk.

##### Part B — Signature Lookup Tables

**B1. Organism buzzwords**

| Clue | Organism |
|---|---|
| Clusters, coagulase+ | *S. aureus* |
| Bacitracin-sensitive, beta-haemolytic chains | Group A strep |
| Optochin-sensitive diplococci | *S. pneumoniae* |
| Optochin-resistant, subacute IE post-dental | Viridans strep |
| Intrinsic cephalosporin resistance | *Enterococcus*, *Listeria* |
| Water source + hyponatraemia + deranged LFTs | *Legionella* |
| Struvite/staghorn stones | *Proteus* (urease) |
| Motile, unpasteurised dairy | *Listeria* |
| Rose spots + relative bradycardia | *Salmonella typhi* |

**B2. CD4 count → opportunistic infection**

| CD4 | Infection |
|---|---|
| <200 | PCP, oesophageal candidiasis |
| <100 | Toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis |
| <50 | CMV retinitis, disseminated MAC |

**B3. Antibiotic → signature toxicity/rule**

| Drug | Rule |
|---|---|
| Aminoglycosides | Nephro/ototoxic — level monitoring |
| Clindamycin | Highest C. diff risk; toxin suppression in nec fasc |
| Linezolid | Serotonin syndrome with SSRIs |
| Daptomycin | Never for pneumonia (surfactant inactivates) |
| Metronidazole | Disulfiram reaction with alcohol |
| Fluoroquinolones ⚑ | Tendon rupture, aortic dissection, QT — restricted use |
| Rifampicin | CYP450 inducer, red body fluids |
| Vancomycin | Red man syndrome (rate-related, not allergy) |

**B4. Resistance mechanism → organism**

| Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|
| Altered PBP2a | MRSA |
| Altered vancomycin target | VRE |
| Beta-lactamase (extended-spectrum) | ESBL Enterobacterales — carbapenems usually still work |
| Carbapenemase | CRE — Reserve-tier agents needed |

docs.text:
Fracture is the disruption of the continuity of the bone, (long bone is more common but flat bone is more severe). Three phases in fracture healing:

- INFLAMMATORY PHASE
- Swelling and hyperaemia
- Organization of fracture haematoma
- Protein growth factors that regulate cell migration and differentiation
- REPARATIVE PHASE
- Primary callus response
- Independent of mechanical factors – dependent on tissue vascularity
- If it unites the two sides it progresses to bridging or hard callus
- REMODELLING PHASE
- Gradual modification of the feature region under influence of mechanical loads with conversion to lamellar bone
- FACTORS THAT PROMOTES HEALING: growth hormone, thyroid hormone, calcitonin, insulin anabolic hormones, vitamin D, vitamin C, exercise weight bearing, youth
- FACTORS THAT INHIBIT HEALING: NSAIDS, steroid, DM, anaemia and decreased oxygenation, vit d deficiency, excessive bone gap or motion, infection, osteoporosis, Paget’s Disease of the Bone, advanced age

![](notes/images/orthopaedics-and-msk-anu/img003.jpg)

**brachial plexus**

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
- NON-DISPLACED: fracture fragments are in anatomic alignment
- DISPLACED: fracture fragments are not in anatomic alignment
- DISTRACTED: fracture fragments are separated by a gap (opposite of impacted)
- IMPACTED: fracture fragments are compressed, resulting in shortened bone
- ANGULATED: direction of fracture apex, e.g. Varus/valgus
- TRANSLATED/SHIFTED: percentage of overlapping bone at fracture site
- ROTATED: fracture fragment rotated about long axis of bone

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
- ABCS
- PRIMARY AND SECONDARY SURVEY (rule out other fractures/injuries)
- HISTORY

- AMPLE (allergies, medications, past medical history, last meal, events surrounding injury)
- Neurological signs
- Past medical history: predisposing conditions that may suggest pathological fracture

- EXAMINATION

- Inspection and palpation for swelling, discolouration, and deformity
- Assessment of active and passive range of motion of suspected joints
- Neurovascular assessment:
- Hands: ulnar, radial and median nerves; radial and ulnar pulses
- Feet: saphenous, dorsolateral, deep fibular, superficial fibular nerves; dorsalis pedis and anterior tibialis pulses

- INVESTIGATIONS

- X-Ray: gold standard for fractures
- Fracture and joint above and below
- CT/MRI if there is evidence of ligament damage
- Ultrasound if there is suspicion for tendon damage, foreign bod

- SUPPORTIVE

- Analgesia: adequate pain relief and muscle relaxant if required
- Antibiotics must in open fractures (broad-spectrum)

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
- PRINCIPLE: restore length, rotation and angulation
- CLOSED:

- Apply traction in the long axis of limb, reverse the mechanism which caused the fracture
- Reduce with iv sedation and muscle relaxation

- INDICATIONS FOR OPEN REDUCTION: “NO CAST”

- Non-union
- Open fracture,
- Neurovascular Compression
- Intra-Articular fracture,
- Salter-harris - 3,4,5
- polyTrauma
- Others: failure of closed reduction, position (e.g. hip), pathological fracture

- Always re-check neurovascular integrity after reduction, and obtain post-reduction x-ray
- MAINTAIN REDUCTION

- External stabilization
- Splints/casts: pad the boney prominance
- If swollen or in a circumferential fracture use front and back slabs instead of a cast to avoid cutting off circulation/compartment’s syndrome
- Traction: sling (by gravity)
- Functional bracing: prevents post-traumatic stiffness by changing from cast to functional brace
- External fixation:Used when there are severe soft tissue injuries or open fractures to reduce likelihood of infection
- Temporizing e.g. In military situations
- Leg lengthening

- Internal Fixation: percutaneous pinning, extra-medullary fixation (screws, plates, wires), IM fixation (rods)

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
AIM

- Reduce pain
- Prevent further damage to skin, soft tissue, blood vessels and nerve
- Facilitate healing and bone union

METHOD

- Splint in a method that will reduce the fracture, and respect soft tissue
- Obtain an x-ray post-reduction

COMPLICATIONS

- Plaster burn:  plaster formation is an exothermic procedure
- Thermal injury: avoid >10 ply cast & >24 degree water
- Pressure sores: formed if there is insufficient padding
- Pressure necrosis: as early as 2 hours post cast
- Nerve palsy: direct compression; avoided by sufficient padding
- Vascular compression
- Splint dermatitis
- Permanent joint stiffness

docs.text:
Generally, fractures will be immobilised for 4-6weeks which may lead to stiffness and muscle weakness in the adjacent joints and muscles. Immobilised in splint, cast, brace, surgically fixated or place in traction.

- Muscle assessment: following immobilisation muscles surrounding the fracture site lose bulk, length and strength. prescribed safe exercise program under supervision of physiotherapist to restore muscle length and balance

- Joint mobilization: joint stiffness often occurs when a limb is not allowed to move for several weeks🡪 improve and restore range of movement of the affected joints once the fracture has healed.Passive: therapist moves joint to maintain ligament and joint capsule
- Active and against resistance: improve muscle power.

- Massage: the release of tight bands and trigger points that occur within muscles following splinting or casting has been shown to reduce pain and restore muscle length.
- Heat and electrotherapy: it is very common for stiffness within soft tissues to occur following prolonged immobilisation. Useful adjuncts to manual treatment and exercise therapy in relieving pain and restoring muscle length. Ice packs help provide analgesia immediately and reduce pain and swelling whereas hear relives pain and stiffness.

- Gait education: if your fracture requires the use of gait aids such as crutches then the physiotherapist can advise you with the most appropriate equipment and way of walking that promotes optimal healing and safety.
- Ergonomic training: training how to use specific body parts for specific activities – i.e. Back pain need to be taught how to lift and carry again
- Functional aids: Cane, crutches, walking aid for lower limb
- Collars or partial splintage for a painful neck
- Footwear such as can-boot

docs.h: Orthopaedics (SNEHA) — Primary haemopoietic tumours — Additional Notes
docs.text: These so called “blood cancers” arise from the blood cells within the bone marrow. Hence, these cancers, which include leukemia, lymphomas and myeloma, are considered to be in the Haemopoietic and lymphoid system (i.e. Distinct from the musculoskeletal system).

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
This is a neoplastic proliferation of plasma cells (activated b-lymphocytes producing immunoglobulins). Overall, it is the commonest tumor that originates in the bone. They present as osteolytic lesions, with infiltration of various organs and associated amyloidosis.

Investigations:

- Protein electrophoresis of blood and urine shows presence of paraproteins (abnormal immunoglobulins produced by tumors 🡪 igg most common.
- Bloods may show raised creatinine
- Radiographs of skull, axial skeleton and proximal long bones
- MRI detects lytic lesions

Treatment:

- High dose chemotherapy with autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation

- Change shoes
- Orthotics [1]splints or spaces bunion toe separators / bunion cushions / bunion splints.

Surgical (if pain is unbearable)

May involve some of the following:

- Realigning the first metatarsal bone

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
Conservative – mild to moderate

Warm water and salt soaks, antibacterial ointment and using dental floss or a gutter splint to provide a track along which the nail may grow is possible.

Surgery – severe or progressive mild ingrown toenails

- Partial avulsion of the lateral nail plate known as a ‘wedge resection; or a complete removal of the toenail
- If it recurs, destruction of the side of the nail bed with anesthesia is recommended.
- Topical abs used post procedure but orals are not recommended as they may delay healing

Nail bracing – less widely used

- Nail braces work by gently lifting the sides of the toenail and eventually retraining the nail to grow to a flatter shape over time. – one full growth of the nail, which is around 1-1.5 years.

Two types: adhesive and nail braces

- POST-SPLENECTOMY: Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants), target cells, thrombocytosis (loss of sequesteration and removal), lymphocytosis (loss of sequestration)
- Vaccinate patients undergoing splenectomy against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcal, HiB, meningococcal)

- TYPES: congenital or acquired (infection, malnutrition, aging, malignancy, iatrogenic e.g. chemo)
- EPIDEMIOLOGY: individual deficiencies are rare

Arthocentesis

- DIAGNOSTIC: determine cause of pain or swelling in the joint
- THERAPEUTIC: removal of excess fluid may help lessen pain and improve antibiotic
- SYNOVIAL FLUID CHARACTERISTIC:
- Crystals: gout (urate), pseudogout (pyrophosphate)
- WCC: bacterial septic; may be slightly elevated in RA, psoaritic and reactive arthritis
- Blood: hemarthrosis from trauma or fracture
- Fat: fracture
- Non-inflammatory: OA

Hypersensivity

- HYPERSENSITIVITY: the immune system, which normally serves a protective role, has a harmful effect. The hypersensitivity reactions can be memorized with the mnemonic ACID: A – Allergic/Anaphylactic/Atopic (Type I); C – Cytotoxic (Type II); I – Immune complex deposition (Type III); D – Delayed (Type IV)
- ALLERGY: abnormal immunological response to an otherwise harmless environmental stimulus
- AUTOIMMUNITY: abnormal immunological response directed against an antigen that is actually part of the body itself

|  | PATHOPHYSIOLOGY | EXAMPLES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TYPE I: IMMEDIATE | IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation →histamine and inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, leukotrienes) | Allergic reactions (food, drug)AnaphylaxisAsthma |
| TYPE II: ANTIBODY-MEDIATED | IgM and IgG antibodies bind to antigens on the cells of particular tissue types→ complement activation and lysis or phagocytosis of cells | Acute haemolytic transfusion reactionPernicious anaemia Goodpasture’sGrave’s diseaseITPHashimoto’s thyroiditisRFMyasthenia gravis |
| TYPE III: IMMUNE-COMPLEX MEDIATED | Antibodies bind to antigens in circulation → immune complex formation and deposition in particular tissues → inflammation | Post-strep GNIgA nephropathySerum sicknessSLE |
| TYPE IV: DELAYED T-CELL-MEDIATED | Contact of antigen with pre-sensitised T lymphocytes → macrophage activation and inflammatory reaction in tissue | Contact dermatitisMultiple sclerosisGBSGraft-versus-host diseaseMantoux testT1DM |

| Definition | Life-threatening type I hypersensitivity reaction which can lead to distributive shock (circulatory failure) |
| --- | --- |
| Aetiology | Exaggerated immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction that leads to systemic vasoactive mediator release (histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins and smooth muscle reactive chemicals) → increased vascular permeability, and vasodilationAllergic (foods e.g. nuts/shellfish, stings, drugs e.g. penicillin/NSAIDs/ACE-I)Non-allergic (exercise-induced) |
| Presentation | Skin or mucous membranes: flushing, urticaria, pruritus, erythema, swelling of the eyelids, or angioedemaRespiratory: nasal congestion, cough, sneezing, hoarseness, chest tightness, stridordyspnoea (bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema)Cardiovascular: hypotension, tachycardia, chest pain (myocardial ischemia due to hypoxia and hypotension)GI: abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting (especially in food allergies) |

| Differentials | Septic shock, asthma, angioedema |
| Management | Withdrawal of offending agent if applicable (e.g., in drug reactions)Airway: examination of airway and intubation if obstruction seems imminent (+ “B” and “C”)IM adrenaline (1:1000) 0.3 – 0.5 mg in lateral thighPaediatric dose of adrenaline: 0.01 mg/kg IM up to 0.5mg q5-15minPositioning: The patient should be placed in a recumbent/supine position with elevation of the lower extremitiesO2 by facemaskIf patient is hypotensive: volume replacement with crystalloid (normal saline 1–2 L IV rapid bolus)Bronchospasm and no benefit of adrenaline: nebulized salbutamolAntihistamines (competitive inhibition of histamine at receptor, reducing histamine-mediated effects and symptoms e.g., increased vascular permeability, vasodilation, swelling, pruritus)H1 antihistamine (e.g., diphenhydramine) IV for urticariaH2 antihistamine (e.g., ranitidine) IVHydrocortisone 100mg IV/methylprednisolone 1mg/kg IV x 24 hoursContinuous monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, heart function, and pulse oximetry; urine output should also be monitored in hypotensive patients receiving resuscitation.Monitor for 4-6 hours in ED minimum and arrange follow up within 24-48 hours (educate about potential second biphasic reaction and avoidance of allergens) |

docs.text:
| Definition | Chronic inflammatory and pruritic skin disease that typically manifests in early child hoodOften associated with other atopic diseases e.g. asthma, allergic rhinitis |
| --- | --- |
| Epidemiology | 10-15% of all children are affected with an age of onset between 3-6 months of ageDisease often improves with age |
| Aetiology | Incompletely understoodGENETIC: polygenic inheritance of predisposition for increased IgE formation and sensitisation in which abnormal Th2 response in the skin → cytokine overproduction → excessive IgE production → allergic dermatitisTRIGGERS: dust, heat, dry/humid climates, emotional stress, infections, skin irritation |
| Presentation | Intense pruritis and dry skinINFANTILE AD (<2 YEARS): eczema (cheeks, face, head, extensors), Dennie-Morgan fold (below eye)CHILDHOOD AD (2-12 YEARS): eczema (flexural creases, skin folds, lichenified lesions (thickened skin)ADULT/ADOLESCENT AD (> 12 YEARS): LICHENIFIED lesions and pruritis of flexor surfaces of extremities), nummular eczema (coin-shaped)ASSOCIATED: asthma, allergic rhinitis, xerosis |
| Diagnostic Criteria | Essential: pruritis, eczema (maculopapular, erythematous lesions that can also have scale, crusting, oozing, or blistering)Important features: early age of onset, atopy, xerosis |
| Differentials | Seborrheic dermatitis (usually more greasy lesions), psoriasis (onset in adolescent years) |
| Management | Avoid triggers e.g. pets, dust, mites, pollens, foods, chemical/clothing irritants, heats, stressKeep skin moist with moisturisers and emollients (reduce skin evaporation to ↑ hydration)In severe AD can add topical steroids, calcineurin inhibitors (immunosuppressant), phototherapy (narrow band UVB) or systemic therapy (cyclosporine, azathioprine, methotrexate) |

Autoimmunity

DEFINITION: Immune reaction against the body’s own cells, due to a loss of immunological tolerance

PRESUMED PATHOGENESIS

- Autoreactive B lymphocytes are eliminated in the bone marrow, spleen, or lymph nodes (can be detected)
- T lymphocytes that attack the body's own cells are amended in the thymus or destroyed in peripheral lymphoid tissues (e.g., lymph nodes, adenoids, Peyer's patches) due to a lack of stimulation (usually cannot detect specific antibodies)
- If the selection mechanisms fail, this results in the immune cells attacking the body's own cells

CAUSES

- Previous infection e.g. GBS, RF through molecular mimicry
- Genetic predisposition

![](notes/images/rheumatology-and-immunology-anu/img004.jpg)

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.h: MSK & Rheumatology Notes — Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
*Sources: Kumar & Clark, Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine, StatPearls, Arthritis Research UK / Versus Arthritis REMS-GALS, BSR guidance. Autoantibody associations cross-checked against Robbins and UpToDate-style summaries. Discriminators **bolded**.*

---

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
##### Inflammatory vs mechanical — the first fork
Almost every rheumatology history hinges on separating **inflammatory** from **mechanical/degenerative** pain. Get this and the differential collapses.

| Feature | **Inflammatory** (RA, spondyloarthropathy, crystal) | **Mechanical** (OA, injury) |
|---|---|---|
| Morning stiffness | **Prolonged, >30–60 min** | Brief (<30 min) |
| Effect of activity | **Better with use** ("warms up") | **Worse with use**, better with rest |
| Effect of rest | Worse (stiffens up) | Better |
| Night pain / waking | Common | Uncommon (except severe OA) |
| Swelling | **Soft-tissue, warm** (synovitis) | Bony (osteophyte) |
| Systemic features | Fatigue, weight loss, fever, rash | Absent |
| Response to NSAIDs | Often marked | Partial |

**Memory hook:** *inflammatory joints hate rest and love movement; mechanical joints are the opposite.*

##### Pattern-spotting: distribution
- **Symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis** → **RA** (also SLE, viral).
- **Asymmetrical large-joint / lower-limb oligoarthritis** → **spondyloarthropathy** (reactive, psoriatic, AS).
- **Axial (spine/sacroiliac) inflammatory back pain in a young adult** → **axial spondyloarthritis**.
- **Monoarthritis, acutely hot** → **septic until proven otherwise**, then crystal (gout/pseudogout).
- **Migratory** → rheumatic fever, gonococcal, some viral.

##### GALS and REMS
- **GALS screen** (Gait, Arms, Legs, Spine) — the rapid MSK screening exam: *"Any pain or stiffness in your muscles, joints or back? Can you dress/wash yourself fully? Can you walk up and down stairs?"* + inspection of gait, arms, legs and spine.
- **REMS** (Regional Examination of the MSK System) — the structured **Look – Feel – Move – (Special tests / function)** approach applied to a region. Always compare sides; assess active then passive movement; screen the joint above and below.

##### Systemic and extra-articular clues (the "it's more than a joint" flags)
Uveitis/red eye (spondyloarthropathy, sarcoid), psoriasis/nail pitting (PsA), oral/genital ulcers (Behçet's, reactive), Raynaud's (connective tissue disease), rash (SLE, dermatomyositis, vasculitis), sicca (Sjögren's), ENT/sinus disease + haemoptysis (GPA), recent GI/GU infection (reactive arthritis).

---

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.h: 3.2 Blood tests and the acute-phase response
docs.text:
**ESR vs CRP** — both rise in inflammation but they are not interchangeable:

| | **CRP** | **ESR** |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Acute-phase protein (hepatic, IL-6 driven) | Rate red cells settle (surrogate for fibrinogen/immunoglobulins) |
| Speed | **Rises and falls fast** (hours–days) | **Slow** to rise and fall (days–weeks) |
| Confounders | Fairly specific to inflammation/infection | Raised by **age, anaemia, pregnancy, paraproteins**; can be very high in myeloma |
| Classic use | Infection, most inflammation | **GCA/PMR, SLE activity** |

⚑ *Useful discordance:* in **active SLE**, **ESR is high but CRP is often normal/only mildly raised** — a rising CRP in a lupus patient should prompt a search for **infection** or serositis rather than being assumed to be a flare.

**Other core bloods:** FBC (anaemia of chronic disease, cytopenias in SLE, eosinophilia in EGPA), U&E (renal involvement — lupus nephritis, vasculitis), LFTs (baseline for hepatotoxic DMARDs), **urate** (gout — but may be normal during an acute attack), **bone profile** (Ca/PO₄/ALP), **CK** (grossly raised in inflammatory myopathy/rhabdomyolysis), vitamin D, urinalysis (an essential, cheap screen for renal involvement — **blood + protein/casts = glomerulonephritis until proven otherwise**).

---

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.h: 3.3 Autoantibodies and immunology *(the highest-yield table in rheumatology)*
docs.text:
**How to use antibodies:** they are **specific but not always sensitive**, and several are for **classification not diagnosis**. Order them to confirm a clinical suspicion, not to screen a well patient.

| Antibody | Strongest association | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **RF (rheumatoid factor)** | RA (sensitive, **not specific** — also Sjögren's, cryoglobulinaemia, chronic infection, healthy elderly) | Positive RF ≠ RA |
| **Anti-CCP (anti-citrullinated peptide)** | **RA — specific**, predicts erosive disease | The RA-defining antibody |
| **ANA (antinuclear antibody)** | **SLE screen** (sensitive, not specific); also many CTDs, some healthy people | **Entry criterion** for SLE classification |
| **Anti-dsDNA** | **SLE — specific**; tracks activity/nephritis | Rises in flare |
| **Anti-Sm (Smith)** | **SLE — specific** (but insensitive) | Confirmatory |
| **Anti-Ro (SSA) / Anti-La (SSB)** | **Sjögren's**; SLE; **neonatal lupus / congenital heart block** in pregnancy | Ro also in subacute cutaneous lupus |
| **Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase)** | **Diffuse** systemic sclerosis | ILD risk |
| **Anti-centromere** | **Limited** systemic sclerosis (CREST) | Pulmonary hypertension risk |
| **Anti-Jo-1 (anti-synthetase)** | **Polymyositis/dermatomyositis** | Antisynthetase syndrome (ILD, mechanic's hands) |
| **Anti-U1-RNP** | **Mixed connective tissue disease** (high titre) | Overlap features |
| **c-ANCA / anti-PR3** | **Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)** | ENT + lung + kidney |
| **p-ANCA / anti-MPO** | **MPA and EGPA** | Pulmonary–renal, eosinophilic |
| **Antiphospholipid** (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2GPI) | **Antiphospholipid syndrome** | Thrombosis + pregnancy loss; **paradoxically prolonged APTT** |

**Complement (C3/C4):** **consumed (low) in active SLE** and in immune-complex disease → a **low complement + high anti-dsDNA** picture = active lupus (especially nephritis). **Memory hook:** *in lupus, complement goes down as the disease goes up.*

---

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
##### Joint aspiration (arthrocentesis) — the reflex investigation of the acute hot joint
**Any acutely hot, swollen, painful joint must be aspirated before antibiotics** (unless it's a prosthetic joint → refer to orthopaedics; don't aspirate a prosthesis in ED). Send fluid for:

1. **Cell count + differential** — the septic-vs-inflammatory gradient (there is overlap, so it's supportive not absolute):

| Appearance / WCC | Suggests |
|---|---|
| Clear, WCC <2,000/mm³, low PMN | **Non-inflammatory** (OA, trauma) |
| Cloudy/yellow, WCC ~2,000–50,000 | **Inflammatory** (RA, crystal, spondyloarthropathy) |
| Turbid/purulent, **WCC >50,000 (often >100,000), PMN >90%** | **Septic arthritis** (but lower counts don't exclude it) |
| Blood-stained (haemarthrosis) | Trauma/ACL, haemophilia, PVNS |

2. **Gram stain + culture** — the definitive septic-arthritis test (may be negative even when infected).
3. **Polarised-light microscopy for crystals:**

| Crystal | Shape | Birefringence | Disease |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Monosodium urate** | **Needle-shaped** | **Negatively** birefringent (yellow when parallel) | **Gout** |
| **Calcium pyrophosphate** | **Rhomboid** | **Positively** birefringent | **Pseudogout (CPPD)** |

**Memory hook:** *"goutt" needles are **N**egative; **P**seudogout is **P**ositive and **P**laty/rhomboid.* ⚑ *Crystals and infection can coexist — finding crystals does not exclude sepsis.*

##### Imaging

| Modality | Best for | Signature findings |
|---|---|---|
| **Plain X-ray** | OA vs RA, fractures | **OA = LOSS** (Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral Sclerosis, Subchondral cysts); **RA = symmetrical joint-space loss, periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions, soft-tissue swelling** (LESS mnemonic) |
| **Ultrasound** | Synovitis, effusion, guided aspiration, **GCA** | **"Halo sign"** around temporal artery in GCA; power-Doppler synovitis |
| **MRI** | **Cord/cauda equina compression**, **sacroiliitis** (early axSpA), osteomyelitis, marrow oedema | Sacroiliac bone-marrow oedema; the emergency spine scan |
| **DEXA** | Bone density (osteoporosis) | **T-score ≤ −2.5 = osteoporosis** (see Section 6/endocrine) |
| **CT** | Complex fractures, staging | — |
| **Temporal artery biopsy** | GCA confirmation | **Granulomatous inflammation, giant cells; skip lesions → don't let a negative biopsy overrule strong clinical GCA** ⚑ |

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Morning stiffness >60 min, better with use | **Inflammatory** arthritis |
| Symmetrical small joints (MCP/PIP), spares DIP | **RA** |
| Asymmetrical lower-limb + enthesitis + HLA-B27 | **Spondyloarthropathy** |
| High ESR but normal CRP in a young woman | **Active SLE** (and a rising CRP → think infection) |
| First and only test in the acute hot joint | **Joint aspiration** (before antibiotics) |
| Synovial WCC >50,000, >90% PMN | **Septic arthritis** (but lower doesn't exclude) |
| Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals | **Gout** (MSU) |
| Rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals | **Pseudogout** (CPPD) |
| Radiographic LOSS | **Osteoarthritis** |
| Antibody specific for RA / for SLE | **Anti-CCP** / **anti-dsDNA or anti-Sm** |
| c-ANCA/PR3 vs p-ANCA/MPO | **GPA** vs **MPA/EGPA** |
| Low C3/C4 + high anti-dsDNA | Active **lupus** (nephritis) |
| Negative temporal artery biopsy but classic GCA | **Still treat** — skip lesions; biopsy is not 100% sensitive |

##### Sources
Kumar & Clark *Clinical Medicine*; Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine (autoantibody and synovial-fluid tables); Robbins (antibody–disease associations); StatPearls (synovial fluid analysis, ANCA); Versus Arthritis / Arthritis Research UK REMS & GALS resources. Synovial-fluid WCC thresholds (>50,000 supporting septic arthritis, with the caveat that no cut-off reliably excludes it) are consistent across StatPearls and Oxford Handbook; crystal birefringence directions cross-checked in ≥2 sources. DEXA T-score threshold (WHO −2.5) confirmed in bone-health guidance.

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.h: Orthopaedics (SNEHA) — Examination of radiographs — Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
AP and lateral films 🡪 look at each radiograph from a wide to medium to close up look.

- Bone – normal shape, size, contour or are they thicker or thinner than normal, shorter/longer or abnormally curved
- Joints – bony components in correct alignment or displaced / angled
- Bone texture – paget’s disease, avascular necrosis, osteoporosis, new bone formation.
- Contours of bone – contours of bine, noting any abnormality en route. Make a list on an anatomical base: assess ligamentous attachments, joint margins, the joint space and the cortical and cancellous bone elements.
- Comparison films
- Oblique projections
- Localized views
- Stress films - radiograph of the joint in use.

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
Additional screening tests include:

- ESR, CRP

- Serum calcium, phosphate and alp

Additional imaging techniques

Functional imaging techniques

- Technetium bone scans – 99mtc-methylene diphosphonate) 🡪 sensitive to areas of unusual bone rebuilding activity since it is taken up by osteoblast cells. 🡪 sensitive to fractures and bone tumors, including metastases

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.h: Orthopaedics (SNEHA) — inflammatory joint diseases — Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
Hyaline cartilage is composed of type 2 collagen, water, proteoglycans and chondrocytes.

- Collagen: resist tensile stresses and transmit force
- Water & proteoglycans: turgor and elasticity
- Chondrocytes: synthesis and digest matrix; secrete degrading enzymes in an inactive form and enrich matrix with enzyme inhibitors

Diseases that destroy articulate cartilage do so by activating catabolic enzyme, decreasing inhibitors 🡪 accelerated rate of matrix breakdown. Cytokines such as il-1 and TNF trigger the degradative process; their sources include chondrocytes, synoviocytes, fibroblasts, and inflammatory cells. Destruction of articular cartilage by indigenous cells is an important mechanism in many joint diseases.

docs.h: Rheumatology & Immunology (ANU) — PLASMA PROTEINS ASSOCIATED WITH INFLAMMATORY REACTIONS (play a role in innate immunity) — Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
- ACUTE PHASE PROTEINS: liver releases 30 acute-phase reactants, including CRP, ferritin, fibrinogen, α1-antitrypsin, haptoglobin, procalcitonin, IL-6
- NOTABLE NEGATIVE ACUTE PHASE REACTANTS: albumin, transferrin, anti-thrombin
- COMPLEMENT SYSTEM: after stimulation from Ab-complexes by pathogens → compliment activation →enhance functions of antibodies and phagocytesClassical pathway: IgM or IgG binds to pathogen (via C1)
- Alternative pathway: direct activation by pathogen rather than Ab-Ag complexes (via C3)
- Causes: opsonisation (C3), bacteria lysis (C5-9) and activation of mast cells/granulocytes (C3/C4/C5)

- PRO-INFLAMMATORY CYTOKINESIFN-α: ↑MHC I expression
- IFN-β: stimulates NK cells and cytotoxic
- IFN-γ: activated macrophages
- TNF-α: pyrogenic, cytotoxic, mediates septic shock
- Interleukins: IL-1, 2, 4, 6
- Arachidonic acid derivatives: PGE2/PGI2 increases pain sensation, vasodilation, and inhibits platelet aggregation and  leukotrienes which cause chemotaxis, exudation and bronchoconstriction
