docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| DIP nodes (Heberden's), 1st CMC squaring, LOSS on X-ray | **Osteoarthritis** |
| Symmetrical MCP/PIP synovitis sparing DIP, morning stiffness >1 h | **Rheumatoid arthritis** |
| RA-specific antibody / anchor drug | **Anti-CCP** / **methotrexate** |
| RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia | **Felty's syndrome** |
| Neck instability in RA to flag before anaesthesia | **Atlantoaxial subluxation** |
| Young man, inflammatory back pain, reduced Schober's, HLA-B27 | **Ankylosing / axial spondyloarthritis** |
| MRI sacroiliitis but normal X-ray | **Non-radiographic axial SpA** ⚑ |
| Bamboo spine | **Ankylosing spondylitis** |
| Nail pitting + dactylitis + pencil-in-cup | **Psoriatic arthritis** |
| Arthritis 1–4 wks after GI/GU infection + conjunctivitis + urethritis | **Reactive arthritis** |
| Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent, 1st MTP | **Gout** |
| Rhomboid, positively birefringent, chondrocalcinosis | **Pseudogout (CPPD)** |
| Target serum urate on ULT | **<0.36 mmol/L** (<0.30 if tophi) ⚑ |
| Test before allopurinol in high-risk ethnicity | **HLA-B*5801** ⚑ |
| Acute hot joint — first action | **Aspirate before antibiotics** |
| Commonest septic arthritis organism / in young sexually active | ***S. aureus*** / ***N. gonorrhoeae*** |
| Ulcer probes to bone in a diabetic foot | **Osteomyelitis** (MRI) |

##### Sources
Kumar & Clark; Robbins; StatPearls (RA, spondyloarthropathies, gout, septic arthritis). **2010 ACR/EULAR RA classification criteria**; **2021 ACR guideline for the treatment of RA** (methotrexate as first-line anchor DMARD; the ORAL Surveillance-derived JAK-inhibitor cardiovascular/malignancy/VTE warning); **2022 ASAS-EULAR axial SpA recommendations** (r-axSpA vs nr-axSpA nomenclature; NSAID→TNFi/IL-17i sequencing); **2020 ACR gout guideline** (treat-to-target, start-low allopurinol with prophylaxis, serum-urate target <6 mg/dL [<0.36 mmol/L], ULT indications, HLA-B*5801 testing) — urate target and ULT indications cross-checked against EULAR gout guidance. Crystal birefringence directions verified in ≥2 sources. Septic-arthritis "aspirate before antibiotics" and organism spectrum from BSR/StatPearls.

| Epidemiology | F>M, peak incidence ~ 20-40 years |

Hypotheses suggest the following factors:Genetic predisposition: HLA-DR4/DR1 in ~93% of patientsEnvironmental: infections, tobaccoHormonal: improves during pregnancy, worsens after birth |

| Differentials | Osteoarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, gout, pseudogout, AI-related (sarcoidosis, SLE, RF) |

| Definition | Derangement in purine metabolism causing hyperuricemiaMonosodium urate crystal deposits in tissue (tophi) and synovium (microtophi)Chronic gout is characterised with progressive joint degeneration due to recurring gout attacks |
| --- | --- |
| Aetiology | RISK FACTORS:Food (SALT): seafood, alcohol, liver/kidney (sugar), turkey (meat)Drugs (FACT): furosemide, aspirin, cytotoxic (cyclosporine), thiazide diureticsCo-morbidities: DM, HTN, hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia, anaemia, renal failure (impacting on excretion)Non-modifiable: age, male gender, genetic mutationsHyperuricemia does not equal gout but ↑ risk of gout and is commonly caused by impaired renal excretion (90%), overproduction (10%) and over-consumption of purine-rich foodPRIMARY HYPERURICEMIA: idiopathicSECONDARY HYPERURICEMIA: ↓ uric acid excretion (most common): MedicationsCRFKetoacidosis/lactic acidosis↑ uric acid production: High cell turnover (tumour lysis, haemolytic anaemia, psoriasis, myeloproliferative neoplasms, chemotherapy, radiation)↑ protein diet and obesityEnzyme defects (Lesh-Nyhan) |
| Pathophysiology | Uric acid is obtained exogenously (diet) or by xanthine oxidase (endogenously)Uric acid is excreted via intestinal (1/3) or urinary (2/3)Hyperuricemia → supersaturation of uric acid in ECF →intra-articular uric crystal precipitation (coated by IgGs) → phagocytised by polymorphonuclear cells → inflammatory mediators and enzymes →local joint inflammationOvertime, tophi causes destruction of cartilage and bone in joints → deformities and arthritis |
| Patterns | AcuteIntercritical (or interval) Chronic and recurrent |
| Presentation | Acute gouty arthritis: severe pain, redness, joint swelling, impaired joint mobilityTophi: urate deposits on cartilage, tendons, bursae, soft tissues and synovial membranesLocations: podagra (usually first MTP), gonagra (knee), chiragra (finger joint), ear helix, olecranon bursae, tendon insertions (Achilles tendon)Kidney: gouty nephropathy, uric acid calculi |
| Investigations | Joint aspirate: >90% show monosodium urate (negatively birefringent, needle-shaped)X-Ray: (in chronic gout): tophi shown as soft tissue swelling, punched-out-lesions, erosion with “over-hanging”Blood: hyperuricemia, ↑WBC, ↑ESRClinical Diagnosis: ≥1 episodes of single joint inflammation, 72 hours, cannot mobilise joint, classic podagra involvement (can be other joints), visible/palpable lesions (tophus) |
| Management | CONSERVATIVE: avoid high purine foods and drugs with hypouricemic effects, ice therapy, weight loss, management of diabetes and blood pressureACUTE GOUT:NSAIDS (COX-2 inhibitors) e.g. indomethacin, naproxen, ibuprofen: discontinue 2-3 days after symptoms resolveColchicine (interferes with neutrophil migration to the joint): 1 tablet (0.5mg) three/four times day; side effects are severe diarrhoea, nephrotoxicity and myelosuppresionCorticosteroid: IA/oral/IM; consider ACTH to prevent adrenal suppressionCHRONIC GOUTIndication

docs.text:
- DEFINITION: transient neurological Sx associated with malignant hypertensive state
- AETIOLOGY: abrupt ↑ BP in a chronically hypertensive state 🡪 BP > cerebral autoregulatory range 🡪 hydrostatic leakage 🡪 cerebral oedema 🡪 neurological deficits and altered medication
- HISTORY: vague (headache, confusion, visual distrubances)
- EXAMINATION: vitals (↑BP), ophthalmoscopy (papilloedema, haemorrhage, exudates, cotton wool spots), neuro exam (altered mental status, weakness)
- INVESTIGATIONS: FBC, EUC and urinalysis (kidney function), cardiac enzymes an ECG (?MI), CT head (rule out stroke), CXR (rule out aortic dissection, a concomitant)
- DIFFERENTIALS: stroke, tumour, encephalitis
- TREATMENT: ICU + regular BP/neurological assessment, return BP to baseline (e.g. labetalol/nicardipine; avoid CNS-affecting agents; excessive BP reduction below baseline may cause cerebral ischemia)
- PROGNOSIS: related to degree of target-organ damage

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
- TYPES
- Primary: glial vs. non-glial (developed on/in the structures of brain including nerves, blood vessels and glands)
- Metastatic (70%): arise from primary sources (lung > breast > kidney > GI > melanoma)
- Main types to know
- Pituitary: craniopharyngioma, prolactinoma, acromegaly
- Posterior fossa (P for paeds): medulloblastoma, ependymoma (both present withhydrocephalus)
- Anterior fossa (A for adults): meningioma, glioblastoma
- Astrocytoma: most common primary intra-axial brain tumour
- PRESENTATION: commonly focal neurological deficits and seizures, headaches worse in AM, progressive N/V
- INVESTIGATIONS: MRI w contrast > CT w contrast, stereotactic biopsy (tissue diagnosis), metastatic work-up, tumour markers (i.e. germ cell)
- TREATMENT
- Conservative: serial history, physical exam and imaging for slow growing/benign lesions
- Medical: corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone, palliative, ↓ cerebral oedema), seizure prophylaxis (e.g. phenytoin), pharmacologic (i.e. pituitary adenoma)
- Surgical: total/partial excision (decompressive, palliative), shunt if hydrocephalus
- Radiotherapy
- Chemotherapy e.g. alkylating agents (vincristine, cyclophosphamide)

docs.text:
*Sources: AHA/ASA 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients with Acute Ischemic Stroke; NICE NG128 (stroke and TIA); European Stroke Organisation guidelines; AHA/ASA spontaneous ICH guideline (2022); AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH guideline (2023); Kumar & Clark; Merck Manual Professional; StatPearls. Scope: the highest-yield acute section. ⚑ marks guidance that has moved since older textbooks.*

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Stroke** — an acute focal neurological deficit of vascular origin lasting >24 hours or with imaging evidence of infarction/haemorrhage. **TIA** — transient focal neurological dysfunction of vascular origin **without infarction on imaging**; ⚑ the definition is now *tissue-based*, not the old "resolves within 24 hours" time-based one.

Roughly **85% ischaemic, 15% haemorrhagic** (of which about two-thirds intracerebral and one-third subarachnoid).

**Modifiable risk factors:** hypertension (the single biggest), atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidaemia, obesity, alcohol, obstructive sleep apnoea, physical inactivity, combined oral contraceptive with migraine with aura. **Non-modifiable:** age, male sex, family history, prior stroke/TIA, ethnicity (higher risk in South Asian, African and Caribbean populations).

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
Symptoms usually last minutes (typically <1 hour). Distinguish from mimics: migraine aura (positive symptoms, slow march), focal seizure (positive symptoms, seconds, post-ictal), syncope (global, not focal), hypoglycaemia, functional.

**Management (NICE NG128):**

- Give **aspirin 300 mg immediately** unless contraindicated.
- **Specialist assessment within 24 hours** for anyone with a suspected TIA in the last 7 days. ⚑ NICE has **abandoned the ABCD² score** for deciding urgency — everyone gets seen within 24 hours.
- Do **not** do CT routinely; MRI (with diffusion-weighted imaging) is the test of choice, ideally on the day of assessment.
- Carotid imaging urgently if the patient is a candidate for carotid intervention.
- Start secondary prevention immediately (see 4.9). **Crescendo TIAs** (≥2 in a week) or TIA on anticoagulation → admit.
- Driving: in the UK, no driving for **1 month** after a TIA or stroke (Group 1 licence), longer and with notification for Group 2.

**Amaurosis fugax** — painless transient monocular visual loss, classically "curtain descending"; think ipsilateral carotid disease or cardiac embolus, and treat as a TIA.

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**TOAST aetiologies:** large-artery atherosclerosis; cardioembolism (AF, endocarditis, recent MI, prosthetic valve, patent foramen ovale); small-vessel occlusion (lacunar); other determined (dissection, vasculitis, thrombophilia, sickle cell, CADASIL, moyamoya); undetermined (cryptogenic).

**Bamford / Oxford (OCSP) classification** — clinical, done at the bedside, predicts prognosis.

| Class | Criteria | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **TACS** — total anterior circulation | **All three**: (1) higher cortical dysfunction (aphasia/neglect), (2) homonymous hemianopia, (3) motor and/or sensory deficit of ≥2 of face/arm/leg | Worst prognosis; large MCA ± ACA |
| **PACS** — partial anterior circulation | **Two of the three**, or higher cortical dysfunction alone, or a limited motor/sensory deficit | Highest early recurrence risk |
| **LACS** — lacunar | **No** cortical signs, no visual field defect: pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, or ataxic hemiparesis | Best prognosis; small perforator |
| **POCS** — posterior circulation | Cranial nerve palsy with contralateral deficit, bilateral deficits, disordered conjugate eye movement, cerebellar signs, **isolated homonymous hemianopia** | Easily missed |

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
| Presentation | Territory |
|---|---|
| Leg > arm weakness, abulia, incontinence | ACA |
| Face/arm > leg, aphasia or neglect, gaze towards lesion | MCA |
| Isolated homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing | PCA |
| Dense equal hemiparesis, no cortical signs, no field defect | Lacunar (internal capsule/pons) |
| Vertigo, ataxia, crossed sensory loss, Horner's, hoarseness | Lateral medullary — PICA/vertebral |
| Sudden reduced consciousness, quadriparesis, pinpoint pupils | Basilar occlusion / pontine |
| Preserved awareness, quadriplegia, vertical eye movement only | Locked-in (ventral pons) |
| Young patient, neck pain, Horner's, after neck trauma or chiropractic manipulation | **Carotid or vertebral dissection** |
| Young patient, migraine, recurrent subcortical strokes, family history, dementia | **CADASIL** (NOTCH3) |
| Stroke in pregnancy/puerperium, headache, seizures | Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, eclampsia, RCVS |

**Five lacunar syndromes:** pure motor hemiparesis (posterior limb of internal capsule — commonest), pure sensory stroke (VPL thalamus), sensorimotor stroke, ataxic hemiparesis (pons/internal capsule), clumsy-hand dysarthria.

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Sequence:** ABC and glucose → NIHSS → **immediate non-contrast CT head** → decide reperfusion → CT angiography (± perfusion) if large-vessel occlusion possible → stroke unit.

**Thrombolysis**

- Agents: ⚑ the 2026 AHA/ASA guideline endorses **either alteplase or tenecteplase** within the 4.5-hour window; tenecteplase is a single bolus (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg) and is increasingly first-line, alteplase is 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg, 10% bolus then infusion over 1 hour). Older textbooks list alteplase only.
- **Window: within 4.5 hours of onset (or last known well)**, for disabling deficits ⚑ **regardless of NIHSS score**.
- **Extended/unknown-onset window:** selected patients **4.5–9 hours**, or wake-up stroke, using advanced imaging — perfusion core/penumbra mismatch (EXTEND) or **DWI–FLAIR mismatch** (WAKE-UP). ⚑ This did not exist in older texts.
- ⚑ For **non-disabling** deficits within 4.5 hours, dual antiplatelet therapy is now preferred over thrombolysis.
- **BP must be <185/110** before thrombolysis and kept **<180/105 for 24 hours** afterwards.
- **Absolute contraindications:** intracranial haemorrhage on imaging, previous ICH, active bleeding, known AVM/aneurysm/intracranial neoplasm at risk, recent significant head injury or intracranial/spinal surgery (<3 months), suspected SAH, GI haemorrhage <21 days, platelets <100, INR >1.7 or therapeutic anticoagulation, DOAC within 48 hours (unless assays normal), **glucose <2.8 mmol/L uncorrected**, uncontrolled BP above the threshold.
- **Complications:** symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (~2–6%), angio-oedema (especially with ACE inhibitors), systemic bleeding.

**Mechanical thrombectomy**

- For **large-vessel occlusion** (intracranial ICA, M1, and selected M2/basilar).
- **Within 6 hours** on standard criteria; **6–24 hours** with perfusion/clinical mismatch selection (DAWN, DEFUSE-3).
- ⚑ Now also offered to patients with **large established ischaemic cores** (SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT, RESCUE-Japan LIMIT) — the old rule "ASPECTS <6 excludes thrombectomy" no longer holds.
- ⚑ **Basilar artery occlusion: thrombectomy within 24 hours with NIHSS ≥10** (ATTENTION, BAOCHE) — a strong recommendation in the 2026 guideline.
- Thrombolysis and thrombectomy are not alternatives: if eligible for both, give thrombolysis and proceed to thrombectomy without waiting for a response.

**Other acute measures**

- **Aspirin 300 mg** as soon as haemorrhage is excluded, or at **24 hours** if thrombolysed (after repeat imaging); continue 300 mg for 2 weeks then switch to long-term antithrombotic.
- **Do not lower BP acutely** in ischaemic stroke unless thrombolysing, or BP >220/120, or another indication (aortic dissection, heart failure, hypertensive encephalopathy). ⚑ Intensive lowering to <140 systolic is **not** recommended even after successful reperfusion.
- Glucose 4–11 mmol/L; treat fever; nil by mouth until swallow screened; VTE prophylaxis with **intermittent pneumatic compression** (not routine heparin); ea

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Causes:** hypertension (deep — basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum), **cerebral amyloid angiopathy** (lobar, elderly, recurrent, microbleeds on SWI), anticoagulation, AVM/aneurysm, tumour, sympathomimetic drugs (cocaine, amphetamine), venous thrombosis.

**Management:**

- ⚑ **Rapid BP lowering to a systolic target of 130–140 mmHg within the first hour**, sustained — as part of a care bundle (INTERACT3, which showed reduced mortality/disability). Avoid dropping >70 mmHg from baseline.
- **Reverse anticoagulation urgently:** warfarin → **IV vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate**; dabigatran → **idarucizumab**; factor Xa inhibitors → **andexanet alfa** (or PCC where unavailable) ⚑.
- Neurosurgery for **cerebellar haemorrhage >3 cm** or with brainstem compression/hydrocephalus (this one is exam-standard), for hydrocephalus (EVD), and for selected lobar clot evacuation (minimally invasive approaches increasingly used ⚑).
- Reverse the reversible: glucose, temperature, seizures (treat, do not prophylax), head up 30°.
- Stop antithrombotics; the timing of restarting is individualised (often ~4–8 weeks if a strong indication such as a mechanical valve or high-risk AF).

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Presentation:** **thunderclap headache** — maximal within seconds, "worst ever", often occipital; ± vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, reduced consciousness, seizure, **subhyaloid/vitreous (Terson's) haemorrhage** on fundoscopy, third nerve palsy (PCom aneurysm), sudden death.

**Causes:** ruptured **saccular (berry) aneurysm** (~85%) — commonest sites: anterior communicating artery, posterior communicating artery, MCA bifurcation; perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal (benign, ~10%); AVM, dissection, trauma.

**Associations:** autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers–Danlos type IV, coarctation, family history, smoking, hypertension, alcohol.

**Diagnosis:** immediate **non-contrast CT** — sensitivity is >98% within 6 hours of onset and falls thereafter; if negative and the story is convincing, **LP at ≥12 hours** for **xanthochromia** (spectrophotometry). Then **CT angiography** to define the aneurysm.

**Management:**

- Neurosurgical/neuroradiology referral; **endovascular coiling is preferred to clipping** where the aneurysm is suitable (ISAT), ideally within 24–72 hours.
- **Nimodipine 60 mg orally 4-hourly for 21 days** — reduces poor outcome from delayed cerebral ischaemia. (Note: it is neuroprotective; it does not simply "prevent vasospasm on angiography".)
- Bed rest, analgesia, laxatives, careful BP control (avoid hypotension), euvolaemia, VTE prophylaxis mechanical initially.

**Complications and their timing:**

| Complication | Timing | Clue |
|---|---|---|
| Rebleeding | First 24–48 h (highest risk) | Sudden deterioration — secure the aneurysm early |
| **Delayed cerebral ischaemia / vasospasm** | **Days 4–14 (peak 7–10)** | New focal deficit or reduced GCS; treat with induced euvolaemia/hypertension, nimodipine, angioplasty |
| Hydrocephalus | Any time; early or late | Deteriorating consciousness; EVD/shunt |
| **Hyponatraemia** | Days | SIADH vs **cerebral salt wasting** (hypovolaemic — treat with salt and fluid, **not** fluid restriction) |
| Seizures | Any | Treat, don't prophylax |
| Neurogenic pulmonary oedema, stunned myocardium | Early | ECG changes mimicking ischaemia |

**Grading:** Hunt and Hess or WFNS (based on GCS and focal deficit) clinically; **modified Fisher** on CT (blood load predicts vasospasm).

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Suspect when:** headache (often progressive over days, worse lying flat or on Valsalva), papilloedema, seizures, focal deficits **crossing arterial territories**, haemorrhagic infarcts in unusual places (parasagittal, temporal), or isolated intracranial hypertension.

**Risk factors:** pregnancy and puerperium, combined oral contraceptive, thrombophilia, dehydration, malignancy, local sepsis (mastoiditis, sinusitis), head injury, nephrotic syndrome, and (rarely) vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia.

**Diagnosis:** **CT or MR venography**. Plain CT may show a dense cord/delta sign but is often normal. D-dimer is unhelpful if negative in isolated headache.

**Treatment:** ⚑ **anticoagulate — with low-molecular-weight heparin — even in the presence of haemorrhagic infarction**, then oral anticoagulation for 3–12 months. Treat raised ICP; decompressive surgery in severe cases. Warfarin remains standard; DOACs are a reasonable alternative in stable patients (RE-SPECT CVT, ACTION-CVT) ⚑ but not where VITT or antiphospholipid syndrome is present.

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
| Setting | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Ischaemic stroke or TIA, non-cardioembolic | **Clopidogrel 75 mg daily** long term (aspirin + dipyridamole if intolerant) |
| **Minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3–5) or high-risk TIA** | ⚑ **Dual antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21 days**, then clopidogrel alone (CHANCE, POINT, THALES). Loading doses used; do not continue DAPT long term — bleeding risk |
| Atrial fibrillation | **DOAC** (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran); warfarin if mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis. Timing: ⚑ **early initiation (within days) is safe and is now supported** by ELAN/OPTIMAS; the old "1-3-6-12 day rule" is being superseded |
| Lipids | High-intensity statin (e.g. atorvastatin 80 mg) — target LDL <1.8 mmol/L (some guidance <1.4) |
| Blood pressure | Long-term target <130/80 in most; start once stable (usually after ~2 weeks) |
| **Symptomatic carotid stenosis 50–99% (NASCET)** | **Carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks** of the event — benefit falls sharply with delay. Stenting in selected younger patients or high surgical risk |
| Asymptomatic carotid stenosis | Best medical therapy; surgery only in selected cases |
| **Patent foramen ovale** in cryptogenic stroke, age <60, high-risk PFO | ⚑ **PFO closure** (CLOSE, REDUCE, RESPECT) plus antiplatelet |
| Lifestyle | Smoking cessation, alcohol reduction, exercise, diabetes control, AF screening |

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Acute complications:** aspiration pneumonia (swallow screen before anything by mouth), malignant cerebral oedema (day 2–5 after large MCA infarct), haemorrhagic transformation, seizures, DVT/PE, pressure ulcers, depression, urinary retention/infection, malnutrition.

**Rehabilitation** is multidisciplinary from day one: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy (both for aphasia and swallowing), dietitian, psychology, stroke nurse specialists. **Post-stroke complications to actively look for:** spasticity (physiotherapy, botulinum toxin), shoulder subluxation and pain, central post-stroke (thalamic) pain, emotional lability, post-stroke depression (common, treatable), fatigue, cognitive impairment/vascular dementia.

**Prognostic notes:** TACS carries the worst outcome (~60% dead or dependent at 1 year); LACS the best. Most functional recovery occurs in the first 3 months.

---

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
- DEFINITION: sudden neurological deficit of a vascular basis with CNS tissue infarction, confirmed by neuroimaging
- RISK FACTORS: non-modifiable (↑age > 65 y/o, F>M, ethnicity e.g. Indigenous, familial), modifiable (TIA, HTN, smoking, cholesterol, ↓ diet, ↓ exercise, obesity, DM, EtOH, AF ↑ risk of thrombosis, coagulopathy in chronic liver disease)
- PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

ISCHEMIC STROKE (80%)

- TOAST Criteria

- LARGE-ARTERY ATHEROSCLEROSIS (embolus/thrombusis)- large artery > 50% occlusion, infarct > 1.5 cm
- CARDIOEMBOLISM- AF, valve disease, ventricular thrombi, cardiomyopathy
- SMALL-VESSEL OCCLUSION (LACUNAR)- a/w HTN, DM and ↑ age 🡪 lipohyalinosis, affecting small penetrating arteries/arterioles that originate from the base of the brain and supply basal ganglia, thalamus, deep white matter and brain-stem; infarct < 1.5cm
- STROKE OF OTHER DETERMINED AETIOLOGY e.g. drugs, arterial dissection, thrombophilia, arteritis, anti-phospholipid syndrome, complex migraine, watershed infarcts
- STROKE OF UNDETERMINED AETIOLOGY- two/more causes, negative/incomplete evaluation

- Hypoxia 🡪 Necrosis at centre of ischemic damage becomes leaky 🡪 K+ and ATP 🡪 further inflammation + oedema of surrounding ischemic penumbra (initially vulnerable tissue salvageable) 🡪 widespread infarction 🡪 liquefaction necrosis 🡪 removed by macrophages 🡪 parenchymal volume loss

HAEMORRHAGIC (20%)

INTRACEREBRAL HAEMORRHAGE (ICH)- BLEEDING DIRECTLY INTO THE BRAIN PARENCHYMA

- Causes: HTN (most common), trauma, small microaneurysm rupture (Charcot-Bouchard), bleeding diatheses, amyloid angiopathy, drugs (amphetamine, cocaine), vasculitis; Sx may not be as sudden like embolism or SAH

SUBARACHNOID HAEMORRHAGE (SAH)- BLEEDING INTO THE CSF WITHIN THE SUBARACHNOID SPACE

- Causes: trauma (common), ruptured aneurysms, coagulopathies, vasculitides, tumour, cerebral artery dissections
- DIFFERENTIALS: drug intoxication, infections, migraines, metabolic, seizures, tumours
- PRESENTATION
- Sudden onset due to sudden ↑ICP, with worsening of symptoms as infarction progresses
- ↑ICP 🡪 headache (worse in morning + bending), N/V, mass effects, focal signs, herniation syndrome, HTN, afebrile
- General- ↓ LOC, altered mental status, confusion, neglect
- Language- dysarthria, aphasia, swallowing difficulty
- Vision- diplopia, eye deviation, asymmetric pupils, visual field defect
- ![](notes/images/neurology-anu/img011.jpg)
Coordination- ataxia, intention tremor, ↓ coordination
- Motor- UMN Sx
- Sensation- ↓ sensation
- Dominant hemisphere: aphasia, contralateral hemiparesis, dysarthria, reading, writing, calculation
- Non-dominant hemisphere: neglect, apraxia (dressing, constructional)
- However, constellation of neurological deficits can point to a certain vascular territory (in table below)
- Anterior circulation ischemia caused by occlusion to one of the carotid arteries/MCA (most common)
- Posterior circulation ischaemia more challenging as motor/sensory limb signs are absent

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
**Pathology:** chronic immune-mediated inflammatory demyelination of the CNS with axonal loss. Plaques are perivenular and favour the periventricular white matter, corpus callosum, juxtacortical region, optic nerves, brainstem/cerebellar peduncles and spinal cord. **Prevalence rises with distance from the equator**; peak onset 20–40 years; female:male ~3:1; risk factors include low vitamin D, **Epstein–Barr virus infection** (now regarded as a near-necessary prerequisite ⚑), smoking, adolescent obesity, and HLA-DRB1*15:01.

**Phenotypes:**

| Phenotype | Course |
|---|---|
| **Clinically isolated syndrome** | First demyelinating episode; may or may not go on to MS |
| **Relapsing–remitting (~85% at onset)** | Discrete relapses with partial or full recovery |
| **Secondary progressive** | Steady progression after an initial relapsing course (most RRMS eventually) |
| **Primary progressive (~10–15%)** | Progressive from onset; older, more male, more spinal cord |
| **Radiologically isolated syndrome** | Incidental typical MRI lesions without symptoms ⚑ — now diagnosable as MS in some circumstances |

**Common presentations:** **optic neuritis** (subacute painful monocular visual loss, pain on eye movement, red desaturation, RAPD), **partial transverse myelitis** (sensory level, Lhermitte's, bladder symptoms), brainstem syndromes (diplopia, **internuclear ophthalmoplegia**, vertigo, trigeminal neuralgia in a young person), cerebellar syndromes, fatigue, cognitive change. **Uhthoff's phenomenon** — transient worsening with heat.

**Diagnosis — dissemination in space (DIS) and time (DIT).** The 2017 McDonald criteria required lesions in ≥2 of four typical locations (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) for DIS, and either a new lesion over time, simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, or **CSF-specific oligoclonal bands** as a substitute for DIT.

⚑ **The 2024 revisions (published 2025) change several things:**
- The **optic nerve** is added as a **fifth topography** for dissemination in space (evidenced by MRI, OCT or visual evoked potentials).
- **Central vein sign** and **paramagnetic rim lesions** are incorporated as MS-specific imaging biomarkers.
- **Kappa free light chains** in CSF are accepted as an alternative to oligoclonal bands.
- When enough topographies are involved, **separate evidence of dissemination in time is no longer required**.
- MS can now be diagnosed in **asymptomatic** individuals (previously labelled radiologically isolated syndrome) when supportive biomarkers are present.
- The stated trade-off is a risk of **overdiagnosis** — the criteria are only valid once mimics have been excluded.

**Investigations:** MRI brain and whole spine with gadolinium (**"Dawson's fingers"** — ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles — are characteristic), CSF for oligoclonal bands unmatched in serum, visual evoked potentials, and blood tests to exclude mimics (**AQP4 and MOG antib

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.h: 8.2 MS — relapse management and disease-modifying therapy
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
**Relapse:** new or worsening symptoms lasting **>24 hours** in the absence of infection or fever, ≥30 days from the last relapse. **First exclude a pseudo-relapse** — infection (especially urinary), fever, metabolic upset unmasking old deficits; treating the infection is the treatment.

**Acute relapse treatment:** **methylprednisolone 500 mg orally for 5 days** (or 1 g IV daily for 3–5 days if severe or unable to take oral). Steroids shorten the relapse but do not change long-term disability. Plasma exchange for severe steroid-refractory relapse.

**Disease-modifying therapy** — for relapsing MS; the direction of travel is towards **earlier use of higher-efficacy agents** ⚑.

| Class/drug | Route | Key risk to remember |
|---|---|---|
| Interferon beta, glatiramer acetate | SC/IM | Modest efficacy; flu-like symptoms; injection reactions; safe in pregnancy |
| **Teriflunomide** | Oral | **Teratogenic** — needs washout with cholestyramine; hepatotoxicity |
| **Dimethyl fumarate** | Oral | Flushing, GI upset, **lymphopenia → PML risk** |
| **Sphingosine-1-phosphate modulators** (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod) | Oral | **First-dose bradycardia**, macular oedema, VZV reactivation, **rebound disease on stopping** |
| **Cladribine** | Oral (short courses) | Lymphopenia, herpes zoster, contraception for 6 months |
| **Natalizumab** (anti-α4-integrin) | IV/SC | **Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy** — risk rises with **JC virus antibody positivity**, long duration and prior immunosuppression |
| **Anti-CD20** (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, rituximab, ublituximab) | IV/SC | Infusion reactions, hypogammaglobulinaemia, infections; **ocrelizumab is the only licensed DMT for primary progressive MS** |
| **Alemtuzumab** (anti-CD52) | IV | Powerful but **secondary autoimmunity — thyroid disease (~40%), ITP, anti-GBM nephritis**; needs 5 years of monthly monitoring |
| **Autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation** | — | For highly active disease failing therapy ⚑ |

**Progressive MS:** ⚑ **ocrelizumab** for early inflammatory PPMS; **siponimod** for active SPMS. Otherwise the focus is symptom control and rehabilitation.

**Symptomatic management:** spasticity — baclofen, tizanidine, gabapentin, botulinum toxin, **nabiximols** in refractory cases; **fatigue** — exercise, sleep, amantadine/modafinil (limited evidence); bladder — anticholinergics, intermittent self-catheterisation (check post-void residual first); neuropathic pain — gabapentinoids, amitriptyline, duloxetine; **fampridine** for walking speed in selected patients; depression, sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis, vitamin D.

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
These are **not** MS and must be identified because MS drugs (interferon, natalizumab, fingolimod) can make NMOSD worse.

| | **Multiple sclerosis** | **NMOSD (AQP4-IgG)** | **MOGAD (MOG-IgG)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Antibody | None | **Aquaporin-4 IgG** (astrocytopathy) | **MOG-IgG** (oligodendrocyte myelin) |
| Demographics | F>M 3:1, 20–40 y, Northern European | **Strong female predominance, often Afro-Caribbean or East Asian, older onset** | Children and adults, no sex bias |
| Optic neuritis | Usually unilateral, mild-moderate | **Bilateral, severe, posterior/chiasmal, poor recovery** | **Bilateral, severe, with optic disc swelling, but good steroid response** |
| Myelitis | Short segment, partial | **Longitudinally extensive (≥3 vertebral segments)** | Longitudinally extensive, often conus |
| Other clues | Dawson's fingers, cognitive change | **Area postrema syndrome — intractable hiccups, nausea and vomiting** | ADEM phenotype in children; steroid-dependent relapses |
| CSF bands | Positive in >85% | Usually **negative** | Usually negative |
| Acute treatment | Steroids | High-dose steroids **plus early plasma exchange** | High-dose steroids (very responsive) |
| Maintenance | MS DMTs | **Rituximab, eculizumab, satralizumab, inebilizumab** ⚑ | Steroid-sparing (azathioprine, MMF, rituximab, IVIg) if relapsing |
| MS drugs | — | **Harmful** | Not indicated |

> **Hook:** *Longitudinally extensive myelitis + bilateral severe optic neuritis + hiccups = check AQP4.*

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.h: 8.4 Optic neuritis, transverse myelitis and ADEM
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
**Optic neuritis:** subacute (hours–days) monocular loss of acuity and colour vision, **pain worse on eye movement**, central scotoma, **RAPD**; the disc is normal in two-thirds ("the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing" — retrobulbar). Recovery over weeks is usual; **optic disc pallor** and a **delayed VEP P100** persist. MRI brain determines the risk of MS. High-dose steroids speed recovery but do not change final acuity. **Atypical features — bilateral, severe, no recovery, disc swelling, older patient — mean test for AQP4/MOG and consider GCA or compressive causes.**

**Transverse myelitis:** acute or subacute cord dysfunction with a sensory level, weakness and sphincter disturbance. Always image urgently to **exclude compression first**. Causes: MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, post-infectious, SLE/Sjögren's, sarcoidosis, infections (VZV, HSV, enterovirus, schistosomiasis), paraneoplastic, and **spinal cord infarction** (which is sudden and painful, with sparing of dorsal columns).

**ADEM:** monophasic, usually post-infectious or post-vaccination, more common in children; **encephalopathy is required** for the diagnosis; large, poorly demarcated, simultaneously enhancing lesions. Treated with high-dose steroids ± IVIg/plasma exchange. **Recurrence should prompt MOG antibody testing.**

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
**Organisms by group:**

| Group | Commonest organisms |
|---|---|
| Neonates | Group B streptococcus, *E. coli*, **Listeria** |
| Children/young adults | *Neisseria meningitidis*, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, (Hib if unvaccinated) |
| Adults | ***Streptococcus pneumoniae*** (commonest overall in adults), *N. meningitidis* |
| **>60 years, pregnancy, immunosuppressed, alcohol excess** | Add ***Listeria monocytogenes*** |
| Post-neurosurgery, shunts, penetrating trauma | Staphylococci, Gram-negatives |
| Basal skull fracture/CSF leak | *S. pneumoniae* |

**Recognition:** the classic triad of fever, neck stiffness and altered mental state is present in fewer than half — **most have at least two of headache, fever, neck stiffness and altered consciousness**. Look for photophobia, vomiting, seizures, focal signs, and the **non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash of meningococcal sepsis** (a late sign; its absence means nothing). Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are specific but insensitive.

**Immediate management (NICE NG240, 2024, and UK Joint Specialist Societies guidance):**
1. Recognise, resuscitate; **blood cultures and bloods (including meningococcal/pneumococcal PCR)**.
2. ⚑ **Antibiotics within 1 hour of arrival** — do not wait for imaging or LP. In the community, benzylpenicillin IM/IV before transfer if meningococcal disease is suspected and transfer will be delayed.
3. **Empirical therapy: IV ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily** (or cefotaxime). **Add amoxicillin/ampicillin 2 g 4-hourly for *Listeria* cover if over 60 years, pregnant, immunosuppressed, or with alcohol excess/malnutrition.** Add vancomycin if there is a risk of penicillin-resistant pneumococcus (recent travel to high-prevalence areas). Aciclovir if encephalitis is also possible.
4. **Dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly for 4 days**, given **with or just before the first dose of antibiotics** — reduces hearing loss and mortality in pneumococcal meningitis. Avoid or stop if meningococcal sepsis or septic shock predominates, or in post-surgical/immunosuppressed cases.
5. **CT before LP** only if: reduced or fluctuating consciousness (GCS <12 or a fall of ≥2), focal neurological signs, new seizures, papilloedema, severe immunocompromise, or signs of raised ICP/shock. **A normal CT does not exclude raised ICP.**
6. **LP as soon as it is safe** (ideally within 1 hour of arrival if no contraindication): opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose (with **paired serum glucose**), Gram stain, culture, PCR, lactate.
7. Contact tracing and **prophylaxis for close contacts** of meningococcal disease: **ciprofloxacin single dose** (first line; rifampicin an alternative), plus vaccination as advised by public health. Notify the local health protection team — meningococcal disease is **notifiable**.

**Complications:** septic shock and DIC, hearing loss (**all survivors need audiology**), hydrocephalus, subdural empyema, cerebral abscess, venous sinus thrombosis, seizures, cognitive impairment, cranial

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
**Encephalitis = brain parenchymal inflammation → altered mental state, personality or behaviour change, seizures, focal deficits, fever.** The discriminator from meningitis is **altered brain function**, not just meningism.

**Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1)** — the commonest sporadic viral encephalitis and the treatable one:
- Fever, confusion, **prominent behavioural and memory change**, dysphasia, seizures.
- MRI: **asymmetric temporal and inferior frontal lobe** oedema/haemorrhage; EEG: **temporal periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges**.
- CSF: lymphocytosis, raised protein, normal glucose, **red cells may be present**; **HSV PCR** (may be falsely negative in the first 24–48 hours — repeat if suspicion is high).
- **Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly immediately on suspicion**, for 14–21 days. Delay is the main determinant of poor outcome; untreated mortality ~70%.

**Other infective causes:** VZV, enterovirus, EBV, CMV and HHV-6 (immunosuppressed), measles (SSPE), mumps, HIV seroconversion, arboviruses (Japanese encephalitis, West Nile, Murray Valley/Kunjin in Australia ⚑, tick-borne encephalitis), rabies, *Listeria* rhombencephalitis, cerebral malaria.

**Autoimmune encephalitis** ⚑ — increasingly recognised and treatable:

| Antibody | Picture | Association |
|---|---|---|
| **Anti-NMDA receptor** | Young woman; prodrome → psychiatric symptoms/psychosis → seizures → **orofacial dyskinesias**, autonomic instability, reduced consciousness | **Ovarian teratoma** — image the pelvis |
| **LGI1** | Older man; hyponatraemia; **faciobrachial dystonic seizures**; amnesia | Rarely tumour |
| **CASPR2** | Morvan syndrome, neuromyotonia, insomnia | Thymoma |
| **GABA-B** | Prominent seizures | Small cell lung cancer |
| Classic paraneoplastic (Hu, Ma2, CV2) | Limbic encephalitis, brainstem, cerebellar | SCLC, testicular, others |

Treatment: **remove the tumour** where present, plus first-line immunotherapy (steroids, IVIg, plasma exchange) and second-line rituximab/cyclophosphamide. Recovery can be slow but is often substantial.

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.h: 8.7 Brain abscess, TB and cryptococcal meningitis
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
**Brain abscess:** headache, fever, focal deficit — but the classic triad is present in a minority. Sources: contiguous (otitis, mastoiditis, sinusitis, dental), haematogenous (endocarditis, lung, cyanotic congenital heart disease with right-to-left shunt), penetrating trauma, neurosurgery. Imaging: **ring-enhancing lesion with a smooth thin wall and restricted diffusion on DWI** (which distinguishes it from tumour). **Do not LP.** Treatment: neurosurgical aspiration/excision plus prolonged IV antibiotics (typically ceftriaxone + metronidazole ± vancomycin), and dexamethasone only for significant mass effect.

**Tuberculous meningitis:** subacute over weeks — headache, low-grade fever, personality change, then **cranial nerve palsies (especially VI), hydrocephalus and basal exudates with enhancement on imaging**; stroke from vasculitis of perforators. CSF: **lymphocytosis, very high protein (often >1–5 g/L), low glucose**, AFB smear (low yield), **Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra**, culture. Treat empirically on suspicion: **RIPE (rifampicin, isoniazid + pyridoxine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months then rifampicin/isoniazid — 12 months total for CNS TB — plus adjunctive corticosteroids**, which reduce mortality.

**Cryptococcal meningitis:** in HIV with CD4 <100 (also other immunosuppression). Insidious headache, fever, **very high opening pressure**. CSF **India ink** and **cryptococcal antigen (CrAg — the test of choice, highly sensitive)**. Treat with **liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine induction, then fluconazole**, and — critically — **serial therapeutic lumbar punctures to control intracranial pressure**, which is the main determinant of early mortality. Beware immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome when antiretrovirals are started.

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
**Neurosyphilis** ("the great imitator") — early forms: asymptomatic, meningeal, meningovascular (stroke in a young person). Late: **general paresis** (dementia, psychiatric change) and **tabes dorsalis** (lightning pains, sensory ataxia, **Argyll Robertson pupils**, absent reflexes, Charcot joints). Diagnose with serum treponemal tests plus CSF (VDRL specific but insensitive; raised protein and lymphocytes). Treat with **IV benzylpenicillin** for 14 days; warn about the **Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction**.

**HIV neurology by CD4 count:**

| CD4 | Condition |
|---|---|
| Any | Seroconversion meningoencephalitis, distal sensory polyneuropathy, HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder, inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy |
| <200 | **Cerebral toxoplasmosis** (multiple ring-enhancing lesions in basal ganglia, treat with pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine; response confirms the diagnosis), **primary CNS lymphoma** (single periventricular enhancing lesion, EBV in CSF, thallium-avid) |
| <100 | **Cryptococcal meningitis**, CMV retinitis and polyradiculitis |
| <50–200 | **Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy** — JC virus; multifocal non-enhancing white matter lesions, no mass effect, progressive deficits; treat by restoring immunity (also seen with natalizumab, rituximab and other immunosuppressants) |

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
**Tetanus:** *Clostridium tetani* toxin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release → **trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, muscle spasms with preserved consciousness**, autonomic instability. Treat with wound debridement, **human tetanus immunoglobulin**, metronidazole, benzodiazepines/magnesium, ventilation, and immunisation (infection does not confer immunity).

**Rabies:** long variable incubation; **hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation** (furious form) or ascending paralysis (paralytic form); **almost invariably fatal once symptomatic** — the whole management is post-exposure prophylaxis (wound washing, vaccine ± immunoglobulin).

**Prion disease (sporadic CJD):** rapidly progressive dementia over months with **myoclonus**, ataxia, visual disturbance, akinetic mutism. Investigations: **EEG periodic sharp wave complexes**, MRI **cortical ribboning and pulvinar/hockey-stick sign (variant CJD)**, CSF **14-3-3 protein and RT-QuIC** (the most useful modern test ⚑). No treatment; invariably fatal. Variants: variant CJD (bovine spongiform encephalopathy, younger, psychiatric onset, painful sensory symptoms), familial (PRNP mutation), iatrogenic.

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
| Syndrome | Antibody | Tumour |
|---|---|---|
| Limbic encephalitis | Hu, Ma2, LGI1, GABA-B | SCLC, testicular |
| **Lambert–Eaton** | **P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel** | **Small cell lung cancer** |
| Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration | **Yo** (also Tr, Hu) | **Breast, ovarian**, Hodgkin lymphoma |
| Opsoclonus–myoclonus | Ri | Neuroblastoma (children), breast/lung |
| Stiff person syndrome | **GAD65**, amphiphysin | Breast |
| Sensory neuronopathy | Hu | SCLC |
| Dermatomyositis | Mi-2, TIF1-γ, NXP2 | Ovarian, lung, GI (adults) |

The general rule: **a subacute, otherwise unexplained neurological syndrome in a smoker or in someone with weight loss deserves antibody testing and a CT chest/abdomen/pelvis ± PET.**

docs.title: Headache and Facial Pain
docs.h: Neurology Master Notes — Headache and Facial Pain

docs.title: Headache and Facial Pain
docs.text:
Most headache is primary (migraine, tension-type, cluster). The job is to spot the small number that are secondary.

**SNOOP4 red flags:** **S**ystemic symptoms or secondary risk factors (fever, weight loss, cancer, HIV/immunosuppression, pregnancy); **N**eurological signs or reduced consciousness; **O**nset sudden (thunderclap); **O**lder — new headache after **50** (giant cell arteritis, tumour); **P**apilloedema; **P**ositional (worse lying flat = raised ICP; worse upright = low pressure); **P**recipitated by Valsalva/exertion; **P**rogressive or a change in an established pattern.

docs.title: Headache and Facial Pain
docs.text:
**Diagnosis (ICHD-3):** ≥5 attacks lasting 4–72 hours, with **≥2 of** unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, aggravated by routine activity, **and ≥1 of** nausea/vomiting or photophobia **and** phonophobia.

**Aura** (in ~25%): fully reversible, develops over **≥5 minutes**, lasts **5–60 minutes**, usually visual (**fortification spectra, scintillating scotoma spreading across the field**), sometimes sensory (marching paraesthesia), rarely dysphasic. **Aura that lasts >60 minutes, is purely negative, or is always on the same side warrants imaging.**

**Phases:** prodrome (yawning, mood change, food craving, hours to days), aura, headache, postdrome.

**Triggers:** stress and stress-relief, sleep change, missed meals, dehydration, alcohol (especially red wine), hormonal (menstrual migraine), specific foods, weather. A headache diary is diagnostic and therapeutic.

**Acute treatment:**
- **Simple analgesia**: aspirin 900 mg or ibuprofen/naproxen, taken **early and at full dose**; add an antiemetic (metoclopramide or prochlorperazine — also helps gastric stasis and absorption).
- **Triptans** (e.g. sumatriptan 50–100 mg oral, or subcutaneous/nasal if vomiting) — 5-HT₁B/₁D agonists. **Contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, previous stroke, and in hemiplegic/basilar migraine.**
- ⚑ **Gepants** (small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonists — rimegepant, ubrogepant) and the ditan **lasmiditan** (5-HT₁F agonist) are alternatives where triptans fail or are contraindicated; they lack vasoconstrictor effects. Rimegepant is licensed both for acute treatment and prevention.
- **Avoid opioids and codeine-containing analgesics** — they promote medication-overuse headache.

**Prevention** (offer if ≥4 debilitating days/month, or acute treatment is failing):
- **Propranolol** (avoid in asthma) — good evidence and first-line for many.
- **Amitriptyline** (helpful with poor sleep or coexisting tension-type headache).
- **Topiramate** — effective but teratogenic: ⚑ Pregnancy Prevention Programme required, and it reduces oral contraceptive efficacy at higher doses.
- **Candesartan** as an alternative.
- ⚑ **CGRP monoclonal antibodies** — erenumab (receptor), fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab (ligand) — monthly/quarterly injections; NICE approves after **3 previous preventives have failed**. **Atogepant/rimegepant** (oral gepants) are also now approved preventives ⚑.
- **Botulinum toxin A** for **chronic migraine** (≥15 headache days/month) after 3 preventives have failed.
- Menstrual migraine: perimenstrual naproxen or frovatriptan/zolmitriptan.
- Non-drug: regular sleep, meals and exercise; riboflavin 400 mg; magnesium; treat medication overuse first.

**Migraine and the combined oral contraceptive:** ⚑ **migraine with aura is an absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraception** (UKMEC 4) — the stroke risk is multiplicative. Migraine without aura is UKMEC 2–3.

docs.title: Headache and Facial Pain
docs.text:
**Tension-type headache:** bilateral, pressing/tightening ("band around the head"), mild-moderate, not aggravated by activity, no vomiting; may have photophobia *or* phonophobia but not both. Manage with simple analgesia used sparingly, stress and posture management, amitriptyline if chronic.

**Medication-overuse headache:** headache on **≥15 days/month** in someone using acute treatment regularly for >3 months — **≥15 days/month** for simple analgesics, **≥10 days/month** for triptans, opioids, ergots or combination analgesics. Treatment is **withdrawal of the overused drug** (abrupt for simple analgesics and triptans; opioids need tapering), with warning that headache worsens for 1–2 weeks first, plus a preventive.

docs.title: Headache and Facial Pain
docs.text:
Maximal intensity within **1 minute** (usually seconds). Assume **subarachnoid haemorrhage** until excluded (see Section 4.7): immediate non-contrast CT, LP at ≥12 hours if CT is negative.

**Differentials:** SAH, **reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome** (recurrent thunderclaps over days, often postpartum or with serotonergic/vasoactive drugs; "sausage-string" vessels on angiography; treat with nimodipine and remove triggers), cervical artery dissection, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, **pituitary apoplexy** (headache + visual loss + ophthalmoplegia + hypopituitarism — needs hydrocortisone and urgent MRI), hypertensive emergency/PRES, spontaneous intracranial hypotension, third ventricular colloid cyst, primary cough/exertional/sexual headache (a diagnosis of exclusion).

docs.title: Headache and Facial Pain
docs.text:
**Suspect in anyone over 50** with new headache. Features: temporal headache and scalp tenderness (pain combing hair), **jaw claudication (the most specific symptom)**, visual symptoms (amaurosis fugax, diplopia, sudden painless visual loss from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy), thickened non-pulsatile temporal artery, systemic upset, and polymyalgia rheumatica in ~40–50%.

**Investigations:** **ESR and CRP** (usually markedly raised; a normal ESR does not exclude it), **temporal artery ultrasound** looking for the **halo sign** ⚑ (now a first-line test in many centres and recommended in the BSR 2020 GCA guideline), **temporal artery biopsy** (skip lesions mean a negative biopsy does not exclude; remains positive for ~2 weeks after starting steroids), consider large-vessel imaging (PET-CT/MRA) for extracranial involvement.

**Treatment — do not wait for tests:**
- **No visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately.**
- **Visual symptoms or jaw claudication: IV methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg daily for up to 3 days**, then high-dose oral, and same-day ophthalmology review.
- **Tocilizumab** ⚑ as a steroid-sparing agent in relapsing or steroid-intolerant disease (NICE-approved).
- Add bone protection, PPI, and aspirin where not contraindicated; taper steroids slowly over 12–24 months.

**The point of urgency:** visual loss in GCA is usually irreversible, and the fellow eye is at risk within days.

docs.title: Headache and Facial Pain
docs.text:
**Typical patient:** a young woman with obesity, or recent weight gain.

**Features:** daily headache worse lying flat and on waking, **pulsatile tinnitus**, transient visual obscurations, **papilloedema**, **sixth nerve palsy** (false localising), enlarging blind spot and constricted fields; **visual acuity is preserved until late** — fields, not acuity, are what to monitor.

**Drug causes to always ask about:** ⚑ **tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline), vitamin A and retinoids (isotretinoin), and — importantly — corticosteroid withdrawal**; also nitrofurantoin, lithium, levothyroxine in children, growth hormone.

**Diagnosis (modified Dandy/Friedman criteria):** papilloedema, normal neurological examination except cranial nerve palsies, **normal neuroimaging including MR venography (to exclude venous sinus thrombosis)**, **CSF opening pressure >25 cmH₂O with normal CSF constituents**.

**Management:** weight loss (the most effective long-term measure, including consideration of bariatric surgery ⚑ — the IIH:WT trial), **acetazolamide** (first-line drug; topiramate as an alternative with the bonus of weight loss), stop the causative drug, serial visual fields and OCT; for threatened vision — **optic nerve sheath fenestration** or **CSF shunting**, with venous sinus stenting in selected cases with stenosis. Repeated LPs are a temporising measure only.

docs.title: Headache and Facial Pain
docs.text:
**Orthostatic headache — worse within minutes of standing, relieved by lying down.** Causes: post-lumbar-puncture (highest with larger, cutting needles; use atraumatic pencil-point needles), spontaneous (connective tissue disorders, disc osteophyte tears), trauma or surgery.

MRI shows **diffuse smooth pachymeningeal enhancement, brain sagging, subdural collections**. Treatment: conservative (fluids, caffeine, lying flat, analgesia) for 24–48 hours, then **epidural blood patch** — highly effective for post-dural-puncture headache. Investigate for a spinal leak (CT/MR myelography) if spontaneous and persistent.

docs.title: Headache and Facial Pain
docs.h: 7.9 Trigeminal neuralgia and other facial pain
docs.text:
**Trigeminal neuralgia:** paroxysms of **severe, electric-shock-like, unilateral facial pain lasting seconds**, in the **V2/V3 distribution**, triggered by light touch, chewing, cold wind or shaving; refractory periods between attacks; **no sensory loss on examination**.

**Cause:** usually neurovascular compression by a loop of the superior cerebellar artery at the root entry zone. **MRI is indicated** to exclude a secondary cause — **bilateral trigeminal neuralgia, onset under 40, sensory loss, or other cranial nerve signs suggest MS or a cerebellopontine angle tumour** and change the diagnosis.

**Treatment:** **carbamazepine is first-line** (monitor sodium — hyponatraemia — and FBC/LFTs; watch for the HLA-B*1502 association with SJS in patients of Han Chinese/Southeast Asian ancestry). Alternatives: oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, baclofen, gabapentin. Refractory cases: **microvascular decompression** (best long-term durability), stereotactic radiosurgery, percutaneous rhizotomy/balloon compression.

**Other facial pain:** post-herpetic neuralgia (after shingles; amitriptyline, gabapentinoids, topical lidocaine), persistent idiopathic facial pain, temporomandibular disorder, dental and sinus causes, **Ramsay Hunt** (see Section 10), and **cluster headache** — which is frequently misdiagnosed as dental or sinus disease.

docs.h: Neurology Master Notes — Movement Disorders and Neurodegeneration
docs.text:
*Sources: MDS clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease (2015); NICE NG71 (Parkinson's disease in adults), NG97 (dementia); consensus criteria for PSP (MDS 2017), MSA (2022), DLB (McKeith 2017); El Escorial/Gold Coast criteria and NICE NG42 (motor neurone disease); TGA and MHRA decisions on anti-amyloid antibodies; Kumar & Clark; Merck Manual Professional; StatPearls. ⚑ = changed from older textbooks.*

---

docs.title: Movement Disorders and Neurodegeneration
docs.text:
**Pathology:** degeneration of dopaminergic neurones in the **substantia nigra pars compacta** with intraneuronal **Lewy bodies containing α-synuclein**. Symptoms appear after ~50–70% of nigral neurones are lost. Braak staging explains the prodrome: the olfactory bulb and dorsal vagal nucleus are affected before the midbrain, which is why **anosmia, constipation, depression and REM sleep behaviour disorder can precede motor symptoms by years** ⚑.

**Cardinal features:** **bradykinesia** (obligatory) plus **rest tremor** and/or **rigidity**.

- **Bradykinesia** — slowness *with decrement in amplitude* on repetitive movement (finger tapping); micrographia, hypomimia, reduced arm swing, hypophonia.
- **Rest tremor** — 4–6 Hz, "pill-rolling", **asymmetric**, worse with distraction (counting backwards), improves on movement.
- **Rigidity** — "lead-pipe", with **cogwheeling** when tremor is superimposed; **positive Froment's manoeuvre** (activation of the other limb).
- Postural instability is a *later* feature — early falls argue against idiopathic PD.

**Diagnosis is clinical** (MDS criteria). NICE: refer untreated to a specialist; **DaTscan** is only for distinguishing PD from essential tremor when there is genuine doubt (it does **not** separate PD from parkinson-plus syndromes, which are also presynaptic).

**Non-motor features (often more disabling than motor):** anosmia, constipation, orthostatic hypotension, urinary urgency, depression and anxiety, apathy, REM sleep behaviour disorder, excessive daytime sleepiness, pain, dementia (~50% within 10 years), psychosis and hallucinations (often drug-related).

**Red flags that argue against idiopathic PD (i.e. suggest a "plus" syndrome or secondary cause):** symmetrical onset, **early falls (<3 years)**, early autonomic failure, early dementia, **early or severe bulbar dysfunction**, vertical gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, pyramidal signs, a rapid course, **poor or absent response to levodopa**, and prominent drug history.

docs.title: Movement Disorders and Neurodegeneration
docs.text:
| Syndrome | Discriminating features | Pathology |
|---|---|---|
| **Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP)** | **Early falls, backwards**; **vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (down-gaze first)**; axial rigidity; surprised/staring facies; pseudobulbar affect; "hummingbird" midbrain on sagittal MRI | **Tau** |
| **Multiple system atrophy (MSA)** | **Early, severe autonomic failure** (postural hypotension, incontinence, impotence); MSA-P parkinsonian or MSA-C cerebellar; inspiratory stridor; **"hot cross bun" sign** in the pons | **α-synuclein** (glial cytoplasmic inclusions) |
| **Corticobasal degeneration** | **Markedly asymmetric** akinetic-rigid limb, **apraxia, alien limb phenomenon**, cortical sensory loss, myoclonus, dystonia | Tau |
| **Dementia with Lewy bodies** | **Dementia within 1 year of parkinsonism**, fluctuating cognition, **visual hallucinations**, REM sleep behaviour disorder, **severe neuroleptic sensitivity** | α-synuclein |
| **Vascular parkinsonism** | **"Lower-body parkinsonism"** — gait predominant, upper limbs spared; pyramidal signs; stepwise; vascular risk factors | Small-vessel disease |
| **Drug-induced parkinsonism** | **Symmetrical**, subacute, after antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, sodium valproate, lithium; resolves over weeks–months on withdrawal | Dopamine blockade |
| **Normal pressure hydrocephalus** | Gait apraxia + urinary incontinence + dementia; ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy | CSF dynamics |
| **Wilson's disease** | Under 50, tremor/dystonia, **Kayser–Fleischer rings**, liver disease, psychiatric change | Copper |

> **Hook:** *PSP falls backwards and can't look down; MSA faints and wets itself; CBD forgets the limb belongs to it; DLB sees things and cannot tolerate haloperidol.*

**Rule for DLB vs Parkinson's disease dementia:** the **"1-year rule"** — dementia within 1 year of (or before) the motor features = **DLB**; dementia arising well after established PD = **Parkinson's disease dementia**.

docs.title: Movement Disorders and Neurodegeneration
docs.text:
| Type | When present | Frequency | Features |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rest** | At rest, improves with action | 4–6 Hz | Asymmetric, pill-rolling — **Parkinson's** |
| **Postural / action (essential tremor)** | Arms outstretched, on action | 6–12 Hz | **Bilateral, symmetric**, head/voice tremor, **improves with alcohol**, family history in ~60%; treat with **propranolol or primidone** |
| **Intention** | Worsens approaching a target | — | Cerebellar disease; with past-pointing and dysmetria |
| **Physiological/enhanced** | Postural | Fine, fast | Anxiety, caffeine, **thyrotoxicosis**, salbutamol, lithium, alcohol withdrawal |
| **Dystonic** | Position-dependent, jerky | Irregular | With dystonic posturing |
| **Functional** | Variable | **Entrainable and distractible** | Sudden onset, variable frequency |

**Essential tremor vs Parkinson's disease** is the classic pairing: essential tremor is **bilateral, postural/kinetic, faster, with head and voice involvement, improved by alcohol, and without bradykinesia**; parkinsonian tremor is **asymmetric, at rest, slower, with bradykinesia and rigidity**.

docs.title: Movement Disorders and Neurodegeneration
docs.text:
**Chorea** — brief, irregular, flowing, non-stereotyped involuntary movements that flit from one body part to another; **motor impersistence** (milkmaid grip, inability to keep the tongue protruded).

**Causes:** Huntington's disease, **Sydenham's chorea** (post-streptococcal, a major Jones criterion), chorea gravidarum, SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, polycythaemia, drugs (levodopa, antipsychotic-induced **tardive dyskinesia**, cocaine, oral contraceptives), Wilson's disease, neuroacanthocytosis, hyperglycaemia (non-ketotic hyperosmolar → hemichorea).

**Huntington's disease:** autosomal dominant, **CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in *HTT* on chromosome 4** (≥40 repeats fully penetrant), with **anticipation** (worse and earlier in successive generations, especially with paternal transmission). Presents in mid-adulthood with the triad of **chorea, cognitive decline (subcortical dementia) and psychiatric disturbance** (depression, irritability, high suicide risk). MRI: **caudate atrophy with box-car ventricles**. No disease-modifying treatment; chorea managed with **tetrabenazine** (or antipsychotics); genetic counselling before predictive testing is mandatory.

**Wilson's disease:** autosomal recessive *ATP7B* mutation → impaired biliary copper excretion. **Always consider in anyone under 50 with a movement disorder, especially with liver disease or psychiatric symptoms.** Features: tremor (classically "wing-beating"), dystonia, dysarthria, parkinsonism, ataxia, **Kayser–Fleischer rings** (near-universal in the neurological form), hepatitis/cirrhosis, haemolysis, psychiatric change. Investigations: **low serum caeruloplasmin, low serum copper, high 24-hour urinary copper**, slit-lamp examination, liver biopsy copper; MRI **"face of the giant panda"** in the midbrain. Treatment: **penicillamine or trientine** (chelation), zinc for maintenance, and liver transplantation in fulminant disease.

docs.title: Movement Disorders and Neurodegeneration
docs.text:
**Dystonia** — sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing twisting postures; often relieved by a **sensory trick (geste antagoniste)**, e.g. touching the chin in cervical dystonia.

- Focal: **cervical dystonia (torticollis)**, blepharospasm, writer's cramp, laryngeal dystonia. Treat with **botulinum toxin**.
- Generalised: **DYT1 (childhood-onset)**; **dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa)** — diurnal variation, dramatic and sustained response to small doses of levodopa, **so every young-onset dystonia deserves a levodopa trial**.
- Acute dystonic reaction: hours after a dopamine antagonist (metoclopramide, antipsychotics) — oculogyric crisis, torticollis; treat with **procyclidine or benztropine**.
- Secondary: Wilson's, cerebral palsy, drugs, stroke.

**Myoclonus** — brief shock-like jerks. Physiological (hypnic jerks, hiccup), essential, epileptic (JME), or symptomatic: **metabolic (uraemia, hepatic — asterixis is negative myoclonus), post-hypoxic (Lance–Adams), CJD, Alzheimer's late stage, drugs (opioids, gabapentinoids in renal failure, SSRIs)**.

**Tics** — brief, stereotyped, **suppressible with rising inner urge and relief on release** — the feature that separates them from chorea and myoclonus. **Tourette syndrome:** multiple motor tics plus ≥1 vocal tic for >1 year with onset before 18; comorbid OCD and ADHD are the rule. Treat behaviourally first (habit reversal/CBIT); drugs (clonidine, aripiprazole, tetrabenazine) if disabling.

docs.title: Movement Disorders and Neurodegeneration
docs.text:
**Acquired:** alcohol (with thiamine deficiency — vermis), stroke, MS, posterior fossa tumour, hypothyroidism, **phenytoin** and lithium toxicity, coeliac disease, paraneoplastic (anti-Yo), vitamin E deficiency, Wernicke's, hydrocephalus.

**Inherited:**

| Disorder | Inheritance/genetics | Clues |
|---|---|---|

docs.title: Movement Disorders and Neurodegeneration
docs.text:
**Definition:** acquired, progressive, global cognitive decline affecting function, with **clear consciousness** (the discriminator from delirium).

| Type | Proportion | Key features | Pathology |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Alzheimer's disease** | ~60% | **Insidious episodic memory loss first**, then language and visuospatial; temporoparietal atrophy, medial temporal lobe atrophy on MRI | **Extracellular β-amyloid plaques and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles** |
| **Vascular dementia** | ~20% | **Stepwise** decline, focal signs, vascular risk factors, executive/processing-speed deficits; white matter disease and infarcts | Ischaemia |
| **Dementia with Lewy bodies** | ~10–15% | **Fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder**; neuroleptic sensitivity; reduced uptake on DaTscan | α-synuclein |
| **Frontotemporal dementia** | ~5% (but commonest under 65 alongside AD) | **Onset 45–65**; behavioural variant — disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, hyperorality, compulsions, **memory relatively spared early**; or primary progressive aphasia (semantic/non-fluent) | Tau or **TDP-43**; overlap with MND; *C9orf72*, *MAPT*, *GRN* |

**Other causes:** Parkinson's disease dementia, Huntington's, prion disease, alcohol-related brain damage/Korsakoff, HIV, neurosyphilis, chronic subdural haematoma, tumour, **B12 or thyroid deficiency**, normal pressure hydrocephalus, depression ("pseudodementia").

**Assessment:** collateral history, cognitive testing (**MoCA, ACE-III, MMSE**), bloods to exclude reversible causes (FBC, U&E, calcium, glucose/HbA1c, LFT, TFT, **B12 and folate**, ± HIV/syphilis), **structural imaging (CT or MRI)**, and specialist tests where the diagnosis is unclear (**FDG-PET, DaTscan for DLB, MIBG cardiac scintigraphy, CSF amyloid/tau, or plasma p-tau217** ⚑ — blood biomarkers are entering practice).

**Management (NICE NG97):**
- **Non-pharmacological first**: cognitive stimulation therapy, exercise, occupational therapy, carer support and education, advance care planning, driving and financial capacity discussions, and **Power of Attorney early**.
- **Cholinesterase inhibitors** (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's, DLB and Parkinson's disease dementia. **Memantine** (NMDA antagonist) for moderate-to-severe AD, or if cholinesterase inhibitors are contraindicated/not tolerated. **Neither is indicated in frontotemporal dementia or pure vascular dementia** — in vascular dementia, treat the vascular risk factors.
- **Behavioural and psychological symptoms:** look for pain, infection, constipation and environmental triggers before drugs. Antipsychotics only for severe distress or risk, at the lowest dose for the shortest time — they increase stroke and mortality risk — and **avoid entirely in DLB** (use quetiapine or clozapine if unavoidable).
- ⚑ **Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies** (lecanemab, donanemab) for early sy

docs.title: Movement Disorders and Neurodegeneration
docs.h: 9.8 Normal pressure hydrocephalus and reversible dementias
docs.text:
**NPH triad — "wet, wacky and wobbly":** **gait apraxia first** (magnetic, wide-based, shuffling), then urinary incontinence, then a subcortical dementia. Communicating hydrocephalus with **ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy** (Evans index >0.3) and a normal or high-normal opening pressure.

**The key test is a large-volume ("tap") lumbar puncture removing 30–50 mL of CSF, or extended lumbar drainage, with objective gait timing before and after.** Improvement predicts benefit from a **ventriculoperitoneal shunt**. Gait improves most; cognition least — so the earlier the shunt, the better.

**Always exclude the treatable:** B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, chronic subdural haematoma, depression, medication (anticholinergic burden, benzodiazepines, opioids), alcohol, sleep apnoea, neurosyphilis, HIV.

docs.title: Movement Disorders and Neurodegeneration
docs.text:
**Degeneration of upper and lower motor neurones, with no sensory involvement.** Median age of onset ~60; median survival **2–5 years** from symptom onset. ~10% familial (*C9orf72* is the commonest, and links MND with frontotemporal dementia; also *SOD1*, *TARDBP*, *FUS*).

**Phenotypes:**

| Variant | Features | Prognosis |
|---|---|---|
| **Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (~70%)** | Mixed UMN + LMN in the same region — **wasted, fasciculating limbs with brisk reflexes** | Typical |
| **Progressive bulbar palsy (~20%)** | Dysarthria, dysphagia, wasted fasciculating tongue, mixed bulbar/pseudobulbar signs | **Worst** |
| Progressive muscular atrophy | LMN only | Slower |
| Primary lateral sclerosis | UMN only | Slowest |

**Recognition:** progressive, painless, **asymmetric** weakness; wasting; **fasciculations**; cramps; **brisk reflexes in a wasted limb** (the single most useful sign); split hand; foot drop; bulbar symptoms; emotional lability (pseudobulbar affect); weight loss; up to 50% have cognitive change and ~15% frank FTD. **No sensory loss, no sphincter disturbance, no eye movement abnormality** — features that, if present, should make you doubt the diagnosis.

**Investigations:** clinical diagnosis supported by **EMG (widespread denervation and fasciculation potentials in ≥2–3 body regions)**, normal nerve conduction sensory studies, MRI brain and cervical spine to exclude compressive myelopathy, and bloods to exclude mimics (CK, anti-GM1 for **multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block** — a treatable mimic — B12, thyroid, paraprotein, HIV, Lyme).

**Management (NICE NG42):** multidisciplinary clinic.
- **Riluzole** — glutamate antagonist; extends survival by ~3 months; monitor LFTs.
- ⚑ **Newer agents** are limited and region-specific: **edaravone** is licensed in some countries; **tofersen** is approved for the rare *SOD1* form; sodium phenylbutyrate–taurursodiol was withdrawn after its confirmatory trial failed ⚑ — a useful reminder to check current status rather than an old textbook.
- **Non-invasive ventilation** — the intervention with the biggest quality-of-life and survival benefit; monitor FVC/SNIP and symptoms of nocturnal hypoventilation.
- **Gastrostomy (PEG/RIG) placed early**, before FVC falls below ~50% predicted.
- Symptom control: **riluzole aside, most of the work is symptomatic** — sialorrhoea (glycopyrronium, hyoscine, botulinum toxin), spasticity (baclofen), cramps (quinine), pseudobulbar affect (amitriptyline, dextromethorphan/quinidine), communication aids, palliative care involvement early, and advance care planning.

---

| After the internal capsule, the neurones pass through the crus cerebri of the midbrain, the pons and into the medulla. The most caudal part of the medulla, the tract divides into two: The fibers within the lateral corticospinal tract (80% of all fibres) decussate in the pyramid of the medulla.
