docs.title: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.parent: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.text:
**How they present:** progressive focal deficit, **new-onset seizure in an adult** (the commonest presentation of a low-grade glioma), features of raised ICP (morning headache worse on lying flat/coughing, vomiting, papilloedema), personality or cognitive change, and — importantly — **any new focal neurology that evolves over weeks**.

**Metastases are more common than primary brain tumours.** Commonest primaries: **lung, breast, melanoma, renal, colorectal**. Typically **multiple, at the grey–white junction, with disproportionate vasogenic oedema and ring enhancement**.

| Tumour | Features |
|---|---|
| **Glioblastoma (IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4)** | Commonest malignant primary brain tumour in adults; rapid course; **irregular thick ring enhancement with central necrosis, crossing the corpus callosum ("butterfly glioma")**; median survival ~12–15 months with maximal treatment |
| **Diffuse astrocytoma / oligodendroglioma (IDH-mutant)** ⚑ | The 2021 WHO classification is **molecular**: adult diffuse gliomas are split by **IDH mutation** and, for oligodendroglioma, **1p/19q co-deletion** — which predicts better prognosis and chemosensitivity |
| **Meningioma** | Commonest primary intracranial tumour overall; **extra-axial, dural-based, homogeneous enhancement with a "dural tail"**, may calcify; usually benign; more common in women, grows in pregnancy (progesterone receptors); often incidental and observed |
| **Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)** | **Cerebellopontine angle**: progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance, then V (corneal reflex loss) and VII involvement; **bilateral = NF2** |
| **Pituitary adenoma** | See 11.2 |
| **Primary CNS lymphoma** | Immunosuppression (HIV) or immunocompetent; periventricular, homogeneously enhancing, **exquisitely steroid-responsive ("ghost tumour" — do not give steroids before biopsy)** |
| **Medulloblastoma / pilocytic astrocytoma / ependymoma** | Childhood posterior fossa tumours — morning headache, vomiting, ataxia, hydrocephalus |

**Management principles:** MRI with contrast; **dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema** (with PPI and glucose monitoring); antiseizure medication if seizures have occurred (not prophylactically); tissue diagnosis; then surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy (**temozolomide with radiotherapy for glioblastoma**, with **MGMT promoter methylation** predicting benefit ⚑). Discuss driving restrictions. Early palliative care involvement for high-grade disease.

docs.title: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.h: 11.2 Pituitary tumours and apoplexy; other skull base lesions
docs.parent: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.text:
**Pituitary adenoma:** presents with **bitemporal hemianopia** (chiasmal compression from below, upper quadrants first), headache, hormonal excess (**prolactinoma** — galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, low libido; **acromegaly**; **Cushing's disease**) or hypopituitarism.

- **Prolactinoma is treated medically first** — **cabergoline** or bromocriptine — not surgically, which is a favourite exam point.
- Non-functioning macroadenomas and GH/ACTH-secreting tumours: **trans-sphenoidal surgery**.
- Always check **visual fields** and a full pituitary hormone profile.

**Pituitary apoplexy:** haemorrhage or infarction into an adenoma → **sudden severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI in the cavernous sinus), reduced consciousness and acute hypopituitarism**. **Give hydrocortisone immediately**, urgent MRI, endocrine and neurosurgical input. Precipitants include pregnancy (Sheehan's is the postpartum pituitary infarction variant), anticoagulation, surgery, dynamic pituitary testing.

**Cavernous sinus syndrome:** CN III, IV, V1/V2 and VI plus sympathetic fibres → ophthalmoplegia, facial sensory loss and a **postganglionic Horner's**, often with proptosis and chemosis. Causes: cavernous sinus thrombosis (from facial/sinus infection), tumour, carotid–cavernous fistula, aneurysm.

docs.title: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.h: 11.3 Metastatic cord compression and paraneoplastic disease
docs.parent: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.text:
**Metastatic spinal cord compression** — see Section 5.5 for the emergency management. Remember the **pain precedes the neurology by weeks**: progressive thoracic back pain, worse lying flat and on coughing, in someone with a cancer history is an indication for **MRI whole spine within 24 hours**, not analgesia and review.

**Paraneoplastic neurological syndromes** — see the antibody table in Section 8.10. The practical rules: (1) the neurological syndrome usually **precedes the cancer diagnosis**; (2) subacute onset in a smoker or someone losing weight should trigger antibody testing and CT chest/abdomen/pelvis ± **FDG-PET**; (3) treating the tumour is the most effective treatment; (4) classic syndromes are limbic encephalitis, cerebellar degeneration (anti-Yo, breast/ovary), LEMS (SCLC), sensory neuronopathy (anti-Hu), opsoclonus–myoclonus and stiff person syndrome.

docs.title: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.parent: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.text:
| Syndrome | Inheritance/gene | Features |
|---|---|---|
| **Neurofibromatosis type 1** | AD, *NF1* (chromosome **17** — "von Recklinghausen, 17 letters") | **≥6 café-au-lait macules**, axillary/inguinal freckling, **≥2 neurofibromas or 1 plexiform**, **Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas)**, **optic pathway glioma**, bony dysplasia, first-degree relative; complications: learning difficulty, phaeochromocytoma, hypertension, scoliosis, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour |
| **Neurofibromatosis type 2** | AD, *NF2* (chromosome **22**) | **Bilateral vestibular schwannomas**, meningiomas, ependymomas, juvenile cataract; far fewer skin signs |
| **Tuberous sclerosis** | AD, *TSC1* (hamartin, 9q) / *TSC2* (tuberin, 16p) | **Ash-leaf macules (Wood's lamp), shagreen patch, facial angiofibromas, periungual fibromas**; cortical tubers and subependymal nodules; **infantile spasms**, epilepsy, learning difficulty, **renal angiomyolipoma**, cardiac rhabdomyoma, lymphangioleiomyomatosis; mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) are used ⚑ |
| **von Hippel–Lindau** | AD, *VHL* (3p) | **Cerebellar and retinal haemangioblastomas**, **renal cell carcinoma**, phaeochromocytoma, pancreatic and renal cysts |
| **Sturge–Weber** | Sporadic, *GNAQ* mosaic | **Port-wine stain in the V1 distribution**, leptomeningeal angioma, **"tram-track" gyriform calcification**, epilepsy, hemiparesis, glaucoma, learning difficulty |

docs.title: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.parent: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.text:
| Disorder | Features | Management |
|---|---|---|
| **Obstructive sleep apnoea** | Snoring, witnessed apnoeas, daytime somnolence (Epworth score), obesity, hypertension, AF; diagnose with polysomnography/oximetry | Weight loss, **CPAP**, mandibular advancement; driving advice |
| **Narcolepsy** | **Excessive daytime sleepiness** plus **cataplexy** (sudden loss of tone triggered by emotion — pathognomonic of type 1), **sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations**; loss of hypothalamic **orexin/hypocretin** neurones, HLA-DQB1*06:02 | Diagnose with multiple sleep latency test ± CSF hypocretin; **modafinil/solriamfetol/pitolisant** for sleepiness ⚑, sodium oxybate for cataplexy and disturbed nights, scheduled naps |
| **REM sleep behaviour disorder** | Acting out dreams, injuries to self or partner; loss of REM atonia | **A strong prodrome of synucleinopathy** (PD, DLB, MSA — most convert within 10–15 years); safety measures, melatonin, clonazepam |
| **Restless legs syndrome** | Urge to move the legs, worse at rest and in the evening, relieved by movement; check **ferritin (aim >75 µg/L)**, renal function, pregnancy, drugs | Iron replacement, **α2δ ligands (gabapentin/pregabalin) preferred first-line over dopamine agonists** ⚑ because of **augmentation** |
| Parasomnias (non-REM) | Sleepwalking, night terrors, confusional arousals in slow-wave sleep, usually children | Safety, sleep hygiene |
| Circadian disorders | Shift work, delayed sleep phase | Light therapy, melatonin timing |

docs.title: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.parent: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.text:
**FND is a positive diagnosis based on internal inconsistency and incongruence, not a diagnosis of exclusion** ⚑ — this is a genuine change from older teaching, and it matters because "no organic cause found" both fails patients and gets marks deducted.

**Positive signs:**

| Sign | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Hoover's sign** | Weak hip **extension** that normalises when the opposite hip is flexed against resistance |
| Hip abductor sign | Similar principle in hip abduction |
| **Give-way / collapsing weakness** | Inconsistent effort rather than fixed weakness |
| **Tremor entrainment** | The tremor takes on the frequency of a voluntarily tapped rhythm, or stops |
| Dragging monoplegic gait | Leg dragged with the hip internally or externally rotated — not seen in pyramidal weakness |
| Functional seizure features | See Section 6.9 — prolonged, waxing and waning, closed eyes |
| Inconsistency over time | Signs vary with distraction and observation |

**Context:** symptoms are real and disabling, not feigned (unlike factitious disorder or malingering). Risk factors include prior physical injury or illness, migraine, chronic pain, fatigue, anxiety and depression, and adverse life events — but a psychological trigger is **not required** for the diagnosis.

**Management:** an explicit, positive explanation ("your nervous system is not working properly rather than being damaged — here is the sign that shows me that"), demonstration of the positive sign to the patient, written information, **physiotherapy with an FND-informed approach for motor symptoms**, **CBT for functional seizures**, treating comorbid depression, anxiety and pain, and avoiding repeated investigation, which entrenches illness beliefs.

---

docs.title: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.parent: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| New seizure in an adult | Image the brain — think tumour |
| Commonest brain tumour overall | Metastases |
| Commonest primary malignant brain tumour in adults | Glioblastoma |
| "Butterfly" lesion crossing the corpus callosum | Glioblastoma |
| Extra-axial dural-based lesion with a dural tail | Meningioma |
| Molecular markers that define adult diffuse gliomas | IDH mutation; 1p/19q co-deletion for oligodendroglioma ⚑ |
| Marker predicting temozolomide benefit in glioblastoma | MGMT promoter methylation |
| Steroid-responsive "ghost tumour" | Primary CNS lymphoma — biopsy **before** steroids |
| Unilateral progressive sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus | Vestibular schwannoma — MRI internal acoustic meatus |
| Bilateral vestibular schwannomas | Neurofibromatosis type 2 (chromosome 22) |
| Bitemporal hemianopia | Pituitary macroadenoma |
| First-line treatment of a prolactinoma | Cabergoline (medical, not surgical) |
| Sudden headache with visual loss and ophthalmoplegia in a pituitary mass | Pituitary apoplexy — hydrocortisone immediately |
| Café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules | NF1 (chromosome 17) |
| Ash-leaf macules, shagreen patch, infantile spasms | Tuberous sclerosis |
| Cerebellar haemangioblastoma with renal cell carcinoma | von Hippel–Lindau |
| Port-wine stain with tram-track calcification and epilepsy | Sturge–Weber syndrome |
| Sudden loss of tone triggered by laughter | Cataplexy — narcolepsy type 1 |
| Neurotransmitter deficient in narcolepsy | Orexin (hypocretin) |
| Acting out dreams in an older adult | REM sleep behaviour disorder — prodrome of synucleinopathy |
| Blood test to check in restless legs syndrome | Ferritin (aim >75 µg/L) |
| Why dopamine agonists are avoided first-line in restless legs | Augmentation ⚑ |
| Sign showing functional leg weakness | Hoover's sign |
| Sign showing functional tremor | Entrainment/distractibility |
| Is FND a diagnosis of exclusion? | **No** — it is a positive diagnosis based on inconsistency ⚑ |

##### Sources
**WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System, 5th edition** (2021) — molecular (IDH, 1p/19q) grouping of adult diffuse gliomas ⚑. NICE **NG99** (brain tumours and metastases) and **NG234** (spinal metastases) — imaging, steroid use, referral pathways. Stupp regimen and MGMT methylation evidence for glioblastoma. UK pituitary and Endocrine Society guidance — prolactinoma medical management, apoplexy treatment. **ICSD-3-TR** and AASM practice parameters — narcolepsy, RBD, restless legs (including the shift to α2δ ligands first-line because of augmentation ⚑). Stone, Carson and colleagues (*Practical Neurology*, *BMJ*) and the FND Society — positive diagnostic signs and management. Merck Manual Professional and StatPearls — neurocutaneous syndrome diagnostic criteria (NF1 criteria cross-checked against the 2021 revised international consensus criteria).

---

docs.title: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.h: Neurology (ANU) — adult tumours — Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.parent: Neuro-oncology, Neurocutaneous, Sleep and Functional Disorders
docs.text:
| Glioblastoma multiforme (Grade IV- high-grade astrocytoma) | Definition: derived from astrocytes (glial cell) in the parenchymaFeatures: most common adult primary tumour, ↑ malignant, found in cerebral hemispheres and only tumour that can cross corpus callosum (“butterfly glioma”, ring-enhancing lesion)Histology: pleomorphic tumour cells that border central areas of necrosis and haemorrhagePrognosis: 1-year median survivalTreatment: resection (↓ prognosis) |
| --- | --- |
| Meningioma | Definition: arise from the arachnoid “cap” cells of the arachnoid villi in the meningesFeatures: common, typically benign, most oven in convexities of hemispheres (near surfaces of brain), extra-axial (external to brain parenchyma), dural attachment (“tail”)Histology: spindle cells concentrically arranged in a whorled pattern, psammoma bodies (laminated calcifications)Prognosis: in favourable locations, 85% curable by surgery; RT stops the growth of meningiomas in up to 80% of cases |
| Haemangio-blastoma | Definition: originate from the vascular system of CNSFeatures: associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome when found with retinal angiomas, most often cerebellarHistology: closely arranged, thin-walled capillaries with minimal interleaving parenchymaPrognosis: very good, if surgical extraction of tumour can be achieved |
| Schwannoma | Definition: nerve sheath tumour composed of Schwann cellsFeatures: often benign, localised to CN VIII (acoustic neuroma → hearing loss, tinnitus and disequilibrium); bilateral acoustic neuroma associated with NF-2Prognosis: resectable or treated with stereotactic radiosurgery |
| Oligo-dendroglioma | Definition: originates from the oligodendrocytes of the brain or from a glial precursor cellFeatures: relatively rare, slow growing, most often in frontal lobesHistology: chicken-wire capillary pattern, “fried egg” cellsPrognosis: currently considered incurable but since slow-growing (good prognosis) |
| Pituitary adenoma | Definition: tumour that arises in the pituitary glandFeatures: benign, microadenoma <1cm, macroadenoma >1cm, mass effects (bitemporal hemianopia, headache)Endocrine effects (↑/↓ pituitarism) Most often prolactinoma causing hyperprolactinema– infertility, amenorrhea, galactorrhea, decreased libidoACTH production – Cushing’s disease and hyperpigmentationGH production – acromegalyDiabetes insipidus Pituitary apoplexy (sudden expansion of mass due to haemorrhage/necrosis)- abrupt onset headache, visual disturbances, ↓ mental status, panhypopituitarismTreatment: resection (trans-sphenoidal approach), appropriate endocrine replacement therapy (DA agonist for prolactinoma, serotonin agonist/↓ cortisol production for Cushing’s, somatostatin analogue for acromegaly) |

seizures/epilepsy

| Definitions | SEIZURES: transient neurological dysfunction caused by excessive/abnormal activity of cortical neurons and electrical activityEPILEPSY: chronic condition characterised by ≥ 2 unprovoked seizuresSTATUS EPILEPTICUS: s

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.h: Neurology Master Notes — Neuroanatomy and localisation

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.text:
| Lobe | Key functions | Lesion syndrome |
|---|---|---|
| Frontal | Motor (precentral gyrus), Broca's area (dominant inferior frontal), executive function, saccades (frontal eye field), continence | Contralateral weakness, expressive aphasia, disinhibition/apathy, primitive reflexes, gaze deviation **towards** the lesion |
| Parietal | Primary sensory (postcentral gyrus), spatial awareness (non-dominant), calculation/praxis (dominant) | Cortical sensory loss, **neglect** (non-dominant), **Gerstmann syndrome** (dominant: acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, left–right disorientation), inferior quadrantanopia |
| Temporal | Auditory cortex, Wernicke's area (dominant superior temporal), memory (hippocampus), Meyer's loop | Receptive aphasia, amnesia, **superior** quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"), complex partial seizures |
| Occipital | Vision | Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, cortical blindness (Anton syndrome if denied) |
| Insula/cingulate | Autonomic, pain affect, motivation | Akinetic mutism (bilateral cingulate) |

**Language.** Broca's = non-fluent, effortful, comprehension intact, patient frustrated. Wernicke's = fluent but empty/paraphasic, comprehension impaired, patient unaware. Conduction aphasia (arcuate fasciculus) = fluent, comprehension intact, **repetition disproportionately impaired**. Global aphasia = all impaired (large dominant MCA territory). Left hemisphere is dominant in ~95% of right-handers and ~70% of left-handers.

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.text:
The **circle of Willis** joins anterior (internal carotid) and posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulations: anterior communicating artery between the two ACAs; posterior communicating arteries linking each ICA to its PCA.

| Artery | Territory | Signature deficit |
|---|---|---|
| Anterior cerebral | Medial frontal and parietal | **Leg > arm** weakness, abulia, urinary incontinence, grasp reflex |
| Middle cerebral | Lateral hemisphere | **Face and arm > leg** weakness, aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant), contralateral homonymous hemianopia, eyes deviate to the side of the lesion |
| Posterior cerebral | Occipital, medial temporal, thalamus | Homonymous hemianopia **with macular sparing**, alexia without agraphia, thalamic pain syndrome |
| Lenticulostriates (MCA branches) | Internal capsule, basal ganglia | **Pure motor lacunar stroke** — dense equal weakness of face/arm/leg with no cortical signs |
| Basilar | Pons, midbrain, cerebellum | Reduced consciousness, quadriparesis, cranial nerve signs, locked-in syndrome |
| PICA | Lateral medulla | **Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome** |
| AICA | Lateral pons, inner ear | Lateral pontine syndrome **with deafness** |
| Anterior spinal | Medial medulla | Contralateral hemiparesis + tongue deviation to lesion + loss of vibration |

**Watershed (borderzone) infarction** — between ACA/MCA and MCA/PCA territories, caused by global hypoperfusion (cardiac arrest, severe hypotension, critical carotid stenosis). Classic picture: **"man-in-a-barrel"** proximal arm and thigh weakness with preserved distal power, plus transcortical aphasia.

**Venous:** superior sagittal sinus, transverse → sigmoid → internal jugular; deep system via internal cerebral veins → vein of Galen → straight sinus. Cortical vein or sinus thrombosis causes infarcts that **cross arterial territories and are often haemorrhagic** — the discriminator.

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.text:
The **internal capsule** packs the entire corticospinal and corticobulbar output into a few millimetres, which is why a small lacunar infarct there causes a dense hemiplegia with no cortical signs. The **posterior limb** carries motor fibres (face → arm → leg, anterior to posterior); the genu carries corticobulbar fibres; the retrolenticular part carries the optic radiation.

**Thalamus** — the relay for essentially everything except olfaction. VPL (body sensation), VPM (face sensation), LGN (vision), MGN (hearing), VL/VA (motor from cerebellum and basal ganglia). Thalamic stroke → contralateral hemisensory loss of all modalities, sometimes followed by **Déjerine–Roussy** central post-stroke pain.

**Basal ganglia** — caudate + putamen (striatum), globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra.

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.text:
**Rules that solve most brainstem questions:**
1. **Crossed signs** = brainstem. Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficit + contralateral long-tract (motor or sensory) deficit.
2. **Which cranial nerve is involved tells you the level** — midbrain III/IV, pons V/VI/VII/VIII, medulla IX/X/XI/XII.
3. **Medial** structures (motor, medial lemniscus, hypoglossal) are supplied by paramedian branches; **lateral** structures (spinothalamic, spinal trigeminal, sympathetic, nucleus ambiguus) by circumferential arteries.

| Syndrome | Vessel/level | Features |
|---|---|---|
| **Weber** | Midbrain, PCA branch | Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis |
| **Benedikt** | Midbrain tegmentum | Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral ataxia/tremor (red nucleus) |
| **Millard–Gubler** | Ventral pons | Ipsilateral CN VI and VII palsy + contralateral hemiparesis |
| **Wallenberg (lateral medullary)** | PICA/vertebral | Ipsilateral: facial pain/temperature loss, Horner's, ataxia, dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), vertigo/nystagmus. **Contralateral: body pain/temperature loss. Face and body dissociated, and no limb weakness** |
| **Medial medullary (Déjerine)** | Anterior spinal | Contralateral hemiparesis + contralateral vibration loss + **tongue deviates towards the lesion** |
| **Locked-in** | Basilar, ventral pons | Quadriplegia + anarthria, **vertical eye movements and blinking preserved**, fully aware |
| **Internuclear ophthalmoplegia** | MLF | Failure of adduction on the side of the lesion + nystagmus of the abducting eye; convergence intact. **Bilateral INO in a young adult = MS until proven otherwise** |

> **Hook for Wallenberg:** "*Don't pick a (PICA) horse that can't eat*" — Horner's, ataxia, dysphagia/hoarseness, crossed sensory loss, and **no weakness**.

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.text:
| CN | Name | Function | Exits skull via | Key lesion sign |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | Olfactory | Smell | Cribriform plate | Anosmia (early PD, frontal meningioma, head injury) |
| II | Optic | Vision | Optic canal | Field defect localised by site (see 2.6) |
| III | Oculomotor | All extraocular muscles except LR/SO; levator; parasympathetic pupil | Superior orbital fissure | "Down and out", ptosis, **mydriasis if compressive** |
| IV | Trochlear | Superior oblique | Superior orbital fissure | Vertical diplopia worse looking down/in; head tilt away |
| V | Trigeminal | Facial sensation, muscles of mastication | V1 SOF, V2 foramen rotundum, V3 foramen ovale | Sensory loss, jaw deviates **towards** weak side |
| VI | Abducens | Lateral rectus | Superior orbital fissure | Failure of abduction; **false localising sign in raised ICP** |
| VII | Facial | Facial muscles, taste anterior ⅔, stapedius, lacrimation/salivation | Internal acoustic meatus → stylomastoid foramen | LMN: whole side including forehead. UMN: forehead spared |
| VIII | Vestibulocochlear | Hearing, balance | Internal acoustic meatus | Sensorineural loss, vertigo |
| IX | Glossopharyngeal | Taste posterior ⅓, gag afferent, parotid | Jugular foramen | Loss of gag sensation |
| X | Vagus | Palate, pharynx, larynx, parasympathetic | Jugular foramen | Uvula deviates **away** from lesion, hoarseness |
| XI | Accessory | SCM, trapezius | Jugular foramen | Weak shoulder shrug and head turn to opposite side |
| XII | Hypoglossal | Tongue | Hypoglossal canal | Tongue deviates **towards** the lesion (LMN) |

> **Hook:** *"Uvula runs away from the lesion, tongue points to it."*

**Third nerve palsy — the exam's favourite discriminator.** Parasympathetic pupillary fibres run on the *outside* of the nerve, so:

- **Pupil-involving ("surgical")** — compressive: posterior communicating artery aneurysm, uncal herniation, tumour. Painful. **Urgent CT angiography.**
- **Pupil-sparing ("medical")** — microvascular infarction of the nerve core: diabetes, hypertension. Usually recovers in ~3 months.

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.text:
Retina → optic nerve → **optic chiasm** (nasal fibres cross) → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiations (**Meyer's loop through temporal lobe carries superior field**; parietal fibres carry inferior field) → occipital cortex.

| Lesion site | Field defect |
|---|---|
| Optic nerve | Monocular visual loss / central scotoma |
| Chiasm | **Bitemporal hemianopia** (pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma) |
| Optic tract | Contralateral homonymous hemianopia (incongruous) |
| Temporal (Meyer's loop) | Contralateral **superior** quadrantanopia |
| Parietal radiation | Contralateral **inferior** quadrantanopia |
| Occipital cortex | Congruous homonymous hemianopia **with macular sparing** |

**Pupillary pathways.** Light reflex: retina → optic nerve → pretectal nucleus → *bilateral* Edinger–Westphal nuclei → CN III → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae (hence the consensual response). **Relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn)** = optic nerve or severe retinal disease (classically optic neuritis) — the swinging-torch test shows paradoxical dilatation. **Argyll Robertson pupil** (neurosyphilis) — small, irregular, accommodates but does not react ("prostitute's pupil"). **Holmes–Adie** — dilated, poorly reactive, slow tonic constriction, absent ankle reflexes, benign, young women.

**Horner's syndrome** (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, enophthalmos) localises along a three-neurone chain:

| Order | Path | Causes | Anhidrosis pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| First (central) | Hypothalamus → cord T1 | Stroke (Wallenberg), cord lesion, MS | Whole side of body |
| Second (preganglionic) | T1 → superior cervical ganglion, over lung apex | **Pancoast tumour**, thyroid/neck surgery, trauma | Face and neck |
| Third (postganglionic) | Along ICA to orbit | **Carotid dissection**, cluster headache, cavernous sinus | Little or none (medial forehead) |

*Painful Horner's with neck pain in a young person = carotid dissection until proven otherwise.*

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.text:
Anatomy: two hemispheres and midline vermis; three peduncles (superior — output to red nucleus/thalamus; middle — input from contralateral pontine nuclei; inferior — input from cord and inferior olive). Functional divisions: **vestibulocerebellum** (flocculonodular — balance, eye movements), **spinocerebellum** (vermis — gait, trunk), **cerebrocerebellum** (hemispheres — limb coordination and planning).

Signs — **DANISH**: Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus (fast phase towards lesion), Intention tremor, Slurred/scanning speech, Hypotonia/heel–shin incoordination.

Discriminator: **cerebellar ataxia does not worsen much on eye closure**; **sensory (dorsal column) ataxia does — a positive Romberg test.**

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.text:
The cord runs from the foramen magnum to the **conus medullaris at L1/L2 in adults** (L3 in neonates); below that the **cauda equina**. There are cervical and lumbar enlargements. Lumbar puncture is therefore performed at **L3/4 or L4/5**, below the conus.

**Tracts to know in cross-section:** dorsal columns posteriorly (gracile medial = legs, cuneate lateral = arms), lateral corticospinal tract laterally, spinothalamic tract anterolaterally.

**Blood supply:** one **anterior spinal artery** (supplies the anterior two-thirds — corticospinal and spinothalamic) and two posterior spinal arteries (dorsal columns), reinforced by radicular arteries including the **artery of Adamkiewicz** (usually T9–T12, left-sided). Anterior spinal artery occlusion → paraplegia and loss of pain/temperature **with preserved vibration and proprioception**.

| Cord syndrome | Cause | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Complete transection | Trauma | Loss of all modalities below, UMN signs below, LMN at level, sphincter loss |
| **Brown-Séquard** (hemisection) | Trauma, tumour, MS | Ipsilateral weakness + dorsal column loss; contralateral pain/temperature loss |
| **Anterior cord** | ASA occlusion, aortic surgery | Weakness + pain/temperature loss; **vibration/proprioception spared** |
| **Central cord** | Hyperextension in cervical spondylosis; syringomyelia | **Arms > legs** weakness; "cape" dissociated sensory loss |
| **Posterior cord** | B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis | Loss of vibration/proprioception, sensory ataxia, positive Romberg |
| **Subacute combined degeneration** | B12/copper deficiency | Dorsal columns + corticospinal: **absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars** |
| **Conus medullaris** | Tumour, trauma | Early symmetrical sphincter dysfunction, mixed UMN/LMN, saddle anaesthesia |
| **Cauda equina** | Central disc prolapse, tumour | Asymmetric **LMN** leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia, late retention |

**Key sensory levels:** C4 shoulder tip, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L1 inguinal, S2–S4 perianal.

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.text:
| Root | Motor | Reflex | Sensory |
|---|---|---|---|
| C5 | Shoulder abduction | Biceps | Lateral arm |
| C6 | Elbow flexion, wrist extension | Supinator | Thumb |
| C7 | Elbow extension, wrist flexion | Triceps | Middle finger |
| C8 | Finger flexion | — | Little finger |
| T1 | Finger abduction | — | Medial arm |
| L2/3 | Hip flexion, adduction | — | Anterior thigh |
| L4 | Knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion (inversion) | Knee | Medial shin |
| L5 | Great toe extension, ankle dorsiflexion, hip abduction | — | Dorsum of foot, first web space |
| S1 | Plantarflexion, eversion | Ankle | Sole, lateral foot |

**Brachial plexus:** roots C5–T1 → trunks (upper, middle, lower) → divisions → cords (lateral, posterior, medial) → branches. **Erb's palsy** (C5/6, upper trunk) = "waiter's tip" adducted internally rotated arm; **Klumpke's** (C8/T1) = claw hand ± Horner's.

| Nerve | Roots | Motor loss | Sensory loss | Classic cause |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Median | C6–T1 | Thumb abduction/opposition (LOAF muscles) | Radial 3½ digits, palmar | Carpal tunnel |
| Ulnar | C8–T1 | Interossei, adductor pollicis (**Froment's sign**), claw hand | Ulnar 1½ digits, dorsal and palmar | Elbow compression |
| Radial | C5–T1 | **Wrist drop**, finger extension | First dorsal web space | Spiral groove ("Saturday night palsy") |
| Axillary | C5/6 | Shoulder abduction | Regimental badge | Shoulder dislocation, humeral neck fracture |
| Common peroneal | L4–S1 | **Foot drop**, eversion | Lateral shin, dorsum foot | Fibular neck compression |
| Tibial | L4–S3 | Plantarflexion, inversion | Sole | Tarsal tunnel |
| Femoral | L2–4 | Knee extension | Anterior thigh, medial calf (saphenous) | Pelvic surgery, haematoma |
| Lateral cutaneous of thigh | L2/3 | None | Lateral thigh | **Meralgia paraesthetica** |

**Foot drop discriminators:** common peroneal palsy — weak dorsiflexion **and eversion**, inversion spared, ankle jerk intact. L5 radiculopathy — weak dorsiflexion **and inversion and hip abduction**, often with back pain. Sciatic — all of the above plus weak plantarflexion and absent ankle jerk.

**Median vs ulnar claw paradox:** the *higher* the ulnar lesion, the *less* the claw ("ulnar paradox"), because flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers is also denervated.

docs.title: Neuroanatomy and localisation
docs.text:
Sympathetic outflow is **thoracolumbar (T1–L2)**, short preganglionic/long postganglionic, mostly noradrenergic. Parasympathetic outflow is **craniosacral (CN III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4)**, long preganglionic/short postganglionic, cholinergic. The vagus supplies viscera to the splenic flexure; S2–S4 ("**S2, 3, 4 keeps the pee off the floor**") supply the distal colon, bladder and genitalia.

**Bladder control:** parasympathetic S2–S4 (detrusor contraction, pelvic nerve), sympathetic T10–L2 (relaxation and sphincter tone), somatic S2–S4 pudendal (external sphincter). A **suprapontine or cord lesion** gives a spastic, small-capacity, reflex bladder with urge incontinence; a **cauda equina/conus lesion** gives a flaccid, atonic bladder with retention and overflow — the discriminator that matters in acute back pain.

Autonomic failure appears in MSA, Parkinson's, diabetes, amyloidosis and GBS: postural hypotension, anhidrosis, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, fixed heart rate.

docs.text:

| Same but **with deafness** | Lateral pontine, AICA |
| Failure of adduction + nystagmus in the abducting eye | Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF) |
| Bilateral INO in a 25-year-old | Multiple sclerosis |
| Third nerve palsy **with** dilated pupil | Compressive — PCom aneurysm; urgent imaging |
| Third nerve palsy sparing the pupil | Microvascular (diabetes/hypertension) |
| Forehead spared in facial weakness | UMN (stroke) |
| Whole hemiface weak, including forehead | LMN (Bell's palsy) |
| Tongue deviates towards the weak side | Ipsilateral CN XII (LMN) lesion |
| Uvula deviates away from the lesion | CN X palsy |
| Bitemporal hemianopia | Chiasmal compression — pituitary adenoma |
| Superior quadrantanopia | Temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) |
| Painful Horner's with neck pain | Carotid dissection |
| Horner's with anhidrosis of the whole body | First-order (central) lesion |
| Horner's + wasted small hand muscles | Pancoast tumour (T1 root, second-order) |
| Ataxia much worse with eyes closed | Sensory (dorsal column) ataxia — Romberg positive |
| Absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars | Subacute combined degeneration (also tabes + MND, Friedreich's) |
| Vibration preserved, pain/temperature and power lost | Anterior spinal artery syndrome |
| Arms weaker than legs after a fall in an elderly patient | Central cord syndrome |
| Foot drop with weak eversion but normal inversion | Common peroneal nerve |
| Foot drop with weak inversion and hip abduction | L5 radiculopathy |
| Conus lesion vs cauda equina | Conus: early symmetrical sphincter loss, mixed UMN/LMN. Cauda: asymmetric LMN, late retention |
| Level of the conus medullaris in adults | L1/L2 |

Guyton & Hall *Textbook of Medical Physiology* (14th ed) — membrane and cerebral circulation physiology, CSF dynamics, autoregulation range. Snell *Clinical Neuroanatomy* and Blumenfeld *Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases* — tracts, brainstem syndromes, cranial nerves. Kumar & Clark and Merck Manual Professional — clinical correlates. StatPearls — Horner's syndrome localisation, Brown-Séquard, anterior cord syndrome. Brain Trauma Foundation Guidelines (4th ed) — ICP >22 mmHg treatment threshold and CPP 60–70 mmHg target ⚑ (older texts quote >20 mmHg; both figures appear in current practice, and the BTF value is the one to quote). docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.text:
*Sources: Kumar & Clark *Clinical Medicine*; Macleod's Clinical Examination; Blumenfeld *Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases*; NICE guidance (head injury NG232, suspected neurological conditions NG127, stroke NG128); Merck Manual Professional; StatPearls. Scope: how to take the history, localise, examine, and choose and interpret investigations.*

---

docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.h: 3.1 The history — four questions that do most of the work
docs.text:
1. **Where is the lesion?** Driven by the *pattern* of deficit (see 3.2).
2. **What is the pathology?** Driven by the *time course*.
3. **Why this patient?** Risk factors, family history, drugs, occupation, travel.
4. **How disabling is it?** Function, driving, work, safety.

**Time course is the single most useful piece of information in neurology:**

| Onset and evolution | Pathology suggested |
|---|---|
| Seconds — maximal at onset | Vascular (ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke), seizure, syncope |
| Seconds–minutes with a spreading "march" | Seizure (seconds), **migraine aura (5–60 min, spreads slowly)** |
| Minutes–hours | Infection, inflammation, metabolic, migraine |
| Days–weeks | Inflammatory/demyelinating, infective (TB, abscess), subdural |
| Weeks–months, progressive | Tumour, degenerative, chronic compressive |
| Months–years | Neurodegenerative, hereditary |
| Relapsing and remitting | MS, migraine, epilepsy, periodic paralysis |
| Fatigable / diurnal | Myasthenia gravis |

> **Hook:** *Stroke is sudden, seizure is fast and stereotyped, migraine aura creeps, tumour crawls.*

docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.text:
Work top-down. The key first split is **UMN versus LMN**, then the distribution.

| Level | Clues that put the lesion here |
|---|---|
| **Cortex** | Higher function involved — aphasia, neglect, apraxia, cortical sensory loss (astereognosis, agraphaesthesia), seizures, homonymous field defect |
| **Subcortical/internal capsule** | Dense, equal face/arm/leg deficit **without** cortical signs |
| **Brainstem** | **Crossed signs**; cranial nerve palsies with contralateral long-tract signs; diplopia, vertigo, dysarthria, dysphagia, reduced consciousness |
| **Cerebellum** | Ataxia, nystagmus, dysmetria, intention tremor — ipsilateral, no weakness |
| **Spinal cord** | A **sensory level**, bilateral signs, sphincter disturbance, UMN below and LMN at the level |
| **Root** | Dermatomal pain and sensory loss, myotomal weakness, lost reflex, worse on cough/strain |
| **Plexus** | Multiple roots/nerves in one limb, pain, patchy |
| **Peripheral nerve** | Individual nerve territory (mononeuropathy), or length-dependent glove-and-stocking (polyneuropathy) |
| **NMJ** | **Fatigable**, no sensory loss, normal reflexes, ocular/bulbar predominance |
| **Muscle** | **Proximal symmetrical** weakness, no sensory loss, reflexes preserved until late, raised CK |

**Weakness pattern shortcut:**

| Pattern | Think |
|---|---|
| Proximal symmetrical | Myopathy |
| Distal symmetrical + sensory loss | Polyneuropathy |
| Fatigable, ocular/bulbar | Myasthenia gravis |
| Asymmetric, mixed UMN and LMN, no sensory signs | **Motor neurone disease** |
| Ascending, areflexic, days | Guillain–Barré syndrome |
| Hemiparesis | Contralateral hemisphere or brainstem |
| Paraparesis with sensory level | Spinal cord |
| Paraparesis, flaccid, asymmetric, saddle anaesthesia | Cauda equina |

docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.text:
**Sequence:** inspection (posture, wasting, fasciculations, tremor, involuntary movements) → tone → power (MRC 0–5) → reflexes → coordination → sensation → gait.

**MRC power grades:** 0 none; 1 flicker; 2 movement with gravity eliminated; 3 against gravity; 4 against resistance but reduced; 5 normal.

**Gait is the highest-yield single observation** and is often the OSCE opener:

| Gait | Description | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| Hemiplegic | Circumduction, flexed arm | Stroke |
| Spastic paraparetic ("scissoring") | Stiff, adducted legs | Cord lesion, cerebral palsy, HSP |
| Ataxic (cerebellar) | Broad-based, unsteady, falls **towards the lesion** | Cerebellar disease, alcohol |
| Sensory ataxic | Stamping, watches feet, **Romberg positive** | Dorsal column disease, B12, tabes |
| Parkinsonian | Small shuffling steps, reduced arm swing, festination, difficulty turning | Parkinson's disease |
| High-stepping | Foot drop | Peroneal palsy, L5 root, peripheral neuropathy |
| Waddling | Trendelenburg, pelvis drops | Proximal myopathy |
| Apraxic ("magnetic", feet stuck) | Wide-based, cautious, upright | **Normal pressure hydrocephalus**, frontal disease |
| Antalgic | Short stance on painful side | Pain |
| Functional | Inconsistent, excessive effort, improves with distraction | Functional neurological disorder |

**Signs worth having a stock answer for:** pronator drift (subtle pyramidal weakness), Hoffmann's sign (cervical myelopathy), Lhermitte's phenomenon (electric shock down spine on neck flexion — cervical cord: MS, cord compression, B12), Uhthoff's phenomenon (heat-induced worsening — MS), Froment's sign (ulnar), Trendelenburg (gluteus medius/L5), Gowers' sign (proximal myopathy in children).

docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.text:
**Glasgow Coma Scale (3–15)** — always report the three components, not just the total.

| Eye opening (4) | Verbal (5) | Motor (6) |
|---|---|---|
| 4 spontaneous | 5 orientated | 6 obeys commands |
| 3 to voice | 4 confused | 5 localises to pain |
| 2 to pain | 3 inappropriate words | 4 withdraws from pain |
| 1 none | 2 incomprehensible sounds | 3 abnormal flexion (decorticate) |
| | 1 none | 2 extension (decerebrate) |
| | | 1 none |

**GCS ≤8 = consider intubation** (loss of airway protective reflexes). Decorticate (flexion) implies a lesion above the red nucleus; decerebrate (extension) implies a lower brainstem lesion and is the worse sign.

**Brainstem reflexes to test in coma** (each tests a specific level): pupillary light (midbrain), corneal (pons — V afferent, VII efferent), oculocephalic/"doll's eyes" and oculovestibular caloric (pons/midbrain, MLF), gag/cough (medulla), respiratory pattern.

**Pupils in coma:**

| Pupils | Localisation/cause |
|---|---|
| Pinpoint, reactive (needs magnifier) | **Pontine** haemorrhage; **opioids** |
| Midposition, fixed | Midbrain lesion |
| Unilateral fixed dilated | **Uncal herniation / CN III compression** |
| Bilateral fixed dilated | Severe hypoxic-ischaemic injury, atropine, deep barbiturate, brain death |
| Normal and reactive with reduced consciousness | Favours **metabolic/toxic** cause |

> **Hook:** *Metabolic coma spares the pupils; structural coma does not.*

docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.text:
| Situation | First test | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Suspected acute stroke | **Non-contrast CT head immediately** | Excludes haemorrhage before thrombolysis; early ischaemic signs (hyperdense MCA, loss of grey–white differentiation, insular ribbon) |
| Stroke being considered for thrombectomy | **CT angiography** ± CT perfusion | Detects large-vessel occlusion; perfusion selects late-window patients |
| Thunderclap headache | Non-contrast CT (sensitivity >98% if within 6 h) then **LP at ≥12 h** if CT negative | Xanthochromia |
| Head injury with NICE criteria | CT head within 1 h (or 8 h for delayed criteria) | Surgical haematoma |
| Suspected MS, cord lesion, posterior fossa, epilepsy workup, tumour | **MRI** | Far better soft-tissue and posterior fossa resolution |
| Suspected cord compression / cauda equina | **Urgent MRI whole spine** | CT misses cord and disc detail |
| Suspected venous sinus thrombosis | **CT venogram or MR venogram** | Plain CT often normal; "empty delta sign" only sometimes |
| Suspected carotid dissection | CT/MR angiography with fat-saturated sequences | Mural haematoma, "string sign" |

**MRI sequences worth naming:** **DWI/ADC** (restricted diffusion = acute infarct within minutes; also abscess, and cortical ribboning in CJD), **FLAIR** (periventricular demyelination, "Dawson's fingers"; DWI–FLAIR mismatch dates a stroke as <4.5 h ⚑ and is used to select wake-up strokes for thrombolysis), **T2\*/SWI** (microbleeds, haemosiderin, cavernoma), **T1 with gadolinium** (BBB breakdown — active plaque, tumour, abscess, meningeal enhancement).

**Contrast patterns:** ring enhancement — think **abscess (thin, smooth, restricts diffusion centrally), glioblastoma (thick, irregular), metastasis (multiple, grey–white junction), toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma, demyelination (incomplete/open ring)**.

docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.text:
**Contraindications / when to CT first:** focal neurological deficit, GCS <10 or falling, new seizure, papilloedema, immunocompromise, age >60 — and always if signs of raised ICP. Also avoid in coagulopathy, platelets <50, local sepsis. Remember: **suspected bacterial meningitis — give antibiotics first, image second, LP third if delayed.**

| Parameter | Normal | Bacterial | Viral | TB / fungal | SAH | MS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Appearance | Clear | Turbid | Clear | Fibrin web | Xanthochromic | Clear |
| Opening pressure | 10–20 cmH₂O | ↑ | Normal/↑ | ↑↑ | ↑ | Normal |
| White cells | <5/mm³ | **>1000, neutrophils** | 10–1000, **lymphocytes** | 100–500, lymphocytes | RBC ± | Normal or mild lymphocytosis |
| Protein | 0.15–0.45 g/L | **>1 g/L** | <1 g/L | **>1–5 g/L (very high)** | ↑ | Normal or mildly ↑ |
| Glucose (CSF:serum) | >0.6 (≥⅔) | **<0.4 (very low)** | Normal | **Low** | Normal | Normal |
| Extra | — | Gram stain, PCR | Viral PCR (HSV, enterovirus) | AFB, TB PCR, CrAg, India ink | **Xanthochromia at ≥12 h**, RBC does not fall between bottles | **Unmatched oligoclonal bands** |

**Albuminocytological dissociation** — high protein with normal cell count — is the classic Guillain–Barré finding, though it may be normal in the first week (present in ~50% at 1 week, ~75% by 3 weeks), so a normal early CSF does not exclude GBS.

**Traumatic tap vs SAH:** in a traumatic tap the red cell count **falls markedly** from bottle 1 to bottle 4 and there is no xanthochromia; in SAH the count stays constant and xanthochromia (from bilirubin, needing ~12 hours to form) is present on spectrophotometry.

docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.text:
| Test | What it shows | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **EEG** | Cortical electrical activity | Classifying epilepsy (not diagnosing "is this a seizure?" — a normal interictal EEG never excludes epilepsy), non-convulsive status, encephalopathy (triphasic waves), **HSV encephalitis (temporal periodic discharges)**, **CJD (periodic sharp wave complexes)**, 3 Hz spike-and-wave in absence epilepsy |
| **Nerve conduction studies** | Velocity and amplitude | Demyelinating (↓velocity, conduction block, prolonged F-waves) vs axonal (↓amplitude) neuropathy; entrapments |
| **Repetitive nerve stimulation** | NMJ safety factor | **Decrement** in myasthenia, **increment** in LEMS |
| **EMG** | Muscle electrical activity | Denervation (fibrillations, positive sharp waves, large polyphasic units) vs myopathy (small short polyphasic units); myotonic discharges |
| **Evoked potentials** | Conduction in a sensory pathway | Visual evoked potentials show **delayed P100** after optic neuritis — evidence of a previous subclinical lesion |

docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.h: 3.8 Blood tests, antibodies and specialist investigations
docs.text:
**Baseline in most presentations:** FBC, U&E, LFT, glucose/HbA1c, calcium, CRP/ESR, TFT, B12 and folate, lipids. Add on pattern:

| Test | When |
|---|---|
| **CK** | Proximal weakness — very high in inflammatory myopathy/rhabdomyolysis |
| ESR (urgent) | ?Giant cell arteritis — but do not delay steroids for the result |
| **AChR antibody**, then **MuSK** | Myasthenia gravis (AChR positive in ~85% generalised, ~50% ocular) |
| **Anti-ganglioside** (GQ1b) | Miller Fisher variant of GBS |
| **Aquaporin-4 (AQP4-IgG)**, **MOG-IgG** | NMOSD and MOGAD — must be checked before calling it MS ⚑ |
| **Oligoclonal bands (CSF, unmatched in serum)** | MS |
| **Anti-NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, Hu, Yo, Ri, Ma2** | Autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis |
| Copper, caeruloplasmin, 24 h urinary copper, slit lamp | **Wilson's disease** in any young person with movement disorder or unexplained tremor plus liver disease |
| Genetic testing | Huntington's (CAG repeat), CMT, SCA, Friedreich's, mitochondrial |
| HIV, syphilis serology | Almost any unexplained neurology |
| Paraprotein/immunofixation | Neuropathy of unclear cause |

docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.h: 3.9 Red flags and the never-miss list
docs.text:
**Headache red flags (SNOOP4):** **S**ystemic features/secondary risk (fever, cancer, immunosuppression, pregnancy), **N**eurological signs, **O**nset sudden (thunderclap), **O**lder (new headache >50 — think GCA), **P**apilloedema, **P**ositional/**P**ostural, **P**recipitated by Valsalva, **P**rogressive/pattern change.

**Back pain red flags:** bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, reduced anal tone, progressive neurological deficit, thoracic pain, age <20 or >55, cancer history, fever, night pain, unexplained weight loss, steroid use, IV drug use.

**The never-miss diagnoses, and the test that catches each:**

| Diagnosis | Immediate action |
|---|---|
| Bacterial meningitis | Blood cultures then **immediate ceftriaxone** ± amoxicillin; dexamethasone; LP when safe |
| Subarachnoid haemorrhage | Non-contrast CT; LP ≥12 h if negative |
| Acute ischaemic stroke | Immediate CT and reperfusion assessment — time is brain |
| Cord compression / cauda equina | Emergency MRI whole spine; dexamethasone if malignant |
| Giant cell arteritis | Immediate high-dose steroid, then temporal artery ultrasound/biopsy |
| Raised ICP with herniation | Head up 30°, osmotherapy, neurosurgical referral |
| Status epilepticus | Benzodiazepine now; treat the cause |
| Guillain–Barré / myasthenic crisis | **Serial FVC** — not oximetry |
| Wernicke's encephalopathy | IV thiamine **before** glucose |
| Herpes simplex encephalitis | Empirical IV aciclovir on suspicion |
| Temporal arteritis of the eye / acute angle closure | Same-day ophthalmology |
| Carotid/vertebral dissection | Angiography; antithrombotic |

---

docs.title: Neurological Assessment
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Deficit maximal at onset | Vascular event |
| Symptoms spreading over 20–30 minutes with visual zig-zags | Migraine aura |
| Symptoms spreading over seconds, stereotyped, positive phenomena | Seizure |
| Fatigable diplopia and ptosis worse in the evening | Myasthenia gravis |
| Sensory level on the trunk | Spinal cord lesion |
| Cortical sensory loss / neglect / aphasia | Cortical lesion |
| Dense hemiparesis with completely normal higher function | Internal capsule lacune |
| Pinpoint pupils in coma | Pontine haemorrhage or opioids |
| Unilateral fixed dilated pupil in coma | Uncal herniation |
| Reactive pupils with deep coma | Metabolic/toxic cause |
| GCS threshold for airway protection | ≤8 |
| Which is worse — decorticate or decerebrate? | Decerebrate (extension) — lower brainstem |
| CSF: >1000 neutrophils, protein >1, glucose <0.4 ratio | Bacterial meningitis |
| CSF: lymphocytes, very high protein, low glucose | TB (or fungal) meningitis |
| CSF: high protein, normal cell count | Albuminocytological dissociation — GBS |
| CSF: unmatched oligoclonal bands | Multiple sclerosis |
| Red cells constant across bottles + xanthochromia | Subarachnoid haemorrhage |
| Red cells falling across bottles, no xanthochromia | Traumatic tap |
| Minimum interval from headache onset to LP for xanthochromia | 12 hours |
| Delayed P100 on visual evoked potentials | Previous optic neuritis |
| Periodic lateralised discharges over the temporal lobe on EEG | HSV encephalitis |
| Periodic sharp wave complexes + cortical ribboning on DWI | Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease |
| 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave | Childhood absence epilepsy |
| MRI sequence positive within minutes of infarction | DWI (with ADC correlate) |
| DWI positive but FLAIR negative | Stroke likely <4.5 h old ⚑ |
| Monitoring parameter in GBS/myasthenic crisis | Forced vital capacity |

##### Sources
Kumar & Clark *Clinical Medicine* (10th ed) and Macleod's *Clinical Examination* — history, examination, gait patterns. Blumenfeld *Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases* — localisation framework. NICE NG128 (stroke and TIA), NG232 (head injury), NG127 (suspected neurological conditions) — imaging indications and timings. Merck Manual Professional and StatPearls — CSF profiles, GCS, coma assessment. CSF values cross-checked between Kumar & Clark and Merck Manual Professional; the CSF:serum glucose ratio cut-off of <0.4 for bacterial meningitis is consistent across both. Albuminocytological dissociation timing in GBS from Brain/Cochrane-cited GBS reviews and StatPearls. ⚑ DWI–FLAIR mismatch as a selection tool for unknown-onset stroke derives from the WAKE-UP trial and is incorporated in current AHA/ASA and ESO stroke guidance.

docs.title: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.parent: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.text:
Normal ICP in adults: **5–15 mmHg**. Treat sustained ICP **>22 mmHg** ⚑ (Brain Trauma Foundation 4th edition; older texts say >20). Remember **CPP = MAP − ICP**, target **60–70 mmHg**.

**Causes:** mass lesion (tumour, haematoma, abscess), oedema (trauma, large infarct, hepatic failure), hydrocephalus, venous outflow obstruction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, hypercapnia.

**Clinical features:** headache worse in the morning / on lying flat / on coughing and straining, vomiting (often without nausea), **papilloedema**, visual obscurations, diplopia from a **false-localising sixth nerve palsy**, reduced consciousness. **Cushing's triad** — **hypertension (widened pulse pressure), bradycardia, irregular breathing** — is a late and ominous sign of brainstem compression.

**Herniation syndromes:**

| Syndrome | Anatomy | Signs |
|---|---|---|
| **Uncal (transtentorial)** | Medial temporal lobe over tentorium | **Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil** (CN III), then contralateral hemiparesis; **Kernohan's notch** phenomenon can give *ipsilateral* (false-localising) hemiparesis |
| Central | Downward diencephalic displacement | Progressive reduced consciousness, small reactive then midposition pupils, Cheyne–Stokes → hyperventilation |
| Subfalcine (cingulate) | Under falx | Often silent; may compress ACA → leg weakness |
| **Tonsillar (coning)** | Cerebellar tonsils through foramen magnum | Neck stiffness, **respiratory arrest**, death — the reason not to LP with raised ICP |

**Management ladder:**
1. Airway, ventilation (**normocapnia PaCO₂ 4.5–5.0 kPa**), oxygenation, avoid hypotension.
2. **Head up 30°**, head midline, loosen collars/ties (venous drainage), treat pain, fever and seizures, avoid hypotonic fluids.
3. **Osmotherapy** — mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or **hypertonic saline**; hypertonic saline is increasingly preferred, especially if hypovolaemic or hypotensive ⚑.
4. Sedation ± neuromuscular blockade; consider ICP monitoring.
5. **Short-term hyperventilation** to PaCO₂ ~4.0–4.5 kPa only as a bridge to definitive treatment — prolonged use causes ischaemia.
6. **Dexamethasone works for vasogenic oedema around tumour and abscess; it does not help traumatic or ischaemic oedema** (CRASH trial showed harm in head injury).
7. Definitive: evacuate the haematoma, resect the mass, EVD for hydrocephalus, decompressive craniectomy.

docs.title: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.parent: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.text:
Coma requires **bilateral hemispheric dysfunction, a brainstem/RAS lesion, or a diffuse metabolic-toxic insult**.

**Structured approach:** ABC, glucose (and empirical thiamine before glucose in anyone at risk), naloxone if opioid features, temperature; then GCS, pupils, eye movements, motor response, respiratory pattern, fundoscopy, meningism, skin/needle marks, breath; then targeted investigation.

| Feature | Metabolic/toxic | Structural |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Gradual | Sudden |
| Pupils | Preserved reactivity | Asymmetric, fixed, or level-specific |
| Focal signs | Usually absent | Present |
| Eye movements | Roving, conjugate | Gaze deviation, disconjugate |
| Tone/movement | Tremor, asterixis, myoclonus | Posturing, focal |

**Causes to work through:** hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, hypercapnia, sepsis, uraemia, hepatic failure, hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia, hypothyroidism (myxoedema coma), adrenal crisis, drugs/alcohol/opioids, Wernicke's, non-convulsive status, stroke/haemorrhage/SAH, trauma, meningitis/encephalitis, tumour, hydrocephalus, hypothermia.

**Locked-in syndrome, vegetative state and minimally conscious state are not coma** — a locked-in patient is fully aware, and the way to detect it is to ask them to look up and blink.

docs.title: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.parent: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.text:
**NICE NG232 — CT head within 1 hour if:** GCS <13 on initial assessment or <15 at 2 hours after injury; suspected open/depressed skull fracture; any sign of basal skull fracture (**haemotympanum, "panda" periorbital eyes, CSF otorrhoea/rhinorrhoea, Battle's sign**); post-traumatic seizure; focal neurological deficit; more than one episode of vomiting. **CT within 8 hours** for loss of consciousness/amnesia plus age ≥65, coagulopathy/anticoagulation, dangerous mechanism, or >30 min retrograde amnesia. ⚑ NG232 also advises CT within 8 hours for anyone on an anticoagulant even without other risk factors.

| | **Extradural haematoma** | **Subdural haematoma** |
|---|---|---|
| Vessel | **Middle meningeal artery** (pterion fracture) | **Bridging veins** |
| Population | Young, trauma | Elderly, alcohol, anticoagulated; minor or no trauma |
| CT shape | **Biconvex/lentiform**, does not cross sutures | **Crescentic**, crosses sutures, not midline |
| Course | **Lucid interval** then rapid deterioration | Acute, subacute or chronic (weeks of confusion, headache, fluctuation) |
| Treatment | Urgent craniotomy | Burr hole/craniotomy if symptomatic; chronic SDH often burr-hole drainage ± middle meningeal artery embolisation ⚑ |

**Diffuse axonal injury** — deceleration shear injury; CT may look near-normal while the patient is deeply unconscious; MRI shows petechial haemorrhages at the grey–white junction, corpus callosum and brainstem.

**Concussion / mild TBI:** transient neurological dysfunction without structural injury; graded return to activity; **second impact syndrome** is the rationale for not returning to sport while symptomatic. Post-concussion syndrome — headache, dizziness, poor concentration, irritability, for weeks to months.

**Other TBI principles:** avoid hypotension and hypoxia (each markedly worsens outcome); **tranexamic acid within 3 hours** reduces head-injury-related death in mild-moderate TBI (CRASH-3) ⚑; seizure prophylaxis with levetiracetam/phenytoin for 7 days in severe TBI; **steroids are contraindicated** (CRASH).

docs.title: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.parent: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.text:
**Definition (ILAE operational):** ⚑ a generalised convulsive seizure lasting **≥5 minutes**, or repeated seizures without recovery of consciousness between them. (The older definition of 30 minutes describes the point at which neuronal injury becomes likely — **t₂** — not the point at which to start treating — **t₁ = 5 min**.)

**Timed ladder:**

| Time | Action |
|---|---|
| 0–5 min | ABC, oxygen, IV access, **check glucose**, thiamine if malnourished/alcohol, monitoring |
| 5 min | **Benzodiazepine**: IV lorazepam 4 mg (0.1 mg/kg), or buccal midazolam 10 mg / rectal diazepam if no access |
| 10 min | **Repeat the benzodiazepine once** (maximum two doses total — further doses mainly cause respiratory depression) |
| 15–20 min | **Second-line IV antiseizure medication**: ⚑ levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g), sodium valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3 g), or phenytoin/fosphenytoin 20 mg/kg. **ESETT showed these three are equally effective (~50% each)** — levetiracetam is usually preferred for ease and safety; avoid valproate in women of childbearing potential |
| 30–60 min (refractory) | **General anaesthesia** — propofol, midazolam or thiopentone infusion, intubation, ICU, continuous EEG |
| >24 h despite anaesthesia | **Super-refractory** — ketamine, immunotherapy, ketogenic diet, treat the underlying cause |

**Always ask why:** poor adherence or withdrawal of antiseizure medication (commonest in known epilepsy), alcohol withdrawal, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, infection (meningitis/encephalitis), stroke or haemorrhage, tumour, eclampsia (**give magnesium sulfate**), drug toxicity, autoimmune encephalitis.

**Non-convulsive status** — unexplained persistent confusion or reduced consciousness, especially after a convulsion that "stopped": diagnose with **EEG**. Consider it whenever a post-ictal patient fails to wake up within 20–30 minutes.

**Complications:** hypoxia, aspiration, rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury, hyperthermia, lactic acidosis, arrhythmia, neuronal injury.

docs.title: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.h: 5.5 Acute cord compression and cauda equina syndrome
docs.parent: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.text:
**Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC)** — commonest primaries: **breast, lung, prostate**, also myeloma, renal, lymphoma. Presents with **progressive back pain, often thoracic, worse on lying flat, coughing or straining**, preceding neurology by weeks — a chance to intervene early.

**Immediate management (NICE NG234):**
1. **Dexamethasone 16 mg daily** (with PPI and glucose monitoring) unless lymphoma is suspected and tissue is needed first.
2. **MRI of the whole spine within 24 hours** (sooner if neurology is progressing) — whole spine because multiple levels are common.
3. Discuss with the MSCC coordinator/oncology and spinal surgery: **surgical decompression** for a good-prognosis patient with a single level or spinal instability, otherwise **radiotherapy**.
4. Flat bed rest with log-roll until spinal stability is assessed; analgesia; VTE prophylaxis; bladder care.

**Cauda equina syndrome** — a surgical emergency, usually a large central disc prolapse (also tumour, abscess, haematoma, trauma).

**Red flags:** bilateral sciatica, **saddle anaesthesia**, **urinary retention with overflow incontinence** (or loss of bladder sensation — an earlier sign than retention), faecal incontinence or loss of anal tone, progressive motor weakness, sexual dysfunction.

**Action: immediate MRI lumbosacral spine and emergency neurosurgical/spinal referral** — decompression ideally within 24–48 hours of onset and as soon as possible; delay predicts permanent sphincter dysfunction. Do not "wait until morning" and do not rely on a post-void residual alone.

| | Conus medullaris | Cauda equina |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Sudden, symmetrical | Gradual, asymmetrical |
| Pain | Less prominent | Severe radicular |
| Motor | Mixed UMN + LMN, symmetrical | **LMN only, asymmetrical** |
| Reflexes | Ankle jerks lost, knee jerks may persist, plantars ↑ | All lost |
| Sensory | Symmetrical saddle, dissociated | Asymmetrical saddle |
| Sphincter | **Early** and severe | Late |

docs.title: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.parent: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.text:
The trap: hypoxia and a falling oxygen saturation are **late** signs. A patient with GBS or a myasthenic crisis fatigues and then decompensates abruptly.

**Monitor forced vital capacity (FVC).** "**20/30/40 rule**": FVC <20 mL/kg, maximum inspiratory pressure less negative than −30 cmH₂O, or maximum expiratory pressure <40 cmH₂O → high risk, involve ICU. ⚑ In practice, **FVC <1–1.5 L, a fall of >30% from baseline, an inability to count to 20 in one breath, or a single-breath count of <15** should trigger ICU review; **FVC <15 mL/kg usually means intubation**.

Other warning signs: inability to lift the head from the pillow, weak cough, bulbar weakness with pooling of secretions, paradoxical abdominal breathing, tachypnoea, orthopnoea, restlessness. **Non-invasive ventilation is usually inappropriate** when there is bulbar weakness — these patients need intubation.

**Note:** in myasthenic crisis, differentiate from **cholinergic crisis** (excess anticholinesterase): the latter has muscarinic excess — miosis, salivation, lacrimation, diarrhoea, bradycardia, fasciculations. Modern practice is to withhold pyridostigmine in crisis and treat with **plasma exchange or IVIg plus steroids**.

docs.title: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.parent: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.text:
| Feature | **Delirium** | **Dementia** |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Hours–days | Months–years |
| Course | **Fluctuating**, worse at night | Slowly progressive |
| Consciousness/attention | **Impaired attention** — the cardinal feature | Clear until late |
| Hallucinations | Common, visual | Less common (except DLB) |
| Reversibility | Usually reversible | Usually not |

**Delirium causes (PINCH ME):** Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication (opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, steroids), Environment/Electrolytes. Also alcohol withdrawal, urinary retention, hypoxia, stroke.

**Management:** identify and treat the cause; non-pharmacological first (orientation, lighting, sleep hygiene, familiar faces, mobility, sensory aids, avoid catheters and restraints). Drugs only for distress or risk: **low-dose haloperidol** short term — **avoid antipsychotics in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies** (use quetiapine or clozapine if unavoidable); benzodiazepines are first-line only in alcohol withdrawal or seizure risk.

docs.title: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.h: 5.8 Toxidromes and metabolic emergencies with neurological signatures
docs.parent: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.text:
| Syndrome | Trigger | Signature | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Neuroleptic malignant syndrome** | Dopamine antagonist (or withdrawal of dopaminergic drug) | Days onset, **"lead-pipe" rigidity**, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, **very high CK**, normal or reduced reflexes | Stop the drug, cool, fluids, dantrolene ± bromocriptine |
| **Serotonin syndrome** | SSRI/SNRI/MAOI/tramadol/linezolid combinations | **Hours** onset, **clonus and hyperreflexia (legs > arms)**, agitation, mydriasis, diarrhoea, hyperthermia | Stop the drug, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine |
| Malignant hyperthermia | Volatile anaesthetics, suxamethonium | Intra-operative rigidity, rising end-tidal CO₂, hyperthermia; RYR1 | Dantrolene |
| Anticholinergic | Antihistamines, TCAs, hyoscine | "Mad, hot, dry, red, blind" — delirium, dry skin, mydriasis, retention | Supportive; physostigmine rarely |
| **Wernicke's encephalopathy** | Thiamine deficiency (alcohol, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, refeeding) | **Confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, ataxia** (all three in <20%) | **IV thiamine (Pabrinex) before any glucose**; untreated → Korsakoff |
| Hepatic encephalopathy | Cirrhosis + precipitant | Asterixis, constructional apraxia, fetor | Lactulose, rifaximin, treat precipitant |
| **Osmotic demyelination** | Over-rapid correction of hyponatraemia | Delayed (days) quadriparesis, dysarthria, locked-in | Prevention: correct Na⁺ ≤8–10 mmol/L per 24 h |
| CO poisoning | Faulty heater, fire | Headache, confusion, cherry-red late, delayed leukoencephalopathy | High-flow O₂ ± hyperbaric |

> **Hook:** *NMS is rigid and slow; serotonin syndrome is clonic and fast.*

docs.title: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.parent: Neurological Emergencies and Disorders of Consciousness
docs.text:
Diagnosed clinically, in a patient with **known irreversible structural brain damage**, **deep apnoeic coma on no sedation**, and **excluded reversible causes** (drugs, hypothermia <34 °C, severe metabolic or endocrine derangement, neuromuscular blockade).

**Brainstem reflex testing — all must be absent:**
- Pupillary response to light (II/III)
- Corneal reflex (V/VII)
- Vestibulo-ocular (caloric) response to ice-cold water (VIII/III/VI)
- Motor response within cranial nerve distribution to supraorbital pressure (V/VII)
- Gag (IX/X) and cough on deep tracheal suction (X)
- **Apnoea test** — no respiratory effort with PaCO₂ allowed to rise above 6.65 kPa (and pH <7.40)

In the UK, testing is performed by two suitably experienced doctors (one a consultant), neither on the transplant team, on two separate occasions. Spinal reflexes may persist and do not exclude the diagnosis. Legal time of death is the time of the **first** set of tests.

---

docs.h: Neurology Master Notes — Neuromuscular and Spinal Disorders
docs.text:
*Sources: ABN/EFNS–PNS guidelines on GBS and CIDP; international consensus guidance for the management of myasthenia gravis (2020 update and subsequent revisions); NICE NG59 (low back pain and sciatica); Kumar & Clark; Merck Manual Professional; StatPearls; Preston & Shapiro *Electromyography and Neuromuscular Disorders*. ⚑ = changed from older textbooks.*

docs.title: Neuromuscular and Spinal Disorders
docs.h: 10.1 Peripheral neuropathy — pattern first, cause second
docs.text:
**Step 1 — what is the pattern?**

| Pattern | Meaning | Typical causes |
|---|---|---|
| **Symmetrical distal sensorimotor (glove and stocking)** | Length-dependent axonal | **Diabetes**, alcohol, B12 deficiency, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, drugs, paraprotein, idiopathic |
| **Predominantly motor, symmetrical, proximal and distal** | Demyelinating | **GBS** (acute), **CIDP** (chronic), CMT1, lead, porphyria |
| **Predominantly sensory / small fibre** | Small fibre or sensory ganglionopathy | Diabetes, amyloid, Sjögren's, **B6 excess**, paraneoplastic (anti-Hu), HIV |
| **Mononeuritis multiplex** — several individual nerves, asymmetric, painful | Vasculitic/infiltrative | **Vasculitis (ANCA, PAN, rheumatoid)**, diabetes, sarcoid, leprosy, HIV, amyloid, lymphoma |
| **Autonomic** | Small fibre/autonomic | Diabetes, amyloidosis, GBS, paraneoplastic |

**Step 2 — is it axonal or demyelinating (nerve conduction studies)?** Axonal = **reduced amplitudes** with relatively preserved velocity. Demyelinating = **slowed conduction velocity, prolonged distal latencies, conduction block, prolonged/absent F-waves**.

**Step 3 — routine screen:** glucose/HbA1c, **B12 and folate**, U&E, LFT, TFT, FBC, ESR/CRP, **serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation**, HIV and syphilis serology; then targeted (ANCA, ANA/ENA, ACE, anti-ganglioside, genetic, nerve biopsy if vasculitis or amyloid suspected).

**Neuropathic pain management** (see Section 12): amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin as first-line options; **capsaicin cream for localised pain**; **carbamazepine only for trigeminal neuralgia**; foot care and falls prevention.

docs.title: Neuromuscular and Spinal Disorders
docs.text:
**GBS — acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.**

- **Trigger** in ~two-thirds: *Campylobacter jejuni* (associated with the axonal AMAN variant and worse recovery), CMV, EBV, *Mycoplasma*, Zika, hepatitis E, HIV, surgery, vaccination (rarely).
- **Presentation:** progressive, **ascending, symmetrical weakness** with **areflexia**, developing over days to a nadir by **≤4 weeks** (usually 2); back and limb pain is common and often precedes weakness; sensory symptoms are usually mild relative to weakness; **autonomic instability** (arrhythmias, labile BP, ileus) in up to two-thirds; **facial and bulbar weakness** and **respiratory failure in ~20–30%**.
- **Investigations:** CSF **albuminocytological dissociation** (raised protein, normal cells — often normal in the first week); nerve conduction studies (demyelinating features, may lag); anti-ganglioside antibodies (**GQ1b in Miller Fisher**); stool/serology for *Campylobacter*. **A CSF pleocytosis >50 cells should make you consider HIV, Lyme, sarcoid or malignant infiltration instead.**
- **Variants:** **Miller Fisher syndrome — ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia (anti-GQ1b)**; AMAN/AMSAN (axonal); pharyngeal-cervical-brachial; Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis.
- **Management:** **monitor FVC and autonomic status closely** (see Section 5.6); **IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days OR plasma exchange** — equally effective, **do not combine**; **steroids are ineffective and should not be used** ⚑ (a common exam point); VTE prophylaxis, pain control (gabapentinoids), physiotherapy, and ICU if FVC falls.
- **Prognosis:** ~80% walk independently at 6 months; mortality 3–7%; poor prognostic markers are older age, rapid onset, need for ventilation, preceding diarrhoea/*Campylobacter*, and low distal motor amplitudes.

**CIDP** — the chronic counterpart: progression over **>8 weeks**, relapsing or progressive, symmetric proximal *and* distal weakness with sensory loss and areflexia. Unlike GBS, **it responds to steroids**, as well as to IVIg and plasma exchange; long-term immunosuppression or maintenance IVIg is often needed.

> **Hook:** *GBS — steroids don't work. CIDP — they do.*

docs.text:
**Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy):** commonest inherited neuropathy; **CMT1A (autosomal dominant, PMP22 duplication)** is the commonest subtype and is demyelinating. Features: childhood-to-early-adult onset, **pes cavus, hammer toes, "inverted champagne bottle" legs**, distal wasting and weakness, foot drop, areflexia, mild sensory loss, palpably thickened nerves. Management is supportive (orthotics, physiotherapy, surgery), plus genetic counselling; **avoid neurotoxic drugs (vincristine)**.

**Diabetic neuropathies — know that there are several:**

| Type | Picture |
|---|---|
| Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy | Commonest; glove-and-stocking, painful, with foot ulceration risk |
| Autonomic neuropathy | Postural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, silent ischaemia, fixed tachycardia |
| **Diabetic amyotrophy (proximal diabetic neuropathy / lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy)** | Severe thigh pain, then proximal wasting and weakness, weight loss; often after improved glycaemic control; usually recovers over months |
| Mononeuropathy | Median, ulnar, or **cranial (classically a pupil-sparing third nerve palsy)** |
| Mononeuritis multiplex | Vasculitic |

docs.title: Neuromuscular and Spinal Disorders
docs.text:
**Cervical radiculopathy:** neck and arm pain in a dermatomal distribution, worse on neck extension/rotation (**Spurling's test**), with segmental weakness and a lost reflex. C6 (biceps/supinator, thumb), **C7 (triceps, middle finger — commonest)**, C8. Most improve with conservative management; MRI and surgery for progressive deficit or myelopathy.

**Cervical myelopathy** — the diagnosis not to miss in an older patient with neck problems: **clumsy hands, gait disturbance, brisk reflexes below the level, Hoffmann's sign, inverted supinator jerk, Lhermitte's, sphincter change**. Requires MRI and surgical opinion; delay causes irreversible cord injury.

**Lumbosacral radiculopathy (sciatica):** radicular leg pain below the knee ± dermatomal sensory loss, myotomal weakness, lost reflex; positive **straight-leg raise**. **L5 (foot drop with weak inversion and hip abduction, first web space) and S1 (weak plantarflexion, absent ankle jerk, lateral foot)** are the commonest. NICE NG59: most settle; **do not offer imaging in a non-specialist setting**; treat with exercise and analgesia (NSAIDs; **not** gabapentinoids for sciatica ⚑), and consider epidural injection or surgery for severe or persistent radicular pain. **Screen every episode for cauda equina red flags.**

**Plexopathy:**
- **Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage–Turner)** — abrupt severe shoulder pain for days to weeks, followed by **patchy proximal arm weakness and wasting as the pain settles**; often post-infection or post-vaccination; recovery over months.
- Traumatic brachial plexus injury; **Erb's palsy** (C5/6, waiter's tip) and **Klumpke's** (C8/T1, claw hand ± Horner's).
- **Pancoast tumour** — lower plexus (C8/T1) pain and wasting with **Horner's syndrome**.
- Radiation plexopathy (painless, with myokymia) vs malignant infiltration (painful, with Horner's) — a classic discriminator in breast cancer follow-up.

docs.title: Neuromuscular and Spinal Disorders
docs.text:
##### Myasthenia gravis

**Pathophysiology:** IgG autoantibodies against the **postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor** (~85% of generalised, ~50% of ocular), or against **MuSK** (~5–8%; more bulbar and respiratory, poor response to anticholinesterases) or LRP4. **Bimodal epidemiology:** young women (20s–30s, associated with **thymic hyperplasia** and other autoimmune disease) and older men (60s–70s, associated with **thymoma**).

**Clinical picture:** **fatigable weakness** — worse with use and at the end of the day, better with rest.
- **Ocular in >50% at onset (and remains purely ocular in ~15%)**: asymmetric ptosis (worsens on sustained upgaze), variable diplopia. **Pupils are always spared** — a crucial discriminator from third nerve palsy and botulism.
- Bulbar: dysarthria that deteriorates as the patient speaks, dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, jaw fatigue.
- Limb: proximal weakness; neck extensor weakness ("dropped head").
- Reflexes and sensation are normal.

**Investigations:** **serum AChR antibodies**, then **MuSK** if negative; **repetitive nerve stimulation showing a decrement**; **single-fibre EMG (most sensitive)**; ice-pack test for ptosis at the bedside; **CT/MRI thorax for thymoma in everyone**; screen for associated thyroid disease and other autoimmunity. (The edrophonium/Tensilon test is largely historical because of cardiac risk ⚑.)

**Treatment:**
1. **Pyridostigmine** (symptomatic; muscarinic side effects — cramps, diarrhoea, salivation).
2. **Corticosteroids** — start low and titrate up, because rapid initiation can transiently worsen weakness; add a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine — check **TPMT** first, mycophenolate, methotrexate, ciclosporin, tacrolimus).
3. **Thymectomy** — mandatory for thymoma; also beneficial in **AChR-positive generalised MG under ~50–65 years without thymoma** (MGTX trial) ⚑.
4. **Crisis or severe exacerbation: IVIg or plasma exchange**, plus ICU-level respiratory monitoring.
5. ⚑ **Newer targeted therapies for refractory generalised MG:** **complement inhibitors** (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan — for AChR-positive disease; require **meningococcal vaccination**) and **neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) blockers** (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab — accelerate IgG clearance). Rituximab is particularly effective in **MuSK-positive** disease.

**Drugs that worsen myasthenia — a favourite exam question:** **aminoglycosides, macrolides, fluoroquinolones**, telithromycin (contraindicated), **beta-blockers**, calcium channel blockers, magnesium (including IV magnesium in obstetrics), **quinine and quinolones**, phenytoin, lithium, penicillamine (can cause MG), procainamide, statins, botulinum toxin, iodinated contrast, and neuromuscular blocking agents (extreme sensitivity to non-depolarising blockers).

**Myasthenic vs cholinergic crisis:**

| | **Myasthenic crisis** | **Cholinergic crisis** |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | Undertreatment, infection, surgery, drugs, pregnancy | Excess anticholinesterase |
