docs.text:
**Recognition:** **symmetrical proximal weakness** (difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, washing hair), **no sensory loss**, preserved reflexes until late, ± myalgia, ± raised CK.

| Group | Examples | Clues |
|---|---|---|
| **Inflammatory** | **Dermatomyositis** — heliotrope rash, **Gottron's papules**, shawl sign; **strong malignancy association in adults**. **Polymyositis**. **Inclusion body myositis** — over 50, **asymmetric, distal involvement (finger flexors and quadriceps)**, **poor steroid response** ⚑. **Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy** — very high CK, anti-HMGCR (statin-associated) or anti-SRP | Raised CK, EMG myopathic, MRI oedema, biopsy; treat with steroids ± immunosuppression (except IBM) |
| **Dystrophies** | **Duchenne** (X-linked, dystrophin absent; Gowers' sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, CK ×10–100, cardiomyopathy) and **Becker** (milder, reduced dystrophin); **myotonic dystrophy type 1** — CTG repeat in *DMPK*, **distal weakness, grip myotonia, frontal balding, cataracts, cardiac conduction block, diabetes, testicular atrophy, anticipation**; **facioscapulohumeral**; limb-girdle | Genetic diagnosis; cardiac and respiratory surveillance; corticosteroids and exon-skipping/gene therapies in DMD ⚑ |
| **Metabolic/endocrine** | Hypothyroid and hyperthyroid myopathy, Cushing's/steroid myopathy (**normal CK**), osteomalacia, hypokalaemia; McArdle disease (**second-wind phenomenon**, exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria) | Treat the cause |
| **Drug-induced** | **Statins** (myalgia to rhabdomyolysis; consider anti-HMGCR necrotising myopathy if it continues after stopping ⚑), corticosteroids, colchicine, amiodarone, antiretrovirals, alcohol | History |
| **Channelopathies** | Hypokalaemic and hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis, myotonia congenita | Episodic weakness, potassium at the time of an attack |
| **Mitochondrial** | MELAS, MERRF, **CPEO/Kearns–Sayre** | Maternal inheritance, ragged red fibres, lactate, multisystem |

**Myotonia** = delayed relaxation after contraction (patient cannot let go of a handshake; percussion myotonia). Seen in myotonic dystrophy, myotonia congenita and paramyotonia; treat with mexiletine if disabling.

docs.title: Neuromuscular and Spinal Disorders
docs.text:
(Anatomy and the full syndrome table are in Section 2.8 — here is the clinical approach.)

**First question in any myelopathy: is it compressive?** Compression is treatable and urgent — **image the whole spine with MRI**. Causes: **degenerative cervical spondylosis** (the commonest), **metastatic disease**, disc prolapse, epidural abscess (fever, back pain, focal tenderness, raised inflammatory markers, IV drug use or bacteraemia), haematoma (anticoagulation), trauma.

**Non-compressive causes:** transverse myelitis (MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, post-infectious), **spinal cord infarction** (sudden, painful, anterior cord pattern, often after aortic surgery or dissection), **B12 or copper deficiency (subacute combined degeneration)**, syringomyelia, dural arteriovenous fistula (a treatable cause of progressive myelopathy in older men), radiation, HTLV-1 myelopathy, hereditary spastic paraplegia.

**Subacute combined degeneration:** B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia, ileal disease, metformin, vegan diet, **nitrous oxide abuse** ⚑ — an increasingly common cause in young people) affecting **dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts**: paraesthesia, sensory ataxia, **absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars**, and cognitive/psychiatric change. **Treat with intramuscular B12; neurological damage may be irreversible if treatment is delayed, and B12 must be replaced before folate** to avoid precipitating deterioration.

**Syringomyelia:** a fluid cavity in the central cord (often with Chiari I malformation, or post-traumatic). Classic picture: **"cape" distribution dissociated sensory loss (pain and temperature lost, dorsal columns preserved)**, painless burns and injuries, wasting of the small hand muscles, then long-tract signs; **Horner's syndrome** if it extends to T1. MRI diagnoses it; treatment is decompression of the underlying cause.

docs.title: Neuromuscular and Spinal Disorders
docs.text:
**Bell's palsy:** acute (<72 h) **lower motor neurone** facial weakness — **the forehead is involved** — with ipsilateral loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, hyperacusis, and sometimes retro-auricular pain.
- **The critical split:** **forehead sparing means an upper motor neurone lesion → stroke.** Bilateral facial palsy suggests **sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, GBS, HIV or bilateral parotid disease**.
- **Treatment: prednisolone 50 mg for 10 days (or 60 mg tapering), started within 72 hours** — clearly beneficial. Antivirals add little for Bell's palsy alone but are used if there is a zoster component. **Eye care is mandatory** — lubricants, taping at night, referral if the cornea is at risk.
- Prognosis: ~85% recover well; incomplete palsy carries the best outlook. Failure to improve by 3 months should prompt imaging (parotid tumour, cholesteatoma).

**Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus):** facial palsy **plus a painful vesicular rash in the ear canal/auricle or palate**, often with vertigo and hearing loss. Worse prognosis than Bell's; **treat with aciclovir plus prednisolone**.

**Third nerve palsy:** see Section 2.5 — pupil involvement means compression until proven otherwise.

**Sixth nerve palsy:** may be a false localising sign in raised ICP; also microvascular, cavernous sinus, and skull base pathology.

docs.title: Neuromuscular and Spinal Disorders
docs.text:
**Step 1 — is it vertigo (an illusion of movement) or something else** (presyncope, disequilibrium, anxiety)?

**Step 2 — peripheral or central?**

| | **Peripheral** | **Central** |
|---|---|---|
| Nystagmus | **Unidirectional, horizontal-torsional, suppressed by fixation** | **Direction-changing, vertical or pure torsional, not suppressed** |
| Hearing | Often affected (Ménière's, labyrinthitis) | Usually spared (except AICA stroke) |
| Other neurology | None | Present (diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, weakness) |
| Gait | Unsteady but can walk | **Cannot stand or walk unaided** |
| **HINTS exam** (in acute continuous vertigo) | **H**ead **I**mpulse **abnormal** (corrective saccade), **N**o direction-changing nystagmus, **N**o **T**est **o**f **S**kew | **Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation = central — HINTS "INFARCT"** ⚑ |

| Condition | Duration and trigger | Discriminator | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BPPV** | **Seconds**, on head turning/lying down | **Dix–Hallpike positive** with rotatory nystagmus and latency/fatigability | **Epley manoeuvre** |
| **Vestibular neuritis** | **Days**, continuous, after viral illness | No hearing loss; abnormal head impulse | Short-course vestibular sedatives (≤3 days), then **vestibular rehabilitation** |
| **Labyrinthitis** | Days | Vertigo **with hearing loss** | As above ± steroids |
| **Ménière's disease** | **Minutes to hours**, episodic | **Fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness** with vertigo | Salt restriction, betahistine, ENT referral |
| **Vestibular migraine** | Minutes–days | Migraine history, photophobia, headache often absent during attacks | Migraine preventives |
| **Posterior circulation stroke/TIA** | Sudden, continuous | Central features, vascular risk factors, **inability to walk** | Stroke pathway |
| Vestibular schwannoma | Chronic | **Progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus** | MRI internal acoustic meatus |

> **Hook:** *Seconds = BPPV; minutes–hours with hearing symptoms = Ménière's; days = neuritis; sudden with an inability to walk = stroke.*

- DEFINITION: illusion of rotational, linear, or tilting movement of self or environment, produced by peripheral (inner ear) or central (brainstem-cerebellum) stimulation
- Important to distinguish vertigo from other causes of “dizziness”
- Sense of balance is dependent on vestibular function (sensation of head position and movement in space), proprioception (joint position sense), and visual function

docs.h: Part C — Confusable pairs, reduced to one separating feature
docs.text:
| Pair | The one thing that separates them |
|---|---|
| **Ischaemic vs haemorrhagic stroke** | Imaging only — clinically indistinguishable (headache and vomiting *hint* at haemorrhage) |
| **Stroke vs Bell's palsy** | **Forehead**: spared = stroke, involved = Bell's |
| **Seizure vs syncope** | Lateral tongue bite and prolonged post-ictal confusion = seizure |
| **Epileptic vs functional seizure** | Eyes forcibly closed, waxing–waning, >5 min = functional |
| **Migraine aura vs TIA** | Aura marches over minutes with **positive** phenomena; TIA is instant and **negative** |
| **Migraine vs cluster** | Migraine lies still; cluster paces |
| **Cluster vs paroxysmal hemicrania** | Indometacin abolishes paroxysmal hemicrania |
| **SAH vs traumatic tap** | Xanthochromia and constant red-cell count = SAH |
| **Extradural vs subdural** | Biconvex, does not cross sutures, lucid interval = extradural |
| **Delirium vs dementia** | Attention: impaired and fluctuating = delirium |
| **DLB vs Parkinson's disease dementia** | The 1-year rule |
| **Parkinson's vs essential tremor** | Rest and asymmetric with bradykinesia = Parkinson's; postural, symmetric, alcohol-responsive = essential |
| **Parkinson's vs PSP** | Early falls **backwards** and down-gaze palsy = PSP |
| **Parkinson's vs MSA** | Early severe autonomic failure = MSA |
| **Parkinson's vs vascular parkinsonism** | Lower-body predominance with normal arms = vascular |
| **Parkinson's vs drug-induced** | Symmetry and a drug history = drug-induced |
| **MS vs NMOSD** | Longitudinally extensive myelitis and severe bilateral optic neuritis = NMOSD (check AQP4) |
| **Optic neuritis vs GCA-related visual loss** | Age, pain on eye movement and recovery = optic neuritis; painless sudden loss over 50 with jaw claudication = GCA |
| **Myasthenia vs Lambert–Eaton** | Fatigues with use = MG; briefly improves with use, hyporeflexic, dry mouth = LEMS |
| **Myasthenia vs botulism** | Pupils: spared in MG, **dilated** in botulism |
| **Myasthenic vs cholinergic crisis** | Miosis, salivation, bradycardia, fasciculations = cholinergic |
| **GBS vs CIDP** | Nadir ≤4 weeks = GBS; progression >8 weeks = CIDP (and CIDP responds to steroids) |
| **GBS vs transverse myelitis** | Sensory level and extensor plantars = cord; areflexia throughout = GBS |
| **Common peroneal palsy vs L5 radiculopathy** | Inversion and hip abduction weak = L5 root |
| **Ulnar lesion at the elbow vs the wrist** | Dorsal hand sensory loss = elbow |
| **Conus medullaris vs cauda equina** | Symmetrical with early sphincter loss = conus |
| **Cord compression vs cord infarction** | Sudden and painful with spared vibration = anterior spinal artery infarction |
| **Central cord vs anterior cord syndrome** | Arms worse than legs = central cord |
| **Myopathy vs neuropathy** | Proximal + no sensory loss + raised CK = myopathy |
| **Polymyositis vs inclusion body myositis** | Asymmetric finger flexor/quadriceps weakness, steroid-resistant, over 50 = IBM

docs.title: Neurophysiology
docs.text:
The resting membrane potential (**−70 mV** in a typical neurone) is set by the K⁺ gradient with a small Na⁺ leak, maintained by the **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in)** — electrogenic, and a major consumer of the brain's 20% share of resting oxygen use.

| Phase | Ionic event |
|---|---|
| Threshold (≈ −55 mV) | Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open |
| Upstroke | Rapid Na⁺ influx → depolarisation to ≈ +35 mV |
| Repolarisation | Na⁺ channel inactivation + delayed-rectifier K⁺ efflux |
| Hyperpolarisation | K⁺ efflux overshoots; absolute then relative refractory period |

**Saltatory conduction:** myelin (oligodendrocytes centrally, Schwann cells peripherally) increases membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so current jumps node-to-node at the **nodes of Ranvier**, where Na⁺ channels are concentrated.

**Why this matters clinically:** demyelination slows or blocks conduction → the *conduction-velocity slowing* of demyelinating neuropathy (GBS, CIDP, CMT1) on nerve conduction studies, versus *reduced amplitude* in axonal neuropathy. Heat worsens conduction block — **Uhthoff's phenomenon** in MS.

| Fibre | Myelin | Function | Clinical note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aα/Aβ | Heavy | Proprioception, vibration, light touch, motor | Lost first in compression; large-fibre neuropathy |
| Aδ | Thin | Fast "first" pain, cold | Sharp, well-localised pain |
| C | None | Slow "second" pain, warmth, autonomic | Burning pain; small-fibre neuropathy (normal NCS) |

> **Hook:** *Pressure kills big fibres, ischaemia kills small fibres* — compression neuropathy loses vibration/proprioception first; vasculitic/diabetic small-fibre disease loses pain/temperature with normal nerve conduction studies.

docs.title: Neurophysiology
docs.text:
Depolarisation opens presynaptic **voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels** → vesicle fusion (SNARE proteins) → transmitter release → postsynaptic receptor binding → EPSP or IPSP → summation at the axon hillock.

| Transmitter | Main role | Key clinical link |
|---|---|---|
| Glutamate | Principal excitatory (AMPA, NMDA) | Excitotoxicity in stroke; anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis; memantine blocks NMDA |
| GABA | Principal inhibitory (GABA-A ionotropic Cl⁻, GABA-B metabotropic) | Benzodiazepines, barbiturates, alcohol; anti-GAD antibodies (stiff person) |
| Glycine | Inhibitory in cord/brainstem | Blocked by strychnine and by tetanus toxin |
| Acetylcholine | NMJ, autonomic ganglia, basal forebrain | Myasthenia, cholinesterase inhibitors in Alzheimer's |
| Dopamine | Nigrostriatal, mesolimbic, tuberoinfundibular | Parkinson's; antipsychotic side effects; prolactin |
| Noradrenaline | Locus coeruleus — arousal | Depression, ADHD drugs |
| Serotonin | Raphe nuclei — mood, pain, sleep | Triptans, SSRIs, serotonin syndrome |

**Toxin logic worth memorising:** **tetanus toxin** blocks release of *inhibitory* glycine/GABA in the cord → spasticity and rigidity; **botulinum toxin** blocks release of *acetylcholine* at the NMJ (cleaves SNARE proteins) → flaccid paralysis. Same family of proteases, opposite clinical picture.

docs.title: Neurophysiology
docs.text:
Nerve action potential → presynaptic **P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels** open → ACh released → binds **nicotinic ACh receptors** on the postsynaptic folds → endplate potential → muscle fibre action potential → T-tubule depolarisation → **dihydropyridine receptor** → **ryanodine receptor** → sarcoplasmic Ca²⁺ release → cross-bridge cycling. ACh is degraded by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft.

There is normally a large **safety factor** (far more ACh released than needed). Disease removes it in different places:

| Disorder | Target | Consequence on repetitive stimulation |
|---|---|---|
| Myasthenia gravis | Postsynaptic ACh receptor (or MuSK/LRP4) | **Decrement** at low frequency; fatigable weakness |
| Lambert–Eaton | Presynaptic P/Q Ca²⁺ channel | **Increment** after exercise/high-frequency; weakness improves briefly with use |
| Botulism | Presynaptic SNARE-mediated ACh release | Descending flaccid paralysis, fixed dilated pupils, autonomic features |
| Organophosphate poisoning | Acetylcholinesterase inhibited | Cholinergic crisis then depolarising block |

docs.title: Neurophysiology
docs.text:
CSF is produced mainly by the **choroid plexus** of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles at roughly **0.35 mL/min ≈ 500 mL/day**, with a standing volume of about **150 mL** — so the whole volume is turned over three to four times daily. Flow: lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → foramina of Luschka/Magendie → subarachnoid space → absorbed at arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus (and, per more recent work, via meningeal lymphatics and the glymphatic system).

Normal opening pressure on lumbar puncture: **10–20 cmH₂O** (adults, lateral decubitus); >25 cmH₂O is clearly raised. ⚑ For idiopathic intracranial hypertension, current diagnostic criteria use **>25 cmH₂O** in adults.

**Monro–Kellie doctrine:** the cranium is a fixed box containing brain (~80%), blood (~10%) and CSF (~10%). An increase in one must be offset by a decrease in another, or ICP rises. Initial compensation is displacement of CSF and venous blood; once exhausted, the pressure–volume curve turns steeply upward — which is why a patient can look stable and then deteriorate abruptly.

**Hydrocephalus split:** *non-communicating (obstructive)* — block within the ventricular system (aqueduct stenosis, colloid cyst, posterior fossa tumour); *communicating* — impaired absorption (post-SAH, post-meningitis) or, rarely, overproduction (choroid plexus papilloma).

docs.title: Neurophysiology
docs.text:
Normal CBF ≈ **50 mL/100 g/min**. Thresholds worth knowing: below ~20 mL/100 g/min electrical function fails (the **ischaemic penumbra** — dysfunctional but salvageable); below ~10 mL/100 g/min membrane failure and infarction follow within minutes. The penumbra is the entire rationale for reperfusion therapy.

**Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) = MAP − ICP.** Target CPP is generally **60–70 mmHg** in traumatic brain injury; ICP is treated when sustained **>22 mmHg** ⚑ (Brain Trauma Foundation 4th edition lowered the older ">20" threshold to >22).

**Autoregulation** keeps CBF constant across a MAP of roughly **60–150 mmHg**, shifted rightward in chronic hypertension (so a "normal" BP may under-perfuse). Autoregulation is impaired or lost in acute stroke and TBI, making CBF pressure-passive — the reason for permissive hypertension after ischaemic stroke and for avoiding hypotension in head injury.

CBF also responds to gases: it rises with **hypercapnia** and falls with hypocapnia (roughly 1–2 mL/100 g/min per mmHg PaCO₂) — the basis of brief hyperventilation as a temporising measure for herniation, and of why it is harmful if prolonged.

docs.title: Neurophysiology
docs.text:
Formed by **tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells**, supported by astrocyte end-feet and pericytes. Lipid-soluble small molecules cross freely; glucose (GLUT1) and amino acids need carriers. **Circumventricular organs** lack a barrier — area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone), median eminence, pineal, subfornical organ.

Clinical consequences: levodopa crosses but dopamine does not (hence peripheral decarboxylase inhibitors); most antibiotics penetrate poorly unless the meninges are inflamed (why meningitic doses are higher); contrast enhancement on CT/MRI marks BBB breakdown (tumour, abscess, active demyelinating plaque).

docs.title: Neurophysiology
docs.text:
The corticospinal tract originates in the precentral gyrus (Betz cells in layer V), descends through the **corona radiata → posterior limb of the internal capsule → cerebral peduncle → pons → medullary pyramids**, where ~85–90% decussate to form the lateral corticospinal tract; the remainder continue as the anterior corticospinal tract and cross at segmental level.

| Feature | Upper motor neurone | Lower motor neurone |
|---|---|---|
| Tone | Increased (spastic, clasp-knife) | Decreased (flaccid) |
| Reflexes | Brisk, clonus | Reduced or absent |
| Plantars | Extensor (Babinski) | Flexor |
| Wasting | Late, disuse only | Early and marked |
| Fasciculations | Absent | Present |
| Weakness pattern | Pyramidal — extensors weak in arm, flexors weak in leg | Follows the nerve/root/segment |

> **Hook:** in the arms an UMN lesion spares the "carrying" muscles — **arm flexors strong, extensors weak; leg extensors strong, flexors weak** — hence the hemiplegic posture of flexed arm and extended leg.

Note that in the first hours to days after an acute UMN lesion (spinal shock, acute stroke) tone and reflexes may be *reduced*; spasticity develops later. This trips people up in exams.

**Reflex arc:** muscle spindle (Ia afferent) → dorsal root → monosynaptic connection to the α-motor neurone → contraction. Golgi tendon organs (Ib) mediate inhibition. Reflex roots worth reciting: **biceps C5/6, supinator C6, triceps C7, knee L3/4, ankle S1/2**.

docs.title: Neurophysiology
docs.text:
| | Dorsal column–medial lemniscus | Spinothalamic (anterolateral) |
|---|---|---|
| Modalities | Vibration, proprioception, fine touch | Pain, temperature, crude touch |
| First-order cell | DRG → ascends **ipsilaterally** in the cord | DRG → synapses in dorsal horn |
| Decussation | **Medulla** (internal arcuate fibres) | **Within 1–2 segments in the cord** (anterior white commissure) |
| Second-order | Nucleus gracilis/cuneatus → medial lemniscus | Lateral spinothalamic tract |
| Third-order | VPL of thalamus → postcentral gyrus | VPL of thalamus → postcentral gyrus |

That difference in where the tracts cross is what generates **Brown-Séquard syndrome**: ipsilateral loss of vibration/proprioception and ipsilateral UMN weakness *below* the lesion, with **contralateral** loss of pain and temperature starting one or two segments below.

**Pain modulation:** the gate control theory (Aβ input inhibits dorsal-horn transmission — why rubbing helps) and descending inhibition from the periaqueductal grey via serotonergic/noradrenergic pathways — the mechanism exploited by tricyclics and SNRIs in neuropathic pain.

docs.title: Neurophysiology
docs.text:
**Cerebellum** — compares intended with actual movement and corrects it. Output is **ipsilateral** (double crossing), so a cerebellar hemisphere lesion causes ipsilateral limb signs. Midline (vermis/flocculonodular) disease causes truncal/gait ataxia and nystagmus; hemispheric disease causes limb dysmetria, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia.

**Basal ganglia circuitry** (know the direction of the arrows, not every synapse):

- **Direct pathway** (facilitates movement): cortex → striatum → (inhibits) internal globus pallidus → (disinhibits) thalamus → cortex. Dopamine at **D1** receptors *excites* this pathway.
- **Indirect pathway** (suppresses movement): cortex → striatum → external globus pallidus → subthalamic nucleus → internal globus pallidus → thalamus. Dopamine at **D2** receptors *inhibits* this pathway.

Net effect: nigrostriatal dopamine promotes movement. Losing it (Parkinson's — degeneration of the substantia nigra pars compacta, with Lewy bodies containing α-synuclein) produces hypokinesia. Losing the striatal GABAergic neurones of the indirect pathway (Huntington's) or the subthalamic nucleus (vascular lesion) produces hyperkinesia — chorea and hemiballismus respectively. Motor symptoms of PD appear only after roughly **50–70% of nigral neurones are lost**, which is why disease is well established at diagnosis.

docs.title: Neurophysiology
docs.text:
Consciousness requires **arousal** (ascending reticular activating system in the upper brainstem tegmentum, projecting via thalamus to cortex) plus **content** (cortex). Therefore coma requires either a **brainstem/upper reticular lesion**, **bilateral hemispheric dysfunction**, or a **diffuse metabolic/toxic insult**. A unilateral hemispheric lesion does not cause coma unless it is large enough to compress the brainstem.

Sleep cycles roughly every 90 minutes through N1–N3 (slow-wave, restorative, where sleepwalking and night terrors occur) and REM (dreaming, muscle atonia, where nightmares and — when atonia fails — **REM sleep behaviour disorder** occur; RBD is a strong predictor of later synucleinopathy, i.e. Parkinson's disease, DLB or MSA).

docs.h: Neurology Master Notes — Seizures and Epilepsy

docs.title: Seizures and Epilepsy
docs.text:
The 2017 framework replaced "partial/simple/complex/secondary generalised" with plainer language. Classify at three levels: **seizure type → epilepsy type → epilepsy syndrome**, always asking about aetiology and comorbidity.

| Old term | ⚑ Current term |
|---|---|
| Simple partial | **Focal aware** |
| Complex partial | **Focal impaired awareness** |
| Secondary generalised | **Focal to bilateral tonic–clonic** |
| Petit mal | Absence |
| Grand mal | Generalised tonic–clonic |

**Onset categories:** focal, generalised, unknown. Focal seizures are further described as **motor** or **non-motor** onset and by awareness. Generalised seizures: tonic–clonic, absence (typical/atypical), myoclonic, tonic, atonic, clonic.

**Aetiological groups:** structural, genetic, infectious, metabolic, immune, unknown.

**Definition of epilepsy (ILAE 2014, still current):** ⚑ any one of —
1. **Two** unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart;
2. **One** unprovoked seizure **plus** a ≥60% recurrence risk over 10 years (e.g. a structural lesion or clearly epileptiform EEG);
3. Diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.

docs.title: Seizures and Epilepsy
docs.text:
| Lobe | Features |
|---|---|
| **Temporal** | Rising epigastric aura, déjà vu/jamais vu, fear, olfactory or gustatory hallucination, **lip-smacking and fumbling automatisms**, post-ictal confusion and dysphasia (if dominant). The commonest focal epilepsy |
| **Frontal** | Brief, nocturnal, hyperkinetic/bizarre motor activity, **Jacksonian march**, **Todd's paresis** post-ictally, head/eye version away from the focus, minimal post-ictal confusion |
| **Parietal** | Contralateral paraesthesia, distorted body image |
| **Occipital** | Simple visual hallucinations — flashes, colours, circles (contrast with the fortification spectra of migraine) |

docs.title: Seizures and Epilepsy
docs.text:
**Immediate questions:** was it a seizure at all (versus syncope, cardiac arrhythmia, functional attack, migraine, TIA, hypoglycaemia, parasomnia)? Was it **provoked**? Is there a structural cause?

**Features favouring a seizure over syncope:** aura, head-turning, unusual posturing, prolonged limb-jerking (>30 s), **lateral tongue biting** (highly specific), incontinence (less specific), cyanosis, prolonged post-ictal confusion (>5 min), amnesia for the event, occurrence in sleep. *Brief myoclonic jerks are common in syncope and do not make it a seizure.*

**Workup:** history from a witness (the single most valuable investigation), examination, ECG (**always — exclude long QT, Brugada, heart block**), glucose, electrolytes including calcium and magnesium, toxicology, pregnancy test where relevant. Then **EEG** (within 2 weeks per NICE; supports classification, does not confirm or exclude epilepsy) and **MRI brain** (NICE: within 6 weeks; especially if focal onset, onset <2 years or >60 years, or refractory).

**When to start treatment:** generally after a **second** unprovoked seizure. Consider after a first if there is a structural lesion, an unequivocally epileptiform EEG, a neurological deficit, or the patient judges the risk of another seizure unacceptable. Treating provoked seizures long-term is usually wrong — treat the provocation.

**Driving (UK DVLA, Group 1):** first unprovoked seizure — **6 months** off driving (12 months if there is an abnormality likely to cause further seizures); established epilepsy — **12 months seizure-free**; seizures only in sleep — may drive after an established pattern of ≥12 months of sleep-only seizures; withdrawal of medication — no driving during the change and for **6 months** afterwards. Group 2 (HGV/PSV) rules are far stricter (typically 10 years seizure-free off medication). **The patient must inform the DVLA; the doctor must document the advice.**

**Safety advice:** showers rather than baths, supervision when swimming, care with heights, ladders, machinery and cooking, and — for those of childbearing potential — pre-conception counselling.

docs.title: Seizures and Epilepsy
docs.text:
| Syndrome | Age | Features | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Childhood absence epilepsy** | 4–10 y | Brief blank spells ×10s/day, induced by hyperventilation; **3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave** | **Ethosuximide** first line |
| **Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy** | Teens | **Early-morning myoclonic jerks** (throwing the cereal bowl), GTCS, absences; photosensitive; sleep deprivation and alcohol provoke it; usually lifelong treatment | Levetiracetam or valproate (valproate restricted — see 6.7); **avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and pregabalin — they aggravate myoclonus and absences; lamotrigine can also worsen myoclonus** |
| **Temporal lobe epilepsy** | Any | As 6.2; often **hippocampal sclerosis** on MRI; frequently drug-resistant | Lamotrigine/levetiracetam; consider surgery |
| **Infantile spasms (West syndrome)** | 3–12 mo | Salaam spasms in clusters, developmental regression, **hypsarrhythmia** on EEG; tuberous sclerosis association | **Vigabatrin** (especially with tuberous sclerosis) and/or steroids/ACTH |
| **Lennox–Gastaut** | 3–5 y | Multiple seizure types, tonic seizures in sleep, slow spike-and-wave <2.5 Hz, learning disability | Valproate, lamotrigine, rufinamide, cannabidiol |
| **Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (benign rolandic)** | 4–10 y | Nocturnal hemifacial twitching, drooling, speech arrest; **excellent prognosis, remits in adolescence** | Often no treatment |
| **Dravet syndrome** | Infancy | Prolonged febrile hemiclonic seizures, SCN1A | Avoid sodium-channel blockers; valproate, clobazam, stiripentol, fenfluramine ⚑ |

docs.title: Seizures and Epilepsy
docs.text:
**Provoked (acute symptomatic):** hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, uraemia, alcohol withdrawal (typically 6–48 h after the last drink), benzodiazepine withdrawal, drugs lowering the threshold (tramadol, bupropion, theophylline, quinolones, clozapine), sepsis, eclampsia, meningitis/encephalitis, stroke, head injury, hypoxia.

**Febrile convulsions** — 6 months to 5 years, with fever, no CNS infection. **Simple** (generalised, <15 min, no recurrence in 24 h) carries a small increased risk of later epilepsy; **complex** (focal, >15 min, or recurrent within 24 h) more so.

**Mimics:** vasovagal syncope, cardiac syncope, functional/dissociative seizures, migraine with aura, TIA, panic attacks with hyperventilation, parasomnias, hypnic jerks, transient global amnesia, paroxysmal movement disorders.

docs.title: Seizures and Epilepsy
docs.text:
| Seizure type | First line | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Focal** | **Lamotrigine or levetiracetam** | ⚑ Carbamazepine is now an add-on/alternative, not first-line monotherapy |
| **Generalised tonic–clonic** | Lamotrigine, levetiracetam **or sodium valproate** | Valproate restricted (6.7) |
| **Absence** | **Ethosuximide** | Then valproate; lamotrigine/levetiracetam if valproate unsuitable |
| **Myoclonic** | **Levetiracetam or sodium valproate** | Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin, pregabalin, tiagabine (**they worsen myoclonus and absences**) |
| **Tonic or atonic** | Lamotrigine or sodium valproate | Often in syndromic epilepsy |
| **Idiopathic generalised epilepsy** | Lamotrigine, levetiracetam or sodium valproate | |

**Principles:** monotherapy at the lowest effective dose, titrate slowly (especially lamotrigine — rapid escalation risks **Stevens–Johnson syndrome**), only add a second drug once monotherapy at maximum tolerated dose has failed, and remember **drug-resistant epilepsy = failure of two appropriate, well-tolerated drugs** → refer to a specialist centre for surgical/vagal nerve stimulator/ketogenic assessment.

docs.title: Seizures and Epilepsy
docs.text:
**Valproate is the most teratogenic of the common antiseizure medications:** ~10% risk of major congenital malformation (neural tube defects, cardiac, facial clefts) and ~30–40% risk of neurodevelopmental disorder in exposed children.

**MHRA/NICE position (2023–2024):** ⚑
- Valproate must **not be started in anyone under 55 years** (male or female) unless **two specialists independently document** that there is no other effective or tolerated option.
- Anyone of childbearing potential taking it must be in a **Pregnancy Prevention Programme** with annual specialist review and a signed risk acknowledgement form.
- ⚑ New: warnings extend to **men** — possible increased risk of neurodevelopmental disorders in children fathered while taking valproate; effective contraception is advised for men and for 3 months after stopping.
- Topiramate: similar Pregnancy Prevention Programme requirements ⚑ (teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental risk).

**Practical pregnancy advice:** **5 mg folic acid daily** pre-conception and through the first trimester; do not stop antiseizure medication abruptly — an uncontrolled tonic–clonic seizure is more dangerous than most drugs; **lamotrigine and levetiracetam have the best pregnancy safety data**; lamotrigine levels fall in pregnancy (oestrogen induces glucuronidation) so doses often need increasing and reducing again postpartum; enzyme-inducing drugs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, topiramate >200 mg) reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraception; breastfeeding is generally encouraged; UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register enrolment.

docs.title: Seizures and Epilepsy
docs.text:
**SUDEP** (sudden unexpected death in epilepsy) — incidence roughly **1 in 1000 patient-years** overall, higher in refractory epilepsy. Risk factors: frequent generalised tonic–clonic seizures (the strongest), nocturnal seizures, poor adherence, polytherapy, sleeping alone, young adult male. Risk reduction: optimise seizure control and adherence; NICE requires SUDEP to be discussed with every patient.

**Refractory options:** epilepsy surgery (anterior temporal lobectomy for hippocampal sclerosis has the best evidence — many become seizure-free), lesionectomy, corpus callosotomy, **vagus nerve stimulation**, responsive neurostimulation/deep brain stimulation, **ketogenic diet** (particularly in children).

docs.title: Seizures and Epilepsy
docs.text:
| Feature | Epileptic seizure | **Functional/dissociative** |
|---|---|---|
| Duration | 1–2 min | Often **prolonged (>5 min), waxing and waning** |
| Motor pattern | Stereotyped, synchronous | **Asynchronous** thrashing, **pelvic thrusting, side-to-side head shaking** |
| Eyes | **Open** | **Forcefully closed, resisting opening** |
| Vocalisation | Early cry, then quiet | Emotional crying, talking during the event |
| Injury/tongue bite | Lateral tongue bite | Tip of tongue, if any |
| Post-ictal | Confusion, prolonged | Rapid recovery or prolonged unresponsiveness with normal vitals |
| Investigations | Ictal EEG abnormal; **prolactin may rise** | Ictal EEG normal; prolactin normal |

Diagnosis is made on **positive** features, not by exclusion; management is psychological (explanation without accusation, CBT), not antiseizure medication. Note that both can coexist in the same patient.

docs.title: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
docs.text:
Cross-checked against KDIGO 2012 AKI guideline, NICE AKI guidance, Merck Manual

Professional, StatPearls, and Kidney360 (2023). AKI is the single highest-yield acute renal topic in finals — it appears in written papers, data interpretation, prescribing, and OSCE emergency stations.

docs.title: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
docs.text:
##### KDIGO definition of AKI — any one of:

- 1. **↑ Creatinine ≥26.5 μmol/L (≥0.3 mg/dL) within 48 hours,** OR
- 2. **↑ Creatinine to ≥1.5 × baseline,** known or presumed to have occurred **within the prior**

**7 days,** OR
- 3. **Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥6 hours**

Note the two different time windows: **48 hours** for the absolute rise, **7 days** for the relative rise.

Examiners test this.

##### KDIGO staging

| Stag e | Serum creatinine | Urine output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1.5–1.9 × baseline OR ↑ ≥26.5 μmol/L (≥0.3 mg/dL) | <0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6–12 hrs |
| 2 | 2.0–2.9 × baseline | <0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥12 hrs |
| 3 | ≥3.0 × baseline OR creatinine ≥353.6 μmol/L (≥4.0 mg/dL) OR initiation of RRT OR (if <18 yrs) eGFR <35 | <0.3 mL/kg/hr for ≥24 hrs OR anuria ≥12 hrs |

###### Three rules that generate exam questions:

- **"Worse-of" rule** — stage by whichever criterion (creatinine or urine output) gives the **higher** stage.
- **RRT override** — starting dialysis = **Stage 3,** regardless of the numbers.

- **Urine output criteria are unreliable** in patients on **diuretics** or with **cirrhosis,** and really require ICU-level monitoring to apply properly.

Prognosis: even Stage 1 AKI roughly doubles long-term CKD risk. Mortality climbs steeply with stage (~9% stage 1 → 30–50% stage 3 requiring RRT).

##### Distinguishing AKI from CKD (and acute-on-chronic)

| Favours CKD | Favours AKI |
| --- | --- |
| Small, echogenic kidneys with poor corticomedullary differentiation on US | Normal-sized kidneys |
| Anaemia (EPO deficiency) | Normal Hb |
| Hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, ↑PTH (established CKD–MBD) | Normal bone profile |
| Previous blood results showing chronically raised creatinine | Previously normal creatinine |
| Renal osteodystrophy on imaging | — |

- **The single most useful investigation is old bloods.** Always look for a baseline creatinine.
- **Exceptions — CKD with normal/large kidneys:** diabetic nephropathy (early), amyloid,

HIV-associated nephropathy, myeloma, ADPKD, infiltration.
- **Acute-on-chronic** is common and behaves like AKI for management purposes — treat the acute insult.

docs.title: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
docs.text:
The pre-renal / intrinsic / post-renal framework is the backbone of every AKI answer. State it explicitly in exams — the structure earns marks.

##### Pre-renal (~60–70% of AKI — the commonest)

Kidney is structurally normal; the problem is perfusion. **Reversible if corrected promptly** — but if prolonged, progresses to ATN.
- **True hypovolaemia:** haemorrhage, GI losses (vomiting/diarrhoea), burns, diuretics, poor intake

- **Reduced effective circulating volume** (despite fluid overload!): **cardiorenal** **syndrome** (heart failure), **hepatorenal syndrome** (cirrhosis), nephrotic syndrome
- **Sepsis / distributive shock** — vasodilatation → renal hypoperfusion
- **Drug-induced haemodynamic AKI** (no structural damage — purely altered glomerular haemodynamics):
  - **NSAIDs** → block prostaglandins → **afferent arteriolar constriction** → ↓GFR
  - **ACEi/ARB** → block angiotensin II → **efferent arteriolar dilatation** → ↓GFR (dangerous in bilateral renal artery stenosis)
  - **Calcineurin inhibitors** (ciclosporin, tacrolimus) → afferent vasoconstriction
  - **The "triple whammy": NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic.** Classic exam vignette.
- **Renal artery stenosis** with ACEi
- **Abdominal compartment syndrome** — see below

##### Intrinsic (renal)

Structural damage. Sub-classify by the compartment injured — this is how a good answer is organised. **Post-renal (obstruction)**

Always exclude — it's **reversible** and missing it is negligent. Requires **bilateral** obstruction (or unilateral in a single functioning kidney) to cause AKI.
- **Intraluminal:** stones, clot, sloughed papillae
- **Intramural:** ureteric stricture, tumour
- **Extramural: prostatic hypertrophy or cancer** (the commonest cause in older men), pelvic/cervical malignancy, **retroperitoneal fibrosis,** aortic aneurysm
- **First test: renal ultrasound** (within 24 hours if cause unclear)
- **Trap:** hydronephrosis may be **absent** in early obstruction, volume depletion, or **retroperitoneal fibrosis/encasing tumour** (ureters trapped, can't dilate)

docs.title: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
docs.text:
##### Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)

- **Ischaemic** (prolonged pre-renal state, hypotension, sepsis, surgery) vs **nephrotoxic** (aminoglycosides, contrast, amphotericin, cisplatin, myoglobin, light chains)
- **Urinalysis: muddy-brown granular casts,** renal tubular epithelial cells; **FeNa >1–2%;**

###### urine osm ~300 (isosthenuric)

- **Three phases** — worth knowing because the diuretic phase is a management trap:
  - 1. **Oliguric phase** (~1–2 weeks) — risk of fluid overload, hyperkalaemia
  - 2. **Polyuric/diuretic phase** — tubules recover GFR before they recover concentrating ability → **massive urine output, risk of hypovolaemia,** **hypokalaemia, hypernatraemia.** Must replace fluids and monitor electrolytes.

- 3. **Recovery phase**
- Usually **reversible over days–weeks** if the insult is removed — but often needs supportive dialysis in the interim

##### Rhabdomyolysis and pigment nephropathy

- **Causes:** crush injury, prolonged immobility ("long lie"), seizures, extreme exertion, **statins** (esp. with fibrates or macrolides), alcohol, illicit drugs, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia
- **Diagnosis: CK >5× upper limit of normal** (i.e. typically **>1000 U/L); AKI risk rises**

###### steeply with CK >15,000–20,000 U/L

- **Classic triad** (myalgia, weakness, tea-coloured urine) is present in **<10%** — don't rely on it
- **Biochemistry — the pattern is very examinable:**
  - ↑↑ **CK,** ↑ **potassium,** ↑ **phosphate,** ↑ **urate, ↓ calcium** (early — deposits in damaged muscle), ↑ AST/ALT/LDH
  - **Late rebound hypercalcaemia** during recovery (calcium released from muscle)

— don't over-treat the early hypocalcaemia
  - **Dipstick blood positive, but NO red cells on microscopy** (it's myoglobin) — the mismatch clue
- **Management: early, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation** (ideally within 6 hours) — the single intervention with clear benefit; treat hyperkalaemia; stop the cause; monitor for compartment syndrome. Urinary alkalinisation and mannitol are traditional but evidence is weak — don't lead with them.

##### Contrast-associated AKI

- Creatinine typically rises at **48–72 hours,** peaks at 3–5 days, usually recovers
- **Risk factors:** pre-existing CKD (the biggest), diabetes, heart failure, hypovolaemia, high contrast volume, age, myeloma
- **Prevention: IV isotonic crystalloid (sodium chloride 0.9%) pre- and post-procedure** is the mainstay; withhold nephrotoxics; use the lowest contrast volume. N-acetylcysteine and bicarbonate have largely fallen out of favour (PRESERVE trial showed no benefit) — worth knowing this has changed.
- **Note the shift in thinking:** the true attributable risk is now believed to be **smaller than** **historically taught** — never withhold a genuinely indicated CT for fear of contrast nephropathy.

##### Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS)

- **When:** after starting chemotherapy in **bulky, chemosensitive tumours** (high-grade lymphoma, ALL, leukaemias); can occur spontaneously

docs.title: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
docs.text:
##### The structured approach (use this framework in any AKI question)

- 1. **Assess and resuscitate — is this patient sick?**
- A–E; treat shock, hyperkalaemia, pulmonary oedema, sepsis first

- 2. **Determine the cause — pre-renal / intrinsic / post-renal**
- History (drugs! fluid losses! systemic symptoms!), fluid status examination, urinalysis, bloods, **ultrasound to exclude obstruction**
- **Immunology screen if intrinsic renal disease suspected** (ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, complement, myeloma screen) — don't miss the treatable, time-critical GNs
- 3. **Fluid management**
- **Hypovolaemic → fluid resuscitate.** Balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's/Plasma-Lyte) or

0.9% saline in **boluses (e.g. 250–500 mL) with reassessment after each.**
  - Avoid large-volume 0.9% saline — hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. Avoid

Hartmann's if hyperkalaemic (contains K⁺), though this is somewhat theoretical.
  - **Avoid starches** (increase AKI and mortality)
- **Fluid overloaded → diurese or dialyse.** Do not reflexively give fluid to every AKI —

###### fluid overload is itself harmful and increases mortality.

- **There is no role for "renal-dose dopamine" or routine furosemide to convert** **oliguric to non-oliguric AKI** — both are ineffective. Classic exam distractor.
- 4. **Stop the nephrotoxics; review every drug**
- **STOP:** NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, aminoglycosides, diuretics (if hypovolaemic), contrast
- **DOSE-ADJUST:** opioids, gabapentin, metformin (stop — lactic acidosis risk), DOACs,

LMWH, digoxin, many antibiotics
- **Sick day rules** — SADMANS-type medication holds during acute illness
- 5. **Treat the cause**
- Sepsis → antibiotics; obstruction → **catheter / nephrostomy;** GN → immunosuppression; hypercalcaemia/myeloma → specific treatment
- 6. **Monitor and support**
- Daily U&Es, fluid balance, **daily weights,** catheterise if urine output monitoring is critical
- Treat complications: hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload, anaemia, bleeding
- Nutrition; avoid hypoglycaemia

##### Indications for urgent dialysis — "AEIOU"

| Letter | Indication | Typical trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Acidosis | Severe metabolic acidosis, pH <7.1–7.2, refractory to medical therapy |
| E | Electrolytes | Refractory hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >6.5 mmol/L, or lower with ECG changes) not responding to medical management |
| I | Ingestion / Intoxication | Dialysable toxins: lithium, salicylates, methanol, ethylene glycol, valproate, metformin (severe lactic acidosis) |
| O | Overload | Pulmonary oedema refractory to diuretics |
| U | Uraemia | Symptomatic: uraemic pericarditis, uraemic encephalopathy, uraemic bleeding (platelet dysfunction), intractable nausea/vomiting |

Memory aid for dialysable toxins: **"I STUMBLED"** or simply remember small, water-soluble, low-protein-bound, low-volume-of-distribution drugs are dialysable — **lithium, methanol,** **ethylene glycol, salicylates** are the four to name.

**Key principle:** dialysis is indicated for **refractory** com

docs.text:
###### Question Answer

| Fastest way to exclude a reversible cause? | Renal ultrasound — obstruction |
| --- | --- |
| Pre-renal or ATN? | FeNa <1%, urine osm >500, bland urine = pre-renal. FeNa >1–2%, urine osm ~300, muddy-brown casts = ATN. If on diuretics, use FeUrea <35% |
| Dipstick blood +++, no RBCs on microscopy? | Rhabdomyolysis — check CK |
| Everything up except calcium, post-chemo? | Tumour lysis syndrome |
| AKI + cirrhosis + urine Na <10 + no response to albumin? | Hepatorenal syndrome — terlipressin + albumin |
| AKI + haemoptysis? | Pulmonary–renal syndrome — anti-GBM or ANCA vasculitis. Urgent immunology + biopsy. |
| AKI + new drug (PPI/NSAID/antibiotic) + rash + eosinophilia? | Acute interstitial nephritis — stop the drug, consider steroids |
| AKI post-angiogram + livedo + eosinophilia? | Cholesterol embolisation |
| When to dialyse urgently? | AEIOU |
| Does "renal-dose dopamine" work? | No. Neither does routine furosemide to boost urine output |

##### Sources

KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (2012; staging criteria and definitions); NICE guidance on AKI; Merck Manual Professional Edition (rhabdomyolysis, CK thresholds, AKI incidence); StatPearls; Kidney360 2023 review (FeNa/FeUrea); UCSF Hospital

Handbook and Osmosis (AEIOU dialysis indications — cutoffs quoted variously as pH <7.1 or

<7.2, and K⁺ >6.5, so both ranges are given). Where guidance has shifted since older textbooks (contrast nephropathy prophylaxis, N-acetylcysteine, renal-dose dopamine), the current position is stated and flagged.

RESPONSES TO  PERFUSION

- Systematic response to maintain CO: vascular tone,  contractility

- Renal graded response

- Maintaining GFR

  - Afferent arteriole relaxation

  - RAAS activation

  - Systemic (shock, splanchnic vasoconstriction, vasodilator) and impaired local mechanisms (renal injury, HTN, DM, RAAS blockade medications, nephrotoxic medications) will impair kidney’s ability to maintain GFR

- Turning off glomerular filtration (self-preservation response)

- ATN: temporary renal injury (delayed recovery)

- Cortical necrosis (irreversible injury)

- When all mechanisms overwhelmed, splanchnic vasoconstriction (gut/renal sacrificed to maintain central circulation)

| Definition | Sudden loss of renal function with a  BUN/creatinine and/or urine output (oliguria) |
|---|---|
| Aetiology | ![](notes/renal/images/nephrology-and-urology-anu/img011.jpg) |

| Presentation |  |

docs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
docs.text:
##### Definition

###### CKD = abnormalities of kidney structure or function, present for ≥3 months, with

**implications for health.** Either:
- **eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²,** OR
- **Markers of kidney damage** (albuminuria ACR ≥3 mg/mmol, urine sediment abnormalities, electrolyte abnormalities from tubular disorders, histological/structural abnormalities, or history of transplant)

The **≥3 months** criterion is what separates CKD from AKI — an isolated abnormal eGFR is not

CKD.

##### KDIGO classification — the "heat map" (CGA)

Staged by **Cause, GFR** category, and **Albuminuria** category. GFR and albuminuria together predict risk **better than either alone.**

###### G stages (eGFR mL/min/1.73 m²):

| Stag e | eGFR | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| G1 | ≥90 | Normal/high (only CKD if other damage marker present) |
| G2 | 60–89 | Mildly decreased (only CKD if other marker present) |
| G3a | 45–59 | Mild–moderate |
| G3b | 30–44 | Moderate–severe |
| G4 | 15–29 | Severe |
| G5 | <15 | Kidney failure |

###### A categories (ACR):

| Category | ACR (mg/mmol) | ACR (mg/g) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | <3 | <30 |
| A2 | 3–30 | 30–300 |
| A3 | >30 | >300 |

- The **heat map** (green → yellow → orange → red) combines G and A to grade risk of progression, cardiovascular events, and death. **A worse albuminuria category shifts a** **patient into a higher-risk box even at the same eGFR** — this is the whole point of the two-dimensional system.
- **G1–G2 require a damage marker to count as CKD;** an eGFR of 75 with no albuminuria/structural abnormality is not CKD.

##### Common causes

**Diabetes and hypertension are the two commonest** (together the majority of ESKD). Then:
- Glomerulonephritis (IgA the commonest primary GN)
- ADPKD
- Obstructive uropathy, reflux nephropathy
- Renovascular disease
- Chronic tubulointerstitial disease (drugs, e.g. lithium, analgesics)

docs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
docs.text:
##### Anaemia of CKD

- **Mechanism:** primarily **reduced EPO production** by peritubular fibroblasts; compounded by **absolute and functional iron deficiency,** uraemia-induced ↓ red cell survival, and blood loss.

- **Hepcidin** (raised in CKD due to reduced renal clearance and inflammation) blocks gut iron absorption and iron release from stores → **functional iron deficiency** (iron present but locked away).
- Typically **normochromic, normocytic.**
- **Management:** correct iron first (often **IV iron** in dialysis/non-dialysis CKD), then **erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs)** if still anaemic. Target Hb ~100–120 g/L — **do NOT normalise Hb** (higher targets increased stroke/CV events in trials, e.g. CHOIR,

TREAT).
- Newer: **HIF prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitors** (e.g. roxadustat) — oral agents that stimulate endogenous EPO; a recent addition worth naming.

##### CKD–Mineral and Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD)

The classic cascade — understand it as a chain reaction:
- 1. **↓ GFR → phosphate retention (hyperphosphataemia)**
- 2. **↓ 1α-hydroxylation → low calcitriol (active vitamin D)** → ↓ gut calcium absorption →

###### hypocalcaemia

- 3. **↑ FGF-23** (early — even before phosphate rises) suppresses calcitriol further
- 4. Hypocalcaemia + hyperphosphataemia + low calcitriol → **secondary** **hyperparathyroidism** (↑PTH, an appropriate compensatory response)
- 5. Chronic drive → **tertiary hyperparathyroidism** (autonomous PTH secretion, often with hypercalcaemia)
- **Consequences: renal osteodystrophy** (high-turnover osteitis fibrosa cystica from

↑PTH; or low-turnover adynamic bone disease), and **vascular/soft-tissue calcification** (a major driver of cardiovascular mortality).
- Memory hook: in CKD-MBD the phosphate is HIGH and calcium is LOW — the opposite of primary hyperparathyroidism.

##### Metabolic acidosis

- Failing kidneys can't excrete the daily acid load or regenerate bicarbonate → **normal-then-raised anion gap metabolic acidosis.**
- Accelerates bone demineralisation, muscle wasting, and CKD progression → treat with **oral sodium bicarbonate** when HCO₃⁻ is persistently low.

##### Hyperkalaemia

- Reduced excretion; worsened by RAAS blockade, which itself is protective — a therapeutic tension. Manage with dietary restriction and potassium binders rather than stopping renoprotective drugs where possible.

##### Cardiovascular disease

- **The leading cause of death in CKD** — patients are far more likely to die of CV disease than reach dialysis. CKD is an independent CV risk factor. Emphasise this in any exam answer on CKD complications.

##### Uraemic syndrome (advanced)

- **Pericarditis** (uraemic — a dialysis indication), **encephalopathy, peripheral** **neuropathy, pruritus, platelet dysfunction → bleeding** (despite normal platelet count/coagulation), nausea, restless legs, sexual dysfunction.

docs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
docs.text:
##### Blood pressure and RAAS blockade

- **ACE inhibitor or ARB** is first-line where there is **albuminuria** — reduces intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, slowing progression. Titrate to the maximum tolerated dose.
- **Expected:** a creatinine rise of **up to ~25–30%** (or eGFR fall up to ~25%) after starting is acceptable and does not warrant stopping — recheck in 1–2 weeks. A larger rise suggests **renovascular disease** → investigate.
- Do **not** routinely combine ACEi + ARB (increased hyperkalaemia/AKI, no benefit).
- BP target: individualised, generally **<130/80** with albuminuria (per KDIGO, aiming for

SBP <120 in selected patients using standardised measurement).

##### SGLT2 inhibitors — now standard of care ⚑ (major recent change)

- **Dapagliflozin/empagliflozin slow CKD progression and reduce CV events and** **mortality — WITH OR WITHOUT diabetes** (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY).
- **Initiation threshold has been lowered to eGFR ≥20 mL/min/1.73 m²;** once started, continue until dialysis/transplant.
- Expect a small **initial "dip" in eGFR** — this is haemodynamic and benign, analogous to

ACEi.
- Side effects: mycotic genital infections, small DKA risk (euglycaemic), volume depletion.

If a textbook lists SGLT2 inhibitors as glucose-lowering drugs only, it predates this evidence.

##### Non-steroidal MRA (finerenone) ⚑

- **Finerenone** (a **non-steroidal** MRA) reduces CKD progression and CV events in **type 2** **diabetic kidney disease** with albuminuria (FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD).
- Add on top of a RAS inhibitor when **eGFR ≥25, normal potassium, and persistent** **albuminuria (ACR ≥3 mg/mmol)** despite maximal RASi.

- **Main risk: hyperkalaemia** — monitor potassium. Differs from spironolactone/eplerenone (steroidal MRAs) in receptor selectivity and side-effect profile.

##### The "four pillars" of modern renoprotection (diabetic CKD)

RAS inhibitor + SGLT2 inhibitor + finerenone + glycaemic control (often with a **GLP-1 receptor** **agonist).** This layered approach is the current direction of travel.

##### CKD-MBD management

- **Dietary phosphate restriction** + **phosphate binders** (calcium-based, or non-calcium e.g. sevelamer/lanthanum to avoid calcium loading and vascular calcification)
- **Active vitamin D analogues** (alfacalcidol, calcitriol) for low calcitriol/secondary hyperparathyroidism
- **Calcimimetics** (cinacalcet) lower PTH by increasing calcium-sensing receptor sensitivity

— for secondary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism
- **Parathyroidectomy** for refractory tertiary hyperparathyroidism

##### Anaemia

- Iron (IV commonly) → ESAs; target homoglobin 100–120 g/L; don't over-correct.

##### Acidosis

- **Oral sodium bicarbonate** for persistent metabolic acidosis (also slows progression).

##### Other

- **Statin** for CV risk (atorvastatin 20 mg per NICE for most CKD)
- Lifestyle: smoking cessation, weight, salt restriction, exercise
- **Avoid nephrotoxins;** sick-day rules; vaccinate

##### Referral to neph

docs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
docs.text:
| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Is this CKD or AKI? | CKD if ≥3 months — small echogenic kidneys, anaemia, CKD-MBD, old bloods |
| What does the heat map add over eGFR alone? | Albuminuria (A category) independently predicts risk — a worse ACR moves you to a higher-risk box at the same eGFR |
| Calcium and phosphate in CKD-MBD? | Phosphate HIGH, calcium LOW, PTH HIGH, calcitriol LOW (opposite of primary hyperPTH) |
| Commonest cause of death in CKD? | Cardiovascular disease — not ESKD |
| Drug that slows CKD with or without diabetes? | SGLT2 inhibitor (eGFR ≥20) |
| Add-on for diabetic CKD with residual albuminuria? | Finerenone (watch potassium) |
| Acceptable creatinine rise after ACEi? | Up to ~25–30%; more → suspect renovascular disease |
| Anaemia of CKD — treat what first? | Iron before ESA; don't normalise Hb |

##### Sources

KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline (definition, classification, SGLT2i threshold); KDIGO 2022

Diabetes-in-CKD update and KDOQI/ADA 2024 commentary (SGLT2i eGFR ≥20; finerenone eGFR ≥25, ACR criteria); DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY, FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD trial reports; NICE NG203 (CKD). Where thresholds differ slightly between agents (e.g. dapagliflozin licensed from eGFR 25 in DAPA-CKD vs guideline ≥20 recommendation), both are noted.

---

docs.text:
##### Renal history — the symptom clusters that matter

| Symptom | What it points to |
| --- | --- |
| Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) / anuria | AKI; anuria specifically suggests obstruction, vascular catastrophe (renal artery/vein occlusion), or severe cortical necrosis — true anuria is not typical of ATN |
| Frothy urine | Nephrotic-range proteinuria (surfactant effect of protein) |
| Haematuria — visible vs non-visible | Visible + painless → think malignancy until proven otherwise. Visible + synpharyngitic (with sore throat) → IgA nephropathy. 1–2 weeks after throat/skin infection → post-streptococcal GN |
| Oedema | Nephrotic (periorbital, worse in morning) vs cardiac/hepatic (dependent, worse in evening) |
| Uraemic symptoms | Nausea, anorexia, metallic taste, pruritus, restless legs, confusion, hiccups — late; suggests advanced CKD/need for RRT |

##### Extra-renal clues (the "why is this a systemic disease?" screen)

- **Rash** — purpuric/vasculitic (ANCA vasculitis, IgA vasculitis/HSP), malar (SLE), livedo (cholesterol emboli)
- **Arthralgia** — SLE, vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemia
- **Haemoptysis** — **pulmonary–renal syndrome:** anti-GBM (Goodpasture) or ANCA vasculitis. This is the emergency pattern to recognise.
- **Sinusitis / nasal crusting / saddle nose** — **GPA (granulomatosis with polyangiitis)**

- **Asthma + eosinophilia** — **EGPA**
- **Sensorineural deafness** — **Alport syndrome** (also lenticonus)
- **Weight loss, bone pain, anaemia** — **myeloma**

##### Drug and exposure history (always ask)

- **NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, diuretics** — the "triple whammy" causing haemodynamic AKI
- **Aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin** — direct tubular toxicity
- **PPIs, penicillins, cephalosporins, allopurinol, NSAIDs** — acute interstitial nephritis
- **Lithium** — nephrogenic DI, chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis
- **Contrast** — recent CT/angiogram
- **Calcineurin inhibitors** (ciclosporin, tacrolimus) — in transplant patients
- Herbal/over-the-counter remedies, illicit drugs, protein/creatine supplements

##### Examination

**Fluid status assessment** (the single most examinable renal skill):
- Hypovolaemia: ↓skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, ↓JVP, postural drop, tachycardia, cool peripheries, prolonged cap refill, ↓urine output
- Hypervolaemia: ↑JVP, peripheral/sacral oedema, pulmonary crackles, S3 gallop, ascites,

↑weight
- Weight charts and fluid balance charts are more reliable than any single sign

###### Other renal-specific signs:

- **AV fistula** — inspect (scar, aneurysmal dilatation), palpate **(thrill),** auscultate **(bruit).**

Absent thrill/bruit = thrombosed fistula.
- **Transplant kidney** — palpable mass in the **iliac fossa** with an overlying hockey-stick scar (transplants are placed extraperitoneally in the iliac fossa, native kidneys usually left in situ)
- **Palpable kidneys** — bilateral, ballotable, irregular → **ADPKD.** Unilateral → tumour, hydronephrosis, compensatory hypertrophy
- **Renal bruits** — renal

docs.text:
##### Dipstick — interpretation and traps

| Finding | Interpretation | Traps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blood | Detects haem (haemoglobin peroxidase activity) | Positive with myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis) and free haemoglobin (haemolysis) — no RBCs on microscopy. Dipstick +ve blood but microscopy shows no red cells = pigment, not haematuria |
| Protein | Detects albumin mainly | Misses light chains (Bence-Jones protein) — a normal dipstick does NOT exclude myeloma. Also false +ve with concentrated urine, alkaline urine, contrast, chlorhexidine |
| Leucocytes/nitrite s | Suggests UTI | Nitrites: only Gram-negatives reduce nitrate → nitrite (false −ve with Enterococcus, Staph saprophyticus, and with frequent voiding). Sterile pyuria: TB, chlamydia, AIN, stones, treated UTI |
| Glucose | Glycosuria | If glucose in urine with normal blood glucose → proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome, SGLT2 inhibitor use) |

##### Urine microscopy — the casts (high-yield)

| Cast/finding | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Red cell casts + dysmorphic RBCs | Glomerulonephritis — pathognomonic of glomerular bleeding |
| White cell casts | Acute interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis |
| Granular / "muddy-brown" casts | Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) — sloughed tubular epithelium |
| Hyaline casts | Non-specific — concentrated urine, dehydration, exercise; can be normal |
| Fatty casts / "Maltese cross" under polarised light | Nephrotic syndrome (lipiduria) |
| Broad, waxy casts | Chronic kidney disease (formed in dilated, atrophic tubules) |
| Crystals | Uric acid (tumour lysis), calcium oxalate (ethylene glycol — envelope-shaped), cystine (hexagonal) |
| Eosinophiluria | Historically for AIN — poor sensitivity and specificity; no longer recommended to rely on it |

##### Reading it the other way — disease → expected urinalysis pattern

The casts table above works from finding to diagnosis. Exams more often hand you a disease (or a vignette) and expect you to predict the urine. Learn it in both directions.

| Condition | Dipstick | Microscopy | Protein quantification | Key discriminator |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-renal AKI | Bland (may be trace protein) | Hyaline casts only | Minimal | FeNa <1%, urine osm >500, concentrated urine |
| Acute tubular necrosis | Trace–1+ protein, ± blood | Muddy-brown granular casts, renal tubular epithelial cells | Mild (<1 g/day) | FeNa >1–2%, urine osm ~300 (isosthenuric) |
| Acute interstitial nephritis | Protein +, blood +, leucocytes +, nitrites −ve | White cell casts, sterile pyuria, ± eosinophiluria | Mild (usually <1 g/day) | Sterile pyuria + drug history (PPI, NSAID, penicillin, allopurinol); ± rash, fever, eosinophilia |
| Nephritic syndrome (any GN) | Blood +++, protein + to ++ | Red cell casts + dysmorphic RBCs | Sub-nephrotic (<3.5 g/day) | Red cell casts = glomerular bleeding; plus hypertension, oliguria, oedema |
| Nephrotic syndrome | Protein ++++, blood −ve/trace | Fatty casts, oval fat bodies, "Maltese crosses

docs.text:
##### eGFR equations

- **CKD-EPI 2021 (creatinine)** is the current standard — this is the **race-free refit,** recommended by the NKF/ASN Task Force after they concluded race is a **social, not** **biological, construct** and should not appear in eGFR equations.
- Compared with the old 2009 race-based equation: for the same creatinine, the 2021 equation gives a **lower eGFR in Black patients** and a **higher eGFR in non-Black** **patients.**
- **MDRD** is older and less accurate at higher GFRs — largely superseded.
- **Cockcroft–Gault** estimates creatinine clearance (not eGFR), uses actual body weight, and is still used for some **drug dosing** (e.g. DOACs) — worth knowing it's a different beast.

##### Limitations of eGFR — when it lies

- **Not valid in AKI / non-steady state.** eGFR assumes a stable creatinine. In rapidly rising creatinine, true GFR is far lower than the eGFR suggests (the equation lags behind reality).
- **Extremes of muscle mass:** overestimates GFR in the cachectic, elderly, amputees, and those with muscle-wasting disease; underestimates in bodybuilders and those on creatine supplements.
- **Diet:** vegan/low-protein diets lower creatinine; a large cooked-meat meal transiently raises it.
- **Not validated** in pregnancy, children, or acute illness.
- Indexed to **1.73 m² body surface area** — misleading at extremes of body size.

##### Cystatin C — when and why

- A protein produced by **all nucleated cells at a constant rate,** freely filtered — so it is **independent of muscle mass,** which is its main advantage.
- **Use it as a confirmatory test when creatinine is likely to be unreliable:** extremes of muscle mass, amputees, cirrhosis, malnutrition, or to confirm eGFR near a clinical decision threshold. NKF specifically suggests it for **eGFRcr 45–59 with ACR <30 mg/g** (i.e. is this really CKD?).
- The **CKD-EPI 2021 creatinine–cystatin C combined equation is the most accurate** of the available equations.

- **But cystatin C has its own confounders: smoking, obesity, inflammation, thyroid** **disorders, and corticosteroids** all affect it.

##### Creatinine pitfalls (drugs that raise creatinine without lowering GFR)

- **Trimethoprim, cimetidine, dolutegravir, cobicistat, fenofibrate, ritonavir** — these **block tubular secretion of creatinine,** producing a rise in serum creatinine with **no** **true fall in GFR.** Recognising this avoids an unnecessary AKI workup.
- Conversely, in advanced CKD, tubular secretion of creatinine means **creatinine** **clearance overestimates true GFR.**

docs.text:
##### Renal ultrasound — first-line

- **The key question: is there obstruction?** US is the first-line test to exclude post-renal

AKI (look for **hydronephrosis).** Do it within 24 hours in AKI of unknown cause.
- **Kidney size:**
  - **Small (<9 cm), echogenic, poor corticomedullary differentiation** → **chronic** disease (irreversible)
  - **Normal or enlarged** → acute process, or specific causes of large kidneys:

###### diabetic nephropathy (early), amyloid, HIV-associated nephropathy,

###### myeloma, ADPKD, infiltration

  - **Asymmetry (>1.5–2 cm difference)** → renovascular disease or unilateral pathology
- **Caveat:** hydronephrosis may be **absent** in early obstruction, volume depletion, or **retroperitoneal fibrosis/encasing malignancy** (the ureters are trapped and cannot dilate).

##### Other imaging

| Modality | Use |
| --- | --- |
| CT KUB (non-contrast) | Gold standard for renal stones — no contrast needed |
| CT with contrast | Renal masses, staging RCC. Weigh contrast-associated AKI risk |
| CT / MR angiography | Renal artery stenosis, vascular anatomy. MRA avoids iodinated contrast, but gadolinium is contraindicated in severe CKD (risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis) |
| DMSA | Static scan — renal cortical scarring and differential function (e.g. reflux nephropathy) |
| MAG3 | Dynamic scan — renal perfusion, drainage, and obstruction (± furosemide to assess drainage) |
| Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) | Vesicoureteric reflux in children |

Memory hook: **DMSA** = **Damage/scarring** (static); **MAG3** = **Movement/drainage** (dynamic).

##### Renal biopsy

###### Indications:

- Nephrotic syndrome in an adult (in children, presumed minimal change → trial steroids first, biopsy only if steroid-resistant)
- Nephritic syndrome / suspected glomerulonephritis / rapidly progressive GN
- AKI of unknown cause where pre-renal and post-renal have been excluded
- Unexplained CKD with normal-sized kidneys
- Systemic disease with renal involvement (SLE — the class determines treatment)
- Transplant dysfunction (to diagnose and classify rejection)

###### Contraindications:

- **Uncorrected bleeding diathesis / anticoagulation / thrombocytopenia** (the main one)
- **Uncontrolled hypertension**
- **Single functioning kidney** (relative — risk of losing the only kidney)
- **Small, shrunken kidneys** — will show end-stage fibrosis only; high risk, no useful answer
- Active UTI, hydronephrosis, uncooperative patient

###### Complications:

- **Bleeding** — the dominant risk: haematuria (visible in ~10%), perinephric haematoma, rarely requiring **transfusion, embolisation, or nephrectomy**
- **Arteriovenous fistula** formation
- Pain, infection, damage to adjacent organs
- Death (rare, <0.1%)

###### What the histology answers — always three modalities:

- 1. **Light microscopy** — architecture: proliferation, crescents, sclerosis, nodules, inflammation
- 2. **Immunofluorescence** — what is deposited and where: linear IgG (anti-GBM),

docs.h: Finals-study-2.pdf — Renal Notes, Section 6: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid-Base Disorders (pages 53-58)
docs.text: Cross-checked against UK Kidney Association hyperkalaemia guideline (2023), European hyponatraemia guidance, and standard texts. This is the single highest-yield section for data-interpretation questions — the algorithms below are what examiners build vignettes around.

docs.title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid-Base Disorders
docs.text:
Key principle: **sodium problems are water problems.** Serum sodium reflects water balance relative to sodium, not total body sodium. Volume status is assessed separately and clinically.

##### Hyponatraemia — the diagnostic algorithm

###### Step 1 — exclude the fakes:

- **Pseudohyponatraemia** (severe hyperlipidaemia/paraproteinaemia — normal measured osmolality)
- **Hyperosmolar hyponatraemia** (hyperglycaemia, mannitol — water pulled out of cells; correct sodium ~+2.4 mmol/L per 5.5 mmol/L glucose rise)

###### Step 2 — assess volume status (the pivot):

| Volume status | Urine Na | Causes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hypovolaemic | <20 (extra-renal loss) | D&V, burns, third-spacing, pancreatitis |
|  | >20 (renal loss) | Diuretics, Addison's, salt-wasting nephropathy, cerebral salt wasting |
| Euvolaemic | Variable (often >20) | SIADH, hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid deficiency, primary polydipsia, low solute intake |
| Hypervolaemic | <20 (usually) | Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome (↓ effective circulating volume); renal failure (>20) |

**Step 3 — urine osmolality:** <100 mOsm/kg → appropriate water excretion (primary polydipsia, beer potomania/low solute); >100 → ADH acting (inappropriately if euvolaemic → SIADH).

##### SIADH

- **Diagnostic criteria:** true **euvolaemia,** hyponatraemia with **low plasma osmolality,** **inappropriately concentrated urine (osm >100), urine Na >30,** normal thyroid/adrenal function, no diuretics.
- **Causes: CNS** (stroke, haemorrhage, meningitis), **pulmonary** (pneumonia, TB, small cell lung cancer), **malignancy** (SCLC — ectopic ADH), **drugs** (SSRIs, carbamazepine, chemotherapy), post-op/pain/nausea.
- **Management: fluid restriction** first-line; treat cause; **tolvaptan** (V2 antagonist) or demeclocycline in resistant cases; hypertonic saline only for severe symptoms.

##### Correction rates & osmotic demyelination

- **Correct slowly:** no more than **~8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours** (some guidance says ≤8 in high-risk).
- **Over-rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia → osmotic demyelination** **syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis)** — delayed quadriparesis, dysarthria, "locked-in", pseudobulbar palsy. Often irreversible. **This is the exam's favourite**

###### iatrogenic catastrophe.

- **Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia** (seizures, coma): **hypertonic (3%) saline** in small boluses — the exception where you act fast, but still cap the 24-hour rise.

##### Hypernatraemia and diabetes insipidus

- Hypernatraemia = **water deficit** relative to sodium (usually inadequate water intake ± losses). Causes: dehydration, DI, osmotic diuresis, hypertonic fluids.
- **Diabetes insipidus:** polyuria + polydipsia + dilute urine.
  - **Cranial DI** (↓ADH production): trauma, tumour, surgery, infiltration → **responds**

###### to desmopressin

  - **Nephrogenic DI** (ADH resistance): lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia →

###### does NOT respond to desmopressin

- **Water deprivation test:** urine

docs.title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid-Base Disorders
docs.text:
##### Hyperkalaemia

- **Causes:** reduced excretion **(AKI/CKD, hypoaldosteronism, ACEi/ARB/MRA, NSAIDs,** **trimethoprim, heparin),** transcellular shift **(acidosis, insulin deficiency/DKA,** **rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, digoxin toxicity, suxamethonium),** increased load, and **pseudohyperkalaemia** (haemolysed sample, thrombocytosis).
- **ECG changes (progressive — this order is examinable):**
  - 1. **Tall, tented T waves**
  - 2. Flattened/absent P waves, **PR prolongation**
  - 3. **Broad QRS**
  - 4. **"Sine wave"** → VF/asystole
- **Emergency management (K⁺ ≥6.5, or ≥6.0 with ECG changes):**
  - 1. **Protect the myocardium: IV calcium gluconate 10% 10–30 mL** (or calcium chloride) — onset minutes, lasts ~30–60 min, repeat if ECG changes persist.

Does **not** lower potassium.
  - 2. **Shift K⁺ into cells: insulin (10 units soluble) + 25 g glucose IV** (monitor for hypoglycaemia, continue glucose infusion if pre-treatment glucose <7); **nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg** as adjunct.
  - 3. **Remove K⁺ from body: sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC)** or patiromer (newer GI binders, now used acutely and chronically ⚑ — largely replacing calcium resonium, which is slow/ineffective acutely); **dialysis** if refractory.
- Bicarbonate is no longer recommended as a routine acute agent unless there is severe acidosis. If your notes still lead with "calcium resonium," that's outdated for acute management.

##### Hypokalaemia

- **Causes:** GI loss (D&V), renal loss **(diuretics** — the commonest, hyperaldosteronism,

RTA types 1&2, Bartter/Gitelman), transcellular shift **(insulin, β-agonists, alkalosis,** **refeeding),** poor intake.
- **ECG changes: flattened T waves, U waves,** ST depression, prolonged QT → risk of arrhythmia.
- **Magnesium: hypokalaemia is often refractory until magnesium is replaced** — low

Mg promotes renal potassium wasting. **Always check and replace magnesium.** A classic exam "why won't the potassium come up?" point.

docs.title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid-Base Disorders
docs.text:
##### Hypercalcaemia

- **Causes: primary hyperparathyroidism** and **malignancy** account for ~90% (bony metastases, PTHrP, myeloma); others: sarcoidosis (↑vitamin D), thiazides, thyrotoxicosis, immobility, milk-alkali.

- **Symptoms: "stones, bones, groans, moans"** (renal stones, bone pain, abdominal pain/constipation, psychiatric); polyuria, short QT.
- **Management: IV 0.9% saline rehydration** first-line; **bisphosphonates** for malignancy; treat cause. (Loop diuretics only once rehydrated and if overloaded — not routine.)

##### Hypocalcaemia

- **Causes:** CKD (low calcitriol), hypoparathyroidism (post-thyroidectomy), vitamin D deficiency, hypomagnesaemia, pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis.
- **Signs: Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs,** perioral tingling, tetany, **prolonged QT,** seizures.
- **Management:** calcium (IV for severe/symptomatic), vitamin D; **correct magnesium.**

##### Phosphate & magnesium

- **Hyperphosphataemia:** CKD, tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis → binds calcium.
- **Hypophosphataemia:** refeeding syndrome, Fanconi, DKA treatment, alcohol.
- **Hypomagnesaemia:** diuretics, PPIs, alcohol, diarrhoea, Gitelman → causes refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia.

docs.title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid-Base Disorders
docs.text:
##### Systematic ABG/VBG interpretation (do it in this order)

- 1. **pH** — acidaemia (<7.35) or alkalaemia (>7.45)?
- 2. **Primary disorder** — is CO₂ or HCO₃⁻ the driver? (Respiratory if CO₂ deranged in the same direction as pH; metabolic if HCO₃⁻ is.)
- 3. **Compensation** — appropriate or is there a second disorder?
- 4. **Anion gap** (if metabolic acidosis)
- 5. **Delta ratio** (if raised anion gap)

##### Anion gap

**Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻);** normal ~8–12 mmol/L (correct for albumin — a low albumin lowers the measured gap).

| Raised anion gap metabolic acidosis (MUDPILES / KULT) | Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) |
| --- | --- |
| Methanol, Uraemia, DKA, Propylene glycol/paraldehyde, Iron/isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates | Diarrhoea (GI HCO₃⁻ loss), RTA, Addison's, acetazolamide, ureteric diversion, saline overload |

##### Osmolar gap and toxic alcohols

- **Osmolar gap = measured − calculated osmolality** (calculated = 2×Na + glucose + urea). Raised (>10) → unmeasured osmoles.
- **Raised anion gap acidosis + raised osmolar gap → toxic alcohol (methanol,** **ethylene glycol)** until proven otherwise. Ethylene glycol → **calcium oxalate crystals** +

AKI. Treat with **fomepizole** (or ethanol) ± dialysis.

##### Delta ratio (in raised anion gap acidosis)

**Δ ratio = (rise in anion gap) / (fall in HCO₃⁻)**
- **<1** → additional **normal anion gap acidosis**
- **1–2** → pure high anion gap acidosis
- **>2** → coexisting **metabolic alkalosis** or pre-existing high HCO₃⁻ (e.g. chronic respiratory acidosis)

##### Metabolic alkalosis

- **Chloride-responsive (urine Cl⁻ <20): vomiting/NG loss, diuretics** — corrects with saline.
- **Chloride-resistant (urine Cl⁻ >20): hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's,**

**Bartter/Gitelman, severe hypokalaemia** — doesn't correct with saline.

##### Compensation rules (quick reference)

- **Metabolic acidosis:** expected CO₂ = **(1.5 × HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2** (Winter's formula)
- **Metabolic alkalosis:** CO₂ rises ~0.7 mmHg per 1 mmol/L rise in HCO₃⁻
- **Acute respiratory:** HCO₃⁻ changes ~1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg CO₂ change; **chronic:**

~4–5 mmol/L per 10 mmHg (renal compensation takes days)
- If compensation is outside the expected range, there is a **second (mixed) disorder.**

docs.title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid-Base Disorders
docs.text:
| Clue | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Hyponatraemia, euvolaemic, urine osm >100, urine Na >30 | SIADH (fluid restrict) |
| Delayed quadriparesis after fast Na correction | Osmotic demyelination — correct ≤8–10 mmol/L/24h |
| Polyuria, dilute urine, responds to desmopressin | Cranial DI (vs nephrogenic = no response) |
| Tall tented T waves | Hyperkalaemia — calcium first |
| Potassium won't correct | Check and replace magnesium |
| Raised anion gap + raised osmolar gap | Toxic alcohol (methanol/ethylene glycol) |
| Normal anion gap acidosis | Diarrhoea or RTA (urine anion gap separates them) |
| Metabolic alkalosis, urine Cl <20 | Chloride-responsive — vomiting/diuretics, give saline |

##### Sources

UK Kidney Association Clinical Practice Guideline: Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults

(2023); NHS trust hyperkalaemia protocols (calcium gluconate/insulin-glucose/salbutamol dosing); European/US hyponatraemia guidance (correction limits, ODS); StatPearls and standard texts (acid–base, anion gap, calcium). Sodium correction limits are quoted slightly differently between guidelines (≤8 vs ≤10 mmol/L/24h in high-risk patients) — the conservative figure is highlighted. Acute potassium-binder practice (SZC) reflects current UK/NHS use, a change from older calcium-resonium-led algorithms.

- Underlying cause

- Saline resistant metabolic alkalosis: remove source of aldosterone or glucocorticoid ± spironolactone
