docs.text:
Cross-checked against KDIGO 2021 Glomerular Diseases guideline and KDIGO 2025

IgAN/IgAV guideline, Robbins, and standard texts. This is the heaviest conceptual section — organise every answer around the nephrotic vs nephritic split.

docs.title: Glomerular Disease
docs.text:
##### Nephrotic vs nephritic — the discriminating framework

|  | Nephrotic | Nephritic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core lesion | Podocyte injury → leaky barrier | Inflammation → glomerular breaks + hypercellularity |
| Proteinuria | Heavy (>3.5 g/day) | Mild–moderate (<3.5 g/day) |
| Haematuria | Absent/minimal | Present — red cell casts, dysmorphic RBCs |
| Albumin | Hypoalbuminaemia | Usually preserved |
| Oedema | Marked | Mild–moderate |
| Blood pressure | Usually normal | Hypertension |
| Renal function | Often preserved initially | Often impaired (↑creatinine, oliguria) |
| Other | Hyperlipidaemia, thrombophilia | — |

Mnemonic: **nephr-O-tic = prOtein; nephr-I-tic = Inflammation/hematurIa.**
- **RPGN (rapidly progressive GN)** — nephritic picture with a **rapid loss of renal** **function over days–weeks;** histology shows **crescents.** The nephrological emergency.

Causes group into three:
  - 1. **Anti-GBM** (linear IF)

- 2. **Immune complex** (granular IF — lupus, IgA, post-infectious)
  - 3. **Pauci-immune** (scanty IF — **ANCA vasculitis)**
- Overlap syndromes exist (e.g. membranoproliferative, diffuse proliferative lupus can show both nephrotic and nephritic features).

docs.title: Glomerular Disease
docs.text:
Definition triad: heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) + hypoalbuminaemia + oedema (± hyperlipidaemia). LM- Light microscopy, IF- immunoflorescence, EM- electron microscopy.

| Disease | Key features | Histology (LM / IF / EM) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal change disease | Commonest in children; steroid-responsive; can follow URTI/Hodgkin; adults too | LM normal; IF negative; EM podocyte foot process effacement |
| FSGS | Commonest primary nephrotic cause in adults (esp. Black patients); primary (permeability factor) vs secondary (HIV, obesity, reflux, heroin, sickle cell); often steroid-resistant | LM focal & segmental sclerosis; IF ±nonspecific; EM foot process effacement |
| Membranous nephropathy | Commonest primary nephrotic in older White adults; anti-PLA2R antibodies (~70% of primary); secondary: malignancy (solid tumours), SLE (class V), hepatitis B, drugs (gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs) | LM thickened GBM, "spikes"; IF granular subepithelial IgG/C3; EM subepithelial deposits |
| Diabetic nephropathy | Commonest cause of ESKD overall; progresses albuminuria → nephrotic → decline; usually with retinopathy | Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules, mesangial expansion, GBM thickening |
| Amyloidosis / light chain deposition | Older patients; myeloma/chronic inflammation; Congo red → apple-green birefringence under polarised light | Amorphous deposits; AL (light chain) or AA (serum amyloid A) |

###### Complications of nephrotic syndrome (the "why it's dangerous" list):

- **Thromboembolism** (loss of antithrombin III, etc.) — **renal vein thrombosis** classically in membranous; VTE, PE. Consider anticoagulation if albumin is very low.

- **Infection** (urinary loss of immunoglobulins/complement) — esp. encapsulated organisms
- **Hyperlipidaemia** (hepatic compensation)
- **Oedema** — manage with salt/fluid restriction + loop diuretics; treat the underlying cause and reduce proteinuria (RAS blockade)

docs.title: Glomerular Disease
docs.text:
| Disease | Key features | Complement | Discriminator |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IgA nephropathy | Commonest primary GN worldwide; young adult; visible haematuria 1–2 days after URTI (synpharyngitic) | Normal | Mesangial IgA on IF |
| IgA vasculitis (HSP) | Children; palpable purpura (buttocks/legs) + arthralgia + abdominal pain + nephritis | Normal | Systemic IgA vasculitis |
| Post-streptococcal GN | Child, 1–2 weeks after throat/skin strep; oedema, hypertension, smoky urine; usually self-limiting | LOW C3 | ↑ASOT/anti-DNas e B; subepithelial "humps" on EM |
| Anti-GBM (Goodpasture) | Pulmonary–renal syndrome (haemoptysis + RPGN); antibodies to type IV collagen | Normal | Linear IgG on IF; anti-GBM antibodies |
| ANCA vasculitis | GPA (c-ANCA/anti-PR3, sinus/lung/kidney), MPA (p-ANCA/anti-MPO), EGPA (asthma, eosinophilia); RPGN | Normal | Pauci-immune on IF; ANCA positive |
| Lupus nephritis | Young woman, multisystem; ANA/anti-dsDNA positive | LOW C3 AND C4 | "Full house" IF (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q); class I–VI |
| Membranoproliferative GN / C3 glomerulopathy | Mixed nephrotic/nephritic; hepatitis C/cryoglobulins (immune-complex type) or complement dysregulation (C3 type) | LOW C3 | "Tram-track" GBM double contour |
| Cryoglobulinaemia | Often hepatitis C; purpura, arthralgia, neuropathy | Low C4 | Cryoglobulins |

**Low-complement GNs — memorise the list** (a favourite exam shortcut):
- **Post-streptococcal GN** (low C3)
- **Lupus nephritis** (low C3 **and** C4)
- **Membranoproliferative GN / C3 glomerulopathy** (low C3)
- **Cryoglobulinaemia** (low C4)
- IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM, and ANCA vasculitis are **normal-complement** — this distinction alone often cracks an SBA.

###### Lupus nephritis classes (ISN/RPS) — why the class matters:

- Class **I–II** (minimal/mesangial): supportive.
- Class **III–IV** (focal/diffuse proliferative): the aggressive forms — **immunosuppression** (steroids + mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide; belimumab/voclosporin add-on).

Biopsy class **directs treatment** — that's why every lupus nephritis patient is biopsied.
- Class **V** (membranous): nephrotic picture.
- Class **VI:** advanced sclerosis.

###### Treatment headlines:

- **ANCA vasculitis / anti-GBM:** urgent **immunosuppression** — high-dose steroids + **rituximab or cyclophosphamide; plasma exchange** for anti-GBM (and severe ANCA with pulmonary haemorrhage/dialysis-dependence). Anti-GBM is a **"treat now, biopsy** **confirms" emergency** — delay costs nephrons.
- **IgA nephropathy** ⚑ (updated 2025): **RAS blockade + SGLT2 inhibitor** as supportive backbone; **targeted-release budesonide (Nefecon)** for those at risk of progression; **sparsentan** (dual endothelin/angiotensin receptor antagonist) as an option. Systemic steroids are now used more cautiously given toxicity. If your notes only say "IgA = ACEi

± fish oil," they predate this.

docs.title: Glomerular Disease
docs.text:
| Disease | Genetics | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alport syndrome | Usually X-linked (COL4A5) — type IV collagen defect | Haematuria + progressive renal failure + sensorineural deafness + ocular (lenticonus); "basket-weave" GBM on EM |
| Thin basement membrane disease (benign familial haematuria) | AD, COL4A3/4 | Persistent isolated haematuria, benign course, normal function — the important "don't over-investigate" differential |

docs.title: Glomerular Disease
docs.text:
##### The immunology screen (know what each tests for)

- **ANA, anti-dsDNA** → SLE
- **ANCA (PR3/MPO)** → ANCA vasculitis
- **Anti-GBM** → Goodpasture
- **Complement C3/C4** → low in the GNs listed above
- **Anti-PLA2R** → primary membranous nephropathy
- **Cryoglobulins** → cryoglobulinaemia (send warm)
- **Hepatitis B/C, HIV serology** → secondary causes
- **Serum free light chains / electrophoresis / urine Bence-Jones** → myeloma/amyloid
- **ASOT / anti-DNase B** → recent streptococcal infection

##### Histology — always three modalities (the biopsy answers all three)

- 1. **Light microscopy** — pattern of injury (proliferation, crescents, sclerosis, nodules, thickening)
- 2. **Immunofluorescence** — what and where: **linear** (anti-GBM), **granular** (immune complex), **mesangial IgA** (IgAN), **full house** (lupus), **pauci-immune** (ANCA)
- 3. **Electron microscopy** — deposit location **(subepithelial** = membranous/PSGN humps; **subendothelial** = lupus/MPGN; **mesangial** = IgA) and foot process effacement (minimal change)

docs.title: Glomerular Disease
docs.text:
| Clue | Diagnosis |
| --- | --- |
| Child, nephrotic, steroid-responsive | Minimal change disease |
| Older adult, nephrotic, anti-PLA2R +ve | Membranous nephropathy |
| Haematuria during a sore throat | IgA nephropathy |
| Haematuria 1–2 weeks after infection, low C3 | Post-streptococcal GN |
| Haemoptysis + AKI, linear IF | Anti-GBM (Goodpasture) |
| Sinusitis + lung nodules + AKI, c-ANCA | GPA (ANCA vasculitis) |
| "Full house" IF, low C3 and C4 | Lupus nephritis |
| Purpura on legs + abdominal pain + nephritis in a child | IgA vasculitis (HSP) |
| Haematuria + deafness + family history | Alport syndrome |
| Isolated persistent haematuria, benign | Thin basement membrane disease |

##### Sources

KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases; KDIGO

2025 IgAN/IgAV guideline (Nefecon, sparsentan, SGLT2i positioning); Robbins & Cotran

Pathologic Basis of Disease; StatPearls. Antibody/complement associations cross-checked across guideline and textbook sources.

docs.title: Renal Anatomy
docs.text:
| Cell | Location | Function | Active agents / molecules | Clinical correlate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Endothelial cells | Innermost layer, lining glomerular capillaries | Fenestrated (70–100 nm pores) → high water/solute permeability but hold back cells; glycocalyx adds negative charge | Produce nitric oxide and tendothelin; respond to podocyte-deri ved VEGF; negatively charged glycocalyx | Endothelial injury = thrombotic microangiopathy (HUS/TTP, pre-eclampsia) |
| Podocytes (visceral epithelial cells) | Outermost layer; foot processes (pedicels) wrap the capillaries | Form the slit diaphragm — the final size/charge barrier; synthesise and maintain the GBM; structural support; secrete VEGF to sustain the endothelium | Nephrin, podocin (slit diaphragm proteins); VEGF; the PLA2R antigen sits on podocytes | Foot process effacement → minimal change/nephrotic; anti-PLA2R → membranous; can't proliferate → injury drives FSGS/glomeruloscl erosis |
| Mesangial cells (intraglomeru lar) | Central, between capillary loops | Structural support of the tuft; contractile — adjust capillary surface area and hence GFR; phagocytic — clear trapped macromolecules/i mmune complexes; lay down mesangial matrix | Contract in response to angiotensin II; relax to ANP; secrete cytokines and prostaglandins | Mesangial expansion (diabetic nephropathy, Kimmelstiel–Wilson); mesangial IgA deposits (IgA nephropathy); proliferation in MPGN |
| Parietal epithelial cells | Line the outer wall of Bowman's capsule | Form Bowman's capsule (simple squamous); act as a podocyte progenitor/stem- cell reservoir | — | Proliferate to form crescents in rapidly progressive (crescentic) GN |

docs.title: Renal Anatomy
docs.text:

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Juxtaglomerula r (granular) cells | Modified smooth muscle in the afferent arteriole wall | Synthesise, store, and release renin; act as an intrarenal baroreceptor (sense afferent pressure) | Secrete renin; stimulated by ↓ perfusion pressure, β1-sympathetic input, and signals from the macula densa | The trigger point of RAAS; renin ↑ in renal artery stenosis |
| Macula densa cells | Specialised cells of the thick ascending limb / early DCT where it touches its own glomerulus | Chemoreceptor — sense luminal NaCl via NKCC2; drive tubuloglomerular feedback and modulate renin release | Sensing ↑ NaCl → release adenosine/ATP (→ afferent constriction, ↓GFR); ↓ NaCl → prostaglandins/N O (→ renin release) | Why loop diuretics (block NKCC2 at the macula densa) stimulate renin; basis of tubuloglomerular feedback |
| Extraglomerular mesangial cells (Lacis / Goormaghtigh cells) | The triangle between afferent arteriole, efferent arteriole, and macula densa | Relay signals between the macula densa and the granular cells/arterioles via gap junctions; may contribute to renin secretion | Gap-junction signalling | Complete the JGA feedback circuit |

docs.h: Finals-study-2.pdf — Renal Notes, Section 11: Exam Preparation and Applied Skills (pages 83-86)
docs.parent: Renal Exam Preparation and Applied Skills
docs.text: This section is applied practice rather than new content — it ties the earlier sections into the formats finals actually test: data interpretation, OSCE stations, and emergency scenarios.

docs.title: Renal Exam Preparation and Applied Skills
docs.parent: Renal Exam Preparation and Applied Skills
docs.text:
##### U&Es — pattern recognition

- **Urea:creatinine ratio:**
  - **High urea:creatinine (disproportionate urea)** → **pre-renal** (dehydration, GI bleed, high catabolic state) — urea is reabsorbed with water
  - **Proportionate rise** → intrinsic renal
- **AKI vs CKD on bloods:** CKD suggested by **anaemia, hyperphosphataemia,** **hypocalcaemia, raised PTH,** and (crucially) **old bloods** showing chronicity.
- **Hyperkalaemia + normal anion gap acidosis + diabetic** → think **type 4 RTA.**

##### ABG/VBG — the drill (always the same 5 steps)

- 1. pH → acidaemia/alkalaemia
- 2. Primary driver → respiratory (CO₂) or metabolic (HCO₃⁻)?
- 3. Compensation appropriate? (Winter's formula for metabolic acidosis: expected CO₂ =

1.5×HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2)
- 4. **Anion gap** (Na − [Cl + HCO₃⁻]); if raised → **MUDPILES**
- 5. **Delta ratio** and **osmolar gap** if indicated (mixed disorders, toxic alcohols)

##### Urinalysis panels — the discriminators (from Section 1)

- **Red cell casts + dysmorphic RBCs** → glomerulonephritis
- **Muddy-brown granular casts** → ATN
- **White cell casts + sterile pyuria** → AIN/pyelonephritis
- **Dipstick blood +ve, no RBCs** → rhabdomyolysis (myoglobin)
- **Dipstick protein −ve but heavy proteinuria** → light chains (myeloma)

##### Renal immunology panels

- **Low C3 only** → post-strep GN, C3 glomerulopathy/MPGN

- **Low C3 AND C4** → lupus nephritis, cryoglobulinaemia
- **Normal complement + pauci-immune** → ANCA vasculitis
- **Linear IF / anti-GBM** → Goodpasture
- **Anti-PLA2R** → primary membranous

##### Common traps built into questions

- A "normal" creatinine in **pregnancy** or a **muscular/cachectic** patient may hide real dysfunction
- **Trimethoprim/cimetidine** raising creatinine without true GFR change
- **Pseudohyponatraemia/hyperkalaemia** (lab artefact)
- **FeNa unreliable on diuretics** → use FeUrea
- Correcting sodium for **hyperglycaemia** before calling it true hyponatraemia

docs.title: Renal Exam Preparation and Applied Skills
docs.parent: Renal Exam Preparation and Applied Skills
docs.text:
##### Fluid status examination (rehearse a slick routine)

- **General:** comfortable/breathless, weight/fluid charts
- **Hypovolaemia:** dry mucous membranes, ↓skin turgor, ↓JVP, postural drop, tachycardia, cool peripheries, prolonged cap refill, low urine output
- **Hypervolaemia:** ↑JVP, peripheral/sacral oedema, lung crackles, S3, ascites
- **Always:** capillary refill, pulse, BP (lying/standing), JVP, oedema, chest, fluid balance chart, weights

##### Examining dialysis access / transplant

- **Fistula: look** (scar, aneurysm, skin changes), **feel** (thrill, warmth), **listen** (machinery bruit); comment you would **never cannulate/BP that arm**
- **Transplant: iliac fossa mass** with **hockey-stick scar;** palpate for tenderness (rejection/infection), auscultate for bruit; look for immunosuppression side effects (cushingoid, gum hypertrophy, skin lesions)

##### Counselling stations (structure: ICE → explain → check understanding → safety-net)

- **Starting dialysis:** modalities (HD vs PD), access, lifestyle impact, conservative option
- **Transplant options:** living vs deceased donor, work-up, immunosuppression and its risks
- **CKD diagnosis:** what it means, progression, modifiable factors, why BP/proteinuria control matters
- **Nephrotoxic drug avoidance:** NSAIDs, sick-day rules, over-the-counter awareness

- **Breaking bad news** (renal failure): **SPIKES** framework — Setting, Perception, Invitation,

Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy/Summary

##### Prescribing station

- **IV fluids:** choose fluid and rate for the volume state; balanced crystalloid for resuscitation; reassess
- **Hyperkalaemia:** the emergency algorithm (calcium → insulin/glucose → salbutamol → definitive removal) — see below

docs.title: Renal Exam Preparation and Applied Skills
docs.parent: Renal Exam Preparation and Applied Skills
docs.text:
##### Hyperkalaemia (the commonest renal emergency)

- 1. **ECG + cardiac monitor;** assess severity
- 2. **IV calcium gluconate 10% (10–30 mL)** if ECG changes — stabilises myocardium (repeat if changes persist)
- 3. **Insulin (10 units) + 25 g glucose IV** — shifts K⁺ into cells (monitor for hypoglycaemia)
- 4. **Nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg** — adjunct shift
- 5. **Remove K⁺:** sodium zirconium cyclosilicate/patiromer; **dialysis if refractory**
- 6. **Stop** contributing drugs (ACEi/ARB, K⁺-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs); treat the cause

##### AKI with fluid overload / pulmonary oedema

- Sit up, high-flow oxygen; **IV loop diuretic** (furosemide); consider **GTN** if hypertensive;

**CPAP** if severe; **urgent dialysis/ultrafiltration** if refractory (the "O" of AEIOU)

##### Severe hyponatraemia (symptomatic — seizures/coma)

- **Hypertonic (3%) saline** in small boluses to raise sodium a few mmol/L and control symptoms
- **Cap the rise at ≤8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours** to avoid **osmotic demyelination**
- Identify and treat the cause; involve seniors early

##### Obstructed, infected kidney (urological emergency)

- **Fever + obstruction (hydronephrosis) = emergency** → **resuscitate, antibiotics, and** **urgent decompression (nephrostomy or ureteric stent)** — do not wait to remove the stone

##### Rhabdomyolysis

- **Early aggressive IV fluid resuscitation** (the key intervention); treat **hyperkalaemia;** monitor CK, U&Es, calcium; watch for **compartment syndrome** and the **polyuric**

###### recovery phase

docs.title: Renal Exam Preparation and Applied Skills
docs.parent: Renal Exam Preparation and Applied Skills
docs.text:
- **AKI:** pre/intrinsic/post; KDIGO staging; **AEIOU** dialysis indications; stop nephrotoxics;

US to exclude obstruction
- **Hyperkalaemia:** ECG → calcium → insulin/glucose → salbutamol → remove
- **CKD:** heat map; complications (anaemia, CKD-MBD, CV death); **RAS + SGLT2i +**

###### finerenone

- **Nephrotic vs nephritic:** protein vs blood/casts; low-complement GN list
- **Hyponatraemia:** volume status → urine Na/osm → correct slowly (ODS)
- **Acid–base:** 5-step drill; MUDPILES; osmolar gap for toxic alcohols
- **Diuretics:** site of action; loops lose calcium, thiazides retain
- **Casts:** RBC = GN, muddy-brown = ATN, WBC = AIN
- **Transplant:** rejection timing; CNI toxicity mimics rejection; CMV/BK/skin cancer

##### Sources

This section synthesises the earlier evidence-based sections (each individually cross-checked) into exam formats; no new factual claims beyond those already sourced. Frameworks (SPIKES,

Winter's formula, the hyperkalaemia algorithm, MUDPILES) are standard teaching aids.

docs.title: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease
docs.h: Finals-study-2.pdf — Renal Notes, Section 9: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease (pages 72-75)
docs.text: Cross-checked against Robbins, StatPearls, KDIGO, and standard texts. Much of this cross-references earlier sections — the value here is seeing the systemic disease as the organising principle.

docs.title: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease
docs.text:
- **The commonest cause of ESKD worldwide.**
- **Natural history:** glomerular hyperfiltration → **microalbuminuria (A2)** → **overt** **proteinuria (A3/nephrotic)** → declining GFR → ESKD.
- **Histology:** mesangial expansion, GBM thickening, **Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules,** hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
- **Screening:** annual **ACR** + eGFR in all diabetics. **Retinopathy usually coexists** — its absence in a diabetic with nephropathy should prompt suspicion of an alternative diagnosis.
- **Management:** glycaemic + BP control, **RAS blockade, SGLT2 inhibitors, finerenone,**

GLP-1 agonists (the "four pillars" — see Section 3).

docs.title: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease
docs.text:
- **Hypertensive nephrosclerosis:** chronic hypertension → arteriolar thickening, ischaemia, glomerulosclerosis → slowly progressive CKD (second commonest cause of

ESKD). Small kidneys, modest proteinuria.
- **Renal artery stenosis: atherosclerotic** (older, vascular disease) or **fibromuscular** **dysplasia** (young women, "string of beads" on angiography).
  - Clues: **resistant hypertension, flash pulmonary oedema, AKI after starting**

**ACEi/ARB,** asymmetric kidneys, renal bruit.
  - Investigate with **duplex US, CT/MR angiography.** Revascularisation (angioplasty/stent) reserved for selected cases (trials e.g. CORAL/ASTRAL showed limited benefit over medical therapy for atherosclerotic disease).

docs.title: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease
docs.text:
- Multiple mechanisms — **know all four:**

- 1. **Cast nephropathy ("myeloma kidney")** — filtered **light chains** precipitate with

Tamm-Horsfall protein → tubular obstruction (the commonest, causes AKI)
  - 2. **Hypercalcaemia** → dehydration, vasoconstriction, nephrocalcinosis
  - 3. **AL amyloidosis** → nephrotic syndrome
  - 4. **Light chain deposition disease,** and hyperuricaemia
- **Red flags:** AKI/CKD + **anaemia + bone pain + hypercalcaemia + raised ESR;** **dipstick misses light chains** — send **serum free light chains, serum/urine** **electrophoresis.**
- Management: treat myeloma, aggressive hydration, treat hypercalcaemia.

docs.title: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease
docs.text:
- **ANCA vasculitis** (GPA/MPA/EGPA), **anti-GBM, SLE (lupus nephritis),** **cryoglobulinaemia** — all covered in Section 4. The renal presentation is usually **nephritic/RPGN;** treat with immunosuppression.
- **Scleroderma renal crisis: acute severe hypertension + AKI + microangiopathic** **haemolysis** in systemic sclerosis → treat urgently with **ACE inhibitors** (the one scenario where ACEi is the treatment for a hypertensive/renal emergency).

docs.title: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease
docs.text:
Triad: **microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA) + thrombocytopenia + organ (renal)** **injury;** blood film shows **schistocytes;** ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, negative Coombs.

|  | HUS (typical) | Atypical HUS | TTP |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cause | Shiga-toxin E. coli O157 (post-bloody diarrhoea) | Complement dysregulation | ADAMTS13 deficiency (auto-antibody or inherited) |
| Predominant organ | Kidney (AKI) | Kidney | Neurological + renal |
| Classic group | Children | Any | Adults |
| Treatment | Supportive (avoid antibiotics in STEC) | Eculizumab (anti-C5) ⚑ | Plasma exchange (urgent) ± steroids, rituximab, caplacizumab |

- **Don't give platelets in TTP** (fuels thrombosis) unless life-threatening bleeding.
- **Pentad of TTP** (fever, MAHA, thrombocytopenia, renal, neuro) — but full pentad is uncommon; treat on the triad.

docs.title: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease
docs.text: - **Hypercalcaemia/hypercalciuria** (macrophage 1α-hydroxylase → ↑calcitriol) → stones, nephrocalcinosis; **granulomatous interstitial nephritis.** Responds to **corticosteroids.**

docs.title: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease
docs.text:
- **Physiological changes:** GFR rises ~50%, so **creatinine falls** (a "normal" non-pregnant creatinine may be abnormal in pregnancy); increased renal size, physiological hydronephrosis (right > left).
- **Pre-eclampsia:** >20 weeks, **hypertension + proteinuria** ± end-organ features; podocyte injury; risk of eclampsia, HELLP; definitive treatment is **delivery.**
- **AKI in pregnancy:** pre-eclampsia/HELLP, **acute fatty liver of pregnancy,** TMA (pregnancy-associated aHUS), sepsis, haemorrhage.

docs.title: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease
docs.text: - Medullary hypoxia/sickling → **papillary necrosis, impaired concentrating ability** **(hyposthenuria), haematuria,** and later FSGS/proteinuria and CKD.

docs.title: Renal Involvement in Systemic Disease
docs.text:
- Classically a **collapsing FSGS** → heavy proteinuria, rapid progression; commoner in patients of African ancestry **(APOL1** risk variants); **large echogenic kidneys.** Treat the

HIV (antiretrovirals) — cornerstone.

docs.text:

docs.title: Renal Pharmacology and Prescribing
docs.text:
| Class | Site & target | Main uses | Key side effects / electrolytes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Loop (furosemide, bumetanide) | Thick ascending limb — NKCC2 | Fluid overload (HF, pulmonary oedema, CKD, nephrotic); the most powerful | Hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypovolaemia, ototoxicity, gout |
| Thiazide (bendroflumethiazide, indapamide) | Distal convoluted tubule — NCC | Hypertension, mild oedema | Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperCALCaemia, hyperuricaemia (gout), hyperglycaemia, hyperlipidaemia |
| Potassium-sparing — ENaC blockers (amiloride, triamterene) | Collecting duct — ENaC | With loops/thiazides to spare potassium; Liddle | Hyperkalaemia |
| Aldosterone antagonists (MRA) (spironolactone, eplerenone) | Collecting duct — aldosterone receptor | Heart failure, ascites, resistant HTN, hyperaldosteronism | Hyperkalaemia; spironolactone → gynaecomastia (eplerenone doesn't) |
| Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide) | Proximal tubule — carbonic anhydrase | Glaucoma, altitude sickness, alkalinisation | Metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia |
| Osmotic (mannitol) | Proximal tubule/loop (osmotic) | Raised ICP, glaucoma | Pulmonary oedema, hyponatraemia then hypernatraemia |

Memory hook — the calcium split: **Loops Lose calcium** (hypoCALCaemia), **thiazides reTain** **calcium** (hyperCALCaemia). This is why thiazides help calcium stones and loops don't.
- **Diuretic resistance:** inadequate response to loops in HF/CKD/nephrotic. Causes: poor absorption/oedematous gut, hypoalbuminaemia, RAAS activation, distal nephron hypertrophy.
- **Sequential nephron blockade:** add a **thiazide (e.g. metolazone) to a loop** to block the compensatory distal sodium reabsorption — potent, but **high risk of profound** **hypokalaemia/hypovolaemia;** monitor closely.

docs.title: Renal Pharmacology and Prescribing
docs.text:
| Class | Example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ACE inhibitors | ramipril, lisinopril | ↓Ang II; dry cough (bradykinin), angioedema, hyperkalaemia, first-dose hypotension |
| ARBs | losartan, candesartan | ↓Ang II at receptor; no cough (use if ACEi cough); hyperkalaemia |
| MRAs | spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone (non-steroidal) | Aldosterone blockade; hyperkalaemia |
| Direct renin inhibitor | aliskiren | Rarely used; avoid combining with ACEi/ARB |

- **Renoprotective** via reduced intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria — first-line in albuminuric CKD/diabetic nephropathy.
- **Expected creatinine rise** after starting: **up to ~25–30% (eGFR fall ≤25%) is** **acceptable** — recheck U&Es in 1–2 weeks. A **larger rise → suspect bilateral renal** **artery stenosis** (efferent dilatation removes the pressure maintaining GFR).
- **When to stop / hold:** significant hyperkalaemia, larger creatinine rise, acute illness/volume depletion **(sick-day rules),** pregnancy (teratogenic).
- Don't routinely combine two RAAS agents (↑AKI/hyperkalaemia).

docs.title: Renal Pharmacology and Prescribing
docs.text:
| Drug | Mechanism of injury |
| --- | --- |
| NSAIDs | Afferent vasoconstriction (↓prostaglandins) → haemodynamic AKI; also AIN, papillary necrosis |
| Aminoglycosides (gentamicin) | Direct proximal tubular toxicity (ATN); also ototoxic; monitor levels |
| Vancomycin | ATN (dose/level-related); monitor levels |
| Contrast media | Contrast-associated AKI (see Section 2) |
| Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, ciclosporin) | Afferent vasoconstriction; acute and chronic nephrotoxicity |
| PPIs | Acute interstitial nephritis (and chronic) |
| Lithium | Nephrogenic DI, chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis |
| Chemotherapy (cisplatin, methotrexate, ifosfamide) | ATN, tubulopathy, crystal nephropathy |
| ACEi/ARB | Haemodynamic (efferent dilatation) — not toxic, but precipitate AKI in the wrong setting |

- **The "triple whammy": NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic** — a classic combination causing

AKI, especially with intercurrent illness.

docs.title: Renal Pharmacology and Prescribing
docs.text:
##### Drugs needing dose adjustment (accumulate in renal impairment)

- **Opioids** (morphine — active metabolites accumulate → use oxycodone/fentanyl/alfentanil with care), **gabapentin/pregabalin, many antibiotics** (aminoglycosides, vancomycin, some penicillins/cephalosporins), **DOACs and LMWH** (bleeding risk), **digoxin, allopurinol, methotrexate, sulfonylureas.**

##### Drugs to avoid / stop

- **Metformin** — stop in significant impairment/acute illness **(lactic acidosis** risk; avoid if eGFR <30).

- **NSAIDs** — avoid in CKD/AKI.
- **Nitrofurantoin** — ineffective and risk of toxicity if **eGFR <45** (needs adequate renal excretion to work in the urinary tract).
- **Potassium-sparing diuretics** — caution (hyperkalaemia).

##### Sick-day rules and medication holds

- Temporarily **hold** certain drugs during acute dehydrating illness (D&V, fever) to reduce

AKI risk — commonly remembered as **"SADMANS": Sulfonylureas, ACE** inhibitors,

**Diuretics, Metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs, SGLT2** inhibitors. Restart when eating/drinking normally.

##### Drugs removed by dialysis

- **Small, water-soluble, low-protein-bound, low-volume-of-distribution** drugs are dialysable — e.g. **lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, metformin, some** **antibiotics (aminoglycosides, vancomycin partly).**
- **Not well dialysed:** highly protein-bound or large-volume-of-distribution drugs (e.g.

digoxin, benzodiazepines, warfarin).
- **Practical points:** time doses of dialysable antibiotics **after** dialysis; and note some toxic ingestions are treated with dialysis (see AEIOU, Section 2).

docs.text: Compiled from Guyton & Hall, Robbins, StatPearls, TeachMePhysiology, Deranged Physiology, and cross-checked against Merck Manual/AJKD core curriculum. Numbers given are the standard "textbook average" figures used in exams — real physiological values vary between individuals.

docs.title: Renal Physiology (Foundation)
docs.text:
##### GFR (Glomerular Filtration Rate)

- **Normal GFR ≈ 120 mL/min (~180 L/day)** in a healthy adult (StatPearls; Guyton).
- Determined by the **Starling forces** across the glomerular capillary and the glomerular filtration barrier (endothelium → basement membrane → podocyte slit diaphragms), which filter by size, shape, and charge.
- **Autoregulated** across a mean arterial pressure of ~50–150 mmHg via:
  - **Myogenic mechanism** — afferent arteriole stretch → reflex constriction.
  - **Tubuloglomerular feedback** — macula densa senses distal NaCl delivery and adjusts afferent arteriolar tone.
- GFR clearance is measured using **inulin** (gold standard, freely filtered, not reabsorbed/secreted) or estimated clinically via **creatinine clearance.**

##### Starling Forces (net filtration pressure)

Net filtration pressure = (glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure − Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure) − (glomerular capillary oncotic pressure − Bowman's space oncotic pressure)

| Force | Effect on GFR |
| --- | --- |
| ↑ Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure | ↑ GFR |
| ↑ Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure (e.g. ureteric obstruction) | ↓ GFR |
| ↑ Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (e.g. dehydration, high plasma protein) | ↓ GFR |
| Afferent arteriole constriction | ↓ RBF and ↓ GFR (FF unchanged) |
| Efferent arteriole constriction (e.g. Angiotensin II) | ↓ RBF but GFR maintained/↑ (FF ↑) — clinically relevant with ACEi/ARB in bilateral renal artery stenosis |
| Prostaglandins | Dilate afferent arteriole, protect GFR in states of ↓ renal perfusion — hence NSAIDs (block PG) risk AKI in hypovolaemia |

##### Creatinine vs Urea

|  | Creatinine | Urea |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | Muscle creatine breakdown | Hepatic protein/amino acid metabolism (urea cycle) |
| Handling | Freely filtered, not reabsorbed; small amount of tubular secretion (so creatinine clearance slightly overestimates true GFR) | Freely filtered, ~40–50% passively reabsorbed (more with low tubular flow/dehydration) |
| Influenced by | Muscle mass, exercise, rhabdomyolysis, certain drugs blocking tubular secretion (e.g. trimethoprim, cimetidine — raise creatinine without truly lowering GFR) | Protein intake, GI bleeding, catabolic states, dehydration, hepatic function |
| Clinical use | Best routine marker of GFR (via eGFR equations) | Raised disproportionately to creatinine ("high urea:creatinine ratio") suggests pre-renal cause (dehydration, GI bleed) |

##### Urea Cycle

**Where it happens:** Only in **hepatocytes** (liver) — it's the only organ with the full enzyme set.

Purpose: converts toxic ammonia (from amino acid breakdown) into water-soluble, non-toxic **urea** for renal excretion.

###### Key exam points:

- **2 nitrogens** go into each urea molecule — one from free ammonia, one from aspartate.
- **CPS1/OTC deficiency** → hyperammonaemia; **OTC deficiency** is the most common urea cycle disorder and is **X-linked** (all others are autosomal recessive).
- Or

docs.title: Renal Physiology (Foundation)
docs.text:
##### Sodium Handling (know the % at each segment — classic exam table)

| Segment | % of filtered Na⁺ reabsorbed | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) | ~65% | Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (basolateral) + NHE3 Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger, Na⁺-glucose/amino acid cotransport (apical). Isosmotic — water follows equally, so tubular fluid remains iso-osmolar throughout. |
| Thick ascending limb (Loop of Henle) | ~25% | Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) — target of loop diuretics (furosemide). Water-impermeable segment → generates the medullary concentration gradient ("diluting segment"). |
| Distal convoluted tubule (DCT) | ~5–10% | Na-Cl cotransporter (NCC) — target of thiazide diuretics. Also water-impermeable. |
| Collecting duct (principal cells) | ~2–5% | ENaC (epithelial Na channel) — aldosterone-sensitive, final fine-tuning; target of potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride blocks ENaC; spironolactone blocks the aldosterone receptor). |
| Final urine | <1% of filtered load | — |

(Figures cross-checked across Deranged Physiology, Khan Academy, and Guyton-based sources — proximal 65%, loop 25%, DCT 5%, CD 2–5% is the standard consensus.)

##### Water Handling

- **PCT reabsorbs ~65% of filtered water** (isosmotic, obligatory, follows Na⁺).
- **Descending thin limb of loop of Henle** — permeable to water only (~10% reabsorbed), impermeable to Na⁺ → concentrates tubular fluid as it descends into the hyperosmotic medulla.
- **Ascending limb (thin + thick)** — impermeable to water, reabsorbs solute only → dilutes tubular fluid ("diluting segment").
- **Countercurrent multiplication:** descending limb (water out) + ascending limb (solute out, no water) generates the corticomedullary osmotic gradient (up to ~1200 mOsm/kg at the papilla), maintained by the **vasa recta** acting as a countercurrent exchanger.

- **Collecting duct** — water permeability is **ADH-dependent** (variable, 0–~19% additional, capable of near-total recovery). Under maximal ADH, urine can be concentrated up to

~1200 mOsm/kg; without ADH, urine is dilute (~50 mOsm/kg).

##### Potassium Secretion

- Net K⁺ handling = **reabsorption in PCT (~65%) and thick ascending limb (~25%)** **regardless of intake,** then **regulated secretion in the principal cells of the late**

**DCT/collecting duct** determines final excretion.
- Principal cell secretion via **ROMK channels** (and BK channels under high flow), driven by the lumen-negative potential generated by ENaC-mediated Na⁺ reabsorption.
- **Increased by:** aldosterone, high distal tubular flow rate, high luminal Na⁺ delivery, alkalosis, hyperkalaemia itself.
- **Intercalated cells** (type A) can reabsorb K⁺ via H⁺/K⁺-ATPase in states of K⁺ depletion.
- Reciprocal relationship with H⁺: hypokalaemia → ↑H⁺ secretion (risk of metabolic alkalosis); hyperkalaemia → inhibits ammoniagenesis, impairing acid excretion (relevant to Type IV RTA).

##### Acid–Base Regulation

- **Filtered bicarbonate load ≈ 4,000–5,000 mmol/day** (GFR × plasma

docs.h: 3. Hormonal Control — site of action in the nephron
docs.text:
###### Hormone Source Main site of Effect

###### action

| RAAS (Renin → Ang I → Ang II) | Renin: juxtaglomerular cells (afferent arteriole). Angiotensinogen: liver. ACE: pulmonary/renal vascular endothelium | Efferent arteriole (Ang II constriction); adrenal cortex (stimulates aldosterone) | ↑BP, efferent constriction maintains GFR when renal perfusion falls, stimulates aldosterone and thirst/ADH release |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Aldosterone | Zona glomerulosa, adrenal cortex (stimulated by Ang II and by hyperkalaemia) | Principal cells of the collecting duct (and late DCT) | ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption via ENaC, ↑ K⁺ secretion via ROMK, ↑ H⁺ secretion by intercalated cells |
| ADH (vasopressin) | Hypothalamus (supraoptic/paraventricular nuclei), released from posterior pituitary | V2 receptors on principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct | Inserts aquaporin-2 channels apically → ↑ water permeability/reabsorption → concentrated urine. (V1 receptors elsewhere cause vasoconstriction.) |
| ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) | Atrial myocytes, released on atrial stretch (↑ blood volume) | Afferent arteriole (dilates) + collecting duct (inhibits ENaC) + inhibits renin/aldosterone release | ↑ GFR, natriuresis and diuresis — opposes RAAS |
| EPO (erythropoietin) | Peritubular fibroblast-like cells of the renal cortex/outer medulla, stimulated by hypoxia (HIF pathway) | Acts on bone marrow (not the nephron itself) | Stimulates erythropoiesis — explains anaemia of CKD |
| Vitamin D activation | Skin (UVB) → cholecalciferol → liver 25-hydroxylation → kidney: PCT mitochondria, 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) converts 25(OH)D → 1,25-(OH)₂D (calcitriol), the active hormone | Acts on gut, bone, distal nephron (DCT calcium channels) | ↑ intestinal Ca²⁺/PO₄³⁻ absorption, ↑ distal tubular Ca²⁺ reabsorption, permits normal bone mineralisation. PTH stimulates 1α-hydroxylase; FGF-23 inhibits it. |
| PTH | Chief cells, parathyroid gland (sensed via Ca-sensing receptor) | PCT (inhibits phosphate reabsorption, stimulates 1α-hydroxylase) + distal nephron (stimulates Ca²⁺ reabsorption) | ↑ serum Ca²⁺, ↑ phosphate excretion, ↑ active vitamin D |

docs.title: Renal Physiology (Foundation)
docs.text:
PCT: 65% Na⁺, 65% water, 65% Ca²⁺, ~all glucose/AA/phosphate reabsorption,

85% HCO₃⁻ reabsorption, ammoniagenesis, 1α-hydroxylase (vitamin D activation)

Thin descending limb: water reabsorbed (impermeable to Na⁺)

Thin/Thick ascending limb: Na⁺/K⁺/Cl⁻ reabsorbed (impermeable to water) — NKCC2 (loop diuretic target)

25% Na⁺, 20-25% Ca²⁺ (paracellular), further HCO₃⁻ reabsorption

DCT: 5-10% Na⁺ (NCC, thiazide target), regulated Ca²⁺ reabsorption (PTH/vitamin D target)

Collecting duct (principal cells): 2-5% Na⁺ (ENaC, aldosterone target), K⁺ secretion,

ADH-regulated water reabsorption (aquaporin-2, V2 receptor)

Collecting duct (intercalated cells): acid-base fine-tuning (Type A: H⁺ secretion;

Type B: HCO₃⁻ secretion via pendrin)

###### Enzyme deficiencies - Inborn errors of metabolism

- **OTC deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder and is X-linked** — every other urea cycle disorder is autosomal recessive. This is a classic exam discriminator.
- Classic neonatal presentation of a urea cycle disorder: **poor feeding, vomiting,** **lethargy, ↑ ammonia, and respiratory alkalosis** (ammonia stimulates the respiratory centre → hyperventilation). The respiratory alkalosis is the tell — it distinguishes this from organic acidaemias, which cause a metabolic acidosis.
- **OTC deficiency → ↑ urinary orotic acid.** Reason: the block is after carbamoyl phosphate, so it accumulates, spills out of the mitochondrion, and gets diverted into **pyrimidine synthesis** → orotic acid.
- **CPS1 deficiency → normal/low orotic acid,** because the block is before carbamoyl phosphate is ever made. (Hyperammonaemia + orotic aciduria = OTC; hyperammonaemia without orotic aciduria = CPS1.)
- **Hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency)** also causes orotic aciduria — but with **no hyperammonaemia,** because the urea cycle is intact. It presents instead with megaloblastic anaemia unresponsive to B12/folate.
- **ASS1 deficiency = citrullinaemia** → markedly **↑ plasma citrulline** (the substrate builds up behind the block).
- **ASL deficiency = argininosuccinic aciduria** → **↑ argininosuccinate** in blood and urine.
- General principle: **the intermediate immediately upstream of the blocked enzyme** **accumulates.** Use this to reason out any urea cycle disorder rather than memorising each.

###### Management of hyperammonaemic crisis

- **Stop all protein intake** and give **IV glucose ± lipids** — provides calories to halt catabolism (endogenous protein breakdown is itself an ammonia source).
- **Sodium benzoate** conjugates with **glycine** → **hippurate,** excreted renally.

- **Sodium phenylbutyrate** (→ phenylacetate) conjugates with **glutamine** → **phenylacetylglutamine,** excreted renally. Both create a **nitrogen escape route that** **bypasses the broken urea cycle.**
- **Arginine or citrulline supplementation** — replenishes cycle intermediates downstream of the block (arginine becomes conditionally essential when the cycle can't make i

docs.title: Renal Replacement Therapy and Transplantation
docs.text:
##### Principles (know the two physical processes)

- **Diffusion** — solutes move down a concentration gradient across a semipermeable membrane (clears small solutes: urea, potassium). The basis of **haemodialysis.**
- **Convection / ultrafiltration** — solvent (water) dragged across by a pressure gradient, carrying solutes ("solvent drag"); removes fluid and larger middle molecules. Dominant in **haemofiltration.**
- **Osmosis** — water drawn across by an osmotic gradient (dextrose in dialysate); the basis of fluid removal in **peritoneal dialysis.**

##### Haemodialysis (HD)

- Blood pumped through a dialyser against countercurrent dialysate; usually **3× weekly,**

**~4 hours** in a unit (or home HD).
- **Vascular access — the key exam topic (in order of preference):**
  - **Arteriovenous fistula (AVF)** — **gold standard;** native artery–vein anastomosis; needs **6–8 weeks to "mature";** lowest infection/thrombosis risk, best longevity.

Complications: stenosis/thrombosis, steal syndrome (distal ischaemia), high-output cardiac failure, aneurysm.
  - **AV graft** — synthetic; used when veins inadequate; higher thrombosis/infection than fistula.
  - **Tunnelled central venous catheter** — immediate use but **highest infection** **and thrombosis risk;** last resort/bridge.
  - "Fistula first" — and **never** take blood, cannulate, or put a BP cuff on a fistula arm.
- **Complications: hypotension** (commonest — during fluid removal), cramps, arrhythmia, **dialysis disequilibrium syndrome** (rapid urea/osmolar shifts → cerebral oedema → headache, confusion, seizures — avoided by gentle initial dialysis), access problems, air embolism, anaphylaxis to membrane.

##### Peritoneal dialysis (PD)

- Uses the **peritoneum as the semipermeable membrane;** dialysate instilled via a

Tenckhoff catheter, dextrose osmotic gradient removes fluid. **CAPD** (manual exchanges) or **APD** (overnight machine).
- **Advantages:** home-based, independence, gentler haemodynamics, preserves residual function.
- **Complications:**
  - **PD peritonitis** — the big one: **cloudy effluent + abdominal pain + fever;** diagnose on effluent WCC (>100 with >50% neutrophils) and culture; usually

**Staph** (skin flora); treat with **intraperitoneal antibiotics.**
  - **Exit-site/tunnel infection,** catheter malfunction, hernias, **encapsulating** **peritoneal sclerosis** (rare, serious — bowel encased in fibrous cocoon → obstruction), membrane failure over time, hyperglycaemia/weight gain from glucose load.

##### Choosing a modality & conservative care

- Modality depends on patient factors (comorbidity, lifestyle, home support, residual function, cardiovascular stability), not just clinical criteria — a shared decision.
- **Conservative (supportive) kidney care** is a legitimate pathway for frail/multimorbid patients in whom dialysis may not improve survival or quality of life — focus on symptom control and advance care planning. **Mentioning this shows exam maturity.**

docs.title: Renal Replacement Therapy and Transplantation
docs.text:
The best treatment for ESKD for suitable patients — better survival and quality of life than dialysis.

##### Work-up and matching

- **Living vs deceased donor** (living gives better graft survival, can be pre-emptive before dialysis).
- **Matching: ABO blood group compatibility** and **HLA matching** (HLA-A, -B, -DR most important; DR mismatch matters most). **Crossmatch** (recipient serum against donor lymphocytes) must be negative — a **positive crossmatch predicts hyperacute** **rejection.**
- Placed **extraperitoneally in the iliac fossa,** anastomosed to iliac vessels and bladder; native kidneys usually left in situ.

##### Immunosuppression (and side effects — very examinable)

Typically **triple therapy:**

| Drug class | Example | Key side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calcineurin inhibitor | Tacrolimus, ciclosporin | Nephrotoxicity (afferent vasoconstriction — mimics rejection!), tremor, diabetes (tacrolimus), hypertension, gum hypertrophy/hirsutism (ciclosporin), neurotoxicity; narrow therapeutic window → drug-level monitoring |
| Antimetabolite | Mycophenolate mofetil | GI upset, bone marrow suppression, teratogenic |
| Corticosteroid | Prednisolone | Diabetes, osteoporosis, weight gain, infection, cushingoid |
| (mTOR inhibitor) | Sirolimus | Poor wound healing, proteinuria, pneumonitis |
| Induction agent | Basiliximab (IL-2R antibody), ATG | Infusion reactions, infection |

Key trap: **calcineurin inhibitor toxicity can look like rejection** — both cause a rising creatinine in a transplant. Biopsy + drug levels distinguish them.

##### Rejection — types and timing

| Type | Timing | Mechanism | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hyperacute | Minutes–h ours | Pre-formed antibodies (ABO/HLA) | Graft thrombosis; now rare due to crossmatching; untreatable → remove graft |
| Acute cellular | Days–mont hs | T-cell mediated | Commonest acute; treat with high-dose steroids, ATG if severe |
| Acute antibody-medi ated | Days–mont hs | Donor-specific antibodies | Treat with plasma exchange, IVIG, rituximab |
| Chronic | Months–ye ars | Immune + non-immune (interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy) | Gradual decline; largely untreatable — leading cause of late graft loss |

##### Long-term complications

- **Infection** (immunosuppression): **CMV** (commonest opportunistic — prophylaxis/monitoring), **BK virus** nephropathy (can mimic rejection), **PJP** (co-trimoxazole prophylaxis), fungal.
- **Malignancy: skin cancers (SCC — very high risk, sun protection essential),** **post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD — EBV-driven).**
- **Cardiovascular disease** — leading cause of death with a functioning graft.
- **Recurrent disease** in the graft (FSGS, IgA, MPGN can recur).
- Drug toxicities, new-onset diabetes after transplant (NODAT), bone disease.

##### Delayed graft function

- Need for dialysis within the first week post-transplant, usually due to **ischaemia-reperfusion ATN** (commoner with deceased/marginal donors and long co

###### Renal Disease Recognition — Formulation

###### & Quick-Spot Summary

A synthesis of the section notes, organised for **pattern recognition:** meet the disease by its presenting syndrome, clinch it with the single differentiating feature. Everything here is cross-checked in the parent section files. Use it as the night-before flick-through.

###### How to use this document

- **Part A** — organised by presenting syndrome (how the patient actually turns up). Find the syndrome, scan the discriminators.
- **Part B** — signature tables: the fastest single-clue lookups (pathognomonic clue, antibody, complement, casts, IF pattern, biochemistry).
- **Part C** — confusable pairs: the head-to-heads students mix up, and the one feature that separates each.

docs.h: A1. Acute kidney injury — which bucket?
docs.parent: Renal Syndrome Recognition and Lookup Tables
docs.text:
###### First split: pre-renal / intrinsic / post-renal

| Bucket | Points towards it | Clinching feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-renal | Hypovolaemia, sepsis, HF, cirrhosis, NSAID/ACEi | FeNa <1%, urine osm >500, bland urine, high urea:creatinine; responds to fluid |
| Intrinsic (ATN) | Prolonged pre-renal/toxins/contrast | FeNa >1–2%, urine osm ~300, muddy-brown casts; no response to fluid |
| Post-renal | Older man, single kidney, pelvic malignancy | Hydronephrosis on US; relieved by catheter/nephrostomy |

###### Then the specific AKI syndromes — each has a one-line tell:

| Syndrome | The clue that clinches it |
| --- | --- |
| Rhabdomyolysis | Dipstick blood +++, no RBCs on microscopy; ↑↑CK, ↑K⁺/PO₄³⁻, ↓Ca²⁺ |
| Tumour lysis syndrome | Post-chemo; ↑K⁺, ↑PO₄³⁻, ↑urate, ↓Ca²⁺ ("everything up except calcium") |
| Contrast-associated AKI | Creatinine rises 48–72 h after contrast, recovers |
| Hepatorenal syndrome | Cirrhosis + AKI + urine Na <10 + no response to albumin; bland urine |
| Cholesterol emboli | Post-angiogram + livedo reticularis + eosinophilia + low complement |
| Acute interstitial nephritis | New drug (PPI/NSAID/penicillin) + sterile pyuria + white cell casts ± eosinophilia |
| Scleroderma renal crisis | Systemic sclerosis + severe HTN + AKI + MAHA → give ACE inhibitor |
| Pulmonary–renal syndrome | Haemoptysis + RPGN → anti-GBM or ANCA vasculitis (urgent) |

| Pair | Separator |
| --- | --- |
| Pre-renal vs ATN | FeNa <1% & urine osm >500 (pre-renal) vs FeNa >1–2%, isosthenuric, muddy-brown casts (ATN). If on diuretics → use FeUrea <35% |
| AKI vs CKD | Small echogenic kidneys, anaemia, ↑PO₄³⁻/↓Ca²⁺, old abnormal bloods → CKD |
| IgA nephropathy vs post-strep GN | Haematuria during infection + normal C3 (IgA) vs 1–2 weeks after + low C3 (post-strep) |
| Minimal change vs FSGS | Both nephrotic; MCD steroid-responsive, child, normal LM; FSGS steroid-resistant, segmental sclerosis, secondary causes |
| Anti-GBM vs ANCA (pulmonary–renal) | Linear IF + anti-GBM antibody vs pauci-immune + ANCA |
| Bartter vs Gitelman | Both hypokalaemic alkalosis/normal BP; Bartter = hyperCALCiuria, Gitelman = hypoCALCiuria + hypomagnesaemia |
| Liddle vs hyperaldosteronism | Both HTN + hypokalaemic alkalosis; Liddle = LOW aldosterone, responds to amiloride not spironolactone |
| HUS vs TTP | HUS = renal + child + diarrhoea; TTP = neuro + ADAMTS13, plasma exchange |
| Cranial vs nephrogenic DI | Cranial responds to desmopressin; nephrogenic does not |
| RTA type 1 vs 2 | Type 1 urine pH >5.5 + stones; Type 2 Fanconi + can acidify below threshold |
| RTA (any) vs diarrhoea (normal anion gap acidosis) | Urine anion gap: positive = RTA, negative = diarrhoea |
| Renal artery stenosis vs essential HTN | RAS: resistant HTN, flash pulmonary oedema, AKI on ACEi, asymmetric kidneys, bruit |
| CNI toxicity vs transplant rejection | Both raise creatinine in a graft — drug levels + biopsy distinguish |
| Glomerular vs urological haematuria | Dysmorphic RBCs + casts + protein = glomerular; isomorphic RBCs + clots = urological |
| Nephrotic vs nephritic | Protein-dominant, bland sediment (nephrotic) vs blood + RBC casts + HTN (nephritic) |

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
##### Types and risk factors

| Stone type | ~Frequency | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calcium oxalate | ~80% (commonest) | Radio-opaque; hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, hypocitraturia; low fluid intake |
| Calcium phosphate |  | Radio-opaque; associated with distal (type 1) RTA, alkaline urine |
| Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) | ~10% | Infection stones (urease-producing organisms — Proteus, Klebsiella); form staghorn calculi; alkaline urine |
| Uric acid | ~5–10% | Radiolucent (won't show on plain film); acidic urine, gout, high purine, tumour lysis |
| Cystine | rare | Inherited cystinuria; hexagonal crystals; from childhood |

##### Presentation and imaging

- **Renal colic:** sudden severe **loin-to-groin pain,** colicky, restless patient (can't get comfortable — contrast with peritonitis where they lie still), nausea, haematuria.
- **Imaging: non-contrast CT KUB is the gold standard** (detects nearly all stones including radiolucent uric acid; ultrasound for pregnancy/children to avoid radiation).

##### Management

- **Analgesia: NSAIDs (e.g. IM/PR diclofenac) are first-line** and superior to opioids for renal colic (caution in AKI/CKD).

- **Most small stones (<5 mm) pass spontaneously; medical expulsive therapy** **(tamsulosin)** may help stones 5–10 mm in the distal ureter.
- **Indications for intervention:** stone unlikely to pass, uncontrolled pain, **obstruction** **with infection (emergency),** AKI, solitary kidney.
- **Modalities: shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL), ureteroscopy + laser, percutaneous** **nephrolithotomy (PCNL)** for large/staghorn stones.
- ⚠ **Obstructed + infected kidney = urological emergency** → **urgent decompression** (nephrostomy or ureteric stent) + antibiotics. Do not delay for stone removal.
- **Prevention:** high fluid intake (>2.5 L/day), reduce salt/animal protein, normal dietary calcium (not low), thiazides for hypercalciuria, potassium citrate, allopurinol for uric acid.

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
| Entity | Features | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lower UTI (cystitis) | Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain; no systemic upset; leucocytes/nitrites | Short-course antibiotics (nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim per local guidance) |
| Pyelonephritis | Fever, rigors, loin pain, nausea/vomiting + LUTS; white cell casts | Broader/longer antibiotics; admit if unwell; image if not improving |
| Complicated UTI | Structural/functional abnormality, stones, catheter, pregnancy, immunosuppression, male | Longer courses; investigate underlying cause |
| Catheter-associate d UTI | Only treat if symptomatic; don't treat colonisation | Remove/change catheter; antibiotics only if symptoms |
| Renal/perinephric abscess | Persistent fever despite antibiotics, flank mass | CT; drainage + antibiotics |

- **Asymptomatic bacteriuria — when to treat:** generally **do NOT treat,** EXCEPT in **pregnancy** (risk of pyelonephritis/preterm labour) and **before urological procedures** with anticipated mucosal breach. Treating otherwise drives resistance. Common exam point.

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
- **Causes:** luminal (stone, clot), mural (stricture, tumour), extrinsic **(BPH/prostate cancer**

— commonest in older men, pelvic malignancy, retroperitoneal fibrosis, AAA).
- **Hydronephrosis** on ultrasound (may be absent early or if ureters encased).
- **Post-obstructive diuresis:** after relieving chronic bilateral obstruction, a **massive** **diuresis** can follow (accumulated solute/urea, tubular dysfunction, volume overload correction) → **monitor fluid balance and electrolytes closely,** replace losses.
- **Benign prostatic hyperplasia:** LUTS (hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, incomplete emptying); can cause **chronic retention → obstructive AKI.** Treat with **α-blockers** **(tamsulosin)** ± **5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride);** catheterise acute retention.

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
##### Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)

- **Genetics: PKD1 (chromosome 16, ~85%, more severe)** or **PKD2 (chromosome 4,** **milder);** autosomal dominant.
- **Renal:** bilateral enlarging cysts → **hypertension** (early), haematuria, cyst infection/haemorrhage, stones, progressive CKD → ESKD.
- **Extra-renal manifestations (examinable): berry (intracranial) aneurysms →** **subarachnoid haemorrhage, hepatic cysts,** mitral valve prolapse, **diverticular** **disease,** abdominal wall hernias.
- **Management:** BP control **(ACEi/ARB),** treat complications; **tolvaptan (V2 receptor** **antagonist)** ⚑ slows cyst growth and eGFR decline in rapidly progressing ADPKD — a relatively recent disease-modifying option (monitor LFTs, causes marked aquaresis/thirst). Screen family; consider MRA screening for aneurysms if family history.

##### Other cystic disease

- **Simple cysts** — very common, benign, incidental; use the **Bosniak classification** to grade malignant potential of complex cysts.
- **Acquired cystic disease** — in long-standing dialysis patients; increased RCC risk.
- **Medullary sponge kidney** — cystic dilatation of collecting ducts; recurrent stones and infection, usually benign.
- (Autosomal recessive PKD — infantile, rarer, severe.)

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
##### Renal cell carcinoma (RCC)

- Arises from **proximal tubular epithelium; clear cell** commonest. Risk: smoking, obesity, **VHL disease,** dialysis-acquired cysts.
- **Classic triad (haematuria + loin pain + flank mass)** is late and uncommon (<10%); most found incidentally on imaging.
- **Paraneoplastic syndromes (a favourite): polycythaemia (EPO), hypercalcaemia**

###### (PTHrP), hypertension (renin), Stauffer syndrome (non-metastatic hepatic

**dysfunction).**
- **Spread:** into **renal vein/IVC** (can cause a **left varicocele** if it obstructs the left gonadal vein), lungs ("cannonball" metastases).
- Management: **surgery (partial/radical nephrectomy);** tyrosine kinase inhibitors/immunotherapy for advanced disease (relatively chemo/radio-resistant).

##### Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma

- Bladder/ureter/renal pelvis; **painless visible haematuria;** risk: **smoking, aromatic** **amines (dye/rubber industry),** cyclophosphamide.
- Diagnosis: **cystoscopy + CT urogram + urine cytology.**

##### Prostate cancer (renal relevance)

- Can cause **bladder outflow / ureteric obstruction → post-renal AKI.** Presents with

LUTS, bone pain (sclerotic mets), raised PSA.

##### Haematuria — the diagnostic pathway

- **Visible (macroscopic) haematuria** → always investigate: **cystoscopy + upper-tract** **imaging (CT urogram),** especially **painless visible haematuria in an older smoker =** **malignancy until excluded.**
- **Non-visible (microscopic):** confirm it's real (not myoglobin/haemoglobin — check microscopy for RBCs), exclude UTI, then assess with imaging/cystoscopy if persistent or with risk factors.
- **Glomerular vs urological bleeding: dysmorphic RBCs, red cell casts, proteinuria**

**→ glomerular (nephrology); isomorphic RBCs, clots, no casts → urological** **(urology).**

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
| Clue | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Loin-to-groin colic, restless patient | Renal stone — CT KUB |
| Radiolucent stone (not on plain film/CT easily) | Uric acid stone |
| Staghorn calculus + urease organism (Proteus) | Struvite (infection) stone |
| Fever + obstructed kidney | Urological emergency — decompress (nephrostomy/stent) + antibiotics |
| Asymptomatic bacteriuria — treat when? | Only in pregnancy / pre-urological procedure |
| Massive diuresis after relieving obstruction | Post-obstructive diuresis — replace fluids, monitor electrolytes |
| ADPKD + sudden severe headache | Ruptured berry aneurysm (SAH) |
| Drug that slows ADPKD progression | Tolvaptan |
| RCC + polycythaemia/hypercalcaemia | Paraneoplastic syndrome |
| Painless visible haematuria, older smoker | Urothelial/bladder cancer until excluded — cystoscopy + CT urogram |
| Dysmorphic RBCs + casts vs isomorphic RBCs + clots | Glomerular (nephrology) vs urological (urology) |

##### Sources

EAU and NICE guidance on urolithiasis, LUTS/BPH, and haematuria; StatPearls (RCC, urothelial carcinoma, ADPKD); NICE/SMC tolvaptan guidance for ADPKD. Stone frequencies and paraneoplastic associations cross-checked across sources.

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
- POTTER SYNDROME: in bilateral renal agenesis or obstructive uropathy (Pulmonary hypoplasia, Oligohydramnios – trigger, Twisted face, Twisted skin, Extremity defects, Renal failure- in utero)

- HORSESHOE KIDNEY: inferior kidney poles fuse and the ureters course medially and anteriorly over joined renal isthmus  can cause hydronephrosis, uteropelvic joint obstruction, renal stones, infection, chromosomal aneuploidy syndromes (Turner syndrome, trisomies 13/18/21), renal cancer

- CONGENITAL SOLITARY FUNCTIONING KIDNEY: one functioning kidney; majority asymptomatic

- UNILATERAL RENAL AGENESIS: complete absence of kidney/ureter

- MULTICYSTIC DYSPLASTIC KIDNEY: non-functional kidney with cysts + connective tissue (bilateral=POTTER)

- DUPLEX COLLECTING SYSTEM: associated with vesicoureteral reflux and/or ureteral obstruction,  risk for UTIs

- POSTERIOR URETHRAL VALVES:  urethral obstruction and bladder outlet obstruction in male infants, and can be diagnosed prenatally by hydronephrosis and dilated/thick-walled bladder on U/S

- RENAL ECTOPIA: Abnormal renal location usually results when a kidney fails to ascend from its origin in the true pelvis. It can cause ureteropelvic junction obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux and multicystic renal dysplasia

- RENAL HYPOPLASIA:  ureteral bud branching; underdeveloped kidney with histologically normal nephrons

- VESICOURETERAL REFLUX DISEASE: most common congenital abnormality and is discovered in utero through a morphology scan at 18 weeks. High grades are associated with renal failure and sclerotic renal lesions.

---

| Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) | Definition: numerous cysts in cortex and medulla A causing bilateral enlarged kidneys ultimately destroying kidney parenchyma Aetiology: PKD1 (85%): inherited mutation on chromosome 16 with an alteration of polycystin-1 PKD2 (15%): inherited mutation of chromosome 4 with an alteration of polycystin-2 Age: adulthood (> 30 years) Characteristics: bilateral, cysts vary in size, multiple extra-renal manifestations Presentation: Flank/abdominal pain, UTI, nephrolithiasis, haematuria, progressive renal failure Extra-renal: Gastro: multiple hepatic cysts (70%), colon diverticula, abdominal/inguinal hernias CVS: arterial HTN, heart valve defects e.g. mitral valve prolapse, LVH CNS: berry aneurysms Diagnostic Criteria (Ravines) <30 years of age: at least 2 unilateral or bilateral cysts 30 – 59 years of age: 2 cysts in each kidney >60 years of age: 4 cysts in each kidney Treatment: Prevent/delay progression to ESRD Analgesia fluid intake (prevent stone formation) Aspiration under CT guidance Avoid nephrotoxic substances ACE-I/ARBs Prevent/treat UTI/cystitis Monitor and treat liver failure Screen for cerebral aneurysm Genetic counselling Laparoscopic cyst fenestration or decortication Kidney transplantation (only curative option) Complications: 50% have ESRD by 60 Poor prognostic factors: chronic HTN, cerebral aneurysms |
|---|---|
| Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) | Definition: cystic dilation of collecting ducts B associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis Aetiology: inherited mutation on chromosome 6 Age: birth to childhood Characteristics: bilateral, equally sized cysts Presentation: Significant oliguric renal failure in utero  potter sequence CRF (haematuria, proteinuria) Obligate liver involvement (portal HTN, hepatomegaly) HTN (can cause CHF) Treatment: as above Concerns beyond neonatal: systemic HTN, progressive renal insufficiency, portal HTN, congenital hepatic fibrosis |
| Medullary cystic disease | Definition: inherited disease causing tubulointerstitial fibrosis and progressive renal insufficiency with inability to concentrate urine Presentation: renal stones, haematuria, recurrent UTIs Imaging: medullary cysts usually not visualized; shrunken kidneys on ultrasound Poor prognosis |
| Simple vs complex renal cysts | Simple cysts are filled with ultrafiltrate (anechoic on ultrasound C). Very common and account for majority of all renal masses. Found incidentally and typically asymptomatic. Complex cysts: alcification, septation, thickened wall, solid component, increased density, contrast enhancement. They require follow-up or removal due to risk of renal cell carcinoma |

| Renal Cell Carcinoma | Epidemiology: 85% of renal cancers, M>F, 60-80 years old Risk Factors: Smoking, pre-existic conditions (cystic kidney disease, renal pelvic stones, obesity, HTN, immunodeficiency, Hep C, sickle cell disease), toxins Hereditary (usually younger age): Von-Hippel-Lindau syndrome (RCC: 3 letters: chrom. 3), tuberous sclerosis Pathophysiology: adenocarcinomas from PCT epithelium (~80% are histologically clear cell RCCs) Histology: highly vascular; polygonal clear cells (lipids-gold colour- and carbohydrates) Presentation: Renal/Oncology: haematuria, palpable flank mass, 2° polycythaemia, colicky flank pain, constitutional Sx, HTN (renin secretion), EPO (anaemia, pallor, lethargy) Triad: haematuria, flank pain, palpable flank mass (5-10% present with this) Paraneoplastic (ectopic EPO, ACTH, PTHrP, renin): HTN, Ca2+, polycythemia, secondary hypercortisolism, Stauffer’s syndrome (non-metastatic  LFT and clotting abnormalities), limbic encephalitis (memory loss, psychosis, depression) Local spread: varicocele, Budd-Chiari (lower limb oedema, ascites, hepatic dysfunction) Symptoms of metastasis: lung, bone Spread: Lymph nodes of renal hilum  para-aortic nodes Growth into the renal vein and IVC  hematogenously to lung and bone Diagnostics: Abdominal CT with contrast: thickened irregular walls, variable enhancement, calcification Renal U/S: renal lesion(s) with variable echogenicity Metastatic disease: bone scan, thoracic CT/MRI (cannonball metastases) Bloods and urinalysis: Hb, Ca2+, AST/ALT/ALP, BUN/Cr, hematuria Renal biopsy not generally recommended Treatment: Stage I: ablation, partial nephrectomy Stage II-IV: radical nephrectomy Immunotherapy and/or targeted therapy (for metastatic disease, rarely curative) Interferon-a (immunotherapy) Recombinant cytokines (interleukin-2) Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (metastatic disease) Resistant to chemotherapy and radiation therapy |

| Definition | Symptoms suggestive of a UTI and evidence of pyuria and bacteriuria on UA or urine MC&S Asymptomatic + 100,000 CFU/mL = asymptomatic bacteriuria |

| Classification | Location: upper (pyelonephritis), lower (cystitis/urethritis) Type: Uncomplicated: lower UTI in a setting of functionally and structurally normal urinary tract Complicated: structural/functional abnormality, mal, immunocompromised, diabetic, iatrogenic (procedure, recent Abx usage), pregnancy, pyelonephritis, catheter-associated, post-menopausal, neurogenic bladder, kidney cysts/stones Recurrent/chronic: ≥ 2 infections/6 months OR ≥ 3 infections/year Nosocomial: hospital-acquired usually from IDC |
| Aetiology | Bacteria (KEEPS): Klebsiella, E. coli (~80%), Enterococcus, Proteus mirabilis, Staph saphrophyticus Viral: adenoviruses (haemorrhagic cystitis) Atypical: candida, Tb, chlamydia trachmatis, mycoplasma Abacterial interstitial cystitis |
| Pathogenesis | Opportunistic or translocation of flora: ascending route through urethra Gram neg anaerobic intestinal flora are highly motile and can produce fimbriae (firm attachment) Some bacteria may also produce biofilm which protects them from host defences |
| Risk Factors | Female: shorter urethra with closer proximity between anal and genital regions Sexual intercourse: also, diaphragm/spermicide disturb vaginal flora Catheter-associated Structural/functional abnormalities: BPH, VUR, urinary bladder diverticulum, urethral stricture, cystocele, neurogenic bladder, calculi, stones (can cause stasis and obstruction) Pregnancy Decreased resistance to organisms: DM, immunocompromise, oestrogen, medications Uncircumcised males Chronic constipation Trauma |

| Investigation | Clinical: especially in healthy women with typical presentation Urine dipstick: positive leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, urine pH>7 (in proteus), haematuria Urinalysis MC&S: Mid-stream (avoid contamination with vaginal/skin flora) or through catherization/suprapubic aspiration Pyuria: >10 WBC/hpf Bacteriuria: presence of bacteria on gram negative stain, leukocyte casts absent in lower UTIs Urine culture: Indicated in: complicated UTI, > 65 y/o, diaphragm use, Abx usage Suspected cystitis in: >7 day duration, recurrent UTIs, suspicion of pyelonephritis/urosepsis Significant bacteriuria defined as ≥ 105 colony forming units/mL serves Imaging: Indication: complicated cystitis, suspicion of structural abnormalities, in children > 24 months U/S:  allows urinary retention to be ruled out, pyelonephritis Cystoscopy: stones, reflux, urinary obstruction, polyps or malignancies, interstitial cystitis CT: stones, obstruction, tumours, cysts, and trauma Intravenous pyelogram (IVP): abnormalities, mainly obstructions |

docs.text:
| Definition | Presence of crystalline stones (calculi) within the urogenital tract |
|---|---|
| Epidemiology | M>F, 30-60 years old |
| Classification | Calcium stones – 80% Oxalate makes up 80% – risk factors include low urine volume, hypercalciuria, hyperuricosuria, hyperoxaluria and hypocitraturia [↓ urinary pH] Phosphate makes up 20% – risk factors include hyperparathyroidism and T1 RTA [↑urinary pH] Uric Acid Stones- 10% Risk factors include ↑ acidic urine, gout, hyperuricemia, drugs e.g. aspirin/thiazide [↓urinary pH] Struvite stones (staghorn/infection stones)- 5-10% Composed of Mg2+, NH4+, and PO43- Risk factors include upper UTIs  (Proteus, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, S. aureus) [↑urinary pH] Complications include obstruction, pyelonephritis, hydronephrosis, renal abscess, sepsis Cystine stones- 1% Caused by cystinuria (autosomal recessive disorder characterised by defective intestinal and renal tubular transport of dibasic amino acids (COAL- cystine, ornithine, arginine, lysine) [↓urinary pH] Complications include obstruction, pyelonephritis, hydronephrosis, sepsis, renal abscess formation |
| Risk Factors | Diet (Na2+/purine/oxalate; K+/fluid) PMHx and FHx Medications (loop diuretics, antacids) Crohn’s Disease (↑oxalate absorption) |
| Pathogenesis | Super-saturation of stone constituents (calcium, oxalate, uric acid) at an appropriate temperature/pH → plaques → attach to basement membrane → erode urothelium → anchored surface for calcium oxalate crystals to attach and grow Stasis, low flow and low urine volume ↓ inhibitory factors (e.g. citrate, magnesium, pyrophosphate) If stone  <5mm, it will pass through The four narrowest points in which stones can get stuck are uteropelvic junction, pelvic brim, under the vas deferens/broad ligament and the ureterovesical junction |
| Presentation | Determined by: localisation, and size (if < 5mm, asymptomatic) Severe unilateral, colicky flank pain (renal colic) Radiates anteriorly to lower abdomen and groin (paroxysmal, progressively worsening) Percussion tenderness Haematuria, dysuria, frequency, urgency Fever, N/V, ↓ bowel sounds |
| Investigations | Bloods: ↑WBC, ↑Ca2+, EUC (GFR, BUN) Urinalysis: pH (>7= urea-splitting organisms/struvite stones, <5=uric acid stones), pyuria, RBC, nitrates, crystals, staining Renal U/S: calcification, dilatation CT non-contrast (gold standard): calcification, hydronephrosis, stone size/site, perinephritic fat stranding KUB X-ray: radiopaque (calcium-containing) vs. weakly x-ray positive (struvite, cystine) vs. radiolucent (uric acid) Intravenous pyelogram |
| Differentials | Acute abdomen, hydronephrosis, testicular torsion, UTI (cystitis, pyelonephritis) |
| Management | Uncomplicated stones < 5 mm Hydration, analgesia (NSAIDs, IV morphine), anti-emetic, Abx (concomitant UTI, infection stones) Uric acid stones: urine alkalisation, allopurinol Hypercalcemia: thiazide diuretics Uncomplicated stones < 10 mm (especially distal stones) Medical: medical expulsion th

| Definition | Urge incontinence: involuntary urine leakage preceded by sudden urge to void (bladder aetiology) Stress incontinence: involuntary leakage of urine with a sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure (urethra/sphincter weakness; post-partum pelvic musculature weakness) Mixed: Urinary leakage associated with urgency and ↑ intra-abdominal pressure Overflow incontinence: urinary incontinence associated with retention (BPH). Impaired detrusor contractility and/or bladder outlet obstruction → chronically distended bladder with ↑ bladder pressure → dribbling of urine when intravesical pressure > outlet resistance |
|---|---|
| Normal physiology | Neural control of micturition: parasympathetic nervous system → S2–S4 ventral root → inferior hypogastric plexus → contraction of the detrusor muscle → voluntary relaxation of the external urethral sphincter muscle via the pudendal nerve → micturition! ![](notes/renal/images/nephrology-and-urology-anu/img018.jpg) |
| Epidemiology | ↑ prevalence with age, F>M Stress/mixed incontinence in female patients; urge incontinence in males |
| Types | ![](notes/renal/images/nephrology-and-urology-anu/img019.jpg) Urge incontinence: Detrusor overactivity: CNS lesion, inflammation/infection, bladder neck obstruction with tumour/stone, BPH ↓ bladder wall compliance: CNS lesion, fibrosis, sphincter/urethral problem Stress incontinence: Post-prostate cancer Tx and pelvic operations Urethral hypermobility: weakened pelvic floor musculature Intrinsic sphincter deficiency: surgery, neurological, aging, hypo-oestrogen |
| Investigations | Urinalysis and culture: exclude UTI U/S: residual urine after micturition Pad test: quantification of urine leaked Micturating cysto-urethrogram: morphological abnormalities Urodynamic studies: bladder pressure, urethral closure pressure Cystoscopy: tumours, fistula (vesicorectal/vesicovaginal) MRI: pelvic floor defects |
| Treatment | General principles: Contributors: ↓drugs, treat reversible causes Lifestyle: weight loss, diet (EtOH, caffeine, carbonated drinks), smoking cessation Physical: absorbent products, catheterisation, urethral occlusion, pessaries/penile compression devices Behavioural: bladder training, Kegel exercises, vaginal-weighted cones, biofeedback Constipation management Topical oestrogen in post-menopausal patients with vaginal atrophy Stress incontinence: general principles, duloxetine (SNRI in women), surgery Urge continence: general principles, anticholinergic, surgery Overflow incontinence: acute intermittent catherization, timed voiding, underlying cause |
| Complications | ↑ contact with urine: dermatitis, skin infections, UTIs |

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
| Definition | Acute/chronic inability to voluntarily empty the bladder |
|---|---|
| Aetiology | ![](notes/renal/images/nephrology-and-urology-anu/img020.jpg) Mechanical obstruction Enlarged prostate: BPH, cancer, prostatitis Urethral narrowing: stricture, carcinoma, posterior urethral valves, urethritis Bladder neck obstruction: calculi, cancer, bladder tamponade Phimosis: congenital/acquired foreskin constriction  inability to retract Functional obstruction Detrusor underactivity and/or sphincter overactivity (neurogenic bladder, spinal cord compression, trauma, MS, PD, pelvic splanchnic nerve  bladder denervation, diabetic autonomic neuropathy) Drug-induced urinary retention: ↓ detrusor activity (anticholinergics, narcotics, TCAs, antipsychotics) and  ↑ urethral sphincter tone (sympathomimetics) Detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia Urethral/bladder trauma Post-operative urinary retention |
| Urethral stricture | Definition: narrowing of the urethra with possible restriction of urinary flow Aetiology: trauma/iatrogenic, post-infectious, congenital, idiopathy Presentation: straining, weak stream, dribbling, pollakiuria, incomplete urination, retention Investigations: uroflowmetry, retrograde urethrography/voiding cystourethrography Treatment: Internal urethrotomy: release stricture/scar tissue Urethroplasty: open reconstruction with xcision of fibrotic urethra and reanastomosis Permanent urethral stents |
| Presentation | History: suprapubic pain, incomplete emptying, weak stream, purulent/bloody meatal discharge Examination: palpable/percussible bladder, ↑ prostate size, ↓ anal sphincter tone Neurological: ↓DTR, ↓ “anal wink”, saddle anaesthesia |
| Investigations | Bloods: FBC, EUC, Cr, BUN U/A and urine MC&S U/S Cystoscopy Urodynamic studies PVR |
| Treatment | Underlying cause Catherization: Immediate transurethral Foley in acute retention, and intermittent in chronic retention Suprapubic catheter if above not possible (e.g. urethral stricture, ↑prostate, contraindications e.g. trauma) Post-operative: encourage ambulation, a-blockers to relax bladder neck outlet |
| Complications | Hydronephrosis Definition: distention/dilation of renal pelvis and calyces with proximal dilatation Aetiology: mechanical (congenital, renal stones, BPH, cervical cancer, ureteral trauma), functional (neuropathic, pharmacological e.g. a-adrenergic, hormonal e.g. pregnancy), VUR Complications: compression, atrophy of renal cortex and medulla |
