docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
- Location: between the bladder and the penis; just in front of the rectum

- Anatomy: urethra runs through the centre of the prostate

- Three zones:

- Peripheral (70% volume):  fibromuscular stroma

- Central (25% volume):  contains secretory ducts

- Transitional (5% volume): proximal to urethra

- Blood supply: inferior vesical artery and middle rectal arteries

- Nerves: parasympathetic (S2-4) and sympathetic (L1-2)

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
- 70% glandular and 30% stromal tissue

- Secretes fluid that nourishes and protects sperm – alkaline to neutralize vaginal acidity, proteolytic enzymes, prostatic acid phosphatase, PSA

- During ejaculation, the prostate squeezes this fluid into the urethra, and it’s expelled with sperm as semen

- The vasa deferentia bring sperm from the testes to the seminal vesicles. The seminal vesicles contribute fluid to semen during ejaculation.

docs.title: Structural and Urological Renal Disease
docs.text:
| Definition | Benign stromal and glandular hyperplasia of the transitional zone of the prostate |
|---|---|
| Epidemiology | Prevalence increases with age (~50% of 50 y/o, ~80% of 80 y/o) |
| Aetiology | DHT: converted from testosterone by 5-α reductase and is a potent prostatic growth factor Gene amplification of androgen receptors: present in glandular epithelial and stromal cells  ↑ androgen receptor sensitivity to androgens  prostatic hyperplasia Androgen-oestrogen imbalance: ↑ oestrogen: testosterone (with ↑ age) Stem cell proliferation and longevity |
| Pathophysiology | Alpha-adrenergic receptors in prostate capsule, stroma and bladder neck which produce DHT Glandular/stromal hyperplasia  prostatic urethral compression  bladder outlet obstruction In bladder outlet obstruction, ↑ detrusor activity (irritative Sx), weakening of bladder wall (UTIs, retention, bladder stones), detrusor muscle hypertrophy (trabeculation/pseudodiverticula) |
| Risk Factors | Cigarette smoking, metabolic syndrome, genetic predisposition |
| AUA BPH Symptom Score | FUNWISE Frequency, Urgency, Nocturia, Weak stream, Intermittency, Straining, Emptying incomplete feeling 0-7: Mildly symptomatic 8-19: Moderately symptomatic 20-35: Severely symptomatic Note: dysuria not included in score but is commonly associated with BPH Initial alpha-adrenergic antagonist monotherapy for <20, combination therapy for >20 |
| Presentation | LUTS: irritative (frequency, urgency, urge incontinence, dysuria) and obstructive symptoms (hesitance, straining, poor/intermittent stream, dribbling, sensation of incomplete voiding) Gross haematuria DRE: symmetrically enlarged, smooth (no nodules), firm, non-tender, rubbery/elastic text |
| Investigations | Urinalysis and urine culture: UTI, haematuria Bloods: PSA (co-existent prostate cancer), renal (BUN, Cr, EUC) Abdominal U/S: ↑ total prostate valud, ↑ post-void residual urine volume (> 100 mL) Transrectal U/S: if prostate cancer suspected from DRE/PSA Uroflowmetry: normal maximal urinary flow rate ↓ and is <15 mL in bladder outlet obstruction and <10 mL is an indication for surgery CTAP: hydronephrosis, mass Cystoscopy/biopsy if indicated (suspected malignancy, surgical intervention) |
| Differentials | Prostate cancer, prostatitis, prostatic abscess, urethral strictures, posterior urethral valves |
| Management | Lifestyle:  limit fluids, bladder training, monitoring Medical therapy: indicated in mild BPH, discomfort from symptoms Alpha-blockers (e.g. tamsulosin, doxazosin. terazosin)  relaxation of smooth muscle of bladder neck and urethra  ↓ resistance to urinary outflow  symptom improvement 5-α reductase inhibitor (e.g. finasteride, dutasteride)  blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT  ↓ prostatic growth, ↑ prostatic apoptosis/involution SE: sexual/erectile/ejaculatory dysfunction, ↓ libido Parasympatholytics/anticholinergics (e.g. oxybutynin, darifenacin) Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors Surgical intervention: indicated in severe B

| Definition | A condition in which the spermatic cord becomes twisted within the scrotum, leading to venous engorgement, arterial compromise and irreversible damage if not resolved after 6-12 hours |
|---|---|
| Epidemiology | Peak incidence in neonatal period and puberty |
| Aetiology | Idiopathic (bell-clap deformity  mobile testes  twists itself  ischemia/toxin), iatrogenic, trauma |

docs.title: Tubulointerstitial and Tubular Disorders
docs.h: Finals-study-2.pdf — Renal Notes, Section 5: Tubulointerstitial and Tubular Disorders (pages 47-51)
docs.text:
Cross-checked against Robbins, StatPearls, and standard renal physiology/clinical texts. The

RTAs and inherited tubulopathies are stable textbook content but very high-yield for data-interpretation questions — this section rewards precise memorisation of the electrolyte/urine patterns.

docs.title: Tubulointerstitial and Tubular Disorders
docs.text:
##### Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN)

- **Mechanism:** hypersensitivity reaction causing inflammation of the renal interstitium →

AKI.
- **Causes:**
  - **Drugs (~70%): NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, penicillins/cephalosporins,**

###### allopurinol, rifampicin, sulfonamides, diuretics

  - **Infection:** pyelonephritis, leptospirosis, legionella
  - **Autoimmune/systemic:** sarcoidosis, Sjögren's, SLE, **TINU** (tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis)
- **Classic triad** (fever, rash, eosinophilia) — present in **<10%,** so its absence doesn't exclude AIN.
- **Investigations:** AKI, **sterile pyuria, white cell casts, eosinophiluria** (poor sensitivity/specificity — no longer relied upon), mild proteinuria.
- **Management: stop the offending drug** (the key step); **corticosteroids** if no improvement or severe. Usually recovers, but can leave chronic damage.

##### Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis

- Slowly progressive interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy.
- **Analgesic nephropathy:** chronic heavy use (esp. old compound analgesics with phenacetin); **papillary necrosis;** look for a "ring sign" on imaging.
- **Lithium nephrotoxicity: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus** (commonest renal effect) and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis; monitor levels and renal function.
- Others: chronic obstruction/reflux, sarcoidosis, heavy metals, aristolochic acid, myeloma.

docs.title: Tubulointerstitial and Tubular Disorders
docs.text:
All RTAs cause a **normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis.** Distinguish by potassium, urine pH, and associated features. Normal anion gap = bicarb loss w/ compensatory hyperchloraemic; vs high anion gap = increased acids added e.g. ketoacid, lactic acid, toxins

|  | Type 1 (Distal) | Type 2 (Proximal) | Type 4 (Hyperkalaemic) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Defect | Distal H⁺ secretion fails (α-intercalated cell) | Proximal HCO₃⁻ reabsorption fails | Aldosterone deficiency/resistance |
| Serum K⁺ | LOW (hypokalaemia) | LOW (hypokalaemia) | HIGH (hyperkalaemia) |
| Urine pH | >5.5 (inappropriately high) — can't acidify urine | Variable; <5.5 once below reabsorptive threshold | <5.5 (appropriately low) |
| Causes | Autoimmune (Sjögren's, RA), hypercalciuria, amphotericin, genetic | Fanconi syndrome, myeloma, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, Wilson's, cystinosis | Diabetes (commonest), Addison's, ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs, heparin, trimethoprim, spironolactone |
| Complication s | Nephrocalcinosis, calcium phosphate stones (alkaline urine, hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia); rickets/osteomalacia | Rickets/osteomalacia; stones uncommon | Mild acidosis |
| Treatment | Oral bicarbonate/citrate; potassium replacement | Bicarbonate (large doses needed) + potassium; thiazide | Fludrocortisone, dietary K⁺ restriction, loop diuretic; stop offending drugs |

**The urine anion gap** (Na⁺ + K⁺ − Cl⁻) — used to work out the cause of a normal-anion-gap acidosis:
- **Negative** ("neg-GUT-ive") → **GI bicarbonate loss (diarrhoea)** — kidney appropriately excreting NH₄Cl
- **Positive** → **RTA** — kidney failing to excrete ammonium

Memory hooks: Type **1** = **one** = distal = high urine pH + stones. Type **2** = proximal = Fanconi.

Type **4** = the only **hyperkalaemic** RTA = **hypoaldosteronism.**

docs.title: Tubulointerstitial and Tubular Disorders
docs.text:
- **Generalised proximal tubular dysfunction** → failure to reabsorb multiple solutes:
  - **Glycosuria (with normal blood glucose),** aminoaciduria, phosphaturia (→ hypophosphataemia → **osteomalacia/rickets),** bicarbonaturia (→ **type 2 RTA),** uricosuria, tubular proteinuria, **hypokalaemia**
- **Causes: myeloma (commonest acquired cause in adults),** drugs **(tenofovir,** ifosfamide, aminoglycosides, expired tetracyclines), heavy metals, **Wilson's disease,** **cystinosis** (commonest inherited, children), Sjögren's.
- Recognise it from the combination: glycosuria + normoglycaemia + hypophosphataemia

+ hypokalaemia + acidosis.

docs.title: Tubulointerstitial and Tubular Disorders
docs.text:
| Disorder | "Acts like" | Defect | Key electrolytes | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bartter syndrome | Loop diuretic (furosemide) | NKCC2 in thick ascending limb | Hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, normal/low BP, hypercalciuria | Presents younger/more severe; normal Mg²⁺; may have nephrocalcinosis |
| Gitelman syndrome | Thiazide | NCC in distal convoluted tubule | Hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, normal/low BP, HYPOcalciuria | Hypomagnesaemia ; milder, older presentation |
| Liddle syndrome | Excess ENaC activity ("always-on" aldosterone effect) | Gain-of-fun ction ENaC | Hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, HYPERTENSION, LOW renin & aldosterone | Treat with amiloride (not spironolactone) |
| Apparent mineralocorticoi d excess | Cortisol acting on MR | 11β-HSD2 deficiency (can't inactivate cortisol) | Hypokalaemia, alkalosis, hypertension, low renin/aldosterone | Also caused by liquorice excess |

###### Discriminators worth locking in:

- **Bartter vs Gitelman:** both look like diuretic abuse (hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, normal/low BP), but **calcium separates them — Bartter = hyperCALCiuria (loop-like),**

###### Gitelman = hypoCALCiuria + hypomagnesaemia (thiazide-like).

- **Liddle vs Bartter/Gitelman:** Liddle is **HYPERtensive with LOW aldosterone** — it mimics hyperaldosteronism but the aldosterone is suppressed, and it responds to **amiloride, not spironolactone.**

##### Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

- **Collecting duct resistance to ADH** → inability to concentrate urine → **polyuria,** **polydipsia, dilute urine despite raised plasma osmolality.**
- **Causes: lithium** (commonest acquired), **hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia,** chronic kidney disease, inherited **(AVPR2** X-linked, or aquaporin-2).
- **Water deprivation test:** urine stays dilute after deprivation AND **fails to concentrate** **after desmopressin** (distinguishes from cranial DI, which does respond to desmopressin).
- **Management:** treat the cause; **thiazides (paradoxical antidiuresis),** **low-salt/low-protein diet, amiloride** (esp. lithium-induced).

docs.title: Tubulointerstitial and Tubular Disorders
docs.text:
| Clue | Diagnosis |
| --- | --- |
| AKI + new PPI/NSAID/antibiotic + sterile pyuria + white cell casts | Acute interstitial nephritis |
| Normal anion gap acidosis, hypokalaemia, urine pH >5.5, stones | Type 1 (distal) RTA |
| Normal anion gap acidosis, hypokalaemia, + glycosuria/phosphaturia | Type 2 (proximal) RTA / Fanconi |
| Normal anion gap acidosis, hyperkalaemia, diabetic | Type 4 RTA (hypoaldosteronism) |
| Hypokalaemic alkalosis, normal BP, high urine calcium | Bartter syndrome |
| Hypokalaemic alkalosis, normal BP, low urine calcium + low Mg | Gitelman syndrome |
| Hypokalaemic alkalosis + hypertension + low renin/aldosterone | Liddle syndrome (treat with amiloride) |
| Polyuria, dilute urine, on lithium, no response to desmopressin | Nephrogenic DI |
| Glycosuria with normal blood glucose | Proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi / SGLT2 inhibitor) |

##### Sources

Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease; StatPearls (RTA, Bartter, Gitelman, Liddle,

Fanconi, nephrogenic DI); standard clinical texts. The RTA and tubulopathy electrolyte/urine patterns were cross-checked across at least two sources; these are stable, well-established facts.

---

docs.title: Tubulointerstitial and Tubular Disorders
docs.text:
Acute/chronic inflammation of the renal tubules and interstitium

##### acute tubulo-interstitial nephritis

| Definition | Rapid (days to weeks) decline in renal function and accounts for 10-20% of all AKI |
|---|---|
| Aetiology | Hypersensitivity: antibiotics (B-lactams, sulphonamides, rifampin, quinolones, cephalosporins), NSAIDs, diuretics, allopurinol, PPIs, phenytoin, acyclovir, methotrexate Infectious: bacterial pyelonephritis, leptospirosis, streptococcus, legionella, CMV, EBV Immune: SLE, Sjogren’s, sarcoidosis Idiopathic Note: Pee (diuretics) Pain (NSAIDs) Penicillins and cephalosporins Proton pump inhibitors RifamPicin |
| Pathophysiology | Hypersensitivity or tubular obstruction/toxicity  inflammatory cells infiltrate interstitium |
| Presentation | Underlying disease symptoms AKI: painless haematuria Hypersensitivity: fever, rash, arthralgia Pyelonephritis: CVA tenderness, flank pain |
| Investigations | Urine: proteinuria, haematuria, pyuria, WBC casts, eosinophils (AIN) Bloods:  urea,  Cr, eosinophilia (drug reaction), metabolic acidosis (RTA), PO43-, K+, Na+ Renal biopsy definite Gallium scan:  signal=infiltrate |
| Management | Discontinue drugs and IVF Antibiotics if infectious Corticosteroids in allergic or immune disease |
| Prognosis | Recovery within 2 weeks if insult can be eliminated |

##### chronic tubulo-interstitial nephritis

| Definition | Slowly progressive renal failure, moderate proteinuria and abnormal tubular function signs |
|---|---|
| Aetiology | Persistent acute TIN UTI/chronic pyelonephritis: tumours, stones, bladder outlet obstruction, VUR Nephrotoxins Analgesic nephropathy: NSAIDs, acetaminophen Crystal-induced: acyclovir, methotrexate, cisplatin, lithium, cyclosporine Heavy metals Vascular disease Malignancies: multiple myeloma, lymphoma Immune: SLE, Sjogren’s, anti-GBM, sarcoidosis Hereditary: cystic disease, sickle cell disease |
| Pathophysiology | prostacyclin synthesis → vasoconstriction of the medullary blood vessels → papillary ischemia/necrosis, fibrosis of interstitium with tubular atrophy, mononuclear cell inflammation |
| Presentation | Painless haematuria, pyuria, fatigue, nausea Underlying aetiology- colicky pain due to papillary necrosis, multiple myeloma Renal papillary necrosis: coagulative necrosis of the renal medullary pyramids and papillae Aetiology (POSTCARDS): pyelonephritis, obstruction, sickle cell disease, Tb, cirrhosis, analgesia, renal transplant rejection, DM, systemic vasculitis Ischemia  necrosis and sloughing of the papillae  ureteral obstruction  scarring |
| Investigations | Tubular dysfunction: e.g. acidosis, electrolyte disturbances e.g. K+ Progressive renal failure: azotemia, uremia Ultrasound: shrunken kidneys with irregular contours |
| Management | Stop offending agent or treat underlying disease Supportive measures: correct metabolic disorders (Ca2+, PO43- and anaemia) Forced diuresis If necessary, plasmapheresis/dialysis |

| Definition | In

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.h: Respiratory Master Notes — Clinical Assessment & Investigation

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
**Cardinal symptoms and their discriminators:**
- **Dyspnoea** — grade with the **mMRC scale (0–4)**: 0 = only on strenuous exercise; 1 = hurrying/slight hill; 2 = walks slower than peers/stops on the level; 3 = stops after ~100 m; 4 = breathless dressing/housebound. Orthopnoea and PND suggest cardiac, but severe COPD/large effusions cause them too.
- **Cough** — dry (ILD, ACE inhibitor, asthma) vs productive (COPD, bronchiectasis, pneumonia). **>8 weeks = chronic**; think asthma, GORD, post-nasal drip (the "big three"), ACEi, and always exclude cancer/TB in a smoker.
- **Sputum** — copious purulent/mucopurulent daily = **bronchiectasis**; "rusty" = pneumococcal pneumonia; pink frothy = pulmonary oedema; **haemoptysis** demands exclusion of cancer, TB, PE, bronchiectasis.
- **Wheeze** (expiratory, polyphonic = airflow obstruction) vs **stridor** (inspiratory, monophonic = **upper-airway obstruction — an emergency clue**).

**Signs by pathology — the classic exam table** (percussion / breath sounds / vocal resonance / mediastinal shift):

| Pathology | Percussion | Breath sounds | Vocal resonance | Trachea/mediastinum |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Consolidation** | Dull | **Bronchial** + crackles | **Increased** | Central |
| **Pleural effusion** | **Stony dull** | Reduced/absent | Reduced | Pushed **away** (if large) |
| **Pneumothorax** | Resonant/hyper-resonant | Reduced/absent | Reduced | Central (**away** if tension) |
| **Collapse (lobar)** | Dull | Reduced | Reduced | Pulled **towards** |
| **Fibrosis** | Normal/dull | **Fine end-inspiratory ("velcro") crackles** | Normal/increased | Central |

*Two discriminators to lock in:* **effusion pushes, collapse pulls** (the mediastinum); and **consolidation increases vocal resonance, effusion decreases it** — the fastest way to separate the two "dull bases."

**Peripheral signs:** finger **clubbing** (lung cancer, ILD/IPF, bronchiectasis, empyema, CF — *not* uncomplicated COPD or asthma), **cyanosis** (central = <~85% sats), **CO₂-retention flap/bounding pulse/warm peripheries**, and cor pulmonale (raised JVP, peripheral oedema, loud P2, RV heave).

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
**Spirometry — the master pattern:**

| Pattern | FEV₁ | FVC | **FEV₁/FVC** | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Obstructive** | ↓↓ | ↓ or normal | **<0.7** (↓) | Asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis |
| **Restrictive** | ↓ | ↓↓ | **≥0.7** (normal or ↑) | ILD/fibrosis, chest-wall, neuromuscular, obesity |
| **Mixed** | ↓↓ | ↓↓ | ↓ | Combined disease |

⚑ **Fixed 0.7 vs the lower limit of normal (LLN):** GOLD still uses a **post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.70** to define COPD, but **ATS/ERS 2022 recommend the LLN (z-score < −1.645)** because the fixed ratio over-diagnoses obstruction in the elderly and under-diagnoses in the young. Know both; quote 0.7 for the COPD definition and mention LLN as the more physiological cut-off.

**Reversibility** ⚑ — the ATS/ERS 2022 criterion for a significant bronchodilator response changed to a **>10% change relative to predicted** FEV₁ or FVC (the older "≥12% *and* ≥200 mL" is still widely quoted and taught). Marked reversibility favours asthma; COPD is by definition not fully reversible.

**Lung volumes** (plethysmography/gas dilution — *not* spirometry): **restriction is confirmed by a low TLC**; **obstruction shows raised RV and TLC (gas trapping/hyperinflation)**.

**DLCO/TLCO** adds the "why":
- **Obstruction + low DLCO → emphysema**; **obstruction + normal/high DLCO → asthma**.
- **Restriction + low DLCO → ILD/parenchymal** (intrinsic lung disease).
- **Restriction + normal DLCO → extra-parenchymal** (chest wall, neuromuscular, obesity — the lungs are fine, they just can't be moved).
- **Isolated low DLCO with normal spirometry → pulmonary vascular disease (e.g. PAH), early emphysema, or anaemia.**

**Flow–volume loops:**
- **Obstruction** — scooped-out (concave) expiratory limb.
- **Fixed obstruction** (e.g. tracheal stenosis, goitre) — **flattening of *both* inspiratory and expiratory limbs**.
- **Variable extrathoracic** (e.g. vocal-cord dysfunction) — flat **inspiratory** limb.
- **Variable intrathoracic** (e.g. tracheomalacia) — flat **expiratory** limb.

**Peak expiratory flow (PEF)** — effort-dependent; used for **asthma diagnosis (diurnal variability >10%) and monitoring/exacerbation severity**, expressed as % of personal best or predicted.

docs.h: 3.3 Arterial Blood Gas Interpretation *(the single highest-yield data skill)*
docs.text:
**A systematic approach:**
1. **Oxygenation** — PaO₂ and the **A–a gradient** (PAO₂ ≈ 150 − PaCO₂/0.8 on room air).
2. **pH** — acidaemia (<7.35) or alkalaemia (>7.45).
3. **Respiratory component** — PaCO₂ (>6.0 kPa/45 mmHg = retention).
4. **Metabolic component** — HCO₃⁻/base excess.
5. **Compensation** and whether the picture is **mixed**.

**Respiratory failure types:**

| | **Type 1** | **Type 2** |
|---|---|---|
| PaO₂ | **Low** (<8 kPa / 60 mmHg) | **Low** |
| PaCO₂ | Normal or low | **High** (>6.0 kPa / 45 mmHg) |
| Core problem | **V/Q mismatch / oxygenation failure** | **Ventilatory (pump) failure** |
| Causes | Pneumonia, PE, oedema, ILD, early asthma | COPD, exhausted asthma, opioids, neuromuscular, chest wall, OHS |

**Acute vs chronic type 2 failure** — the exam trap: look at the **pH and bicarbonate**.
- **Acute** T2RF: high CO₂, **low pH, normal HCO₃⁻** (no time to compensate) — e.g. tiring asthmatic (a **normal or rising CO₂ in acute asthma is a red flag** — the patient is exhausting).
- **Chronic** T2RF: high CO₂, **near-normal pH, high HCO₃⁻** (renal compensation) — e.g. stable COPD.
- **Acute-on-chronic**: high CO₂, low pH **and** high HCO₃⁻.

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
**Chest X-ray — read systematically** (patient details → adequacy [RIPE: Rotation, Inspiration ≥6 anterior ribs, Penetration, Exposure] → ABCDE: Airway/trachea, Breathing/lung fields, Cardiac, Diaphragm/costophrenic angles, Everything else/bones/soft tissue).
- **Silhouette sign** — loss of a normal border localises pathology: a lost **right heart border = right middle lobe**; lost **left heart border = lingula**; lost **hemidiaphragm = lower lobe**.
- **Consolidation** = air bronchograms, no volume loss. **Collapse** = volume loss (raised hemidiaphragm, tracheal/mediastinal shift *towards*, crowded ribs). **Effusion** = homogeneous opacity with a **meniscus**, blunted costophrenic angle. **Pneumothorax** = a lung edge with absent lung markings peripherally; **tension** = mediastinal shift *away* + depressed hemidiaphragm (but tension is a **clinical** diagnosis — don't wait for the film).

**CT:**
- **HRCT** — the investigation for **ILD** (reticulation, honeycombing, ground-glass) and **bronchiectasis** (signet-ring, tram-track).
- **CTPA** — first-line for **PE**.
- **Staging CT (chest/abdomen ± PET)** for lung cancer.

**Solitary pulmonary nodule pathway** — features favouring malignancy: **larger size, spiculated/irregular margins, upper lobe, older age, smoker, growth over time**; benign clues: **fat (hamartoma), popcorn/laminated/central calcification, stability >2 years**. Size-based CT surveillance vs PET vs biopsy per the risk (British Thoracic Society/Fleischner algorithms).

**Other:** **bronchoscopy** (± **EBUS-TBNA** for mediastinal node sampling/staging), **pleural aspiration/biopsy** (see Section 8), sputum MC&S/AFB/cytology, and blood biomarkers (NT-proBNP to exclude cardiac dyspnoea, D-dimer for PE probability, eosinophils to guide ICS, precipitins/autoantibodies for ILD).

---

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Dull base, **increased** vocal resonance, bronchial breathing | Consolidation |
| **Stony** dull base, **reduced** breath sounds & resonance | Pleural effusion |
| Mediastinum pushed **away** | Large effusion / tension pneumothorax |
| Mediastinum pulled **towards** | Lobar collapse |
| Fine end-inspiratory "velcro" crackles | Pulmonary fibrosis |
| Inspiratory **stridor** | Upper-airway obstruction (emergency) |
| Clubbing + lung disease | Cancer, IPF, bronchiectasis, empyema, CF (**not** COPD/asthma) |
| FEV₁/FVC <0.7 | Obstructive |
| FEV₁/FVC ≥0.7 with low FVC & low TLC | Restrictive |
| Restriction + **low** DLCO | Intrinsic (ILD) |
| Restriction + **normal** DLCO | Extra-parenchymal (chest wall/neuromuscular/obesity) |
| Isolated low DLCO, normal spirometry | Pulmonary vascular disease / early emphysema / anaemia |
| Flat **both** loop limbs | Fixed large-airway obstruction |
| Flat **inspiratory** limb only | Variable extrathoracic (e.g. vocal-cord dysfunction) |
| High CO₂, low pH, **normal** HCO₃⁻ | **Acute** type 2 failure |
| High CO₂, normal pH, **high** HCO₃⁻ | **Chronic** type 2 failure (compensated) |
| Rising/normal CO₂ in acute severe asthma | **Exhaustion — life-threatening** |
| Lost right heart border on CXR | Right middle lobe |
| Lost left heart border on CXR | Lingula |

##### Sources
ATS/ERS Technical Standard on spirometry & interpretation (2019/2022 — LLN, revised reversibility threshold); GOLD 2025 (fixed 0.70 for COPD); BTS/ARTP PFT guidance; Merck Manual Professional (PFTs, ABG, respiratory failure); Talley & O'Connor *Clinical Examination*; BTS/Fleischner pulmonary nodule guidance. Numeric thresholds (reversibility, FEV₁/FVC, respiratory-failure cut-offs) cross-checked between ATS/ERS and GOLD/Merck.

docs.title: Interstitial (Diffuse Parenchymal) Lung Disease
docs.h: Respiratory Master Notes — Interstitial (Diffuse Parenchymal) Lung Disease

docs.title: Interstitial (Diffuse Parenchymal) Lung Disease
docs.text:
ILD = a heterogeneous group causing **inflammation and/or fibrosis of the lung interstitium** → **restrictive** spirometry, **low DLCO**, and **fine "velcro" crackles**. The workup triangulates **HRCT pattern + serology + exposure/drug history**, discussed at an **ILD MDT**; biopsy only when the diagnosis remains unclear.

**Two anchors that solve most ILD questions:**

**(a) Zone of predominance:**

| Upper-zone fibrosis — **"CHARTS"** | Lower-zone fibrosis |
|---|---|
| **C**oal worker's pneumoconiosis / **C**ystic fibrosis | **I**diopathic pulmonary fibrosis |
| **H**ypersensitivity pneumonitis | Connective-tissue disease (RA, systemic sclerosis) |
| **A**nkylosing spondylitis | **A**sbestosis |
| **R**adiation | Drugs (amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin) |
| **T**uberculosis / **S**arcoidosis / **S**ilicosis | |

**(b) UIP vs NSIP pattern:**
- **UIP (usual interstitial pneumonia)** — **peripheral, basal, reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, heterogeneous/patchy**; the pattern of **IPF** (and chronic HP, asbestosis, RA).
- **NSIP** — **more uniform ground-glass, less honeycombing, subpleural sparing**; associated with **connective-tissue disease**; steroid-responsive.

docs.title: Interstitial (Diffuse Parenchymal) Lung Disease
docs.text:
Progressive fibrosing ILD of **unknown cause**, older patients, **UIP pattern**. Clinical: insidious exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, **fine bibasal velcro crackles, clubbing**; restrictive PFTs with low DLCO. Diagnosis by **HRCT UIP pattern** (MDT), excluding CTD/exposure. Poor prognosis (median survival ~3–5 years).

⚑ **Antifibrotics — a genuine change in management:** **pirfenidone** and **nintedanib** *slow the decline in FVC* (they don't reverse fibrosis) and are now standard for IPF and other **progressive fibrosing ILD phenotypes**. Steroids/immunosuppression **do not help IPF** (and can harm — the PANTHER trial) — a classic exam contrast with the CTD-associated/NSIP ILDs, which *are* steroid-responsive. Supportive: oxygen, pulmonary rehab, treat reflux, **lung transplant** in suitable candidates.

docs.title: Interstitial (Diffuse Parenchymal) Lung Disease
docs.text:
Multisystem **non-caseating granulomatous** disease, commonest in young adults (and, classically, higher incidence/severity in African-Caribbean patients). Lung is involved in >90%.
- **CXR staging:** 0 (normal), **1 = bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) alone**, 2 = BHL + infiltrates, 3 = infiltrates alone, 4 = fibrosis.
- **Löfgren syndrome** = **BHL + erythema nodosum + arthralgia ± fever** — an **acute, good-prognosis** presentation, often self-limiting.
- Extra-pulmonary: skin (**lupus pernio**, erythema nodosum), eyes (uveitis), **hypercalcaemia** (macrophage 1α-hydroxylase → ↑vitamin D activation), cardiac (arrhythmia/heart block), neuro, parotid.
- Bloods: **raised serum ACE** (non-specific), **hypercalcaemia/hypercalciuria**; biopsy shows **non-caseating granulomas**. Management: many need **no treatment** (observe); **corticosteroids** for organ-threatening disease (eye, cardiac, neuro, hypercalcaemia, progressive lung).

docs.title: Interstitial (Diffuse Parenchymal) Lung Disease
docs.text:
**Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis)** — immune reaction to inhaled organic antigens: **bird fancier's lung** (avian proteins), **farmer's lung** (thermophilic actinomycetes in mouldy hay). **Acute** (flu-like hours after exposure, reversible) vs **chronic** (upper/mid-zone fibrosis). **Discriminator: symptoms relate to exposure** — take an occupational/hobby/pet history.

**Pneumoconioses (inorganic dust):**

| Disease | Exposure | Signature |
|---|---|---|
| **Coal worker's pneumoconiosis** | Coal dust | Upper-zone nodules; **Caplan syndrome** (+ RA → nodules) |
| **Silicosis** | Sandblasting, mining, quarrying | Upper-zone nodules, **"eggshell" hilar node calcification**; ↑**TB** risk |
| **Asbestosis** | Asbestos (latency decades) | **Lower-zone** fibrosis; **pleural plaques** (benign marker of exposure); risk of **mesothelioma** and bronchial carcinoma |
| **Berylliosis** | Aerospace, electronics | Sarcoid-like granulomas |

*Discriminator:* **pleural plaques = exposure marker (benign)**; **asbestosis = the fibrosis**; **mesothelioma = the malignancy** — three different things from the same fibre.

docs.title: Interstitial (Diffuse Parenchymal) Lung Disease
docs.text:
Always screen for connective-tissue disease in new ILD (**RA, systemic sclerosis** [commonly NSIP], **dermatomyositis/anti-synthetase — anti-Jo-1, "mechanic's hands"**, SLE, Sjögren): symptoms, autoantibodies (ANA, ENA, RF/anti-CCP, myositis panel). **Drug-induced ILD** — the classic culprits: **amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin** (and now several biologics/checkpoint inhibitors → pneumonitis). Management is to remove the cause and treat the (often steroid-responsive) inflammation.

---

docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |

| Restrictive PFTs + low DLCO + velcro crackles | Interstitial lung disease |

##### Sources

Zone-of-predominance and UIP/NSIP features cross-checked between Robbins pathology and radiology standards.

docs.h: Respiratory (ANU) — cystic fibrosis — Interstitial (Diffuse Parenchymal) Lung Disease
docs.text:
| Definition | Autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation in cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene |
| --- | --- |
| Pathophysiology | Mutated CFTR gene → defective Cl- channel → inability to transport intracellular Cl- across the membrane → exocrine glands (sweat, mammary, salivary) produce hyperviscous secretions → accumulation of secretions and blockage of glands → chronic inflammation → organ damage |
| Presentation | GASTROINTESTINALFrequent in infancyMeconium ileus in first 24-48 hours of birthPancreatic insufficiency: steatorrhea, malabsorption, diarrhoea, ↓ vitamin A/D/E/K, diabetesLiver and bile duct: cholecystolithiasis, cholestasis, cirrhosis, portal HTNRESPIRATORYFrequent in adulthoodChronic lung infections: S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, B. cepacian, aspergillus fumigatusObstructive lung disease with bronchiectasisExpiratory wheeze, barrel chest, digital clubbingSWEAT GLANDS: salty sweatMUSCULOSKELETAL: osteopenia, frequent fractures, kyphoscoliosisUROGENITAL: nephrolithiasis, frequent UTIsGENITAL: ↓ fertility, males (obstructive azoospermia, absent VD, undescended testes), females (viscous cervical mucus, menstrual abnormalities) |
| Investigations | Sweat chloride test: ≥60 mmol/L on two occasionsCTFR gene mutation: via CVS/amniocentesis sampling, or in sweat-test -ve but suspicious adultsAbnormal nasal potential difference test: voltage measurements before and after CFTR chloride transport stimulation show abnormal epithelial secretion of chloridePFTs: ↓FEV1:FVC (obstructive pattern) |
| Management | General: chest physiotherapy, diet (high calorie), pancreatic enzyme and vitamin supplements, preventative annual vaccine (influenza, pneumococcal)Bronchodilators: salbutamol ± ipratropium bromideMucolytic: to reduce mucus viscosityHypertonic saline nebulisationAntibiotics: treating pulmonary infectionsGlucocorticoids: in chronic rhinosinusitis |

docs.h: Respiratory (ANU) — sarcoidosis — Interstitial (Diffuse Parenchymal) Lung Disease
docs.text:
| Definition | Idiopathic noncaseating granulomatous multi-system disease with lung involvement in 90%Now, numerous HLA antigens have been shown to play a role (thus familial sarcoidosis recognised) |
| --- | --- |
| Epidemiology | Commonly found in African American females and Northern European Caucasians |
| Pathophysiology | T-cell dysfunction and ↑ B-cell activity → local immune hyperactivity and inflammation→non-caseating granulomas commonly in the lungs and lymphatic system → pulmonary fibrosisAffects lungs, liver, eyes, skin nervous system, heart and kidney |
| Presentation | Mnemonic: GRUELINGGranulomas, General (fever, cough, malaise, weight loss, dyspnoea)aRthritisUveitisErythema nodosumLymphadenopathyInterstitial fibrosisNegative TB testGammaglobulinemia |

docs.title: Lung Cancer & Mediastinal Disease
docs.h: Respiratory Master Notes — Lung Cancer & Mediastinal Disease

docs.title: Lung Cancer & Mediastinal Disease
docs.text:
Leading cause of cancer death; **smoking** is the dominant risk (also asbestos, radon, occupational carcinogens; note **adenocarcinoma is the commonest type in non-smokers**). **The treatment-defining split is small-cell vs non-small-cell.**

| | **NSCLC (~85%)** | **SCLC (~15%)** |
|---|---|---|
| Subtypes | **Adenocarcinoma** (commonest, peripheral, non-smokers), **squamous** (central, cavitates, **hypercalcaemia via PTHrP**), large cell | Neuroendocrine, **central**, aggressive |
| Behaviour | Slower; **staged surgically if early** | **Very aggressive**, usually **metastatic at diagnosis** |
| Treatment | Surgery/SABR (early) → chemo-radiotherapy, **targeted therapy & immunotherapy** by molecular markers | **Chemotherapy ± radiotherapy** (rarely surgical); often responds then relapses |
| Paraneoplastic | **Squamous → hypercalcaemia (PTHrP)** | **SIADH, ectopic ACTH (Cushing's), LEMS** |

**Presentation:**
- **Local:** cough, haemoptysis, dyspnoea, recurrent/non-resolving pneumonia, wheeze, chest pain.
- **Local invasion syndromes:** **Pancoast tumour** (apex) → **Horner syndrome** (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) + T1 wasting/arm pain; **hoarseness** (recurrent laryngeal nerve); **SVC obstruction** (facial/arm swelling, distended veins, Pemberton's sign — **an oncological emergency**); phrenic nerve → diaphragm palsy; dysphagia; malignant effusion.
- **Metastatic:** liver, bone (pain, hypercalcaemia), brain (headache, seizures, focal signs), adrenal.
- **Paraneoplastic:** **SIADH** (SCLC), **ectopic ACTH** (SCLC), **hypercalcaemia** (squamous, PTHrP), **Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome** (SCLC), **clubbing/hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy**.

⚑ **Staging — TNM 9th edition (in clinical use from 1 January 2025):** the framework is unchanged but nodal and metastatic categories are subdivided for prognostic precision:
- **N2 is now split** into **N2a** (single ipsilateral mediastinal/subcarinal nodal station) and **N2b** (multiple N2 stations) — because single-station N2 has a better prognosis. (N1 and N3 unchanged.)
- **M1c is split** into **M1c1** (multiple extrathoracic metastases in a **single** organ system) and **M1c2** (multiple organ systems). (T categories and M1a/M1b unchanged.)
- Investigations: **contrast CT chest/upper abdomen**, **PET-CT** for staging, **MRI brain**, and **tissue** via bronchoscopy/**EBUS-TBNA** (also samples mediastinal nodes) or image-guided biopsy; **molecular testing (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, PD-L1, etc.)** guides targeted therapy in NSCLC.
- **Modern therapy:** **targeted agents** (EGFR/ALK inhibitors) and **immune checkpoint inhibitors** (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) have substantially changed advanced-NSCLC outcomes — a key contrast with older "chemo only" teaching. ⚑
- **Screening:** **low-dose CT** screening for high-risk (heavy) smokers is now recommended/implemented in several countries. ⚑

docs.title: Lung Cancer & Mediastinal Disease
docs.text: A single ≤3 cm rounded opacity. Weigh malignancy risk: **larger, spiculated/irregular, upper-lobe, older, smoker, growth** favour cancer; **benign calcification patterns (central, laminated, popcorn = hamartoma), fat, and 2-year stability** favour benign. Manage by risk with **CT surveillance vs PET-CT vs biopsy/resection** (BTS/Fleischner algorithms). *(A nodule >8 mm with intermediate/high risk generally goes to PET-CT ± biopsy.)*

docs.title: Lung Cancer & Mediastinal Disease
docs.text:
Localise by compartment (see Section 2): **anterior = 4 Ts** (**Thymoma** — associated with **myasthenia gravis, red-cell aplasia, hypogammaglobulinaemia**; **Teratoma/germ-cell**; **Lymphoma**; retrosternal **Thyroid**); **middle** = lymphadenopathy, vascular, cysts; **posterior** = **neurogenic tumours**. Metastatic disease to the lung is common (breast, colon, renal, sarcoma → "cannonball" metastases with renal/choriocarcinoma).

---

docs.title: Obstructive Airway Disease
docs.h: Respiratory Master Notes — Obstructive Airway Disease

docs.title: Obstructive Airway Disease
docs.text:
Chronic **reversible** airway inflammation → variable airflow obstruction, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, wheeze, cough, chest tightness, breathlessness (diurnal, triggered by allergens/exercise/cold/viruses).

**Diagnosis (objective confirmation — the pathway has changed)** ⚑: don't diagnose on symptoms alone. Supportive objective tests: **spirometry showing obstruction with bronchodilator reversibility**, **raised FeNO** (eosinophilic inflammation), **PEF variability >10%**, or bronchial challenge. *(NICE and GINA differ slightly on the order/first test — the shared principle for finals is "confirm objectively, don't treat on history alone.")*

⚑ **Chronic management — GINA 2025 "Track 1" (preferred):** the biggest change from older teaching. **SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended** (it increases severe exacerbation and death risk). Instead, everyone gets **ICS-containing treatment**, using **low-dose ICS–formoterol as the reliever**:
- **Steps 1–2:** *as-needed* low-dose **ICS–formoterol** (AIR — anti-inflammatory reliever).
- **Steps 3–5:** low-dose then medium-dose **ICS–formoterol as both maintenance and reliever (MART)**, escalating to add **LAMA**, then **biologics** / high-dose ICS for severe disease.
- **Track 2** (alternative, when Track 1 not possible): ICS whenever SABA taken / regular ICS + SABA reliever.

**Acute asthma — severity stratification (BTS/SIGN), memorise the thresholds:**

| Severity | Key features |
|---|---|
| **Moderate** | PEF 50–75% best/predicted, no features of severe |
| **Acute severe** | **PEF 33–50%**, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, **can't complete sentences** |
| **Life-threatening** | **PEF <33%**, **SpO₂ <92%**, silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, exhaustion, arrhythmia, hypotension, altered consciousness, **normal PaCO₂** |
| **Near-fatal** | **Raised PaCO₂** ± need for ventilation |

*The single most important trap: a **normal or rising CO₂ in acute asthma means the patient is tiring — call ICU.*** A silent chest is ominous (no air moving), not reassuring.

**Acute management — "O SHIT ME" / stepwise:** high-flow **Oxygen** (target 94–98%), nebulised **Salbutamol** (SABA, back-to-back/continuous), **Ipratropium** (SAMA) if severe/life-threatening, **steroids** (oral prednisolone or IV hydrocortisone), and — if not responding — **IV magnesium sulfate**, consider IV salbutamol/aminophylline and ICU. **Antibiotics only if infection**. Escalate to NIV/intubation for exhaustion/rising CO₂.

**Special phenotypes:** **occupational asthma** (symptoms better on days off/holidays — ask about work); **aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease** (asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin/NSAID sensitivity = **Samter's triad**); **ABPA** (asthma + fleeting infiltrates + **very high IgE, Aspergillus precipitins, eosinophilia, central bronchiectasis**).

docs.title: Obstructive Airway Disease
docs.text:
Persistent airflow limitation from **noxious exposure** (smoking >>; also biomass, occupational dust, **α₁-antitrypsin deficiency** in the young/non-smoker with **basal/panacinar** emphysema and liver disease). Chronic bronchitis (clinical: productive cough ≥3 months over 2 years) and emphysema (pathological) coexist.

**Diagnosis:** **post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.70** (GOLD). Grade airflow limitation by FEV₁ % predicted (GOLD 1 ≥80%, 2 = 50–79%, 3 = 30–49%, 4 <30%).

⚑ **GOLD "ABE" assessment (2023 onward — replaced the old ABCD):** combine **symptoms** (mMRC/CAT) with **exacerbation history**:
- **Group A** — low symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation (no hospitalisation): **a bronchodilator**.
- **Group B** — high symptoms, 0–1 exacerbation: **LABA + LAMA**.
- **Group E** — **≥2 moderate or ≥1 hospitalised exacerbation** (regardless of symptoms): **LABA + LAMA**, and **add ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300 cells/µL**.
- (Add/withhold ICS by eosinophils; **avoid ICS if eos <100** or frequent pneumonia. Roflumilast/azithromycin for selected frequent exacerbators.)

**Non-pharmacological (mortality/quality benefit):** **smoking cessation** (the only intervention that slows FEV₁ decline), **pulmonary rehabilitation**, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID), and **LTOT** where criteria met.

**Acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD):**
- **Controlled oxygen — target SpO₂ 88–92%** with a **28% Venturi** in known/at-risk retainers; get an ABG.
- Nebulised **salbutamol + ipratropium**; **oral prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days**; **antibiotics if increased sputum purulence/volume or consolidation**.
- **NIV (BiPAP)** for **persistent respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35 with PaCO₂ >6.0) despite maximal medical therapy** — a core exam indication. Intubation if NIV fails/contraindicated.

**Chronic complications:** chronic type 2 respiratory failure, **cor pulmonale**, secondary polycythaemia, weight loss, pneumothorax (bullae).

**LTOT criteria** ⚑ (assessed when stable, ≥2 ABGs 3 weeks apart, non-smoker): **PaO₂ ≤7.3 kPa (55 mmHg)**; **or 7.3–8.0 kPa** *with* cor pulmonale/pulmonary hypertension/secondary polycythaemia/nocturnal hypoxaemia. Used ≥15 h/day. (LTOT improves survival **only in chronic hypoxaemia**; it does not help isolated exertional or mild desaturation.)

docs.title: Obstructive Airway Disease
docs.text:
Permanent, abnormal **bronchial dilatation** from the **"vicious cycle"** of infection → inflammation → airway damage → impaired clearance → more infection. Causes: **post-infective** (childhood pneumonia, TB, whooping cough), **CF**, immunodeficiency, **ABPA**, primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener = situs inversus + bronchiectasis + sinusitis + infertility), connective-tissue disease, and traction (from fibrosis).

**Clinical:** chronic cough with **copious purulent/mucopurulent sputum**, recurrent infections, haemoptysis, coarse crackles. **HRCT is diagnostic**: **signet-ring sign** (airway wider than its accompanying vessel), **tram-track lines**, lack of tapering. Common colonisers: *Haemophilus influenzae* (commonest), and ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa*** (marks more severe disease/worse prognosis). Management: **airway clearance/physiotherapy**, treat exacerbations with **prolonged (often 14-day) targeted antibiotics**, long-term **azithromycin** for frequent exacerbators, treat the underlying cause, vaccination.

docs.title: Obstructive Airway Disease
docs.text:
**Autosomal recessive**, mutation in the **CFTR** chloride channel (commonest **ΔF508**), → thick secretions across exocrine organs.
- **Respiratory:** bronchiectasis, chronic infection (**Staph aureus early; Pseudomonas and Burkholderia cepacia later**), nasal polyps, ABPA.
- **GI/other:** pancreatic insufficiency (malabsorption, steatorrhoea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency), **meconium ileus** in neonates, CF-related diabetes, biliary disease, **male infertility (absent vas deferens)**, salt loss.
- **Diagnosis:** newborn screening (raised immunoreactive trypsinogen), confirmed by the **sweat test (chloride >60 mmol/L)** and/or genetics.

⚑ **CFTR modulator therapy** has transformed prognosis: **elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor** ("triple therapy", *Trikafta/Kaftrio*) for eligible genotypes markedly improves lung function and reduces exacerbations — a major shift from purely supportive care. Alongside: airway clearance, mucolytics (**dornase alfa, hypertonic saline**), pancreatic enzyme replacement + vitamins, aggressive infection treatment, and MDT care.

docs.title: Pleural Disease & Pneumothorax (acute — high yield)
docs.text:
Fluid in the pleural space. **Step one is always: transudate or exudate?** — because it splits the differential in half.

⚑ **Light's criteria** — the fluid is an **exudate** if **any one** of:
1. Pleural **protein / serum protein > 0.5**, or
2. Pleural **LDH / serum LDH > 0.6**, or
3. Pleural **LDH > two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH**.

*Light's criteria are sensitive for exudates but mislabel ~25% of transudates as exudates; if the clinical picture says transudate (e.g. heart failure on diuretics) but Light's says exudate, check the **serum–pleural albumin gradient (>12 g/L favours transudate)**.*

| | **Transudate** (protein <25 g/L) | **Exudate** (protein >35 g/L) |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | ↑hydrostatic / ↓oncotic pressure | ↑capillary permeability (inflammation) |
| Causes | **Heart failure** (commonest), cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia | **Pneumonia (para-pneumonic), malignancy, TB, PE, pancreatitis, RA/SLE** |

**Other pleural-fluid clues (the lookup table):**

| Finding | Suggests |
|---|---|
| **pH <7.2** in a para-pneumonic effusion | **Empyema / complicated effusion → chest drain** |
| **Low glucose** | Empyema, **RA**, TB, malignancy |
| **Very high amylase** | Pancreatitis, oesophageal rupture |
| **Milky (high triglyceride)** | Chylothorax (thoracic duct) |
| **Blood-stained** | Malignancy, PE, trauma, TB |
| **↑Adenosine deaminase / lymphocytes** | **TB** |
| Positive cytology | Malignant effusion |

Investigate an undiagnosed exudate with **pleural aspiration (protein, LDH, pH, glucose, cytology, microbiology, ADA)**, then **contrast CT and image-guided/thoracoscopic pleural biopsy** if malignancy suspected. Management: treat the cause; **therapeutic aspiration/drainage** for symptoms; **indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis** for recurrent malignant effusions. **A unilateral undiagnosed effusion in a smoker is cancer until proven otherwise.**

docs.title: Pleural Disease & Pneumothorax (acute — high yield)
docs.text:
Air in the pleural space → lung collapse.
- **Primary spontaneous** — no underlying lung disease; **tall, thin, young males, smokers** (apical bleb rupture).
- **Secondary spontaneous** — underlying disease (**COPD**, asthma, CF, ILD, PJP) — more dangerous because of poor reserve.
- **Traumatic/iatrogenic** — subclavian line, pleural procedure, ventilation.
- **Tension pneumothorax** — a **one-way valve** progressively traps air → mediastinal shift, obstructed venous return, cardiovascular collapse.

⚑ **Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis — do NOT wait for a CXR.** Signs: severe respiratory distress, hypotension/tachycardia, **tracheal deviation *away***, absent breath sounds + hyper-resonance, raised JVP. **Immediate treatment: large-bore needle decompression** (traditionally **2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line**; ⚑ many guidelines now favour the **4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line** — the same site as a chest drain — as more reliable in adults), then a chest drain.

⚑ **Updated (BTS 2023) management pathway — a shift from a purely size-based algorithm to a symptom-based one:** the primary question is now **"is the patient symptomatic and stable?"** rather than a fixed size cut-off.
- **Minimal symptoms and stable** → often **conservative (observation)**, even for larger primary pneumothoraces, with review.
- **Symptomatic** → **needle aspiration or drainage**; **ambulatory devices** (e.g. Heimlich-type one-way valves) are now an option in selected patients.
- **Secondary** pneumothorax and any instability → lower threshold to drain and admit.
- Recurrence prevention: **VATS pleurodesis/pleurectomy**; advise **no flying until resolved and no diving ever** (for those with a history).

docs.title: Pleural Disease & Pneumothorax (acute — high yield)
docs.text:
**Mesothelioma** — malignancy of the pleura, strongly linked to **asbestos** (long latency, 20–40 years); presents with **breathlessness, pleuritic pain, unilateral pleural effusion/thickening**; poor prognosis; **industrial compensation** implications — always take an occupational history. **Pleural metastases** (lung, breast, ovary, lymphoma) are the commonest cause of a malignant effusion. **Haemothorax** (blood), **chylothorax** (lymph, thoracic duct injury/lymphoma), and **empyema** (pus) complete the "what's in the space" differential.

docs.text:

| Exudate if… | Pleural/serum protein >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6, or LDH >⅔ ULN |
| Commonest transudate | Heart failure |
| Para-pneumonic effusion pH <7.2 | Empyema → **chest drain** |
| Low pleural glucose | Empyema, RA, TB, malignancy |
| Milky pleural fluid | Chylothorax |

docs.title: Pulmonary Vascular Disease (acute — high yield)
docs.text:
Usually embolus from a **DVT** (Virchow's triad: stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability). Presentation ranges from silent to pleuritic chest pain + dyspnoea + haemoptysis, to **haemodynamic collapse** (massive PE). Signs: tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypoxia, signs of DVT; ABG classically **type 1 failure with low CO₂ (respiratory alkalosis)**. ECG: sinus tachycardia (commonest); **S1Q3T3** is classic but uncommon; RV strain (T-wave inversion V1–V4).

**Diagnostic pathway (probability-first):**
- **Two-level Wells score** → **PE likely (>4)** vs **unlikely (≤4)**.
- **PE unlikely → D-dimer**: if negative, PE excluded (use an **age-adjusted cutoff = age × 10 µg/L for patients >50** to reduce false positives ⚑). If positive → imaging.
- **PE likely → CTPA** directly (don't delay for D-dimer). **V/Q scan** if CTPA contraindicated (renal impairment, contrast allergy, pregnancy — where a low-dose perfusion scan is often preferred).
- Interim/therapeutic anticoagulation should be started while awaiting imaging if there's any delay.

**Risk-stratify (drives disposition):** **sPESI** and haemodynamics —
- **High-risk (massive)** = **haemodynamic instability** (hypotension/shock) → **systemic thrombolysis** (e.g. alteplase), or embolectomy/catheter-directed therapy if lysis contraindicated.
- **Intermediate/low-risk** = anticoagulate; consider outpatient management if sPESI 0 and stable.

**Anticoagulation** ⚑: **DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) are first-line** for most — no bridging needed, oral from the start. Exceptions: **antiphospholipid syndrome (use warfarin)**, severe renal impairment, and **pregnancy/cancer considerations** (LMWH in pregnancy; DOACs or LMWH in cancer-associated VTE).
- **Duration:** provoked by a **transient major risk factor → 3 months**; **unprovoked or ongoing risk factor → ≥3–6 months, often long-term** (weigh bleeding risk); **cancer-associated → continue while active**.

**PE in pregnancy:** avoid D-dimer (physiologically raised); use compression Doppler first if DVT symptoms; **V/Q or CTPA** per local protocol; treat with **LMWH** (DOACs and warfarin avoided).

docs.title: Pulmonary Vascular Disease (acute — high yield)
docs.text:
⚑ **Definition updated (2022 ESC/ERS):** **mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) >20 mmHg at rest** (previously ≥25). Sub-classify with right heart catheter:
- **Pre-capillary PH:** mPAP >20, **PAWP ≤15 mmHg**, **PVR >2 Wood units** (the PVR threshold also fell, from >3) ⚑.
- **Post-capillary PH (left-heart disease):** PAWP **>15 mmHg**.

**The 5 WHO groups:**

| Group | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — PAH** | Pulmonary **arterial** | Idiopathic, heritable, connective-tissue disease (systemic sclerosis), congenital shunts, drugs |
| **2** | **Left heart disease** (commonest overall) | HFrEF/HFpEF, valve disease |
| **3** | **Lung disease/hypoxia** | COPD, ILD, OSA (→ cor pulmonale) |
| **4** | **Chronic thromboembolic (CTEPH)** | Organised PE — potentially **curable by pulmonary endarterectomy** |
| **5** | Multifactorial/unclear | Sarcoid, haematological, metabolic |

**Clinical:** exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, syncope, and signs of RV failure (raised JVP, **loud P2**, RV heave, tricuspid regurgitation, peripheral oedema). **Echo** screens (estimates PA pressure, RV size/function); **right heart catheter confirms**. **Cor pulmonale** = right heart failure due to lung disease/pulmonary hypertension.

**Treatment:** treat the underlying cause (groups 2/3 — optimise heart/lung disease; **do not give PAH-specific vasodilators in group 2/3**, can worsen). **Group 1 PAH** gets targeted therapy: **endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan/ambrisentan/macitentan), PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil/tadalafil), prostacyclin analogues (epoprostenol), riociguat**; **CCBs only if vasoreactive**. **CTEPH (group 4)** → assess for **pulmonary endarterectomy** ± riociguat.

docs.title: Pulmonary Vascular Disease (acute — high yield)
docs.text:
**Pulmonary AVMs** — cause right-to-left shunt (hypoxia unresponsive to O₂), risk of paradoxical embolism/stroke and brain abscess; associated with **hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu)**. **Pulmonary vasculitis** (GPA/EGPA) — see the systemic-disease overlap. **Fat embolism** (post-long-bone fracture: dyspnoea + petechiae + confusion) and **amniotic fluid embolism** are non-thrombotic embolic syndromes.

NORMAL VALUES

- pH: 7.35-7.45
- pCO2: 4.5-6.0 kPa
- pO2: 11-13 kPa
- HCO3-: 22-26 mmol/L
- BE: -2 to +2
- SaO2: > 95%
- PaO2 should ~ FiO2­% - 10
- Alveolar arterial gradient: < 10 (increased in emphysema, fibrosing alveolitis, age)
- Lactate: <2

INTERPRETATION

- Assess oxygenation: hypoxia, alveolar-arterial gradient
- pH status
- Respiratory component (respiratory acidosis= ↓pH, ↑PaCO2; respiratory alkalosis= ↑pH, ↓PaCO3). If PaCO2 doesn’t agree with pH, ignore until step 5
- Metabolic component (metabolic acidosis = ↓pH, ↓HCO3-; metabolic alkalosis=↑pH, ↑HCO3-). If HCO3- doesn’t agree with the pH, ignore until step 5
- Determine primary disturbance and assess compensation

- Acidosis may be compensated by:Respiratory compensation: ↑ RR to blow off CO2 (will result in ↓CO2)
- Metabolic compensation: ↑HCO3- production by kidney (will result in ↑HCO3-)

- Alkalosis may be compensated byRespiratory compensation: ↓RR to retain CO2 (will result in ↑CO2)
- Metabolic compensation: ↓HCO3- production by kidney (will result in ↓HCO3-)

**Pathology**

LARGE AIRWAYS:

- Mucous gland enlargement
- Goblet cell hyperplasia
- Columnar cells replaced by squamous cells (potential carcinogenesis, ↓ mucociliary clearance)

SMALL AIRWAYS:

- Goblet cell hyperplasia
- Replacement of surfactant-secreting clara cells with mucous secreting cells
- Mononuclear cells
- Smooth muscle thickening

PARENCHYMAL DESTRUCTION:

- Reduced surfactant: compounding
- Reduced elastic recoil → hyperinflation → dynamic airway collapse
- Fibrosis: decreased gas exchange
- Reduced SA for gas exchange
- Luminal narrowing: mucus, oedema, infiltration

- Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of mucus-secreting glands in bronchi (Reid index > 50%)

- Daily productive cough

docs.title: Respiratory Anatomy
docs.text: *Written out as prose + tables (not image-only) — pair with `respiratory_anatomy_sheet.svg`.*

docs.title: Respiratory Anatomy
docs.text:
Air passes nose/mouth → pharynx → **larynx** (the protective sphincter and voice box; vocal cords at C5–6) → **trachea** (C6 to the **carina at ~T4/5, sternal angle**) → main bronchi → lobar → segmental bronchi → bronchioles → **terminal bronchioles** (end of the **conducting zone**, ~generation 16) → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → **alveoli** (the **respiratory zone**, gas exchange).

Structural gradient as you descend (worth a table):

| Feature | Trachea/large bronchi | Bronchioles | Alveoli |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cartilage | Yes (C-rings/plates) | **None** (collapse-prone) | None |
| Smooth muscle | Present | **Prominent** (site of bronchospasm) | None |
| Epithelium | Pseudostratified ciliated columnar | Cuboidal, fewer cilia | Type I (gas exchange) + Type II (surfactant) pneumocytes |
| Goblet/mucus | Yes | Club (Clara) cells | None |

The **mucociliary escalator** (cilia + mucus) clears debris upward; smoking, CF and primary ciliary dyskinesia paralyse it → recurrent infection and bronchiectasis. The **conducting zone is anatomical dead space (~150 mL)** — ventilated but no gas exchange.

docs.title: Respiratory Anatomy
docs.text:
- **Right lung: 3 lobes** (upper, middle, lower), divided by the **oblique (major)** and **horizontal (minor)** fissures.
- **Left lung: 2 lobes** (upper, lower) + the **lingula** (the middle-lobe equivalent) + a **cardiac notch**. Only an oblique fissure.
- **Discriminator — the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical**, so **aspirated material and inhaled foreign bodies lodge on the right** (posterior segment of RUL if supine, basal segments if upright). *Memory: "things fall down the right."*

Each lung has ~10 **bronchopulmonary segments** — functionally independent units (own segmental bronchus and artery) that can be resected individually; they explain **postural drainage** positioning and the segmental distribution of aspiration pneumonia.

docs.title: Respiratory Anatomy
docs.h: 2.3 Blood Supply, Lymphatics and the Pleura
docs.text:
**Dual circulation:**

| Circulation | Origin | Job | Pressure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pulmonary** | RV → pulmonary arteries (carry **deoxygenated** blood) | **Gas exchange** | Low (~25/8 mmHg) |
| **Bronchial** | Aorta/intercostals | **Nutritive** supply to airway walls | Systemic (high) |

Bronchial arteries are the usual source of **massive haemoptysis** (systemic pressure) — relevant to bronchial artery embolisation. The pulmonary circulation is **low-pressure, low-resistance and high-compliance**, and recruits/distends to accept increased flow — which is why pulmonary hypertension appears late.

**Lymphatic drainage** ascends through **intrapulmonary → hilar → mediastinal (paratracheal, subcarinal) → scalene/supraclavicular** nodes — the anatomical basis of **lung-cancer N-staging** (and why a supraclavicular node is sampled).

**Pleura:** the **visceral** pleura hugs the lung (insensate); the **parietal** pleura lines the chest wall (**pain-sensitive**, somatic + phrenic innervation) — hence **pleuritic pain** localises to the chest wall or refers to the shoulder tip (diaphragmatic/phrenic, C3–5). The **pleural space** holds a thin film of fluid; it becomes an effusion, pneumothorax, empyema or haemothorax when air/fluid/blood collect.

docs.title: Respiratory Anatomy
docs.h: 2.4 The Mediastinum, Diaphragm and Surface Anatomy
docs.text:
**Mediastinal compartments** and the exam-favourite masses:

| Compartment | Key contents | Classic mass |
|---|---|---|
| **Anterior** | Thymus, fat, nodes | **The 4 Ts**: Thymoma, Teratoma (germ cell), (terrible) Lymphoma, Thyroid (retrosternal) |
| **Middle** | Heart, great vessels, trachea, nodes | Lymphadenopathy, bronchogenic cyst, aneurysm |
| **Posterior** | Oesophagus, aorta, sympathetic chain | **Neurogenic tumours**, oesophageal lesions |

**Diaphragm:** the principal muscle of inspiration, innervated by the **phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5 — "keeps the diaphragm alive")**. Three key openings: **T8 IVC** (vena cava), **T10 oesophagus** (+ vagi), **T12 aorta** (+ thoracic duct, azygos). *Memory: "I 8 10 EGGS AT 12" → IVC 8, oEsophagus 10, Aorta 12.* Accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, intercostals) recruit in distress — visible accessory-muscle use is a sign of severe respiratory compromise.

**Surface anatomy for procedures:**
- **Oblique fissure** ≈ line from T2 spinous process to the 6th rib in the midclavicular line; **horizontal fissure** ≈ 4th rib.
- **Chest drain "triangle of safety"**: bordered by the lateral edge of **pectoralis major**, the anterior edge of **latissimus dorsi**, and a horizontal line at the **nipple (5th intercostal space)** — the base is the axilla apex. Drains and aspiration go **just above a rib** to avoid the **neurovascular bundle** running below each rib.

---

| Carina level | T4/5 (**sternal angle of Louis**) |
| End of the conducting zone / dead space volume | Terminal bronchiole; ~150 mL |
| Pain-sensitive pleura | **Parietal** (visceral is insensate) |
| Shoulder-tip pain from the chest | Diaphragmatic/phrenic irritation (C3–5) |
| Source of **massive** haemoptysis | **Bronchial** (systemic-pressure) arteries |
| Anterior mediastinal mass | **4 Ts** — Thymoma, Teratoma, Lymphoma, Thyroid |
| Posterior mediastinal mass | Neurogenic tumour |
| Phrenic nerve roots | **C3, 4, 5** |
| Diaphragm openings | IVC T8 · oEsophagus T10 · Aorta T12 |
| Needle/drain position relative to rib | **Above** the rib (avoid the sub-costal neurovascular bundle) |
| Triangle of safety borders | Pec major (ant), lat dorsi (post), 5th ICS/nipple line (inf) |

docs.parent: Respiratory Failure, Sleep & Ventilation (acute — high yield)
docs.text:
**Definition:** PaO₂ <8 kPa (60 mmHg) on room air. **Type 1** = hypoxaemia with normal/low CO₂ (oxygenation/**V-Q** failure — pneumonia, oedema, PE, ILD). **Type 2** = hypoxaemia **+ PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa (45 mmHg)** (ventilatory/**pump** failure — COPD, exhausted asthma, opioids, neuromuscular, chest wall, obesity). (See Section 3.3 for acute vs chronic.)

**Oxygen as a drug — targets (BTS):**
- **Most acutely unwell patients: SpO₂ 94–98%.**
- **At risk of hypercapnic (type 2) failure: SpO₂ 88–92%** — start with a **28% Venturi** and check an ABG; titrate to avoid both hypoxia and CO₂ narcosis.
- Devices by delivery: nasal cannulae (low flow, variable FiO₂) → simple mask → **Venturi** (fixed FiO₂, ideal for retainers) → **non-rebreathe reservoir mask** (~15 L, high FiO₂ for the critically hypoxic) → **high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO)** (heated, humidified, high flow — some CPAP-like effect).

**LTOT** (chronic — see Section 4.2): survival benefit only in **chronic hypoxaemia** (PaO₂ ≤7.3 kPa, or 7.3–8.0 with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia), ≥15 h/day.

docs.title: Respiratory Failure, Sleep & Ventilation (acute — high yield)
docs.parent: Respiratory Failure, Sleep & Ventilation (acute — high yield)
docs.text:
**Match the mode to the failure:**

| Mode | What it does | Core indications |
|---|---|---|
| **CPAP** | Continuous pressure (splints airways/alveoli open) — improves **oxygenation** | **Type 1** failure: **cardiogenic pulmonary oedema**, OSA; some pneumonia/COVID |
| **BiPAP (NIV)** | Two pressures (IPAP > EPAP) — augments **ventilation**, clears **CO₂** | **Type 2** failure: **AECOPD with respiratory acidosis**, neuromuscular/chest-wall hypoventilation, OHS |

**The classic exam indication:** **NIV (BiPAP) for AECOPD with pH <7.35 and PaCO₂ >6.0 kPa persisting despite ≥1 h of maximal medical therapy and controlled oxygen.** If pH <7.25 or NIV fails → consider intubation/ICU. Contraindications to NIV: reduced consciousness, vomiting/aspiration risk, facial trauma, untreated pneumothorax, haemodynamic instability.

**ARDS** — acute, diffuse inflammatory lung injury → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and refractory hypoxaemia. Causes: **sepsis/pneumonia** (commonest), aspiration, pancreatitis, trauma, transfusion (TRALI).

⚑ **ARDS — New Global Definition (2023)** updates the 2012 Berlin definition:
- **Timing:** within **1 week** of a known insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms.
- **Imaging:** **bilateral opacities** on CXR/CT **or ultrasound**, not fully explained by effusions/collapse; oedema not fully explained by cardiac failure/fluid overload.
- **Oxygenation:** may now use **SpO₂/FiO₂ (≤315, with SpO₂ ≤97%)** as an alternative to PaO₂/FiO₂.
- **New category — non-intubated ARDS:** diagnosable in patients on **HFNO ≥30 L/min** or **CPAP/NIV with PEEP ≥5 cmH₂O** (Berlin required intubation/PEEP ≥5 with a PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤300).
- **Intubated severity (PEEP ≥5):** **mild** PaO₂/FiO₂ 200–300, **moderate** 100–200, **severe** ≤100.
- **Resource-limited settings:** SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤315 without a PEEP/flow requirement.

**Management of ARDS:** treat the cause; **lung-protective ventilation** (**low tidal volume ~6 mL/kg ideal body weight**, plateau pressure <30 cmH₂O, permissive hypercapnia), adequate PEEP, conservative fluids, **prone positioning** for moderate–severe, neuromuscular blockade in selected cases, and ECMO in refractory cases.

docs.title: Respiratory Failure, Sleep & Ventilation (acute — high yield)
docs.parent: Respiratory Failure, Sleep & Ventilation (acute — high yield)
docs.text:
**Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)** — repetitive upper-airway collapse in sleep → apnoeas/hypopnoeas, fragmented sleep. Presentation: **loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, daytime somnolence** (Epworth score), morning headache, obesity, hypertension; increases cardiovascular and RTA risk. Screen with **STOP-BANG** (Snoring, Tiredness, Observed apnoea, Pressure/BP, BMI >35, Age >50, Neck >40 cm, male). Diagnose with **polysomnography** (AHI ≥5 with symptoms). Treatment: weight loss, avoid alcohol/sedatives, **CPAP** (first-line for moderate–severe), mandibular device for mild.

**Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS)** = obesity + **awake daytime hypercapnia** (not explained by other cause), often with OSA → type 2 respiratory failure; treat with weight loss and **NIV/CPAP**. **Neuromuscular/chest-wall causes** (Guillain–Barré, motor neurone disease, myasthenia, muscular dystrophy, kyphoscoliosis) cause **restrictive** ventilatory failure — monitor with **FVC** (falling FVC, e.g. <15 mL/kg or <1 L, signals impending failure — a key GBS/myasthenic-crisis alarm).

docs.title: Respiratory Infections
docs.text:
**Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)** — fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, dyspnoea; signs of **consolidation** (bronchial breathing, dull percussion, increased vocal resonance, crackles); CXR consolidation.

**Severity — CURB-65** (1 point each): **C**onfusion (AMTS ≤8), **U**rea >7 mmol/L, **R**espiratory rate ≥30, **B**P <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic, age **≥65**.
- **0–1** → home/oral; **2** → hospital (consider); **≥3** → severe, consider ICU. *(CRB-65 omits urea for primary-care use.)*

**Typical vs atypical:**

| | Typical | Atypical |
|---|---|---|
| Organisms | ***Strep pneumoniae*** (commonest overall), *H. influenzae*, *Moraxella*, *Staph aureus* | *Mycoplasma*, *Legionella*, *Chlamydophila*, *Coxiella* |
| Features | Lobar consolidation, rusty sputum | Extra-pulmonary features, dry cough, CXR worse than exam |
| Antibiotic | β-lactam (amoxicillin) | **Macrolide/tetracycline/fluoroquinolone** (atypicals lack a cell wall → β-lactams don't work) |

**Empirical therapy** (per local/NICE guidance): **low severity → amoxicillin** (or doxycycline/macrolide if penicillin-allergic); **moderate → amoxicillin + macrolide**; **high severity → co-amoxiclav (or cephalosporin) + macrolide**, IV. Add **antipseudomonal cover** in bronchiectasis/structural disease. Review at 48–72 h; step down.

**Organism-specific clues (exam gold):**

| Clue | Organism |
|---|---|
| **Hyponatraemia, deranged LFTs, air-con/hotel/water source, diarrhoea** | ***Legionella*** (urinary antigen) |
| Young adult, **erythema multiforme, haemolytic anaemia (cold agglutinins), dry cough** | ***Mycoplasma*** |
| **Cavitation, post-influenza, IVDU** | ***Staph aureus*** |
| Abattoir/farm animal/parturient exposure | ***Coxiella burnetii*** (Q fever) |
| Bird exposure | *Chlamydophila psittaci* (psittacosis) |
| **HIV/immunocompromised, exertional desaturation, dry cough, bilateral perihilar infiltrates, ↑LDH** | ***Pneumocystis jirovecii*** (PCP → high-dose **co-trimoxazole**) |
| Currant-jelly sputum, alcoholic/diabetic, upper-lobe cavitation | *Klebsiella* |

**Complications:** **para-pneumonic effusion → empyema** (see Section 8 — pleural fluid **pH <7.2 needs a chest drain**), **lung abscess** (swinging fever, cavity with air–fluid level; aspiration/anaerobes), sepsis, respiratory failure.

**Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP)** (>48 h after admission) and **VAP** — Gram-negatives (incl. *Pseudomonas*), MRSA; broader empirical cover. **Aspiration pneumonia** — dependent segments (right lower/posterior upper lobe), anaerobes; risk in stroke, reduced consciousness, swallowing disorders.

docs.title: Respiratory Infections
docs.text:
*Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, spread by respiratory droplets. **Primary** (Ghon focus + hilar node = Ghon complex, often asymptomatic) vs **post-primary/reactivation** (apical, cavitating). **Latent TB** = infected, asymptomatic, non-infectious; can reactivate (risk ↑ with **HIV, anti-TNF, immunosuppression, diabetes**).

**Clinical:** chronic cough, **haemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats, fever**, lethargy. **Extra-pulmonary:** lymphadenitis (scrofula), pleural, **miliary** (haematogenous), CNS (meningitis, tuberculoma), spinal (**Pott's disease**), GU, adrenal, pericardial.

**Diagnosis:** **≥3 sputum samples for AFB smear (Ziehl–Neelsen) and culture** (culture is the gold standard but slow), **NAAT/GeneXpert** (rapid, detects rifampicin resistance), CXR (apical cavitation, upper-lobe fibrosis). **Latent TB:** **IGRA** or **tuberculin skin test (Mantoux)** — neither distinguishes latent from active.

**Standard treatment — "RIPE" for 2 months, then RI for 4 (6 months total):** **R**ifampicin, **I**soniazid, **P**yrazinamide, **E**thambutol. Learn the toxicities:

| Drug | Signature toxicity |
|---|---|
| **Rifampicin** | **Orange secretions**, enzyme **inducer** (↓ OCP/warfarin), hepatitis |
| **Isoniazid** | **Peripheral neuropathy** (give **pyridoxine/B6**), hepatitis |
| **Pyrazinamide** | Hepatitis, **hyperuricaemia/gout** |
| **Ethambutol** | **Optic neuritis** (colour vision/acuity — check before starting) |

**MDR-TB** (resistant to rifampicin + isoniazid) needs prolonged specialist regimens. TB is **notifiable**; do **contact tracing**; supervise adherence (DOT) where needed.

docs.title: Respiratory Infections
docs.text:
**Influenza** — sudden fever, myalgia, dry cough; **oseltamivir** if early/high-risk; complications include secondary bacterial (especially **Staph**) pneumonia. **COVID-19** — spectrum from mild URTI to viral pneumonitis/ARDS; risk-stratify by hypoxia. **Aspergillus spectrum:** **aspergilloma** (fungus ball in a pre-existing cavity — haemoptysis), **ABPA** (asthmatics — see Section 4), **invasive aspergillosis** (immunocompromised — angioinvasion, halo sign). **Paediatric-relevant:** bronchiolitis (RSV, infants), croup (parainfluenza — barking cough, stridor), whooping cough (*Bordetella pertussis* — paroxysmal cough, whoop). Always consider the **immunocompromised host** (PCP, CMV, fungi, atypical mycobacteria).
