docs.h: Respiratory Master Notes — Respiratory Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
##### 11.1 Inhaled Therapies

The core inhaler classes (know target, onset, and the key adverse effect):

| Class | Examples | Action | Key adverse effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SABA** | Salbutamol | Short-acting β₂-agonist (bronchodilate) | Tremor, tachycardia, **hypokalaemia**, lactate |
| **LABA** | Salmeterol, formoterol | Long-acting β₂-agonist | As SABA; **never as monotherapy in asthma** (mortality risk) ⚑ |
| **SAMA** | Ipratropium | Short-acting antimuscarinic | Dry mouth, urinary retention, glaucoma (nebulised) |
| **LAMA** | Tiotropium, glycopyrronium | Long-acting antimuscarinic | Dry mouth; caution in prostatism/glaucoma |
| **ICS** | Beclometasone, budesonide, fluticasone | Inhaled corticosteroid (anti-inflammatory) | **Oral candidiasis, dysphonia** (rinse mouth), pneumonia risk in COPD |

**Combination inhalers** reduce inhaler burden: **ICS–formoterol** is now central to asthma (**AIR/MART** — reliever *and* maintenance); **LABA–LAMA** is the COPD backbone (± ICS, eosinophil-guided). **Device/technique** is examinable: check inhaler technique at every review; use **spacers** with pMDIs; consider dry-powder devices where inspiratory flow is adequate.

**Biologics for severe (type 2/eosinophilic) asthma** ⚑: **anti-IgE (omalizumab)**; **anti-IL-5/5R (mepolizumab, benralizumab, reslizumab)**; **anti-IL-4/13 (dupilumab)** — for uncontrolled severe asthma despite high-dose ICS-LABA, guided by IgE/eosinophils/FeNO.

##### 11.2 Other Respiratory Drugs

- **Oral corticosteroids** (prednisolone) — exacerbations and maintenance in severe disease; watch the long-term burden (osteoporosis, diabetes, adrenal suppression — don't stop abruptly).
- **Theophylline/aminophylline** — methylxanthine bronchodilator; **narrow therapeutic index** → nausea, arrhythmia, seizures; **levels rise with enzyme inhibitors** (macrolides, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine) and fall with inducers (smoking, rifampicin). Monitor levels.
- **Leukotriene receptor antagonists** (montelukast) — add-on in asthma; note neuropsychiatric warnings.
- **Antifibrotics** (pirfenidone, nintedanib) — slow FVC decline in IPF/progressive fibrosing ILD (Section 5).
- **CFTR modulators** (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) — transformative in eligible CF (Section 4).
- **Mucolytics** — carbocisteine; **dornase alfa/hypertonic saline** in CF.
- **PAH-targeted drugs** — endothelin antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors, prostacyclins, riociguat (Section 6).
- **Oxygen** — prescribe with a **target saturation range**; it is a drug with a therapeutic window.
- **Smoking cessation** — behavioural support + **NRT / varenicline / bupropion**; the single highest-value intervention across respiratory medicine.

##### 11.3 Prescribing and Safety

- **Antibiotics** — match to setting/severity (Section 7); remember **atypicals need a macrolide/tetracycline/quinolone**, and structural lung disease needs antipseudomonal cover.
- **Anti-tuberculous toxicities** (Section 7): rifampicin (orange, inducer, hepatitis),

docs.title: Respiratory Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
*Synthesis only — no new facts; every discriminator here traces back to the section notes. This is the **source of truth** for the Section 12 "Key Differentials Quick-Reference" (that section is a view of this document). Organised three ways: **A** by presenting syndrome, **B** signature lookup tables, **C** confusable pairs. British/Australian spelling.*

---

##### Part A — By Presenting Syndrome

###### A1. Breathlessness (acute)
Scan for the discriminator, then confirm:

| If you also see… | Think | Clincher |
|---|---|---|
| Pleuritic pain + haemoptysis + risk factors, clear-ish CXR, low CO₂ | **PE** | CTPA; type 1 failure with respiratory alkalosis |
| Wheeze, known asthma, PEF ↓ | **Acute asthma** | PEF %; **normal/rising CO₂ = life-threatening** |
| Smoker, purulent sputum, prior COPD | **AECOPD** | ABG: ↑CO₂, pH <7.35 → NIV |
| Fever, focal crackles, consolidation | **Pneumonia** | CURB-65, CXR |
| Sudden, pleuritic, tall thin (or COPD) | **Pneumothorax** | absent breath sounds, hyper-resonant; trachea away = tension |
| Orthopnoea, raised JVP, bibasal crackles, pink froth | **Pulmonary oedema (cardiac)** | ↑NT-proBNP, CXR bat-wing; CPAP |
| Stridor (inspiratory) | **Upper-airway obstruction** | emergency — secure airway |

###### A2. Breathlessness (chronic/progressive)
- **Obstructive** picture (wheeze, ↓FEV₁/FVC): asthma (variable, reversible, ↑FeNO) vs COPD (smoker, fixed, ↓DLCO) vs bronchiectasis (copious sputum, HRCT signet-ring).
- **Restrictive** picture (velcro crackles, clubbing, ↓DLCO): **ILD/IPF** — then use zone (upper = CHARTS; lower = IPF/CTD/asbestos).
- **Isolated low DLCO, clear lungs**: pulmonary vascular disease (**PAH/CTEPH**) or anaemia.

###### A3. Haemoptysis
| Clue | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| Weight loss, smoker, mass/collapse on CXR | **Lung cancer** |
| Night sweats, apical cavitation, risk factors | **TB** |
| Pleuritic pain, tachycardia, risk factors | **PE** |
| Copious daily purulent sputum, HRCT signet-ring | **Bronchiectasis** |
| Fungus ball in an old cavity | **Aspergilloma** |
| Haematuria + haemoptysis (pulmonary–renal) | **Goodpasture / ANCA vasculitis** |
| Massive volume, systemic-pressure bleed | **Bronchial artery** source → embolisation |

###### A4. Chronic cough (>8 weeks)
The "big three" (asthma, GORD, upper-airway/post-nasal drip) + **ACE-inhibitor** cough; always exclude **cancer/TB** in a smoker, and **ILD** if velcro crackles. Dry + fibrosis → ILD; productive daily → bronchiectasis/COPD.

###### A5. Pleuritic chest pain
PE, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pericarditis (positional/ECG), musculoskeletal, and (with effusion) malignancy/TB. The **ECG + CXR + troponin/D-dimer** triage separates the emergencies.

###### A6. The abnormal CXR (localise first)
Consolidation (air bronchogram) vs collapse (volume loss, shift *towards*) vs effusion (meniscus, shift *away*) vs pneumothorax (lung edge) vs mass (cancer) vs bilateral reticulation (ILD) vs BHL (sarcoid/lymphoma/TB).

---

##### Part B — Signature

docs.title: Respiratory Physiology
docs.text:
**Lung volumes** — four volumes that don't overlap and four capacities (sums of volumes):
- **Tidal volume (TV)** ~500 mL; **IRV** ~3000 mL; **ERV** ~1100 mL; **residual volume (RV)** ~1200 mL.
- **Capacities**: IC = TV+IRV; **FRC = ERV+RV** (volume at end of quiet expiration — the relaxed equilibrium); VC = TV+IRV+ERV; **TLC = VC+RV**.
- **Discriminator:** spirometry **cannot measure RV, FRC or TLC** (anything containing RV) — you need **body plethysmography or gas dilution**. This is why a "restrictive picture" on spirometry needs lung volumes to confirm.

**Compliance** = ΔV/ΔP (distensibility). High compliance (floppy, easy to inflate) = **emphysema**; low compliance (stiff) = **fibrosis, oedema, ARDS**. The lung's elastic recoil comes from tissue elastin *and* surface tension.

**Surfactant** (type II pneumocytes) lowers alveolar surface tension. By **Laplace (P = 2T/r)** small alveoli would otherwise empty into large ones; surfactant lowers tension *more in small alveoli*, stabilising them and preventing collapse. It also increases compliance and keeps alveoli dry. **Memory hook: surfactant = the lung's "anti-collapse detergent."** Deficiency → neonatal RDS; disruption → part of ARDS.

**Airway resistance** is highest in the **medium-sized bronchi**, not the tiny ones — because the huge *total cross-sectional area* of the many small airways in parallel drops resistance (this is why small-airway disease is "silent" early). During forced expiration the **equal pressure point** moves the point of dynamic collapse into the airways; in emphysema (loss of radial traction) this causes **dynamic airway collapse** and air trapping.

docs.title: Respiratory Physiology
docs.text:
**Alveolar gas equation:** PAO₂ = FiO₂(P_atm − P_H₂O) − PaCO₂/R ≈ (on room air at sea level) **150 − PaCO₂/0.8**.

**A–a gradient** = PAO₂ − PaO₂. Normal ≈ **5–10 mmHg** in the young; rises with age (rough rule: ≈ age/4 + 4). **This is the single most useful number for classifying hypoxaemia** (see 1.3).

**Oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve** — sigmoid. **P50 ≈ 27 mmHg** (the PO₂ at 50% saturation).
- **Right shift (offloads O₂ to tissues)**: ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺/↓pH (**Bohr effect**), ↑temperature, ↑2,3-BPG. *Memory: "exercise conditions" — hot, acidic, high CO₂ — dump O₂ where it's needed.*
- **Left shift (holds O₂)**: the opposites, plus **carbon monoxide, methaemoglobin, and fetal Hb (HbF)**.

**CO₂ transport**: ~70% as **bicarbonate** (via carbonic anhydrase in RBCs, chloride shift), ~23% as **carbamino compounds**, ~7% dissolved. **Haldane effect**: deoxygenated Hb carries more CO₂ — so oxygenation in the lung *promotes* CO₂ release (the mirror of the Bohr effect).

**Diffusion** follows **Fick's law** (∝ area × ΔP / thickness). **DLCO/TLCO** (CO uptake) is the clinical measure of the alveolar–capillary membrane.
- **↓DLCO:** emphysema (destroyed surface area), **ILD/fibrosis**, PE/pulmonary vascular disease, anaemia.
- **↑DLCO:** **alveolar haemorrhage** (extra Hb in alveoli soaks up CO), polycythaemia, left-to-right shunt, asthma.
- **Discriminator:** obstruction with **low DLCO = emphysema**; obstruction with **normal/high DLCO = asthma**.

docs.title: Respiratory Physiology
docs.text:
Ideal V/Q ≈ **0.8** overall. Gravity makes both ventilation and perfusion greater at the **base**, but perfusion increases more — so **V/Q is high at the apex** (more ventilation relative to perfusion → alveolar dead-space-like) and **low at the base** (shunt-like). **V/Q = ∞** is pure dead space (ventilated, not perfused, e.g. PE); **V/Q = 0** is pure shunt (perfused, not ventilated, e.g. consolidation, collapse).

**The five causes of hypoxaemia** — and how to separate them:

| Cause | A–a gradient | Corrects with 100% O₂? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hypoventilation** | **Normal** | Yes | Opioids, T2RF, neuromuscular |
| **Low inspired PO₂** | **Normal** | Yes | Altitude |
| **Diffusion limitation** | Raised | Yes (largely) | ILD, exercise |
| **V/Q mismatch** | Raised | Yes | COPD, asthma, PE, pneumonia |
| **Right-to-left shunt** | Raised | **No** (poorly) | Consolidation, collapse, cardiac shunt, AVM |

**Two discriminators worth memorising:** (1) a **normal A–a gradient** points to hypoventilation or low FiO₂ — the lungs themselves are fine; (2) **failure to correct with high-flow oxygen = shunt**, because shunted blood never meets the alveolar gas.

docs.title: Respiratory Physiology
docs.text:
- **Central chemoreceptors** (medulla) respond to **CSF pH / CO₂** — the *dominant minute-to-minute driver*.
- **Peripheral chemoreceptors** (carotid + aortic bodies) respond mainly to **PaO₂**, but only kick in hard when **PaO₂ falls below ~60 mmHg** (the flat part of the sat curve) — plus CO₂ and pH.

**Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV):** unique to the lung — hypoxia *constricts* pulmonary vessels (systemically hypoxia dilates). It diverts blood from poorly-ventilated areas, improving V/Q matching. **Chronic, global HPV → pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale** (the mechanism in COPD and OSA).

⚑ **The "hypoxic drive" caveat:** the old teaching that giving oxygen to a CO₂-retainer "removes their drive to breathe" is **oversimplified and largely wrong**. Hypercapnia after O₂ in COPD is mostly due to **worsened V/Q matching (reversal of HPV) and the Haldane effect**, not loss of central drive. The practical point stands — **target SpO₂ 88–92%** in known/at-risk CO₂ retainers — but the *mechanism* examiners now expect is V/Q, not "knocking out the drive."

---

docs.title: Respiratory Physiology
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Which volumes can spirometry **not** measure? | Anything containing **RV**: RV, FRC, TLC |
| Stiff lung, low compliance | Fibrosis / ARDS / oedema |
| Floppy lung, high compliance | Emphysema |
| Right shift of O₂ curve (offloads O₂) | ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺, ↑temp, ↑2,3-BPG |
| Left shift | CO, metHb, HbF, alkalosis, cold |
| Obstruction + **low** DLCO | Emphysema |
| Obstruction + **normal/high** DLCO | Asthma |
| Raised DLCO | Alveolar haemorrhage (also polycythaemia, L→R shunt) |
| Hypoxaemia with **normal** A–a gradient | Hypoventilation or low FiO₂ |
| Hypoxaemia that **won't** correct on 100% O₂ | Right-to-left shunt |
| Hypoxia *constricts* these vessels | Pulmonary (HPV) — drives cor pulmonale |
| SpO₂ target in a CO₂ retainer | 88–92% |

##### Sources
Guyton & Hall *Textbook of Medical Physiology* (respiration & gas transport chapters); West *Respiratory Physiology: The Essentials*; Merck Manual Professional (respiratory physiology). The mechanism of oxygen-induced hypercapnia (V/Q + Haldane rather than "loss of hypoxic drive") is consistent across BTS oxygen guidance and current respiratory physiology texts.

CONDUCTING ZONE

- Function: warms, humidifies and filters the air but does not participate in gas exchange
- Components: large airways (nose, nasopharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi) and small airways (bronchioles)
- Smooth muscle: sympathetic adrenergic β2 receptors → relaxation and dilation; parasympathetic cholinergic activate muscarinic receptors → contraction and constriction
- Cartilage
- Goblet cells
- Pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells transition to cuboidal cells at the beginning of terminal bronchioles

RESPIRATORY ZONE

- Function: gas exchange
- Components: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli
- No smooth muscle
- Cilia terminate in respiratory bronchioles
- Respiratory bronchioles contain mostly cuboidal cells, then simple squamous cells up to alveoli
- Alveoli have
- Type I pneumocytes: 97% of alveolar surfaces; squamous; thin for optimal gas diffusion
- Type II pneumocytes: These are cuboidal and clustered, secreting surfactant from lamellar bodies → ↓ surface tension, prevents alveolar collapse, ↓ lung recoil and ↑ compliance
- Macrophages

docs.h: Respiratory (ANU) — 1. ventilation of alveoli — Respiratory Physiology
docs.text:
- MUSCLES OF INSPIRATION: diaphragm, external intercostals, accessory muscles
- MUSCLES OF EXPIRATION (NORMALLY PASSIVE): abdominal muscles, internal intercostals
- SURFACTANT: prevents alveolar collapse and alveoli can overcome surface tension and adequately expand

BREATHING CYCLE

- At rest:

- Alveolar pressure = atmospheric pressure
- Intrapleural pressure is negative (lung trying to collapse and chest wall trying to expand)

- During inspiration:

- Diaphragm contracts 🡪↑ volume of thorax 🡪 alveolar pressure ↓ to less than atmospheric 🡪 air flows into lungs
- Intrapleural pressure becomes more negative

- During expiration:

- Elastic force of lungs 🡪 increases alveolar pressure 🡪 air flows out of lungs 🡪 lung volume returns to FRC
- Intrapleural returns to normal during passive expiration
- During forced expiration 🡪 intrapleural pressure becomes positive 🡪 compresses airway

VENTILATION RATE

**VA =VE x VD**

- VA=alveolar ventilation= volume of gas per unit time that reaches alveoli
- VE=minute ventilation=total volume of gas entering lungs per minute= VT (tidal volume) x RR
- VD =physiological dead space

docs.title: Respiratory Physiology
docs.text:
- O2 diffuses from the alveoli into the blood and CO2 diffuses from the blood into the alveoli according to their concentration gradients. Thus [O2] in alveoli > blood and [CO2] in alveoli < blood.
- Diffusion is affected by thickness of membrane and surface area
- O2 binding to Hb is dependent on PaO2 – where oxygen carriage is sigmoid
- ![](notes/images/respiratory-anu/img008.jpg)
CO2 dissolved in plasma, bound to Hb, and as HCO3- (mostly)

CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3-; conversion by carbonic anhydrase

- BOHR’S EFFECT:
- Tissues: ↑ CO2 levels shifts O2-Hb curve to the right, aiding O2 unloading
- Lungs: ↓CO2 levels shifts O2-Hb curve to the left, aiding O2 loading
- HALDANE’S EFFECT
- Tissues: deoxygenated Hb has higher affinity for CO2 carriage
- Lungs: oxygenated Hb has lower affinity for CO2 carriage
- FACTORS THAT CAUSE A RIGHT SHIFT (CADET): CO2, acid, 2,3-DPG, exercise, temperature increase


---

docs.title: Respiratory Physiology
docs.text:
- ELASTIC RECOIL: tendency for lungs to collapse inward and chest wall to spring outward
- AT FRC:
- Inward pull of lung is balanced by outward pull of chest wall, and system pressure is atmospheric
- Airway + alveolar pressures are 0
- Intra-pleural pressure is negative (prevents atelectasis)
- When pressure outside lungs is negative, lungs expand and lung volume increases
- Similarly, when pressure outside lungs is positive, lungs collapse
- HIGH COMPLIANCE: lung easier to fill (emphysema, normal aging); surfactant increases compliance
- LOW COMPLIANCE: lung harder to fill (pulmonary fibrosis, pneumonia, NRDS, pulmonary oedema)

docs.title: Respiratory Physiology
docs.text:
![](notes/images/respiratory-anu/img009.jpg)

- TIDAL VOLUME (VT): volume of air inspired/expired with a normal breath (400-500ml or 5ml/kg body weight)
- RESIDUAL VOLUME (RV): volume of gas left in the lung after maximal expiration; stabilises the alveoli
- FORCED VITAL CAPACITY (FVC): the total volume of air expelled from the lungs after maximum inspiratory effort followed by maximum forced expiration
- FUNCTIONAL RESIDUAL CAPACITY (FRC): volume of air left in the lungs after normal expiration; including respiratory reserve volume and residual volume
- FORCED EXPIRATORY VOLUME (FEV1): The volume of air exhaled in 1 second
- TOTAL LUNG CAPACITY (TLC): Total gas volume in the lung when it is maximally inflated.
